Open wound Break in skin continuity • Example laceration abrasion • Closed wound Skin remains intact but underlying tissue is damaged • Example contusion • Acute wound Usually heals in an expected time • Example surgical incision • Chronic/non healing wound Fails to progress normally through healing • Example diabetic or pressure ulcer • Surgical wounds may also be classified as clean clean contaminated contaminated and dirty/infected --- **8 Wound Healing** • **Definition** Wound healing is the biological process by which the body repairs damaged tissue and restores tissue continuity • **Phases** 1 Hemostasis stops bleeding 2 Inflammation removes bacteria and debris 3 Proliferation granulation tissue collagen angiogenesis and epithelialization 4 Remodeling collagen reorganization and scar maturation --- **9 Gangrene** • **Definition** Gangrene is tissue necrosis caused by inadequate blood supply infection or both • **Types** • Dry gangrene Usually due to ischemia • Wet gangrene Necrotic tissue with infection • Gas gangrene Rapidly progressive infection with gas formation --- **10 Cellulitis** • **Definition** Cellulitis is an acute bacterial infection of the skin and deeper subcutaneous tissues • **Clinical features** • Redness • Warmth • Swelling • Pain/tenderness • Fever may occur • **Treatment** Antibiotics elevation and treatment of the underlying cause --- **11 Abscess** • **Definition** An abscess is a localized collection of pus within a tissue or body cavity usually caused by infection • **Clinical features** • Pain • Swelling • Redness • Warmth • Fluctuant/pus filled swelling • Fever may occur • **Treatment** Drainage when indicated appropriate antibiotics --- **12 Amputation** • **Definition** Amputation is the surgical removal of part or all of a limb • **Indications** Severe trauma gangrene peripheral vascular disease uncontrolled infection and malignancy • **Types** Above knee below knee above elbow and below elbow amputations • **Rehabilitation** Stump care strengthening ROM prosthetic training and gait training --- **13 Phantom Limb** • **Definition** Phantom limb sensation is the feeling that an amputated limb is still present • **Phantom limb pain** Pain perceived in the missing limb • **Features** Burning tingling shooting pain or sensation of movement • **Management** Desensitization mirror therapy graded motor imagery appropriate prosthetic rehabilitation and medical pain management --- **14 Varicose Veins** • **Definition** Varicose veins are dilated elongated and tortuous superficial veins usually of the lower limbs caused mainly by venous valve incompetence • **Features** Visible twisted veins aching heaviness ankle edema and skin changes • **Management** Exercise leg elevation compression when appropriate and selected surgical/endovenous treatment --- **15 Craniotomy** • **Definition** Craniotomy is a neurosurgical procedure in which a portion of the skull is temporarily removed to provide access to the brain and is usually replaced after surgery • **Indications** Brain tumour aneurysm hematoma vascular lesions and other intracranial conditions • **Difference** In craniectomy the bone flap is not immediately replaced --- **16 Laminectomy** • **Definition** Laminectomy is a spinal operation involving removal of part or all of the vertebral lamina to decompress the spinal cord or nerve roots • **Indications** Spinal stenosis nerve root compression selected disc disease and spinal tumours • **Complications** Dural tear/CSF leak infection bleeding neurological injury and spinal instability --- **18 Postoperative Complications** • **Definition** Postoperative complications are unwanted conditions occurring after surgery that may delay recovery or cause morbidity • **Common complications** • Shock • DVT • Wound infection • Atelectasis • Pneumonia • UTI • Pressure injuries • Hemorrhage • Wound dehiscence • Ileus • **Physiotherapy prevention** Early mobilization breathing exercises circulation exercises ROM positioning and functional rehabilitation /////////////////////// **Craniotomy Overview Indications and Complications** --- **Definition** A craniotomy is a neurosurgical procedure in which a portion of the skull is temporarily removed as a bone flap to provide access to the brain for diagnosis or treatment the bone flap is usually replaced at the end of surgery --- **1 Overview of Craniotomy** A craniotomy provides the surgeon with access to intracranial structures while attempting to minimize damage to normal brain tissue The location and size of the craniotomy depend on the pathology being treated **Common types according to location** • Frontal craniotomy • Temporal craniotomy • Parietal craniotomy • Occipital craniotomy • Pterional craniotomy • Retrosigmoid/suboccipital craniotomy It may be performed under general anesthesia while selected procedures involving areas responsible for speech or movement may be performed as an awake craniotomy to allow neurological monitoring during surgery **Basic procedure** 1 Patient is positioned and anesthetized 2 A scalp incision is made 3 Burr holes are created 4 A section of skull is removed as a bone flap 5 The dura is opened to expose the brain 6 The required intracranial procedure is performed 7 The dura is closed 8 The bone flap is replaced and fixed 9 The scalp is closed --- **2 Indications of Craniotomy** Craniotomy may be performed for diagnostic therapeutic or decompressive purposes **A Brain tumours** • Meningioma • Glioma • Metastatic brain tumour • Pituitary and parasellar lesions • Other intracranial tumours **B Cerebrovascular conditions** • Cerebral aneurysm • Arteriovenous malformation AVM • Intracerebral hemorrhage • Selected vascular malformations **C Traumatic brain injury** • Epidural hematoma • Acute subdural hematoma • Depressed skull fracture • Intracranial foreign body **D Raised intracranial pressure / brain swelling** • Selected cases of severe cerebral edema or swelling following trauma or stroke **E Infectious lesions** • Brain abscess • Subdural empyema **F Other indications** • Epilepsy surgery to remove a seizure focus • Microvascular decompression for selected cranial nerve disorders • Biopsy or removal of intracranial lesions • Selected functional neurosurgical procedures --- **3 Complications of Craniotomy** Complications can be neurological surgical systemic or wound related **A Neurological complications** • Brain injury • New neurological deficit • Limb weakness or paralysis • Sensory impairment • Speech or language disturbance • Visual disturbance • Problems with balance and coordination • Cognitive or memory changes • Seizures • Stroke • Cerebral edema **B Hemorrhagic complications** • Intracranial hemorrhage • Epidural or subdural hematoma • Excessive blood loss • Venous sinus injury **C CSF related complications** • Cerebrospinal fluid CSF leak • Hydrocephalus • Pneumocephalus **D Infectious complications** • Surgical site infection • Meningitis • Bone flap infection • Brain abscess or empyema **E Other complications** • Headache • Nausea and vomiting • Scalp numbness or pain • Cosmetic deformity • Temporalis muscle weakness/atrophy • Deep vein thrombosis and other complications related to immobility --- **4 Physiotherapy Implications** Although the question focuses on craniotomy this section is useful for a physiotherapy university answer **Assessment** The physiotherapist should assess • Level of consciousness • Motor power • Muscle tone • Sensation • Balance and coordination • Cranial nerve related deficits • Respiratory status • Functional mobility • Activities of daily living **Physiotherapy management** • Appropriate positioning and pressure area care • Respiratory assessment and treatment when clinically indicated • Passive/active ROM exercises • Prevention of contractures and muscle weakness • Early and progressive mobilization when medically stable • Bed mobility and transfer training • Sitting and standing balance exercises • Gait training • Progressive strengthening and endurance training • Functional and ADL rehabilitation • Patient and caregiver education Treatment must be modified according to neurological status surgical precautions intracranial pressure concerns and medical stability //////////////////////// **Decompressive Craniectomy in Traumatic Brain Injury TBI** --- **Definition** • Decompressive craniectomy DC is a neurosurgical procedure in which a large portion of the skull is removed and the bone flap is not immediately replaced creating additional intracranial space to reduce raised intracranial pressure ICP and prevent or treat brain herniation • It may be performed as part of the surgical treatment of severe traumatic brain injury particularly when intracranial hypertension remains refractory to appropriate medical treatment --- **1 Objectives** • Reduce intracranial pressure ICP • Increase intracranial compliance • Improve cerebral perfusion • Reduce secondary brain injury • Prevent cerebral herniation • Prevent further neurological deterioration • Reduce mortality in appropriately selected patients --- **2 Indications in TBI** • Severe TBI with refractory intracranial hypertension despite appropriate medical treatment • Severe cerebral edema with raised ICP • Significant traumatic brain swelling • Acute subdural hematoma with severe brain swelling or brain bulging after evacuation • Intracranial hematoma associated with significant mass effect • Neurological deterioration due to raised ICP • Clinical or radiological evidence of impending brain herniation • Diffuse cerebral edema with medically refractory intracranial hypertension **Important examination point** • Secondary decompressive craniectomy for late refractory ICP elevation is recommended to improve mortality and favorable outcomes • Current guidelines do not recommend routine early secondary DC simply for modest ICP elevation that is still medically manageable --- **3 Types** **A Primary decompressive craniectomy** • Performed during the initial surgery for a traumatic mass lesion • The bone flap is left out after evacuation of the hematoma or other traumatic lesion • Commonly considered with severe acute subdural hematoma and significant cerebral swelling **B Secondary decompressive craniectomy** • Performed later when intracranial pressure remains refractory to medical treatment • May be unilateral or bifrontal depending on the pattern of brain swelling --- **4 Surgical Steps** 1 General anesthesia • Patient is anesthetized and appropriately positioned 2 Scalp incision • A large scalp incision is made according to the planned decompression 3 Creation of burr holes • Multiple burr holes are created in the skull 4 Removal of large bone flap • A large portion of the skull is removed • In severe unilateral injury a large frontotemporoparietal decompression may be performed 5 Evacuation of traumatic lesion • Hematoma such as subdural or epidural hematoma may be evacuated when indicated 6 Opening of dura • The dura mater is opened widely to allow the swollen brain to expand 7 Duraplasty • The dura may be enlarged using a graft to provide additional space 8 Hemostasis • Bleeding is controlled and the brain is carefully inspected 9 Bone flap not replaced • Unlike craniotomy the removed bone flap is not immediately replaced 10 Closure • The scalp is closed over the decompressed area 11 Later cranioplasty • After the acute phase has resolved the skull defect is usually reconstructed by cranioplasty when appropriate --- **5 Complications** **Early complications** • Intracranial bleeding or hematoma expansion • Cerebral edema • External cerebral herniation • CSF leak • Subdural hygroma • Wound infection • Seizures • Hydrocephalus • Contralateral hematoma **Late complications** • Syndrome of the trephined/sinking skin flap syndrome • Hydrocephalus • Persistent subdural collections • Neurological deterioration • Cosmetic skull defect • Complications related to subsequent cranioplasty --- **6 Physiotherapy Implications** **Assessment** • Level of consciousness/GCS • Pupillary response as documented by the medical team • Motor power • Muscle tone • Sensory function • Balance and coordination • Respiratory status • Vital signs and SpO2 • Functional mobility **Physiotherapy management** • Proper positioning and pressure area care • Respiratory assessment and treatment when indicated • Passive and active ROM exercises • Prevention of contractures • Prevention of pressure injuries • Gradual mobilization when medically stable • Bed mobility and transfer training • Sitting and standing balance exercises • Gait training • Progressive strengthening and functional rehabilitation • Family/caregiver education **Precautions** • Avoid pressure or trauma to the craniectomy defect • Appropriate head protection should be used according to neurosurgical recommendations • Avoid treatment that may significantly increase ICP • Monitor neurological status and vital signs closely • Stop treatment and seek medical review if there is acute neurological deterioration vomiting reduced consciousness seizures or significant cardiorespiratory instability ///////////////////// **Laminectomy Definition Indications Procedure and Complications** --- **Definition** • Laminectomy is a spinal surgical procedure in which part or all of the lamina of a vertebra is removed to decompress the spinal cord or nerve roots • It is commonly performed to relieve pressure caused by spinal stenosis disc disease tumors or other compressive lesions --- **1 Indications** Laminectomy may be indicated in • Spinal canal stenosis causing neurological symptoms • Compression of spinal cord or nerve roots • Herniated intervertebral disc in selected cases • Severe radiculopathy or sciatica due to compression • Spinal tumors • Epidural abscess or other space occupying lesions • Traumatic spinal cord compression • Some cases of degenerative spinal disease • Cauda equina compression when urgent decompression is required • Persistent neurological symptoms not responding adequately to conservative treatment --- **2 Procedure / Surgical Steps** **A Pre operative preparation** • Patient assessment and informed consent • Appropriate imaging such as X ray CT or MRI • General anesthesia is usually administered • Patient is positioned prone on the operating table **B Surgical procedure** 1 Skin incision • A midline incision is made over the affected vertebral levels 2 Exposure • Paraspinal muscles are carefully separated from the vertebral structures • The lamina and spinous processes are exposed 3 Identification of affected level • The surgeon confirms the appropriate spinal level 4 Removal of lamina • Part or all of the lamina is removed using appropriate surgical instruments • This creates additional space within the spinal canal 5 Decompression • Compressed spinal cord or nerve roots are decompressed • Additional procedures such as discectomy or foraminotomy may be performed when indicated 6 Hemostasis • Bleeding is controlled 7 Closure • Muscles and soft tissues are returned to position • The wound is closed in layers 8 Post operative care • Neurological status pain wound condition and mobility are monitored • Early mobilization is encouraged when medically appropriate **Flowchart** Anesthesia Prone position Skin incision Muscle exposure Identify vertebral level Remove lamina Decompress neural structures Hemostasis Wound closure Rehabilitation --- **3 Complications** **A Neurological complications** • Nerve root injury • Spinal cord injury • New weakness or paralysis • Sensory disturbances • Persistent or recurrent radicular pain **B Surgical complications** • Bleeding/hematoma • Infection • Dural tear and CSF leak • Wound problems • Injury to surrounding tissues **C Musculoskeletal complications** • Spinal instability • Post operative back pain • Muscle weakness • Reduced spinal mobility • Recurrent spinal stenosis • Adjacent segment degeneration in some patients **D Other complications** • Deep vein thrombosis • Pulmonary complications related to prolonged immobility • Need for further spinal surgery --- **4 Physiotherapy Implications** Although not specifically requested this earns useful marks in a physiotherapy surgery exam **Assessment** • Pain and neurological symptoms • Muscle strength • Sensory status • ROM • Posture • Balance • Functional mobility • Gait • Respiratory and cardiovascular status **Physiotherapy management** • Proper positioning • Breathing and circulation exercises • Early mobilization when medically stable • Bed mobility and transfer training • Gentle ROM exercises • Progressive strengthening • Gait training • Postural education • Gradual functional rehabilitation • Patient education regarding spinal precautions and safe body mechanics **Precautions** • Avoid excessive spinal flexion extension rotation or loading during the early healing period according to surgical instructions • Avoid heavy lifting until medically cleared • Protect the surgical wound • Monitor for new weakness sensory changes increasing pain fever or wound discharge and report appropriately ////////////////////// **Aneurysm Clipping vs Coiling** --- **Definition of Cerebral Aneurysm** • A cerebral aneurysm is a localized abnormal dilatation or ballooning of a blood vessel in the brain due to weakness of the arterial wall • Rupture can cause subarachnoid hemorrhage SAH which is a neurological emergency --- **1 Aneurysm Clipping** **Definition** • Surgical clipping is an open neurosurgical procedure in which a small metal clip is placed across the neck of the aneurysm to prevent blood from entering the aneurysm **Surgical Steps** 1 General anesthesia is given 2 A scalp incision is made 3 A craniotomy is performed 4 The surgeon exposes the aneurysm 5 The parent artery and aneurysm neck are identified 6 A small metal clip is placed across the aneurysm neck 7 Blood flow into the aneurysm is stopped 8 Hemostasis is achieved 9 The bone flap is replaced and the wound is closed **Advantages** • Provides direct visualization of the aneurysm • Usually provides durable occlusion • Lower risk of aneurysm recurrence compared with coiling in many cases • Useful for some complex aneurysms and aneurysms with anatomy unfavorable for endovascular treatment **Disadvantages / Complications** • Requires craniotomy • More invasive • Longer recovery • Risk of brain or blood vessel injury • Intracranial bleeding • Stroke or neurological deficit • Seizures • Infection • CSF leak --- **2 Aneurysm Coiling** **Definition** • Endovascular coiling is a minimally invasive procedure in which detachable coils are introduced through a catheter into the aneurysm causing thrombosis and preventing blood flow into the aneurysm **Surgical Steps** 1 Local or general anesthesia is administered 2 A catheter is introduced through an artery commonly through the groin or wrist 3 The catheter is guided through the arterial system to the cerebral circulation 4 The aneurysm is identified using angiography 5 A microcatheter is passed into the aneurysm 6 Soft platinum coils are deployed inside the aneurysm 7 Coils promote clot formation within the aneurysm 8 Blood flow into the aneurysm is reduced or stopped 9 The catheter is removed 10 The access site is closed and monitored **Advantages** • Minimally invasive • No craniotomy is required • Generally shorter recovery than surgical clipping • Particularly useful when open surgery carries greater risk • Endovascular treatment can be advantageous in selected patients with ruptured aneurysms **Disadvantages / Complications** • Aneurysm may recanalize or recur • May require repeat treatment and follow up imaging • Thromboembolic complications • Vessel injury • Intracranial hemorrhage • Stroke or neurological deficit • Contrast related complications • Some wide neck aneurysms may require balloon or stent assisted techniques --- **4 Factors Affecting Choice of Treatment** The decision between clipping and coiling depends on • Aneurysm size • Aneurysm location • Shape and neck width • Ruptured or unruptured status • Patients age • General medical condition • Presence of brain swelling or vasospasm • Accessibility of the aneurysm • Experience of the treating neurosurgical/endovascular team --- **5 Physiotherapy Implications** • Assess • Level of consciousness • Motor power • Sensory function • Muscle tone • Balance and coordination • Respiratory status • Functional mobility • Maintain appropriate positioning • Provide respiratory physiotherapy when clinically indicated • Perform ROM exercises to prevent stiffness and contractures • Begin early and progressive mobilization when medically stable • Provide balance gait and functional training • Monitor neurological status during treatment • Educate patient and family regarding safe mobility and rehabilitation ///////////////////// **Postoperative Complications Shock DVT Wound Infection Atelectasis Pneumonia UTI and Pressure Sores** --- **Definition** Postoperative complications are unwanted conditions that develop after a surgical procedure and may delay recovery impair normal body function increase hospital stay or threaten life --- **1 Shock** **Definition** • Shock is a state of inadequate tissue perfusion and oxygen delivery resulting in cellular dysfunction and organ failure **Causes after surgery** • Hemorrhage • Severe fluid loss • Sepsis • Cardiac dysfunction • Anaphylaxis **Clinical features** • Hypotension • Tachycardia • Cold clammy skin • Rapid breathing • Reduced urine output • Confusion or reduced consciousness **Physiotherapy implications** • Do not mobilize an unstable patient • Monitor BP HR respiratory rate and SpO2 • Position appropriately according to the medical condition • Once stabilized gradually initiate mobility and rehabilitation --- **2 Deep Vein Thrombosis DVT** **Definition** • DVT is the formation of a blood clot within a deep vein most commonly in the lower limb **Risk factors** • Prolonged immobilization • Major surgery • Reduced mobility • Dehydration • Previous DVT • Cancer **Clinical features** • Unilateral leg swelling • Calf pain or tenderness • Warmth • Redness • Increased calf circumference **Physiotherapy implications** • Encourage early mobilization when medically appropriate • Ankle pump and active limb exercises • Avoid vigorous massage of a suspected DVT • If DVT is suspected stop treatment and seek medical assessment • Anticoagulation and mechanical prophylaxis may be prescribed according to risk --- **3 Wound Infection** **Definition** • Wound infection is infection of a surgical incision or wound by microorganisms causing local and/or systemic inflammatory response **Clinical features** • Increased pain • Redness • Swelling • Warmth • Purulent discharge • Fever • Delayed wound healing **Physiotherapy implications** • Inspect the wound before treatment • Maintain strict hand hygiene and infection control precautions • Avoid direct pressure or vigorous massage over an infected wound • Modify or postpone treatment if the patient is systemically unwell • Maintain mobility of unaffected areas • Follow wound care and surgical precautions --- **4 Atelectasis** **Definition** • Atelectasis is partial or complete collapse of alveoli resulting in reduced ventilation of the affected lung area **Causes** • Shallow breathing due to pain • Anesthesia • Prolonged bed rest • Retained secretions • Abdominal or thoracic surgery **Clinical features** • Breathlessness • Reduced oxygen saturation • Reduced chest expansion • Decreased breath sounds • Tachypnea **Physiotherapy management** • Upright positioning • Deep breathing/thoracic expansion exercises • Supported coughing • Early mobilization • Airway clearance techniques when clinically indicated • Monitor SpO2 and respiratory status --- **5 Pneumonia** **Definition** • Pneumonia is an infection causing inflammation of the lung parenchyma/alveoli often with consolidation and impaired gas exchange **Clinical features** • Fever • Cough • Sputum production • Breathlessness • Chest discomfort • Reduced oxygen saturation • Fatigue **Physiotherapy implications** • Positioning to optimize ventilation • Breathing exercises • Airway clearance techniques when indicated • Early mobilization • Progressive walking and exercise • Monitor respiratory rate HR and SpO2 --- **6 Urinary Tract Infection UTI** **Definition** • UTI is an infection affecting any part of the urinary tract including the bladder urethra ureters or kidneys **Postoperative risk factors** • Urinary catheterization • Prolonged catheter use • Immobility • Inadequate hydration • Urinary retention **Clinical features** • Burning or pain during urination • Increased urinary frequency • Urgency • Lower abdominal discomfort • Fever in more significant infection • Cloudy or foul smelling urine **Physiotherapy implications** • Encourage early mobilization when appropriate • Encourage adequate mobility and hydration according to medical advice • Maintain catheter safety during transfers and walking • Maintain infection control measures • Monitor for fever or systemic deterioration --- **7 Pressure Sores / Pressure Injuries** **Definition** • A pressure injury is localized damage to the skin and/or underlying tissue usually occurring over a bony prominence due to prolonged pressure or pressure combined with shear **Risk factors** • Prolonged bed rest • Reduced consciousness • Poor nutrition • Incontinence • Reduced sensation • Immobility **Common sites** • Sacrum • Heels • Greater trochanters • Elbows • Occiput **Physiotherapy management** • Regular repositioning • Pressure relieving positions and surfaces • Early mobilization • ROM exercises • Reduce prolonged pressure over bony prominences • Strengthening and functional mobility • Patient and caregiver education • Coordinate with the wound care team /////////////////////// **Physiotherapy Management After Surgery** --- **Definition** • Physiotherapy management after surgery is the planned use of physiotherapy assessment exercises positioning mobilization and education to prevent postoperative complications restore physical function and promote safe recovery --- **Main Physiotherapy Management** **1 Assessment** • Check vital signs HR BP RR and SpO2 • Assess pain • Assess respiratory status • Assess ROM and muscle strength • Assess bed mobility transfers and gait • Check surgical wound and precautions **2 Respiratory Physiotherapy** • Deep breathing exercises • Thoracic expansion exercises • Supported coughing • Airway clearance techniques when indicated • Appropriate positioning • Helps prevent atelectasis and pneumonia **3 Circulatory Exercises** • Ankle pump exercises • Active limb movements • Early mobilization • Helps reduce venous stasis and risk of DVT **4 Early Mobilization** • Bed mobility • Sitting at bedside • Sit to stand • Transfer training • Progressive walking • Prevents deconditioning weakness and pressure injuries **5 ROM and Strengthening** • Passive/active ROM as appropriate • Isometric exercises when indicated • Progressive strengthening • Prevents stiffness muscle weakness and contractures **6 Patient Education** • Teach safe bed mobility and log rolling when appropriate • Wound protection during coughing and movement • Posture and body mechanics • Activity progression and home exercises • Educate about warning signs requiring medical review **Goals** • Prevent postoperative complications • Reduce pain and improve mobility • Maintain muscle strength and ROM • Improve respiratory and cardiovascular function • Restore functional independence and ADLs //////////////////// **Mastectomy Complications and Physiotherapy Management** --- **1 Definition of Mastectomy** • Mastectomy is a surgical procedure in which part or all of the breast tissue is removed most commonly for the treatment of breast cancer • It may be performed on one breast unilateral or both breasts bilateral **Types** • Simple/total mastectomy removal of the whole breast • Modified radical mastectomy removal of the breast with axillary lymph node dissection • Skin sparing mastectomy breast tissue is removed while preserving most of the breast skin • Nipple sparing mastectomy breast tissue is removed while preserving the nipple areola complex • Radical mastectomy extensive removal of breast chest wall muscles and lymph nodes now rarely performed --- **2 Complications After Mastectomy** **Early complications** • Pain at the surgical site • Wound infection • Bleeding or hematoma • Seroma which is accumulation of fluid around the surgical site • Wound healing problems • Reduced shoulder movement • Arm and shoulder stiffness • Numbness or altered sensation around the chest or arm • Fatigue **Late complications** • Lymphedema of the arm hand breast or chest wall particularly after lymph node removal or radiotherapy • Shoulder dysfunction or frozen shoulder • Post mastectomy pain syndrome • Scar adhesion and tissue tightness • Axillary web syndrome cording • Postural abnormalities especially rounded shoulders • Muscle weakness and reduced physical activity • Reduced functional independence • Psychological problems related to altered body image --- **3 Physiotherapy Management After Mastectomy** **A Physiotherapy Assessment** • Assess pain and surgical wound • Assess shoulder and upper limb ROM • Assess muscle strength • Assess posture • Assess sensation • Assess upper limb swelling and signs of lymphedema • Assess respiratory status • Assess functional activities and ADLs --- **B Respiratory Physiotherapy** • Deep breathing exercises • Thoracic expansion exercises • Supported coughing when required • Appropriate positioning • Early mobilization • Helps prevent respiratory complications after surgery --- **C Shoulder and Upper Limb Exercises** • Begin gentle exercises according to surgical instructions • Shoulder flexion exercises • Shoulder abduction exercises • Elbow flexion and extension • Wrist and finger movements • Scapular movements • Gradually restore full shoulder ROM Breast surgery rehabilitation commonly includes postoperative shoulder exercises to maintain or restore arm mobility --- **D Lymphedema Prevention and Management** • Encourage regular gradual arm and shoulder movement • Avoid prolonged inactivity of the affected arm • Maintain healthy body weight and regular physical activity • Protect the skin from cuts burns and infection • Monitor for • Arm swelling • Heaviness • Tightness • Reduced ROM • Refer to a specialist lymphedema service if lymphedema develops For established lymphedema decongestive lymphatic therapy may include exercise compression skin care and specialist manual lymphatic drainage --- **E Postural Correction** • Encourage upright sitting and standing • Avoid rounded shoulders • Perform scapular retraction exercises • Maintain normal thoracic mobility • Correct protective postures caused by pain Good posture helps maintain shoulder function and may reduce muscular tension --- **F Scar Management** • Once the wound is fully healed scar mobility can be assessed • Gentle scar mobilization may be used when appropriate • Stretching exercises can help reduce tissue tightness • Monitor for excessive scar formation or adhesions --- **G Functional Rehabilitation** • Bed mobility training • Transfer training • Progressive walking • Upper limb functional activities • Progressive strengthening • Gradual return to ADLs • Gradual return to work exercise and recreational activities according to medical clearance --- **H Patient Education** • Follow wound care instructions • Avoid heavy lifting and strenuous activity until medically cleared • Perform prescribed exercises regularly • Protect the affected arm from cuts burns and infection • Maintain good skin care • Recognize early signs of lymphedema • Maintain regular physical activity • Seek medical advice for increasing swelling redness wound discharge or severe pain --- **4 Physiotherapy Goals** • Reduce pain and stiffness • Restore shoulder and upper limb ROM • Maintain muscle strength • Prevent or manage lymphedema • Prevent postural abnormalities • Improve functional independence • Prevent complications of immobility • Improve quality of life and return to normal activities //////////////////// **Amputation Definition Indications Levels Complications Stump Care Phantom Limb Prosthetic Rehabilitation and Cineplasty** --- **1 Definition** • Amputation is the surgical removal of part or all of a limb or extremity because of disease trauma or other conditions in which the limb cannot be preserved • The remaining portion of the limb is called the residual limb or stump --- **2 Indications of Amputation** • Severe trauma with an unsalvageable limb • Severe peripheral vascular disease/ischemia • Diabetic foot with irreversible tissue damage • Gangrene • Severe infection or uncontrolled osteomyelitis • Malignant bone or soft tissue tumour • Congenital limb deformity in selected cases • Severe burns or frostbite with non viable tissue • Failed previous reconstruction or repeated infection --- **3 Levels of Amputation** **Lower limb** • Hemipelvectomy • Hip disarticulation • Transfemoral amputation above knee • Knee disarticulation • Transtibial amputation below knee • Symes amputation • amputation below elbow • Wrist disarticulation • Partial hand/finger amputation **Principle** Preserve the maximum useful limb length and whenever possible preserve important joints to optimize functional and prosthetic outcomes --- **4 Complications of Amputation** **Early complications** • Hemorrhage • Hematoma • Infection • Wound breakdown • Edema • Skin necrosis • Pain • Poor wound healing **Late complications** • Joint contracture • Muscle weakness • Residual limb pain • Neuroma • Phantom limb sensation • Phantom limb pain • Poor prosthetic fit • Skin problems due to prosthetic pressure • Reduced mobility and functional independence --- **5 Stump / Residual Limb Care** • Inspect the stump daily for redness swelling pressure areas and skin breakdown • Maintain good stump hygiene • Keep the healed residual limb clean and dry • Control edema using appropriate compression/shrinker techniques when prescribed • Shape the stump appropriately for prosthetic fitting • Use correct positioning to prevent contractures • Perform regular ROM exercises • Strengthen the residual limb and remaining muscles • Perform desensitization when appropriate • Care for the scar after adequate wound healing • Avoid excessive pressure or friction • Protect the opposite limb particularly in patients with vascular disease or diabetes --- **6 Phantom Limb** **Definition** • Phantom limb sensation is the feeling that the amputated limb is still present • Phantom limb pain PLP is painful sensation perceived in the missing limb **Features** • Burning pain • Shooting or electric like pain • Cramping • Tingling • Feeling of movement or position of the missing limb **Management** • Patient education and reassurance • Desensitization techniques • Gentle tapping and massage of the healed residual limb • Graded motor imagery • Mirror therapy may be used as part of rehabilitation • Appropriate prosthetic use when suitable • Psychological support when required • Medical and intact limbs • Improve balance • Improve cardiovascular endurance • Desensitize the residual limb • Train transfers and mobility • Teach ADLs **B Prosthetic fitting** • Assess residual limb condition • Select an appropriate prosthesis • Ensure proper socket fit • Teach donning and doffing • Teach prosthetic hygiene and skin inspection • Gradually increase wearing time **C Prosthetic training** • Weight shifting • Standing balance • Parallel bar training • Gait training • Walking with assistive devices initially when required • Stair training • Uneven surface training • Functional and community mobility **D Follow up** • Regular assessment of skin and residual limb • Prosthetic adjustment as limb volume changes • Gait assessment • Maintenance of prosthetic components • Long term functional and psychological support --- **8 Cineplasty** **Definition** • Cineplasty is a surgical technique in which a muscle tendon unit of the residual limb is brought through the stump and movement **Advantages** • Provides more direct control of the prosthesis • Provides sensory feedback through muscle activity • May improve functional control of some prosthetic devices • Can be particularly useful in selected upper limb amputees --- **9 Physiotherapy Goals After Amputation** • Reduce pain and edema • Prevent contractures • Maintain and improve muscle strength • Improve balance and coordination • Develop independence in transfers and ADLs • Prepare the residual limb for prosthetic fitting • Train safe prosthetic use • Restore gait and functional mobility • Promote psychological adjustment and community reintegration /////////////////////// **Vascular Disorders Varicose Veins Peripheral Arterial Occlusive Disease DVT and Surgical Management** --- **1 Varicose Veins** **Definition** • Varicose veins are dilated elongated and tortuous superficial veins most commonly in the lower limbs caused by failure of venous valves leading to venous reflux and pooling of blood **Clinical features** • Visible twisted and enlarged veins • Leg pain or aching • Heaviness and fatigue of legs • Ankle swelling • Itching • Skin pigmentation or eczema in chronic disease • Venous ulceration in severe cases • Superficial thrombophlebitis may occur **Management** • Regular exercise and weight management • Leg elevation • Compression therapy when appropriate • Endothermal ablation • Ultrasound guided foam sclerotherapy • Surgical ligation/stripping when other interventions are unsuitable --- **2 Peripheral Arterial Occlusive Disease PAOD** **Definition** • Peripheral arterial occlusive disease is a condition in which arterial blood flow to the limbs is reduced due to narrowing or blockage of peripheral arteries most commonly because of atherosclerosis **Clinical features** • Intermittent claudication pain in the limb during walking that improves with rest • Cold extremity • Pale or bluish skin • Reduced or absent peripheral pulses • Shiny thin skin • Loss of hair • Delayed wound healing • Ischemic ulcers • Severe disease may cause rest pain and gangrene **Management** • Smoking cessation • Regular/supervised exercise • Control of diabetes hypertension and Anesthesia

Types: General, Spinal and Local — Systemic Effects

1. Definition

* Anesthesia is a medically induced, temporary and usually reversible state in which sensation, especially pain, is reduced or abolished, with or without loss of consciousness, to permit surgical or diagnostic procedures. 

⸻

2. Types of Anesthesia

A. General Anesthesia

Definition

* General anesthesia is a drug-induced state of unconsciousness with loss of sensation and reduced protective reflexes during surgery. 

Features

* Patient is unconscious.
* Pain sensation is suppressed.
* Protective airway reflexes are reduced.
* Muscle relaxation may be produced.
* Airway support/ventilation may be required.

Uses

* Major abdominal surgery.
* Thoracic surgery.
* Neurosurgery.
* Major orthopaedic surgery.
* Procedures that require prolonged immobility.

⸻

B. Spinal Anesthesia

Definition

* Spinal anesthesia is a regional anesthetic technique in which a local anesthetic is injected into the subarachnoid/intrathecal space, producing temporary sensory and motor blockade. 

Features

* Patient is usually conscious.
* Produces numbness and weakness below the level of the block.
* Commonly used for lower abdominal, pelvic and lower-limb surgery. 

Common effects/complications

* Hypotension.
* Bradycardia.
* Urinary retention.
* Post-dural puncture headache.
* Temporary motor weakness.
* Rare neurological complications. 

⸻

C. Local Anesthesia

Definition

* Local anesthesia produces temporary loss of sensation in a specific, limited area without causing loss of consciousness. 

Examples

* Local infiltration for wound suturing.
* Dental anesthesia.
* Minor skin procedures.
* Peripheral nerve blocks.

Mechanism

* Local anesthetics block voltage-gated sodium channels, preventing nerve impulse transmission. 

⸻

3. Systemic Effects of Anesthesia

A. Respiratory System

* Respiratory depression, particularly with general anesthesia and sedative/opioid drugs.
* Reduced cough and airway-protective reflexes.
* Hypoventilation.
* Reduced functional respiratory capacity.
* Risk of atelectasis and postoperative pulmonary complications.

B. Cardiovascular System

* Hypotension.
* Bradycardia or tachycardia.
* Reduced vascular tone.
* Changes in cardiac output.
* Significant spinal blockade may produce hypotension and bradycardia. 

C. Central Nervous System

* Loss of consciousness with general anesthesia.
* Reduced awareness and reflexes.
* Drowsiness and dizziness after anesthesia.
* Temporary confusion or memory impairment may occur, particularly in susceptible patients. 

D. Gastrointestinal System

* Nausea and vomiting.
* Reduced gastrointestinal motility.
* Postoperative ileus may occur after major surgery.

E. Urinary System

* Urinary retention, particularly following neuraxial anesthesia and some surgical procedures. 

F. Musculoskeletal System

* Muscle relaxation during general anesthesia.
* Temporary weakness after regional/spinal anesthesia.
* Reduced mobility following surgery.
* Increased risk of deconditioning with prolonged immobilization.

G. Temperature Regulation

* Hypothermia may occur during and after surgery.
* Shivering may occur, particularly after spinal anesthesia. 

⸻

4. Physiotherapy Implications

* Assess HR, BP, RR and SpO₂ before treatment.
* Assess level of consciousness and neurological status.
* Check motor and sensory recovery after spinal anesthesia.
* Begin mobilization only when the patient is medically stable and adequate motor/sensory function has returned.
* Perform deep-breathing exercises when indicated.
* Encourage ankle-pump and limb exercises.
* Progress from bed mobility → sitting → standing → walking.
* Monitor for:
    * Dizziness.
    * Hypotension.
    * Desaturation.
    * Excessive weakness.
    * Altered consciousness.
* Use appropriate positioning and airway-clearance techniques when clinically indicated.//////////////////////1. CELLULITIS — 

Definition

* Cellulitis is an acute bacterial infection of the skin and subcutaneous tissues.

Causes / Risk Factors

* Bacterial entry through cuts, wounds or abrasions.
* Insect bites.
* Fungal skin infection.
* Diabetes mellitus.
* Lymphoedema.
* Poor circulation.
* Immunosuppression.

Clinical Features

* Redness.
* Warmth.
* Swelling.
* Pain and tenderness.
* Fever and chills.
* Malaise.
* Regional lymph-node swelling.

Complications

* Abscess formation.
* Lymphangitis.
* Osteomyelitis.
* Sepsis.
* Necrotizing soft-tissue infection.
* Recurrent cellulitis.

Diagnosis

* Clinical examination.
* Blood tests if systemic infection is suspected.
* Wound culture if there is discharge.
* Imaging if deep infection is suspected.

Treatment

* Appropriate antibiotics.
* Analgesics.
* Limb elevation when appropriate.
* Treatment of underlying conditions.
* IV antibiotics/hospitalization for severe infection.

Physiotherapy Implications

* Assess pain, swelling and mobility.
* Avoid vigorous massage over acute cellulitis.
* Elevate the affected limb when appropriate.
* Maintain mobility of unaffected areas.
* Gradually resume exercises after infection improves.
* Educate regarding skin care and prevention.

⸻

2. ABSCESS — 10 Marks

Definition

* An abscess is a localized collection of pus within a tissue or body cavity, usually caused by infection.

Causes

* Bacterial infection.
* Infected wound.
* Blocked skin glands/hair follicles.
* Infected cyst.
* Foreign body.
* Diabetes and reduced immunity.

Types

* Cutaneous abscess.
* Subcutaneous abscess.
* Deep abscess.
* Intra-abdominal abscess.
* Pelvic abscess.
* Liver abscess.
* Lung abscess.

Clinical Features

* Painful swelling.
* Redness.
* Warmth.
* Tenderness.
* Fluctuant swelling.
* Pus discharge.
* Fever.
* Malaise.

Complications

* Cellulitis.
* Spread of infection.
* Sepsis.
* Tissue destruction.
* Recurrence.
* Fistula formation.

Diagnosis

* Clinical examination.
* Ultrasound for selected collections.
* CT/MRI for deep abscesses.
* Culture of pus when appropriate.

Treatment

* Incision and drainage is the main treatment for many abscesses.
* Antibiotics when clinically indicated.
* Analgesics.
* Wound dressing.
* Treatment of underlying disease.

Physiotherapy Implications

* Avoid direct pressure over acute abscess.
* Avoid vigorous massage over infected tissue.
* Maintain mobility of unaffected areas.
* Provide postoperative respiratory and mobility exercises when indicated.
* Monitor for systemic infection.
* Follow wound-care precautions.

⸻

3. GANGRENE — 10 Marks

Definition

* Gangrene is the death of body tissue, usually due to loss of blood supply, infection, or both.

Causes

* Peripheral arterial disease.
* Diabetes mellitus.
* Severe infection.
* Trauma.
* Atherosclerosis.
* Arterial obstruction.
* Burns or frostbite.

Types

* Dry gangrene: Usually due to severe ischemia.
* Wet gangrene: Necrotic tissue associated with infection.
* Gas gangrene: Severe bacterial infection with gas production in tissues.
* Internal gangrene: Affects internal organs following loss of blood supply.

Clinical Features

* Black, brown, purple or discoloured tissue.
* Coldness.
* Loss of sensation.
* Pain.
* Swelling.
* Blisters or ulcers.
* Foul-smelling discharge in infected gangrene.
* Fever and systemic illness.

Complications

* Severe infection.
* Sepsis.
* Shock.
* Extensive tissue loss.
* Amputation.
* Death if untreated.

Treatment

* Restore blood supply when possible.
* Surgical debridement.
* Antibiotics for infection.
* Vascular surgery when indicated.
* Amputation for irreversible tissue damage.

Physiotherapy Implications

* Assess circulation and functional status.
* Avoid pressure or trauma to ischemic tissue.
* Maintain ROM of unaffected joints.
* After amputation:
    * Stump care.
    * ROM exercises.
    * Strengthening.
    * Balance training.
    * Prosthetic rehabilitation.

⸻

4. TUBERCULOSIS (TB) — 10 Marks

Definition

* Tuberculosis (TB) is an infectious disease caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis, most commonly affecting the lungs.

Types

* Pulmonary TB: Affects the lungs.
* Extrapulmonary TB: Affects organs outside the lungs, such as:
    * Lymph nodes.
    * Spine.
    * Bones and joints.
    * Kidneys.
    * Brain/meninges.
    * Skin.

Risk Factors

* Close contact with infectious TB.
* HIV infection.
* Diabetes mellitus.
* Malnutrition.
* Smoking.
* Immunosuppression.
* Overcrowded living conditions.

Clinical Features

* Persistent cough.
* Sputum production.
* Coughing blood may occur.
* Chest pain.
* Fever.
* Night sweats.
* Weight loss.
* Loss of appetite.
* Fatigue.

Diagnosis

* Sputum examination.
* Rapid molecular diagnostic tests.
* Chest X-ray.
* Culture and drug-susceptibility testing.
* TST or IGRA for TB infection.

Treatment

* Combination anti-tuberculosis drugs.
* Common first-line drugs:
    * Rifampicin.
    * Isoniazid.
    * Pyrazinamide.
    * Ethambutol.
* Complete the prescribed treatment course to prevent treatment failure and drug resistance.

Complications

* Pulmonary fibrosis.
* Bronchiectasis.
* Hemoptysis.
* Respiratory impairment.
* Pleural disease.
* TB meningitis.
* Spinal TB.
* Bone and joint destruction.
* Disseminated/miliary TB.

Physiotherapy Implications

* Assess respiratory status and exercise tolerance.
* Monitor HR, RR and SpO₂.
* Breathing exercises when indicated.
* Gradual aerobic and functional exercise.
* Postural and chest mobility exercises.
* Energy-conservation techniques.
* Follow airborne infection-control precautions for infectious pulmonary TB.////////////////Hospital-Acquired Infections (HAI)

1. Definition

* Hospital-acquired infection (HAI), also called healthcare-associated infection, is an infection that a patient acquires while receiving healthcare or during/after hospitalization, which was not present or incubating at the time of admission. 
* HAIs are often preventable and are an important cause of increased morbidity, mortality and hospital stay. 

⸻

2. Common Types of Hospital-Acquired Infections

* Catheter-associated urinary tract infection (CAUTI)
    * Associated with urinary catheterization.
* Surgical-site infection (SSI)
    * Infection occurring at or near the surgical site after an operation.
* Central-line-associated bloodstream infection (CLABSI)
    * Bloodstream infection associated with a central venous catheter.
* Hospital-acquired pneumonia

* Poor nutritional status.
* Diabetes mellitus.
* Immunosuppression.
* Severe underlying illness.
* Reduced mobility.
* Prolonged hospitalization.

Treatment/procedure-related factors

* Surgery.
* Urinary catheterization.
* Central venous catheterization.
* Mechanical ventilation.
* Prolonged antibiotic use.
* Invasive procedures.
* Poor wound care.

* Chills.
* Increased heart rate.
* Increased respiratory rate.

1. Stereotactic Surgery

Definition

* Stereotactic surgery is a minimally invasive neurosurgical technique that uses a three-dimensional coordinate system with CT/MRI guidance to accurately locate and treat a specific area of the brain. 

Overview

* Uses precise anatomical targeting.
* May use a stereotactic frame or frameless navigation.
* Can be used for:
    * Deep brain stimulation.
    * Brain biopsy.
    * Lesioning procedures.
    * Stereotactic radiosurgery.
    * Treatment of selected brain tumours and vascular lesions. 

Indications

* Brain tumours.
* Arteriovenous malformations.
* Movement disorders.
* Parkinson’s disease.
* Essential tremor.
* Dystonia.
* Epilepsy.
* Selected functional neurological disorders.

Complications

* Intracranial bleeding.
* Infection.
* Seizures.
* Neurological deficit.
* Brain edema.
* Headache.
* Injury to surrounding brain structures.
* Radiation-related complications when radiosurgery is used. 

⸻

2. Deep Brain Stimulation (DBS)

Definition

* Deep Brain Stimulation is a treatment in which electrodes are implanted into specific areas of the brain to deliver controlled electrical impulses, with a pulse generator usually implanted under the skin of the chest. 

Overview

* DBS is a reversible neuromodulation technique.
* Common targets include:
    * Subthalamic nucleus (STN).
    * Globus pallidus internus (GPi).
    * Ventral intermediate nucleus (VIM) of the thalamus.
* The electrodes are connected by wires to an implanted pulse generator. 

Indications

* Parkinson’s disease.
* Essential tremor.
* Dystonia.
* Treatment-resistant obsessive-compulsive disorder in selected patients.
* Selected refractory epilepsy.
* Other indications may be considered in specialist centres. 

Complications

* Intracranial hemorrhage.
* Stroke.
* Infection.
* Seizures.
* Lead displacement or malfunction.
* Hardware failure.
* Headache.
* Confusion.
* Speech or balance problems.
* Tingling or muscle contractions due to stimulation.
* Mood changes. 

⸻

3. Rhizotomy

Definition

* Rhizotomy is a surgical procedure in which selected nerve roots or their sensory fibres are partially or completely divided/ablated to reduce abnormal nerve activity or pain.

Overview

* It may be performed using surgical, radiofrequency or other lesioning techniques depending on the nerve and condition.
* The aim is to interrupt abnormal sensory or motor pathways.

Indications

* Severe chronic pain in selected patients.
* Trigeminal neuralgia in selected cases.
* Spasticity in selected patients, particularly through selective dorsal rhizotomy.
* Certain refractory neurological conditions.

Complications

* Numbness or loss of sensation.
* Weakness.
* Neuropathic pain.
* Infection.
* Bleeding.
* Unintended nerve injury.
* Recurrence of symptoms.

* Assess sensory and motor function.
* Manage weakness and altered sensation.
* Improve balance and gait when required.
* Stretching and strengthening for patients treated for spasticity.

Definition

* Thalamotomy is a surgical procedure in which a small, precisely targeted area of the thalamus is destroyed or lesioned to reduce abnormal neurological activity.

Overview

* It is usually performed using stereotactic guidance.
* Modern techniques may include radiofrequency lesioning or focused ultrasound.
* VIM thalamotomy targets the ventral intermediate nucleus and is primarily used for tremor. 

Indications

* Severe essential tremor.
* Selected tremor-dominant Parkinson’s disease.
* Medication-resistant tremor when appropriate.
* Selected unilateral movement disorders.

Complications

* Speech disturbance/dysarthria.
* Ataxia.
* Balance and gait disturbance.
* Weakness.
* Sensory disturbance.
* Cognitive or neurological deficits depending on the target.
* Hemorrhage or infection with invasive procedures.

⸻

Definition

* Neural implants are medical devices implanted in or near the nervous system to record neural activity or deliver electrical stimulation to modify nervous-system function.

* Vagus nerve stimulators.
* Responsive neurostimulation systems.
* Spinal cord stimulators.
* Cochlear implants.

Indications

* Parkinson’s disease.
* Essential tremor.
* Epilepsy.
* Chronic neuropathic pain.
* Hearing loss.
* Selected movement disorders.
* Selected psychiatric or neurological conditions.

Complications

* Infection.
* Bleeding.
* Device malfunction.
* Lead migration or breakage.
* Pain at the implantation site.
* Nerve or brain injury.
* Stimulation-related adverse effects. ////////////Radiological Interpretation of OA and RA

<USER_REQUEST>
Fractures of the Upper limb —
General causes

* Fall on an outstretched hand (FOOSH)
* Direct blow or trauma
* Road-traffic accidents
* Sports injuries
* Twisting or rotational injuries
* Occupational injuries
* Osteoporosis/pathological bone weakness

General clinical features

* Pain and tenderness
* Swelling and bruising
* Deformity or abnormal movement
* Loss of function and restricted ROM
* Crepitus
* Shortening or abnormal alignment
* Neurovascular deficit in complicated fractures

General complications

* Neurovascular injury
* Compartment syndrome
* Infection in open fractures
* Delayed union/non-union
* Malunion
* Joint stiffness
* Post-traumatic arthritis
* Complex regional pain syndrome

⸻

1. Fractures of Clavicle and Scapula

A. Fracture of clavicle

Definition:
Fracture of the clavicle, most commonly involving the middle third.

Causes

* Fall directly on the shoulder
* Fall on an outstretched hand
* Direct blow to clavicle
* Road-traffic or sports injury

Clinical features

* Pain and tenderness over clavicle
* Swelling and deformity
* Patient supports the affected arm
* Shoulder drooping forwards and downwards
* Abnormal mobility/crepitus
* Difficulty in shoulder movements
* Check distal neurovascular status

Complications

* Malunion
* Non-union
* Neurovascular injury
* Skin perforation
* Brachial plexus injury
* Pneumothorax
* Shoulder stiffness

Conservative management

* Arm sling or figure-of-eight brace
* Analgesics
* Ice/elevation initially
* Early elbow, wrist and hand movements
* Gradual shoulder ROM after pain subsides

Surgical management

* ORIF with plate and screws
* Indications: open fracture, neurovascular injury, significant displacement/shortening, threatened skin, or selected unstable displaced fractures.

B. Fracture of scapula

Causes

* Usually high-energy trauma
* Direct blow
* RTA
* Fall from height
* Indirect injury through shoulder

Clinical features

* Severe shoulder/scapular pain
* Swelling and tenderness
* Painful shoulder movements
* Reduced shoulder ROM
* Associated chest injuries may be present

Complications

* Associated rib and chest injuries
* Pneumothorax
* Neurovascular injury
* Malunion
* Shoulder stiffness
* Glenohumeral instability

Management

* Conservative: sling, analgesia, rest followed by early ROM.
* Surgical: ORIF for significantly displaced body/neck fractures, intra-articular glenoid fractures, open fractures or fractures associated with instability. 

⸻

2. Fractures of Greater Tuberosity and Neck of Humerus

A. Greater tuberosity fracture

Causes

* Fall on shoulder/FOOSH
* Shoulder dislocation
* Direct trauma

Clinical features

* Pain and tenderness over greater tuberosity
* Swelling
* Painful and restricted abduction
* Weakness of rotator cuff
* Difficulty raising arm

Complications

* Malunion
* Shoulder stiffness
* Rotator cuff dysfunction
* Subacromial impingement
* Non-union

Management

* Conservative: sling, analgesics and early passive ROM when appropriate.
* Surgical: ORIF for significantly displaced fragments, particularly when displacement causes impingement or affects shoulder mechanics.

B. Fracture of neck of humerus

Causes

* FOOSH
* Fall directly on shoulder
* Osteoporotic fall in elderly
* High-energy trauma in young adults

Clinical features

* Pain and swelling around shoulder
* Tenderness
* Inability to move shoulder
* Bruising
* Deformity
* Check axillary nerve and distal circulation

Complications

* Axillary nerve injury
* Vascular injury
* Avascular necrosis of humeral head
* Malunion/non-union
* Shoulder stiffness
* Rotator cuff dysfunction

Management

* Conservative: sling/shoulder immobilizer, analgesia and progressive ROM for undisplaced/stable fractures.
* Surgical: ORIF or arthroplasty for displaced, unstable, comminuted or selected fracture-dislocations. 

⸻

3. Fracture Shaft of Humerus

Definition:
Fracture of the humeral diaphysis between the surgical neck and supracondylar region.

Causes

* Fall
* Direct blow
* RTA
* Sports injury
* Pathological fracture

Clinical features

* Pain and swelling of arm
* Deformity
* Abnormal mobility and crepitus
* Loss of arm function
* Radial nerve palsy: wrist drop, inability to extend wrist/fingers and sensory changes over the dorsum of hand

Complications

* Radial nerve injury
* Brachial artery injury
* Non-union
* Malunion
* Infection
* Shoulder/elbow stiffness

Conservative management

* Coaptation splint or hanging arm cast initially
* Functional brace after swelling decreases
* Analgesia
* Maintain elbow, wrist and hand movements
* Regular radiographic follow-up

Surgical management

* ORIF with plate and screws
* Intramedullary nailing
* External fixation in selected open/severe injuries
* Indications include open fracture, vascular injury, multiple injuries, unacceptable alignment, pathological fracture and failure of conservative treatment. 

⸻

4. Supracondylar Fracture of Humerus

Definition:
Fracture of the distal humerus just above the elbow condyles, commonly seen in children.

Causes

* Fall on outstretched hand
* Fall onto flexed elbow
* Sports injury

Clinical features

* Severe elbow pain
* Swelling and deformity
* Loss of elbow movement
* Tenderness
* Abnormal carrying angle
* Assess brachial artery and median, radial and ulnar nerves

Complications

* Brachial artery injury
* Median/anterior interosseous nerve injury
* Compartment syndrome
* Volkmann ischaemic contracture
* Cubitus varus
* Elbow stiffness
* Malunion

Conservative management

* Gartland type I: above-elbow cast/splint with elbow flexed appropriately and neurovascular monitoring.
* Regular X-ray follow-up.
* Avoid excessive elbow flexion because it may compromise circulation. 

Surgical management

* Closed reduction and percutaneous pinning (CRPP) for displaced/unstable fractures.
* Open reduction and internal fixation when closed reduction fails or in selected complicated fractures.
* Urgent surgery if there is vascular compromise or an open injury.

⸻

5. Side-Swipe Injury of Elbow

Definition:
A side-swipe injury is a high-energy injury to the elbow produced by a direct blow, classically when the elbow is struck by a passing vehicle.

Causes

* Direct high-energy blow to the elbow
* Road-traffic accident

Clinical features

* Severe pain and swelling
* Open wound commonly present
* Deformity around elbow
* Restricted elbow movement
* Fracture-dislocation may occur
* Possible vascular and nerve injury

Complications

* Infection
* Neurovascular injury
* Compartment syndrome
* Elbow stiffness
* Non-union/malunion
* Post-traumatic arthritis

Conservative management

* Usually limited because these are commonly high-energy, unstable injuries.
* Initial splintage
* Analgesia
* Wound care
* Antibiotics and tetanus prophylaxis for open injuries
* Neurovascular monitoring

Surgical management

* Urgent irrigation and debridement for open injury
* Reduction of dislocation
* ORIF of associated fractures
* External fixation when there is severe soft-tissue injury or instability.

⸻

6. Fractures of Radius and Ulna

Both-bone forearm fracture

Definition:
Fracture of both the radius and ulna, usually involving their shafts.

Causes

* Direct blow
* FOOSH
* RTA
* Sports injury
* Twisting injury

Clinical features

* Pain and swelling
* Deformity and shortening
* Abnormal movement/crepitus
* Loss of pronation and supination
* Neurovascular assessment is essential

Complications

* Compartment syndrome
* Malunion
* Non-union
* Loss of pronation/supination
* Nerve and vascular injury
* Infection
* Radioulnar synostosis

Management

* Conservative: closed reduction and above-elbow cast in selected children/undisplaced fractures.
* Surgical: ORIF with plates and screws is commonly required in adults because accurate restoration of radial bow and forearm rotation is important.

Chauffeur fracture

Important correction: Chauffeur fracture is NOT a fracture of both radius and ulna. It is an intra-articular fracture of the radial styloid process. 

Management

* Undisplaced: splint/cast.
* Displaced or unstable: reduction and fixation, commonly ORIF.

⸻

7. Fractures of Capitulum, Radial Head and Olecranon

A. Capitulum fracture

Causes

* FOOSH
* Direct trauma
* Elbow dislocation

Clinical features

* Elbow pain and swelling
* Tenderness over lateral elbow
* Restricted flexion-extension
* Mechanical locking may occur

Complications

* Non-union
* Malunion
* Elbow stiffness
* Post-traumatic arthritis

Management

* Undisplaced: immobilization followed by early ROM.
* Displaced: ORIF with screws; excision of small non-reconstructable fragments may be considered in selected cases.

B. Radial head fracture

Causes

* FOOSH
* Valgus force at elbow
* Direct trauma

Clinical features

* Lateral elbow pain
* Tenderness over radial head
* Painful pronation and supination
* Restricted elbow movement
* Elbow effusion

Complications

* Elbow stiffness
* Non-union
* Malunion
* Instability
* Post-traumatic arthritis

Management

* Undisplaced: sling briefly followed by early movement.
* Displaced/unstable: ORIF; radial head replacement may be required for severely comminuted fractures.

C. Olecranon fracture

Causes

* Direct fall on elbow
* Triceps contraction
* RTA

Clinical features

* Posterior elbow pain and swelling
* Tenderness
* Palpable fracture gap
* Inability to actively extend elbow in displaced fractures

Complications

* Non-union
* Elbow stiffness
* Loss of extension
* Post-traumatic arthritis
* Ulnar nerve symptoms

Management

* Undisplaced and stable: above-elbow splint/cast with monitoring.
* Displaced: ORIF using tension-band wiring or plate fixation. 

⸻

8. Monteggia and Galeazzi Fractures

A. Monteggia fracture-dislocation

Definition:
Fracture of the proximal or middle ulna associated with dislocation of the radial head at the radiocapitellar joint. 

Causes

* FOOSH
* Direct blow
* RTA
* Hyperpronation injury

Clinical features

* Pain and swelling of forearm/elbow
* Deformity
* Restricted elbow movement
* Prominent/displaced radial head
* Possible posterior interosseous nerve palsy

Complications

* Radial/PIN injury
* Malunion
* Non-union
* Elbow stiffness
* Chronic radial-head dislocation
* Compartment syndrome

Management

* Children: closed reduction and cast immobilization may be successful when stable.
* Adults/unstable injuries: ORIF of ulna, followed by reduction and assessment of radial head stability. 

B. Galeazzi fracture-dislocation

Definition:
Fracture of the middle/distal third of the radial shaft with disruption or dislocation of the distal radioulnar joint (DRUJ). 

Causes

* FOOSH with hyperpronation
* RTA
* High-energy trauma

Clinical features

* Pain and swelling of forearm/wrist
* Radial deformity
* Prominent ulnar head
* Restricted pronation and supination
* DRUJ tenderness/instability

Complications

* DRUJ instability
* Malunion
* Non-union
* Loss of forearm rotation
* Chronic wrist pain
* Post-traumatic arthritis

Management

* Children: closed reduction and long-arm immobilization may be used when stable.
* Adults: ORIF of radius with plate and screws; DRUJ stability is assessed after fixation and stabilized if necessary. 

⸻

9. Fractures of Wrist and Hand Complex – Smith’s Fracture

Smith’s fracture

Definition:
Smith’s fracture is a fracture of the distal radius with volar displacement/angulation of the distal fragment, often considered the reverse of a typical Colles’ fracture.

Causes

* Fall onto the dorsum of the flexed wrist
* Direct blow to the back of the wrist
* RTA

Clinical features

* Pain and swelling around wrist
* Tenderness over distal radius
* Volar deformity
* Restricted wrist and finger movements
* Possible median nerve symptoms
* Reduced grip strength

Complications

* Malunion
* Median nerve compression/carpal tunnel syndrome
* Wrist stiffness
* Tendon problems
* Post-traumatic arthritis
* Complex regional pain syndrome

Conservative management

* Closed reduction
* Below-elbow or above-elbow cast depending on stability
* Elevation and analgesics
* Regular X-rays to detect loss of reduction
* Finger and later wrist ROM exercises

Surgical management

* ORIF, commonly with a volar locking plate, for displaced/unstable or intra-articular fractures.
* External fixation may be used in selected severe comminuted injuries.///////////////////////Dislocations of the Upper Limb —-

Definition

Dislocation is the complete loss of normal articular contact between the articular surfaces of a joint due to trauma or other causes.

The shoulder is the most commonly dislocated major joint, with anterior dislocation being the most common type. 

⸻

1. Shoulder Dislocation

Mechanism of injury

* Anterior dislocation: Fall on an outstretched arm or forceful combination of abduction, extension and external rotation.
* Posterior dislocation: Direct blow to the anterior shoulder with the arm adducted and internally rotated.
* Violent muscle contraction, such as during seizures or electrical injury, may cause posterior dislocation. 

⸻

A. Anterior dislocation of shoulder

Clinical features

* Severe pain following trauma
* Patient supports the affected arm
* Arm held in abduction and external rotation
* Loss of normal rounded contour of shoulder
* Prominent acromion, producing a squared-off shoulder
* Humeral head may be palpable anteriorly
* Complete restriction of active and passive movements
* Check axillary nerve and distal vascular status

Complications

* Axillary nerve injury
* Axillary artery injury
* Greater tuberosity fracture
* Hill-Sachs lesion
* Bankart lesion
* Rotator cuff injury
* Recurrent dislocation
* Joint stiffness

Axillary nerve injury is particularly important and should be assessed before and after reduction. 

⸻

B. Posterior dislocation of shoulder

Clinical features

* Severe shoulder pain
* Arm held in adduction and internal rotation
* Inability to externally rotate the arm
* Flattening of the anterior shoulder
* Prominent posterior humeral head may be palpable
* Restricted shoulder movements

Complications

* Reverse Hill-Sachs lesion
* Fracture of surgical neck or tuberosity
* Neurovascular injury
* Rotator cuff injury
* Recurrent instability
* Osteoarthritis

Posterior dislocation is uncommon and may be missed clinically, particularly when the patient presents with a guarded internally rotated arm. 

⸻

Conservative Management of Shoulder Dislocation

1. Reduction

The dislocation is reduced by closed manipulation, preferably with adequate analgesia/sedation and muscle relaxation.

Kocher’s manoeuvre

1. Patient supine.
2. Arm adducted to the side.
3. Elbow flexed to 90°.
4. Slowly externally rotate the arm until resistance is felt.
5. Elevate/flex the arm while maintaining external rotation.
6. Adduct the arm.
7. Internally rotate the shoulder to complete reduction. 

Note: Forceful Kocher manoeuvre should be avoided because it can cause fractures and soft-tissue injury.

Hippocrates manoeuvre

1. Patient lies supine.
2. The affected arm is gently grasped.
3. Axillary counter-traction is applied.
4. Longitudinal traction is applied to the limb.
5. Gentle manipulation is continued until the humeral head returns to the glenoid.

The classical Hippocratic technique is now generally not preferred because of the risk of brachial plexus and vascular injury. 

After reduction

* Confirm reduction clinically and radiologically.
* Reassess neurovascular status.
* Apply sling/immobilizer.
* Analgesics.
* Gradual ROM exercises.
* Physiotherapy for rotator-cuff and scapular-muscle strengthening.

⸻

Surgical Management

Indications

* Irreducible dislocation
* Recurrent dislocation
* Associated fracture
* Significant bone loss
* Persistent instability
* Major labral injury
* Failed conservative treatment

Important operations

1. Bankart repair

* Repair of the detached anteroinferior glenoid labrum and capsule.
* May be performed arthroscopically or by open technique.
* Common procedure for recurrent anterior instability.

2. Putti-Platt operation

* A historical/non-anatomic stabilization procedure.
* Involves shortening and tightening the subscapularis and anterior capsule.
* Reduces external rotation and therefore limits instability.
* It has largely been replaced by anatomic Bankart repair in modern practice. 

3. Latarjet procedure

* Coracoid transfer to the anterior glenoid.
* Used particularly when there is significant glenoid bone loss or recurrent instability.

⸻

2. Recurrent Dislocation of Shoulder

Definition

Repeated episodes of shoulder dislocation or subluxation following an initial traumatic dislocation.

Causes

* Inadequate healing of capsule/labrum
* Bankart lesion
* Glenoid bone loss
* Hill-Sachs lesion
* Ligamentous laxity
* Inadequate rehabilitation

Clinical features

* Repeated episodes of dislocation
* Apprehension during abduction and external rotation
* Pain and instability
* Reduced confidence in shoulder movements
* Positive apprehension test

Management

Conservative

* Activity modification
* Shoulder immobilization when indicated
* Physiotherapy
* Rotator-cuff strengthening
* Scapular stabilization exercises
* Proprioceptive training

Surgical

* Arthroscopic/open Bankart repair
* Putti-Platt procedure
* Latarjet procedure
* Remplissage or other bone/soft-tissue procedures depending on associated lesions.

Recurrent instability is particularly common in young active patients after traumatic anterior dislocation. 

⸻

3. Dislocation of Elbow

Mechanism of injury

* Commonly due to fall on an outstretched hand
* Hyperextension and valgus/varus forces
* Sports injuries
* Road-traffic accidents

Clinical features

* Severe pain
* Swelling
* Obvious deformity
* Loss of elbow movement
* Prominent olecranon or abnormal relationship of bony landmarks
* Neurovascular assessment is essential

Complications

* Brachial artery injury
* Median, ulnar or radial nerve injury
* Fracture associated with dislocation
* Elbow stiffness
* Chronic instability
* Heterotopic ossification
* Post-traumatic arthritis

Conservative management

1. Closed reduction under adequate analgesia/sedation.
2. Confirm reduction with X-ray.
3. Short period of immobilization.
4. Early active ROM once stability permits.
5. Physiotherapy.

Early mobilization is important because prolonged immobilization increases the risk of elbow stiffness and poor functional outcome. 

Surgical management

* Open reduction if irreducible.
* Repair/reconstruction of collateral ligaments in unstable injuries.
* Fixation of associated fractures.
* External fixation for severe instability when required.

⸻

4. Hand Injuries

A. Crush Injuries

Definition

Injury caused by compression of the hand between two objects, resulting in damage to skin, muscles, tendons, nerves, vessels and bones.

Clinical features

* Pain and swelling
* Bruising
* Skin and soft-tissue damage
* Fracture/dislocation
* Loss of movement
* Sensory loss
* Vascular compromise

Complications

* Compartment syndrome
* Tissue necrosis
* Infection
* Tendon adhesions
* Nerve injury
* Stiffness
* Contracture
* Amputation

Management

Conservative

* Elevation
* Analgesia
* Wound dressing
* Splintage
* Antibiotics when indicated
* Early controlled ROM when safe

Surgical

* Thorough wound exploration and debridement
* Repair of tendons, nerves and vessels
* Fracture fixation
* Fasciotomy for compartment syndrome
* Skin graft/flap coverage
* Amputation when tissue is non-viable.

⸻

5. Flexor Tendon Injuries

Causes

* Sharp cuts
* Glass injuries
* Crush injuries
* Lacerations

Clinical features

* Loss of active finger flexion
* Open wound
* Altered resting finger position
* Loss of grip
* Sensory or vascular injury may coexist

Management

Conservative

* Wound care and splintage in selected partial injuries.
* Early protected rehabilitation after repair.

Surgical

* Primary tendon repair for complete lacerations when appropriate.
* Secondary tendon reconstruction if primary repair is not possible.
* Postoperative controlled tendon-gliding exercises and splinting.

⸻

6. Extensor Tendon Injuries

Causes

* Laceration
* Crush injury
* Direct trauma
* Closed tendon rupture

Clinical features

* Loss of active finger extension
* Finger deformity depending on level of injury
* Weak grip
* Open wound in lacerations

Complications

* Adhesions
* Extensor lag
* Rupture of repair
* Joint stiffness
* Deformity

Management

Conservative

* Splinting in appropriate position for selected injuries.
* Controlled mobilization.

Surgical

* Tendon repair for appropriate complete lacerations.
* Tendon graft or transfer for chronic injuries.
* Postoperative splinting and rehabilitation.

⸻

7. Burn Injuries of Hand

Definition

Burn injury is tissue damage caused by thermal, chemical, electrical or other energy sources.

Clinical features

* Pain
* Erythema
* Blistering
* Swelling
* Loss of skin and soft tissue in deep burns
* Reduced ROM
* Circumferential burns may compromise circulation.

Complications

* Infection
* Edema
* Skin and tendon damage
* Hypertrophic scar
* Contracture
* Web-space contracture
* Burn claw deformity
* Loss of finger movement
* Functional disability

Conservative management

1. Assess burn depth and extent.
2. Clean and dress the wound.
3. Elevate the hand to reduce edema.
4. Maintain adequate analgesia.
5. Splint in anti-deformity/intrinsic-plus position:
    * Wrist: approximately 20–30° extension
    * MCP joints: 70–90° flexion
    * IP joints: extension
    * Thumb: abducted
6. Early supervised ROM when safe.
7. Scar management and pressure therapy during healing.
8. Physiotherapy/occupational therapy.

These measures are important because edema, scarring and prolonged immobilization can rapidly destroy hand function, which humans apparently decided was worth preserving only after discovering fire. 

Surgical management

* Escharotomy for circumferential burns with vascular compromise.
* Early excision/debridement of deep burns.
* Skin grafting for deep partial-thickness and full-thickness burns.
* Flap reconstruction when tendons, joints or other deep structures are exposed.
* Scar release and grafting/flap procedures for established contractures.////////////////////Fractures of the Lower Limb —

General causes

* Road-traffic accidents
* Fall from height or fall on the limb
* Direct blow
* Twisting injuries
* Sports injuries
* Osteoporosis/pathological conditions

General clinical features

* Pain and tenderness
* Swelling and bruising
* Deformity and shortening
* Loss of function
* Abnormal mobility and crepitus
* Restricted joint movements
* Neurovascular deficit in complicated injuries

General complications

* Neurovascular injury
* Compartment syndrome
* Infection in open fractures
* Delayed union/non-union
* Malunion
* Joint stiffness
* Post-traumatic arthritis
* Fat embolism, particularly with long-bone fractures

⸻

1. FRACTURE NECK OF FEMUR

Definition

Fracture of the femoral neck occurring between the femoral head and trochanteric region. It is an intracapsular fracture and may compromise the blood supply of the femoral head. 

Causes

* Fall in elderly patients, commonly with osteoporosis
* Direct trauma
* Road-traffic accidents
* Fall from height
* Pathological weakening of bone

Classification

A. Anatomical classification

1. Subcapital – immediately below femoral head
2. Transcervical – through middle of neck
3. Basicervical – at junction of neck and trochanters 

B. Garden classification

* Type I: Incomplete/valgus impacted fracture
* Type II: Complete but undisplaced fracture
* Type III: Complete fracture with partial displacement
* Type IV: Complete fracture with complete displacement

C. Pauwels classification

* Type I: Fracture angle <30°
* Type II: 30–50°
* Type III: >50° and most vertically oriented/unstable. 

Clinical features

* Pain in groin/hip
* Inability to bear weight
* Limb appears shortened
* Limb lies in external rotation
* Tenderness around hip
* Pain on hip movement
* In impacted fractures, the patient may still be able to walk

Complications

* Avascular necrosis of femoral head
* Non-union
* Malunion
* Infection
* Implant/fixation failure
* Thromboembolism
* Hip stiffness
* Post-traumatic osteoarthritis 

Conservative management

Reserved mainly for patients who are medically unfit for surgery or selected stable/impacted fractures.

* Bed rest initially
* Analgesics
* Skin traction for pain relief when indicated
* Prevention of pressure sores and DVT
* Chest physiotherapy
* Early mobilization with walking aids as tolerated
* Regular radiographic follow-up

AO notes that non-operative treatment is generally reserved for medically infirm patients who cannot tolerate surgery. 

Surgical management

Undisplaced/impacted fractures

* Percutaneous cannulated cancellous screws
* Femoral neck system in selected cases

Displaced fractures

Young patients:

* Urgent reduction
* Internal fixation with cannulated screws/DHS/FNS depending on fracture pattern

Elderly patients:

* Hemiarthroplasty
* Total hip arthroplasty in selected active patients

Current AO guidance includes cannulated screws, femoral neck system, hemiarthroplasty and total hip arthroplasty according to fracture pattern and patient factors. 

⸻

2. FRACTURES OF TROCHANTERS

Definition

Fractures involving the greater and/or lesser trochanter, commonly including intertrochanteric fractures.

Causes

* Fall in elderly patients
* Direct trauma
* RTA
* Fall from height
* Osteoporosis

Clinical features

* Severe hip pain
* Inability to bear weight
