* Swelling and tenderness over hip
* Shortening of limb
* External rotation
* Painful hip movements
* Bruising around hip/thigh

Complications

* Blood loss
* Malunion with varus deformity
* Non-union
* Limb shortening
* Implant failure
* DVT and pulmonary embolism
* Infection
* Hip stiffness

Conservative management

Used only in selected patients who are unsuitable for surgery.

* Bed rest
* Analgesics
* Traction for selected cases
* Prevention of pressure sores and DVT
* Physiotherapy
* Gradual mobilization with walking aids

Surgical management

Preferred in most medically fit patients.

* Dynamic hip screw (DHS)
* Proximal femoral nail (PFN)
* Cephalomedullary nail
* Dynamic condylar screw in selected patterns
* Trochanteric stabilization plate for selected unstable fractures

AO describes sliding hip screw, trochanteric stabilization and intramedullary nailing among operative options for trochanteric fractures. 

⸻

3. FRACTURE SHAFT OF FEMUR

Definition

Fracture involving the diaphysis of the femur, extending between the lesser trochanter and the distal metaphyseal region.

Mechanism of injury

* High-energy trauma: RTA, fall from height
* Direct blow
* Twisting force
* Pathological fracture
* Low-energy injury in osteoporotic elderly patients

Clinical features

* Severe thigh pain
* Swelling
* Deformity
* Shortening
* Abnormal mobility
* Crepitus
* Inability to bear weight
* Significant blood loss may occur
* Assess distal neurovascular status

Complications

* Hemorrhagic shock
* Fat embolism syndrome
* Compartment syndrome
* Neurovascular injury
* Infection
* Delayed union
* Non-union
* Malunion
* Knee/hip stiffness

Conservative management

Used mainly in selected children or patients unsuitable for surgery.

* Skin/skeletal traction
* Manipulation and reduction
* Functional bracing in selected cases
* Analgesics
* Physiotherapy
* Gradual weight bearing after union

Surgical management

Preferred in most adult femoral shaft fractures.

* Intramedullary interlocking nail: commonly preferred
* ORIF with plate and screws in selected cases
* External fixation for severe open fractures/polytrauma
* Early mobilization and rehabilitation

AO identifies antegrade nailing and bridge plating among established methods for femoral shaft fractures. 

⸻

4. SUPRACONDYLAR FRACTURE OF FEMUR

Definition

Fracture of the distal femur occurring just above the femoral condyles.

Causes

* High-energy RTA
* Fall from height
* Direct trauma
* Osteoporosis in elderly
* Pathological fracture

Clinical features

* Severe knee/thigh pain
* Swelling
* Deformity
* Shortening
* Inability to bear weight
* Restricted knee movement
* Possible open wound
* Neurovascular assessment is essential

Complications

* Popliteal artery injury
* Nerve injury
* Compartment syndrome
* Malunion
* Non-union
* Knee stiffness
* Post-traumatic arthritis
* Infection

Conservative management

For selected undisplaced fractures or patients unsuitable for surgery:

* Above-knee cast/brace
* Traction when indicated
* Analgesia
* Regular X-rays
* Quadriceps exercises
* Gradual knee ROM and weight bearing

Surgical management

* ORIF with locking compression plate
* Retrograde intramedullary nail
* External fixation in selected open/complex injuries
* Bone grafting for selected non-unions

⸻

5. FRACTURES OF THE CONDYLES OF FEMUR

Definition

Fractures involving the medial or lateral femoral condyle, which may extend into the knee joint.

Causes

* High-energy trauma
* Direct blow
* Fall
* Twisting injury
* Osteoporosis

Clinical features

* Knee pain
* Swelling and haemarthrosis
* Tenderness over affected condyle
* Restricted knee movement
* Inability to bear weight
* Deformity in displaced fractures

Complications

* Knee stiffness
* Malunion
* Non-union
* Joint incongruity
* Post-traumatic osteoarthritis
* Neurovascular injury
* Infection

Conservative management

For undisplaced and stable fractures:

* Above-knee immobilization
* Analgesics
* Elevation
* Regular radiographs
* Quadriceps exercises
* Gradual ROM and weight bearing

Surgical management

For displaced/intra-articular fractures:

* Open reduction and internal fixation
* Lag screws
* Buttress/locking plates
* Bone grafting when required
* Early controlled knee movement after stable fixation

⸻

6. FRACTURE PATELLA

Definition

Fracture of the patella, commonly caused by direct trauma or sudden forceful contraction of the quadriceps.

Causes

* Direct fall onto knee
* Direct blow
* RTA
* Sudden forceful quadriceps contraction

Types

* Transverse
* Vertical
* Comminuted
* Marginal
* Osteochondral

Clinical features

* Anterior knee pain
* Swelling and haemarthrosis
* Tenderness
* Bruising
* Inability to extend knee actively in displaced fractures
* Palpable gap between fragments

Complications

* Non-union
* Malunion
* Extensor lag
* Knee stiffness
* Post-traumatic arthritis
* Quadriceps weakness
* Infection after surgery

Conservative management

For undisplaced fractures with intact extensor mechanism:

* Knee immobilizer/above-knee cast
* Knee in extension
* Analgesia
* Quadriceps exercises
* Gradual ROM
* Progressive weight bearing

Surgical management

Indicated for displaced fractures or disruption of the extensor mechanism.

* ORIF with tension-band wiring
* Cannulated screws with tension band
* Plate fixation for comminuted fractures
* Partial patellectomy for selected non-reconstructable inferior/superior pole fragments
* Total patellectomy only in exceptional severely comminuted cases

⸻

7. FRACTURES OF TIBIAL CONDYLES

Definition

Fractures involving the proximal tibial articular surface, also called tibial plateau fractures.

Causes

* RTA
* Fall from height
* Sports injuries
* Valgus/varus stress
* Axial loading
* Osteoporosis

Clinical features

* Severe knee pain
* Swelling
* Haemarthrosis
* Tenderness over tibial plateau
* Inability to bear weight
* Restricted knee movements
* Deformity
* Possible ligament/meniscal injury

Complications

* Compartment syndrome
* Neurovascular injury
* Knee stiffness
* Malunion
* Non-union
* Post-traumatic osteoarthritis
* Ligament instability
* Infection

Conservative management

For undisplaced/minimally displaced stable fractures:

* Knee immobilization/hinged brace
* Ice and elevation
* Analgesics
* Non-weight bearing
* Quadriceps and ankle exercises
* Gradual ROM
* Progressive weight bearing after radiological healing

Surgical management

For displaced, unstable or significantly depressed articular fractures:

* Closed reduction and percutaneous fixation in selected cases
* ORIF with plates and screws
* Elevation of depressed articular surface
* Bone graft/substitute where required
* External fixation for severe soft-tissue injury/high-energy fractures

AO includes ORIF with conventional or locking plate techniques among operative methods for proximal tibial fractures. 

⸻

8. BOTH-BONE FRACTURE OF TIBIA AND FIBULA

Definition

Fracture of both the tibial and fibular shafts, usually caused by significant trauma.

Causes

* RTA
* Direct blow
* Fall from height
* Sports injury
* Twisting injury
* Crush injury

Mechanism

* Direct bending force
* Indirect twisting force
* Combination of bending and rotational forces

Clinical features

* Severe pain
* Swelling
* Deformity and shortening
* Abnormal mobility
* Crepitus
* Inability to bear weight
* Open wound may be present
* Neurovascular deficit may occur

Complications

* Compartment syndrome
* Infection, particularly in open fractures
* Delayed union
* Non-union
* Malunion
* Limb shortening
* Neurovascular injury
* Knee/ankle stiffness
* Chronic osteomyelitis

Conservative management

For selected stable/undisplaced fractures:

* Closed reduction
* Above-knee cast initially
* Below-knee cast after adequate stability/union as appropriate
* Elevation and analgesia
* Regular X-rays
* Non-weight bearing followed by progressive weight bearing
* Physiotherapy

Surgical management

Common indications include displaced/unstable fractures, open fractures, vascular injury, compartment syndrome and failure of conservative treatment.

* Intramedullary interlocking nail for tibia
* ORIF with plate and screws in selected fractures
* External fixation for severe open fractures and major soft-tissue injury
* Bone grafting for selected delayed/non-unions
* Early rehabilitation after stable fixation

⸻

Dupuytren’s Fracture

Important examination correction: Dupuytren’s fracture is not the usual name for a shaft fracture of both tibia and fibula. It traditionally refers to an ankle injury involving a proximal fibular fracture with disruption of the distal tibiofibular syndesmosis and associated medial-sided ankle injury, historically related to Maisonneuve-type injury patterns.

If your university syllabus specifically lists “Both bones fracture of tibia and fibula – Dupuytren’s”, write the above tibia/fibula fracture answer and add:

Dupuytren’s fracture

* Usually produced by external rotation and abduction forces at the ankle.
* Associated with disruption of the distal tibiofibular syndesmosis.
* May be associated with medial malleolar or deltoid ligament injury.
* Clinical features include ankle pain, swelling, tenderness and difficulty bearing weight.
* Management depends on stability; unstable syndesmotic injuries generally require reduction and fixation./////////////////Dislocations of Lower Limb—-

Anterior, Posterior and Central Dislocation of Hip
Mechanism of Injury

* Usually caused by high-energy trauma, especially road-traffic accidents.
* Posterior dislocation: hip flexed and adducted, with a force directed along the femur, classically when the knee strikes the dashboard.
* Anterior dislocation: forced abduction and external rotation of the hip.
* Central dislocation: severe axial force directed through the femoral head, causing it to be driven medially through the acetabulum, usually with an acetabular fracture. 

⸻

1. Anterior Dislocation of Hip

Definition

Displacement of the femoral head anteriorly from the acetabulum.

Mechanism

* Forceful abduction + external rotation.
* May occur with extension or flexion depending on the subtype.
* Commonly occurs in RTA or falls. 

Types

1. Superior/anterior (pubic)
2. Inferior/anterior (obturator)

Clinical Features

* Severe hip pain
* Inability to bear weight
* Limb usually lies in abduction and external rotation
* Superior type: hip is relatively extended
* Inferior type: hip is flexed and abducted
* Femoral head may be palpable anteriorly
* Limb may appear shortened
* Restricted and painful hip movements
* Neurovascular examination is essential. 

Complications

* Femoral nerve/artery/vein injury
* Femoral head fracture
* Acetabular fracture
* Avascular necrosis of femoral head
* Post-traumatic osteoarthritis
* Recurrent instability
* Sciatic nerve injury is less common than in posterior dislocation. 

Management

* Immediate trauma assessment and neurovascular examination
* X-ray to confirm dislocation and identify associated fracture
* Urgent closed reduction under adequate sedation/anesthesia
* Post-reduction X-ray/CT to confirm concentric reduction and identify associated injuries
* Open reduction if irreducible, unstable or associated with fractures requiring fixation. 

⸻

2. Posterior Dislocation of Hip

Definition

Displacement of the femoral head posteriorly from the acetabulum. It is the most common type of traumatic hip dislocation. 

Mechanism

* Hip is flexed, adducted and internally rotated.
* Sudden force is transmitted along the femur.
* Classical example: dashboard injury during an RTA. 

Clinical Features

* Severe hip pain
* Inability to bear weight
* Limb is:
    * Flexed
    * Adducted
    * Internally rotated
    * Shortened
* Prominent greater trochanter
* Femoral head may be palpable posteriorly
* Severe restriction of hip movements
* Assess sciatic nerve function. 

Complications

* Sciatic nerve injury
* Avascular necrosis of femoral head
* Femoral head fracture
* Acetabular fracture
* Post-traumatic osteoarthritis
* Recurrent dislocation
* Chondral injury
* Associated knee injuries. 

Management

Conservative/closed

* Urgent closed reduction under adequate sedation/anesthesia.
* Allis manoeuvre is commonly used for posterior dislocation.
* Reassess neurovascular status after reduction.
* Post-reduction X-ray and usually CT to detect associated fractures or intra-articular fragments.
* Protected weight bearing and rehabilitation according to associated injuries.

Surgical

* Open reduction when:
    * Closed reduction fails
    * Dislocation is irreducible
    * Reduction is non-concentric
    * Associated femoral head/neck or acetabular fracture requires fixation
    * Hip remains unstable after reduction. 

⸻

3. Central Dislocation of Hip

Definition

Central dislocation is a medial displacement of the femoral head through a fractured acetabulum. It is therefore essentially a fracture-dislocation of the acetabulum, rather than a simple dislocation.

Mechanism

* Severe axial loading transmitted through the femoral shaft.
* Fall from height
* RTA
* Direct blow to the greater trochanter
* Force drives the femoral head medially into/through the acetabular floor.

Clinical Features

* Severe hip pain
* Inability to bear weight
* Marked restriction of hip movements
* Swelling around hip
* Limb may appear shortened
* Abnormal position of femoral head may be difficult to appreciate clinically
* Associated pelvic injuries may be present
* Neurovascular assessment is essential.

Complications

* Acetabular fracture
* Pelvic/visceral injury
* Blood loss
* Sciatic nerve injury
* Avascular necrosis
* Post-traumatic osteoarthritis
* Hip stiffness
* Heterotopic ossification
* Malunion/non-union of acetabular fracture

Management

Initial

* ATLS assessment
* Analgesia
* Neurovascular examination
* X-ray pelvis/hip
* CT scan to define acetabular fracture pattern.

Conservative

* Skeletal traction may be used in selected stable, minimally displaced injuries.
* Analgesics
* Non-weight bearing
* Physiotherapy and gradual mobilization.

Surgical

* Indicated for displaced acetabular fractures, incongruent hip joint or instability.
* Open reduction and internal fixation (ORIF) of the acetabulum.
* Associated femoral head/neck fractures are treated appropriately.
* Total hip arthroplasty may be required in selected severe injuries or secondary arthritis. ///////////////////////////Fracture of Cervical Spine ——

Definition

A cervical spine fracture is a break in the continuity of one or more cervical vertebrae, with or without associated ligament injury, dislocation or spinal cord injury. Cervical spine trauma may cause spinal cord compression and neurological deficit, including quadriplegia. 

⸻

Causes

* Road-traffic accidents
* Fall from height
* Diving into shallow water
* Sports injuries
* Direct blow to the head or neck
* Hyperflexion or hyperextension injuries
* Axial loading of the cervical spine
* Crush injuries

⸻

Mechanism of Injury

1. Hyperflexion

* Sudden forward bending of the neck.
* May cause vertebral body compression, flexion-distraction injury or fracture-dislocation.
* Can produce spinal cord injury.

2. Hyperextension

* Sudden backward bending of the neck.
* Common in road-traffic accidents and falls.
* May cause extension injuries and spinal cord compression.

3. Axial compression

* Force transmitted vertically through the head.
* Common in diving accidents and falls onto the head.
* May produce burst-type fractures.

4. Rotation

* Rotational force may produce facet injuries and fracture-dislocations.

5. Combined mechanism

* Flexion, extension, rotation and axial loading may occur together in high-energy trauma.

⸻

Clinical Features

Local features

* Severe neck pain
* Cervical muscle spasm
* Tenderness over cervical spine
* Swelling
* Restricted neck movement
* Deformity or abnormal neck position

Neurological features

Depending on the level and severity of spinal cord injury:

* Weakness or paralysis of limbs
* Loss of sensation
* Tingling/numbness
* Loss of reflexes initially
* Respiratory difficulty
* Bladder and bowel dysfunction

Quadriplegia

Quadriplegia/tetraplegia is paralysis or significant impairment of motor and/or sensory function in the four limbs and trunk due to cervical spinal cord injury.

High cervical injuries may cause:

* Paralysis of all four limbs
* Loss of sensation
* Respiratory muscle paralysis
* Loss of bladder and bowel control
* Autonomic dysfunction

The neurological level and completeness of spinal cord injury should be assessed using the ASIA/ISNCSCI neurological examination. 

⸻

Management of Cervical Spine Fracture

1. Initial Management

A. Immobilization

Until cervical spine injury is excluded, maintain spinal precautions.

* Keep patient supine.
* Maintain manual in-line stabilization during handling and airway procedures.
* Apply a properly fitted rigid cervical collar when indicated.
* Avoid unnecessary neck movements.
* Log-roll the patient while maintaining spinal alignment.
* Assess airway, breathing and circulation.
* Perform repeated neurological examinations.

Rigid cervical immobilization is particularly important when there is neurological deficit or suspected significant cervical injury. 

B. Investigation

* Cervical spine CT scan is commonly used to identify fractures and alignment abnormalities.
* MRI is useful for spinal cord, disc, ligament and soft-tissue abnormalities, particularly when neurological deficit is present. 

⸻

2. Management for Stabilization

Conservative management

Used for stable fractures without significant displacement or neurological compromise.

* Rigid cervical collar
* Cervical orthosis/brace
* Analgesics
* Activity restriction
* Regular radiographs/CT as required
* Physiotherapy after adequate healing

Stable cervical compression fractures may be treated with a cervical collar for several weeks. 

Halo immobilization

* Halo vest may provide rigid external immobilization.
* Used in selected stable or reducible cervical injuries.
* Requires careful monitoring for complications.

Surgical stabilization

Indications:

* Unstable fracture
* Significant displacement or deformity
* Fracture-dislocation
* Progressive neurological deficit
* Spinal cord compression
* Failure of conservative treatment
* Significant ligamentous disruption

Procedures:

* Anterior cervical decompression and fusion
* Posterior cervical fixation and fusion
* Combined anterior and posterior stabilization when required
* Removal of compressive bone/disc fragments when indicated

The choice of surgical approach depends on the fracture pattern, instability, neurological status and site of spinal cord compression. 

⸻

3. Management of Quadriplegia

Immediate management

1. Maintain cervical immobilization and spinal alignment.
2. Maintain a patent airway.
3. Provide oxygen and ventilatory support when required.
4. Monitor respiratory function continuously.
5. Maintain adequate circulation and blood pressure.
6. Perform complete neurological assessment.
7. CT/MRI to identify spinal cord compression.
8. Urgent spine/neurosurgical consultation.
9. Surgical decompression and stabilization when indicated.
10. Prevent secondary complications.

Prevention of complications

* Regular repositioning
* Pressure sore prevention
* Chest physiotherapy
* Assisted coughing and respiratory care
* DVT prophylaxis
* Bladder and bowel management
* Prevention of contractures
* Passive ROM exercises
* Physiotherapy and occupational therapy
* Psychological and social rehabilitation

Patients with cervical spinal cord injury may require prolonged multidisciplinary rehabilitation. 

⸻

4. Clay-Shoveler’s Fracture

Definition

A Clay-shoveler’s fracture is an avulsion fracture of the spinous process, most commonly involving C7, but it may involve C6 to T3. 

Mechanism

* Direct blow to the posterior neck
* Sudden forceful flexion
* Sudden muscular/ligamentous traction on the spinous process
* Sports injuries
* RTA

Clinical features

* Sudden localized neck pain
* Pain between the shoulder blades
* Local tenderness
* Swelling
* Restricted cervical movements
* Usually no neurological deficit

Complications

* Chronic neck pain
* Neck stiffness
* Rare neurological injury
* Non-union may occasionally cause persistent pain

Management

Conservative

* Rest
* Analgesics/NSAIDs
* Hard cervical collar for comfort
* Gradual return to activity
* Physiotherapy after pain subsides

Most isolated clay-shoveler’s fractures are stable injuries and heal with conservative treatment. 

Surgical

* Rarely required.
* Excision of the painful non-united fragment may be considered in persistent symptomatic cases. 

⸻

5. Hangman’s Fracture

Definition

A Hangman’s fracture is a traumatic fracture through the bilateral pars interarticularis/neural arch of C2, often associated with traumatic C2-C3 spondylolisthesis. 

Mechanism

* Hyperextension
* Axial loading
* Often associated with high-energy trauma
* Examples: RTA, fall from height, diving injury

Clinical features

* Severe neck pain
* Neck stiffness
* Tenderness
* Restricted cervical movements
* Possible C2-C3 deformity
* Neurological deficit is relatively uncommon in typical injuries because the spinal canal may become widened. 

Complications

* C2-C3 instability
* Non-union
* Malunion
* Chronic neck pain
* Neurological injury in severe displacement
* Vertebral artery injury
* Post-traumatic deformity

⸻

Classification of Hangman’s Fracture

Levine-Edwards classification

Type I

* Hyperextension and axial compression
* Minimal displacement
* Stable injury

Type II

* Hyperextension and axial loading followed by flexion
* Significant displacement and angulation
* Unstable

Type IIA

* Flexion-distraction injury
* Significant angulation
* Usually little horizontal displacement

Type III

* Type I injury associated with bilateral C2-C3 facet dislocation
* Highly unstable. 

⸻

Management of Hangman’s Fracture

Conservative

For stable/minimally displaced injuries:

* Rigid cervical collar
* Analgesics
* Regular radiological follow-up
* Halo immobilization for selected unstable but reducible injuries
* Gradual mobilization after healing

Type I injuries can commonly be treated with a rigid cervical collar. 

Surgical

Indications:

* Significant displacement
* Severe angulation
* Failure of closed reduction
* C2-C3 facet dislocation
* Severe instability
* Neurological compression
* Failure of conservative treatment

Procedures:

* Posterior C2-C3 fixation and fusion
* Anterior C2-C3 fusion in selected cases
* Combined fixation for complex injuries ///////////////////Fractures of Thoracic and Lumbar Spine —

Definition

A thoracic or lumbar spine fracture is a break in one or more vertebral structures of the thoracic or lumbar spine, with or without associated ligament, spinal cord or nerve-root injury.

Thoracolumbar fractures commonly occur around the T11-L2 region, which represents the transition between the relatively rigid thoracic spine and mobile lumbar spine. 

⸻

1. Mechanism of Injury

Thoracolumbar fractures commonly result from:

1. Flexion-compression

* Sudden forward flexion of the spine.
* Produces compression/wedge fractures.
* Common after falls and road-traffic accidents.

2. Axial compression

* Vertical force transmitted through the spine.
* Produces burst fractures with compression of the vertebral body and possible retropulsion into the spinal canal.

3. Flexion-distraction

* Excessive forward bending with distraction of the posterior elements.
* Produces Chance fracture.
* Classically associated with seat-belt injuries.

4. Hyperextension

* Forced backward bending.
* May produce anterior column injury and extension-type fractures.

5. Rotation/shear

* High-energy rotational or translational forces.
* May produce fracture-dislocation and severe spinal instability.

⸻

2. Common Thoracic and Lumbar Fractures

A. Compression/Wedge Fracture

Definition

Collapse of the anterior portion of the vertebral body, producing a wedge-shaped vertebra.

Causes

* Osteoporosis
* Fall
* RTA
* Axial loading

Clinical features

* Localized back pain
* Tenderness
* Muscle spasm
* Increased pain with movement
* Kyphotic deformity may develop
* Usually no neurological deficit in a simple stable fracture

Management

Conservative

* Analgesics
* Short period of rest
* Thoracolumbosacral orthosis (TLSO) in selected cases
* Early mobilization
* Physiotherapy
* Osteoporosis management where appropriate

Surgical

* Rare in stable fractures.
* Consider vertebral augmentation or fixation in selected patients with persistent severe pain, progressive deformity or instability.

⸻

3. Burst Fracture

Definition

A burst fracture occurs when axial compression causes the vertebral body to fracture in multiple directions, potentially pushing bone fragments into the spinal canal.

Mechanism

* Severe axial loading
* Fall from height landing on feet
* RTA
* Diving injury

Clinical features

* Severe back pain
* Local tenderness
* Muscle spasm
* Restricted spinal movements
* Possible kyphosis
* Neurological deficit may occur due to canal compromise.

Complications

* Spinal cord/conus injury
* Nerve-root compression
* Progressive kyphosis
* Chronic pain
* Neurological deterioration
* Spinal instability

Conservative management

For stable fractures without neurological deficit:

* Analgesics
* TLSO brace in selected patients
* Early mobilization
* Physiotherapy
* Serial radiographs

Surgical management

Indications include:

* Significant instability
* Progressive deformity
* Neurological deficit with compression
* Significant canal compromise in appropriate clinical settings
* Failure of conservative treatment

Procedures:

* Posterior pedicle-screw fixation
* Decompression when indicated
* Vertebral reconstruction/corpectomy in selected severe injuries
* Fusion when instability requires it.

AO describes non-operative treatment for selected stable thoracolumbar injuries and operative stabilization for unstable patterns. (surgeryreference.aofoundation.org￼)

⸻

4. Chance Fracture

Definition

A Chance fracture is a flexion-distraction injury extending horizontally through the vertebral body and posterior elements.

Mechanism

* Sudden flexion-distraction
* Classically caused by a lap seat belt during RTA.

Clinical features

* Severe back pain
* Local tenderness
* Paraspinal muscle spasm
* Possible abdominal bruising/seat-belt sign
* Neurological deficit may occur.

Complications

* Spinal instability
* Kyphotic deformity
* Chronic back pain
* Neurological injury
* Associated abdominal/visceral injury

Management

Conservative

* Selected stable bony injuries with intact posterior ligamentous complex
* TLSO brace
* Analgesia
* Regular radiological follow-up
* Physiotherapy

Surgical

* Indicated for ligamentous disruption, significant displacement, instability, progressive deformity or neurological compromise.
* Posterior pedicle-screw fixation and fusion is commonly used.

⸻

5. Fracture-Dislocation of Thoracolumbar Spine

Mechanism

* High-energy trauma
* Severe flexion, extension, rotation or shear forces
* RTA
* Fall from height

Clinical features

* Severe back pain
* Obvious deformity
* Severe muscle spasm
* Inability to move
* Neurological deficit may be present

Complications

* Spinal cord/conus injury
* Cauda equina syndrome
* Permanent neurological deficit
* Spinal instability
* Deformity
* Chronic pain

Management

Initial

* Full spinal immobilization
* ABC assessment
* Neurological examination
* CT/MRI as indicated

Surgical

* Usually requires reduction and internal fixation with pedicle screws and rods, often with fusion.
* Decompression if neural structures are compressed.
* Postoperative rehabilitation.

These injuries are generally considered unstable and require specialist spinal management. (surgeryreference.aofoundation.org￼)

⸻

6. General Clinical Features of Thoracic and Lumbar Fractures

Local features

* Severe localized back pain
* Vertebral tenderness
* Paraspinal muscle spasm
* Swelling
* Restricted spinal movements
* Kyphotic deformity
* Bruising

Neurological features

Depending on the level and severity:

* Lower-limb weakness/paralysis
* Numbness or paraesthesia
* Altered reflexes
* Sensory loss
* Bladder and bowel dysfunction
* Sexual dysfunction
* Cauda equina/conus symptoms in lower thoracolumbar injuries

Associated injuries

High-energy trauma may be associated with:

* Rib fractures
* Chest injury
* Abdominal injury
* Pelvic fractures
* Long-bone fractures

⸻

7. General Management

A. Initial Management

1. Spinal precautions and immobilization
2. ABC assessment
3. Maintain adequate oxygenation and circulation
4. Neurological examination
5. Analgesia
6. CT scan for bony injury
7. MRI when neurological deficit, ligamentous injury or spinal cord compression is suspected.

⸻

B. Conservative Management

Indicated mainly for stable fractures without neurological deficit.

* Bed rest only for a short period when necessary
* Analgesics
* TLSO brace where appropriate
* Early mobilization
* Physiotherapy
* Back and abdominal muscle strengthening
* Gradual return to activities
* Regular radiological follow-up

Prolonged bed rest should generally be avoided because it increases complications such as DVT, pressure sores and deconditioning.

⸻

C. Surgical Management

Indications

* Unstable fracture
* Progressive kyphosis
* Significant displacement
* Neurological deficit due to compression
* Spinal cord/conus/cauda equina compression
* Disruption of posterior ligamentous complex
* Fracture-dislocation
* Failure of conservative treatment

Procedures

* Posterior pedicle-screw fixation
* Posterior spinal fusion
* Decompression/laminectomy when indicated
* Anterior decompression and fusion in selected cases
* Combined anterior and posterior fixation for severe injuries

⸻

8. Fracture of Coccyx

Definition

A coccygeal fracture is a break in one or more segments of the coccyx, usually caused by a direct fall onto the buttocks.

Causes

* Fall directly on the buttocks
* Fall from height
* Direct blow
* Childbirth
* Occasionally repetitive trauma

Mechanism

* Direct axial force on the coccyx
* Sudden backward bending of the coccyx
* Direct impact while sitting/falling.

Clinical Features

* Pain over coccyx (coccydynia)
* Local tenderness
* Pain while sitting
* Pain during rising from a chair
* Pain during defecation
* Pain during prolonged sitting
* Bruising/swelling may be present
* Pain on direct palpation

Complications

* Chronic coccydynia
* Non-union
* Malunion
* Painful sitting
* Difficulty with defecation
* Rare rectal injury

⸻

Conservative Management

Most coccygeal fractures are treated conservatively.

1. Analgesics/NSAIDs
2. Avoid prolonged sitting.
3. Use a coccygeal cushion or wedge cushion.
4. Sit leaning slightly forward to reduce pressure on the coccyx.
5. Ice during the acute phase.
6. Stool softeners if painful defecation is present.
7. Gradual return to normal activity.
8. Physiotherapy for persistent symptoms.

Surgical Management

Surgery is rarely required.

* Considered for severe persistent pain despite prolonged conservative treatment.
* Coccygectomy may be performed in carefully selected patients with chronic refractory coccydynia.////////////////////FRACTURE OF RIB CAGE —

Definition

A fracture of the rib cage is a break in the continuity of one or more ribs or the sternum, usually caused by direct or indirect trauma. Severe chest trauma may be associated with pneumothorax, haemothorax, pulmonary contusion or flail chest.

⸻

1. FRACTURE OF RIBS

Mechanism of Injury

* Direct trauma: A blow to the chest causes the rib to bend and fracture at the site of impact.
* Indirect trauma: Compression of the chest from the sides may fracture ribs at their point of maximum curvature.
* RTA
* Fall
* Sports injury
* Crush injury
* Severe coughing may rarely cause stress fractures.

Clinical Features

* Severe localized chest pain
* Pain aggravated by:
    * Deep inspiration
    * Coughing
    * Sneezing
    * Movement
* Local tenderness over the fractured rib
* Swelling and bruising
* Painful and shallow breathing
* Crepitus may be present
* Reduced chest expansion on the affected side
* Respiratory distress in severe injuries

Complications

* Pneumothorax
* Haemothorax
* Pulmonary contusion
* Pneumonia
* Atelectasis
* Respiratory failure
* Flail chest
* Injury to underlying organs

Management

Conservative

* Assess airway, breathing and circulation.
* Analgesics, including multimodal analgesia when required.
* Ice application during the acute phase.
* Encourage deep breathing and coughing exercises.
* Incentive spirometry where appropriate.
* Chest physiotherapy.
* Early mobilization.
* Treat associated pneumothorax/haemothorax if present.

Important: Routine tight chest binding is avoided because it restricts ventilation and may increase pulmonary complications.

Surgical

Usually not required for uncomplicated rib fractures.

Indications may include:

* Severe chest wall instability
* Flail chest in selected patients
* Multiple severely displaced fractures
* Persistent respiratory compromise
* Failure of conservative treatment

Surgical stabilization of rib fractures (SSRF) may be performed using plates and screws in selected patients.

⸻

2. FRACTURE OF STERNUM

Definition

A fracture of the sternum is a break in the continuity of the breastbone, commonly occurring after high-energy blunt trauma.

Mechanism of Injury

* Direct blow to anterior chest
* RTA, particularly impact against steering wheel or restraint system
* Fall onto the chest
* Compression injury
* Severe chest trauma

Clinical Features

* Severe anterior chest pain
* Localized tenderness
* Swelling and bruising
* Pain on deep inspiration
* Pain on coughing
* Crepitus or palpable deformity
* Reduced chest movement
* Associated respiratory distress if there are intrathoracic injuries

Complications

* Myocardial injury
* Arrhythmias
* Pulmonary contusion
* Pneumothorax
* Haemothorax
* Rib fractures
* Rare vascular injury
* Respiratory complications

Because sternal fractures can indicate significant blunt chest trauma, associated cardiac and thoracic injuries must be assessed.

Management

Conservative

For uncomplicated, stable fractures:

* Analgesics
* Ice application
* Rest initially
* Deep-breathing exercises
* Coughing exercises
* Chest physiotherapy
* Early mobilization
* Monitor for associated cardiopulmonary injury

Surgical

Rarely required.

Indications:

* Severe displacement
* Unstable fracture
* Persistent severe pain
* Non-union
* Associated chest-wall instability
* Failure of conservative treatment

ORIF with plates and screws may be performed when surgical stabilization is indicated.

⸻

3. FRACTURE OF PELVIS

Definition

A pelvic fracture is a break in one or more bones forming the pelvic ring, including the ilium, ischium, pubis or sacrum. Pelvic fractures range from stable injuries to life-threatening unstable pelvic-ring injuries.

Mechanism of Injury

1. High-energy trauma

* RTA
* Fall from height
* Crush injury
* Industrial accidents

2. Low-energy trauma

* Falls in elderly osteoporotic patients

Mechanisms of pelvic-ring injury

* AP compression: pelvis opens like a book.
* Lateral compression: inward compression of the pelvic ring.
* Vertical shear: upward displacement of one side of the pelvis.
* Combined mechanisms may occur.

⸻

Clinical Features

Local

* Severe pelvic/hip pain
* Inability to stand or walk
* Pelvic tenderness
* Swelling and bruising
* Limb-length discrepancy
* Pelvic deformity
* Pain on movement

Associated features

* Shock due to major blood loss
* Abdominal injury
* Urethral/bladder injury
* Rectal injury
* Nerve injury
* Lower-limb vascular injury

Complications

* Massive haemorrhage and hypovolaemic shock
* Pelvic organ injury
* Bladder/urethral injury
* Rectal injury
* Neurovascular injury
* DVT and pulmonary embolism
* Infection
* Malunion
* Chronic pelvic pain
* Gait abnormality
* Sexual dysfunction

⸻

Management of Pelvic Fracture

A. Initial Management

Pelvic fractures are managed initially according to trauma principles.

1. Airway and breathing assessment
2. Circulation assessment
3. Control external haemorrhage
4. Avoid repeated manipulation of the pelvis.
5. Apply a pelvic binder when an unstable pelvic-ring injury with suspected haemorrhage is present.
6. Establish IV access.
7. Fluid and blood-product resuscitation as required.
8. Assess for abdominal, urinary, neurological and vascular injuries.
9. Imaging with X-ray/CT according to the patient’s condition.

A pelvic binder is used as an early temporary measure for suspected unstable pelvic-ring injury and should be positioned appropriately around the greater trochanters.

⸻

B. Conservative Management

Used mainly for stable, minimally displaced pelvic fractures.

* Bed rest initially when required
* Analgesics
* Pelvic support where appropriate
* DVT prophylaxis
* Early mobilization
* Walking aids
* Physiotherapy
* Progressive weight bearing
* Regular radiological follow-up

⸻

C. Surgical Management

Indications

* Unstable pelvic-ring fracture
* Significant displacement
* Open pelvic fracture
* Persistent haemodynamic instability
* Failure of conservative management
* Associated organ/vascular injury

Methods

* External fixation
* Pelvic packing for uncontrolled pelvic haemorrhage in appropriate settings
* Angioembolization for arterial bleeding
* ORIF with plates and screws
* Percutaneous screw fixation in selected fractures ////////////////INFLAMMATION AND REPAIR —-

Introduction to Soft-Tissue Healing

Definition of Inflammation

Inflammation is a protective response of living vascularized tissue to injury, infection or irritation, which removes the injurious stimulus and initiates the process of healing and repair.

⸻

1. Causes of Inflammation

* Trauma and mechanical injury
* Burns
* Infection
* Chemical irritants
* Foreign bodies
* Tissue necrosis
* Ischaemia
* Immune reactions

⸻

2. Types of Inflammation

A. Acute inflammation

* Rapid onset
* Usually lasts for a short duration
* Predominantly involves neutrophils
* Characterized by vascular changes, exudation of fluid and inflammatory cells.

B. Chronic inflammation

* Develops gradually or persists for a longer duration
* Predominantly involves lymphocytes, macrophages and plasma cells
* Associated with tissue destruction and fibrosis.

⸻

3. Cardinal Signs of Inflammation

1. Rubor – redness
2. Calor – heat
3. Tumor – swelling
4. Dolor – pain
5. Functio laesa – loss of function

⸻

4. Basic Process of Inflammation

Vascular response

* Brief vasoconstriction
* Vasodilation
* Increased blood flow
* Increased vascular permeability
* Formation of inflammatory exudate
* Stasis of blood flow

Cellular response

* Margination of leukocytes
* Rolling
* Adhesion
* Transmigration/diapedesis
* Chemotaxis
* Phagocytosis
* Destruction/removal of microorganisms and damaged tissue

⸻

5. Definition of Repair

Repair is the restoration of tissue continuity following injury by replacement of damaged tissue with new tissue.

Repair occurs through two major processes:

1. Regeneration
2. Scar formation

Regeneration

Replacement of damaged cells by cells of the same type, restoring normal tissue structure and function.

Scar formation

Replacement of damaged tissue by connective tissue, resulting in fibrosis and scar formation.

⸻

6. Soft-Tissue Healing

Soft-tissue healing is the process by which injured skin, muscle, tendon, ligament and other soft tissues restore their structural integrity and function following injury.

Healing occurs through overlapping phases.

Phase 1: Haemostasis

Immediately after injury

* Vasoconstriction
* Platelet aggregation
* Formation of blood clot
* Fibrin clot formation
* Provides temporary wound stability
* Releases growth factors that initiate healing

⸻

Phase 2: Inflammatory Phase

Approximately first few days

* Vasodilation and increased vascular permeability
* Neutrophils migrate to the wound
* Macrophages subsequently predominate
* Removal of bacteria, dead cells and debris
* Release of cytokines and growth factors
* Prepares the wound for tissue formation

⸻

Phase 3: Proliferative Phase

Usually begins within a few days and continues for several weeks.

Main events

* Fibroblast proliferation
* Collagen synthesis
* Formation of granulation tissue
* Angiogenesis
* Re-epithelialization
* Wound contraction

Initially, the wound contains predominantly type III collagen.

⸻

Phase 4: Remodeling/Maturation

Begins after the proliferative phase and may continue for months to years.

* Collagen is reorganized
* Type III collagen is gradually replaced by stronger type I collagen
* Collagen cross-linking increases
* Vascularity decreases
* Scar becomes paler and flatter
* Tensile strength progressively increases but does not normally return completely to that of uninjured tissue.

The inflammatory, proliferative and remodeling phases overlap rather than occurring as completely separate stages.

⸻

7. Factors Affecting Soft-Tissue Healing

Local factors

* Poor blood supply
* Infection
* Tissue damage
* Foreign body
* Excessive tension
* Repeated trauma
* Haematoma
* Excessive movement

Systemic factors

* Age
* Poor nutrition
* Diabetes mellitus
* Smoking
* Anaemia
* Immunosuppression
* Certain medications, particularly corticosteroids

⸻

8. Types of Wound Healing

Primary intention

* Wound edges are closely approximated.
* Minimal tissue loss.
* Less granulation tissue.
* Small scar.
* Example: clean surgical incision.

Secondary intention

* Wound edges cannot be approximated.
* Greater tissue loss.
* Extensive granulation tissue.
* More wound contraction.
* Larger scar.

Tertiary intention

* Wound is initially left open because of contamination/infection and is closed later after the wound is adequately clean./////////////1. Sprain

Definition: Injury to a ligament caused by excessive stretching or tearing, usually due to sudden twisting or abnormal joint movement.

Features: Pain, swelling, tenderness and joint instability.

2. Strain

Definition: Injury to a muscle or tendon caused by overstretching or excessive force.

Features: Pain, muscle spasm, weakness and swelling.

3. Contusion

Definition: Injury to soft tissue caused by a direct blunt blow, producing damage to underlying tissues without breaking the skin. 
/////2. Meniscal Injuries of Knee

Mechanism

* Twisting of a weight-bearing knee
* Sudden change of direction
* Deep squatting
* Direct trauma
* Degenerative injury in older individuals

Clinical Features

* Joint-line pain and tenderness
* Swelling, often developing after activity
* Locking or catching
* Clicking
* Restricted knee movement
* Pain on squatting
* Positive McMurray test and/or Apley compression test

⸻

3. Cruciate Ligament Injuries of Knee

Mechanism

ACL injury

* Sudden deceleration
* Pivoting/change of direction
* Hyperextension
* Valgus force with rotation

PCL injury

* Dashboard injury
* Fall onto a flexed knee
* Hyperflexion
* Posteriorly directed force on the tibia

Clinical Features

* Pain and swelling
* Acute haemarthrosis, particularly with ACL injury
* Feeling of instability or giving way
* Restricted ROM
* ACL: Positive Lachman and anterior drawer tests
* PCL: Positive posterior drawer test and posterior sag sign

⸻

4. Medial and Lateral Collateral Ligament Injuries

Mechanism

MCL

* Valgus stress applied to the knee
* Commonly associated with contact sports

LCL

* Varus stress applied to the knee
* May occur with high-energy trauma

Clinical Features

* Pain and tenderness over the injured ligament
* Local swelling
* Pain on stress testing
* Medial instability with valgus stress in MCL injury
* Lateral instability with varus stress in LCL injury
* Difficulty in weight bearing

⸻

5. Lateral Ligament Injury of Ankle

Mechanism

Most commonly caused by inversion injury of a plantar-flexed ankle.

Commonly injured ligaments:

* Anterior talofibular ligament (ATFL)
* Calcaneofibular ligament (CFL)
* Posterior talofibular ligament (PTFL)

Clinical Features

* Pain around lateral ankle
* Swelling
* Bruising
* Tenderness over lateral ligaments
* Difficulty in weight bearing
* Reduced ankle ROM
* Instability in severe injury
* Positive anterior drawer/talar tilt tests when appropriate

⸻

6. Wrist Sprain

Mechanism

* Fall on an outstretched hand (FOOSH)
* Sudden hyperextension or hyperflexion
* Twisting injury
* Direct trauma

Clinical Features

* Wrist pain
* Swelling
* Tenderness
* Painful and restricted wrist movement
* Reduced grip strength
* Bruising
* Pain during loading of the wrist/////Strains, Contusions and Tendon Ruptures—-

1. Strains

Definition: A strain is an injury involving a muscle or musculotendinous unit, caused by excessive stretching or forceful contraction.

A. Quadriceps strain

Mechanism: Sudden forceful contraction, sprinting, kicking or jumping.
Clinical features:

* Anterior thigh pain
* Tenderness
* Swelling/bruising
* Pain on resisted knee extension
* Weakness of quadriceps

B. Hamstring strain

Mechanism: Sudden sprinting, acceleration or excessive hip flexion with knee extension.
Clinical features:

* Posterior thigh pain
* Tenderness
* Bruising/swelling
* Pain on resisted knee flexion
* Reduced running ability

C. Calf strain

Mechanism: Sudden push-off, jumping or running.
Clinical features:

* Calf pain
* Tenderness
* Swelling
* Pain on resisted plantar flexion
* Difficulty walking

D. Biceps strain

Mechanism: Sudden forceful elbow flexion or lifting.
Clinical features:

* Anterior arm pain
* Tenderness
* Pain on resisted elbow flexion/supination
* Weakness

E. Triceps strain

Mechanism: Forceful elbow extension or throwing activity.
Clinical features:

* Posterior arm pain
* Tenderness
* Pain on resisted elbow extension
* Weakness and swelling

⸻

2. Contusions

Definition: A contusion is a blunt-trauma injury causing damage to muscle and small blood vessels without disruption of the skin.

A. Quadriceps contusion

* Usually caused by direct blow to the thigh.
* Pain, swelling and bruising
* Reduced knee flexion
* Muscle stiffness
* Severe cases may develop myositis ossificans

B. Gluteal contusion

* Direct fall or blow to buttock.
* Pain and tenderness
* Swelling and bruising
* Pain while sitting or walking

C. Calf contusion

* Direct blow to calf.
* Pain and swelling
* Bruising
* Tenderness
* Painful walking and plantar flexion

D. Deltoid contusion

* Direct blow to shoulder.
* Shoulder pain and tenderness
* Swelling/bruising
* Painful shoulder movement
* Reduced abduction

General management: Protection/rest initially, ice, compression and elevation where appropriate, followed by gradual ROM and strengthening.

⸻

3. Tendon Ruptures

A. Achilles Tendon Rupture

Mechanism

* Sudden forceful plantar flexion
* Jumping or sprinting
* Sudden eccentric loading of calf muscles

Clinical features

* Sudden severe pain in posterior ankle
* Feeling of being kicked in the calf
* Difficulty walking
* Weak/absent plantar flexion
* Palpable gap above calcaneus
* Positive Thompson test

Management

* Immobilization in plantar flexion for selected patients
* Functional rehabilitation
* Surgical tendon repair in selected active patients, complete ruptures and appropriate cases.

⸻

B. Rotator Cuff Tendon Rupture

Mechanism

* Fall on an outstretched arm
* Forceful shoulder movement
* Repetitive overhead activity
* Degenerative tendon changes

Clinical features

* Shoulder pain
* Painful arc
* Weakness of shoulder elevation
* Difficulty with overhead activities
* Night pain
* Positive rotator-cuff tests

Management

* Rest/activity modification
* Analgesics
* Physiotherapy: ROM and progressive rotator-cuff/scapular strengthening
* Surgical repair for selected acute traumatic tears, significant weakness or failure of conservative treatment.//////////////////AMPUTATIONS

Definition and Levels of Amputation
—
Definition

Amputation is the partial or complete removal of a limb or part of a limb through a surgical procedure or as a result of trauma.

The main aims of amputation are to remove non-viable or diseased tissue, control infection or pain, and create a functional residual limb suitable for rehabilitation and prosthetic fitting.

⸻

1. Levels of Upper-Limb Amputation

A. Finger and Hand

1. Distal phalanx amputation
2. Middle phalanx amputation
3. Proximal phalanx amputation
4. Metacarpal amputation
5. Ray amputation – removal of a digit with its corresponding metacarpal.
6. Transmetacarpal amputation – through the metacarpals.

B. Wrist and Forearm

7. Wrist disarticulation – separation through the wrist joint.
8. Transradial amputation – through the forearm, below the elbow.

C. Elbow and Arm

9. Elbow disarticulation – through the elbow joint.
10. Transhumeral amputation – through the arm, above the elbow.

D. Shoulder

11. Shoulder disarticulation – removal of the upper limb through the shoulder joint.
12. Forequarter amputation – removal of the upper limb together with part of the shoulder girdle.

⸻

2. Levels of Lower-Limb Amputation

A. Foot and Ankle

1. Toe amputation
2. Ray amputation
3. Transmetatarsal amputation
4. Lisfranc amputation – through the tarsometatarsal joints.
5. Chopart amputation – through the transverse tarsal joint.
6. Syme’s amputation – ankle disarticulation with preservation of the heel pad.

B. Leg

7. Transtibial amputation – through the tibia and fibula below the knee.

C. Knee

8. Knee disarticulation – amputation through the knee joint.

D. Thigh and Hip

9. Transfemoral amputation – through the femur above the knee.
10. Hip disarticulation – removal of the limb through the hip joint.
11. Hemipelvectomy – removal of the lower limb with part of the pelvis.

⸻

3. Indications for Amputation

* Severe traumatic injury
* Peripheral vascular disease with irreversible tissue loss
* Uncontrolled infection/gangrene
* Malignant tumour
* Severe congenital deformity
* Non-functional painful limb
* Severe burns or crush injury
* Irreversible ischemia

⸻

4. Principles of Selecting the Level

The level should be selected to:

* Remove all non-viable or diseased tissue.
* Preserve maximum useful limb length.
* Preserve viable skin and soft-tissue coverage.
* Maintain adequate blood supply.
* Preserve important joints whenever possible.
* Produce a stable, painless and functional residual limb.
* Allow effective prosthetic fitting./////////////////////Traumatic Spinal Cord Injuries—

Definition

Traumatic spinal cord injury (SCI) is an acute injury to the spinal cord caused by an external mechanical force, resulting in temporary or permanent impairment of motor, sensory and autonomic functions below the level of injury. 

⸻

Causes

* Road-traffic accidents
* Falls from height
* Sports injuries, especially diving
* Direct blow to the spine
* Gunshot or penetrating injuries
* Crush injuries
* Hyperflexion or hyperextension injuries
* Fracture-dislocation of the vertebral column

⸻

Clinical Features

Clinical presentation depends mainly on the level, severity and completeness of spinal cord injury.

1. Motor disturbances

* Muscle weakness or paralysis below the level of injury
* Paraplegia: paralysis of both lower limbs
* Quadriplegia/tetraplegia: paralysis of all four limbs following cervical cord injury
* Loss of voluntary movements
* Muscle weakness may be flaccid initially because of spinal shock
* Later, spasticity and hyperreflexia may develop in upper motor neuron lesions

⸻

2. Sensory disturbances

* Loss or reduction of sensation below the level of injury
* Loss of:
    * Pain
    * Temperature
    * Touch
    * Pressure
    * Vibration
    * Proprioception
* Paraesthesia or numbness
* A clearly defined sensory level may be present.

⸻

3. Reflex changes

Spinal shock

Immediately after a significant acute SCI:

* Flaccid paralysis
* Loss of deep tendon reflexes
* Loss of superficial reflexes
* Absent bulbocavernosus reflex may occur
* Areflexia below the level of injury

As spinal shock resolves, reflexes may return and become exaggerated in upper motor neuron injuries. 

⸻

4. Autonomic disturbances

Bladder dysfunction

* Urinary retention
* Urinary incontinence
* Neurogenic bladder

Bowel dysfunction

* Constipation
* Faecal incontinence
* Neurogenic bowel

Sexual dysfunction

* Erectile/ejaculatory dysfunction
* Altered sexual sensation

Other autonomic abnormalities may include impaired sweating and temperature regulation. 

⸻

5. Respiratory Features

Respiratory impairment depends on the level of injury.

* Difficulty in deep inspiration
* Weak cough
* Retained respiratory secretions
* Reduced vital capacity
* Respiratory muscle paralysis
* Respiratory failure in high cervical injuries

Injury involving C3–C5 can compromise diaphragmatic function because the phrenic nerve arises from these cervical segments. 

⸻

6. Cardiovascular Features

Particularly with cervical and high thoracic injuries:

* Hypotension
* Bradycardia
* Peripheral vasodilation
* Neurogenic shock
* Cardiac rhythm disturbances

Neurogenic shock results from loss of sympathetic outflow and is particularly associated with injuries above approximately T6. 

⸻

7. Clinical Patterns of Incomplete SCI

A. Central Cord Syndrome

* Usually follows cervical hyperextension injury.
* Upper limbs are affected more than lower limbs.
* Hand weakness may be prominent.
* Sensory disturbance may occur.

B. Brown-Séquard Syndrome

Due to hemisection of the spinal cord:

* Ipsilateral motor weakness
* Ipsilateral loss of proprioception/vibration
* Contralateral loss of pain and temperature

C. Anterior Cord Syndrome

* Motor paralysis below the lesion
* Loss of pain and temperature
* Relative preservation of dorsal-column functions such as vibration and proprioception. 

⸻

8. Complete and Incomplete Injury

Complete SCI

* No sensory or motor function is preserved in the sacral segments S4–S5.
* No sacral sparing.
* Classified as AIS/ASIA Grade A. 

Incomplete SCI

* Some sensory and/or motor function is preserved below the neurological level, including sacral function.
* Classified as AIS B–D depending on the amount of preserved function.
* AIS E: normal motor and sensory examination. 

⸻

9. Clinical Examination

Assessment should include:

* Level of neurological injury
* Motor power
* Sensory examination
* Deep tendon reflexes
* Anal sensation and voluntary anal contraction
* Muscle tone
* Respiratory function
* Bladder and bowel function
* Autonomic function

The International Standards for Neurological Classification of Spinal Cord Injury (ISNCSCI/ASIA examination) is used to determine the neurological level and severity of injury. 

⸻

10. Important Complications

* Respiratory failure
* Neurogenic shock
* Spinal shock
* Pressure sores
* Deep-vein thrombosis and pulmonary embolism
* Urinary tract infection
* Neurogenic bladder and bowel
* Contractures
* Spasticity
* Autonomic dysreflexia
* Chronic pain
* Permanent paralysis/////////////////

injuries /////////////////////// **Dislocations of the Upper Limb** **Definition** Dislocation is the complete loss of normal articular contact between the articular surfaces of a joint due to trauma or other causes The shoulder is the most commonly dislocated major joint with anterior dislocation being the most common type --- **1 Shoulder Dislocation** **Mechanism of injury** • Anterior dislocation Fall on an outstretched arm or forceful combination of abduction extension and external rotation • Posterior dislocation Direct blow to the anterior shoulder with the arm adducted and internally rotated • Violent muscle contraction such as during seizures or electrical injury may cause posterior dislocation --- **A Anterior dislocation of shoulder** **Clinical features** • Severe pain following trauma • Patient supports the affected arm • Arm held in abduction and external rotation • Loss of normal rounded contour of shoulder • Prominent acromion producing a squared off shoulder • Humeral head may be palpable anteriorly • Complete restriction of active and passive movements • Check axillary nerve and distal vascular status **Complications** • Axillary nerve injury • Axillary artery injury • Greater tuberosity fracture • Hill Sachs lesion • Bankart lesion • Rotator cuff injury • Recurrent dislocation • Joint stiffness Axillary nerve injury is particularly important and should be assessed before and after reduction --- **B Posterior dislocation of shoulder** **Clinical features** • Severe shoulder pain • Arm held in adduction and internal rotation • Inability to externally rotate the arm • Flattening of the anterior shoulder • Prominent posterior humeral head may be palpable • Restricted shoulder movements **Complications** • Reverse Hill Sachs lesion • Fracture of surgical neck or tuberosity • Neurovascular injury • Rotator cuff injury • Recurrent instability • Osteoarthritis Posterior dislocation is uncommon and may be missed clinically particularly when the patient presents with a guarded internally rotated arm --- **Conservative Management of Shoulder Dislocation** **1 Reduction** The dislocation is reduced by closed manipulation preferably with adequate analgesia/sedation and muscle relaxation **Kochers manoeuvre** 1 Patient supine 2 Arm adducted to the side 3 Elbow flexed to 90 4 Slowly externally rotate the arm until resistance is felt 5 Elevate/flex the arm while maintaining external rotation 6 Adduct the arm 7 Internally rotate the shoulder to complete reduction Note Forceful Kocher manoeuvre should be avoided because it can cause fractures and soft tissue injury **Hippocrates manoeuvre** 1 Patient lies supine 2 The affected arm is gently grasped 3 Axillary counter traction is applied 4 Longitudinal traction is applied to the limb 5 Gentle manipulation is continued until the humeral head returns to the glenoid The classical Hippocratic technique is now generally not preferred because of the risk of brachial plexus and vascular injury **After reduction** • Confirm reduction clinically and radiologically • Reassess neurovascular status • Apply sling/immobilizer • Analgesics • Gradual ROM exercises • Physiotherapy for rotator cuff and scapular muscle strengthening --- **Surgical Management** **Indications** • Irreducible dislocation • Recurrent dislocation • Associated fracture • Significant bone loss • Persistent instability • Major labral injury • Failed conservative treatment **Important operations** **1 Bankart repair** • Repair of the detached anteroinferior glenoid labrum and capsule • May be performed arthroscopically or by open technique • Common procedure for recurrent anterior instability **2 Putti Platt operation** • A historical/non anatomic stabilization procedure • Involves shortening and tightening the subscapularis and anterior capsule • Reduces external rotation and therefore limits instability • It has largely been replaced by anatomic Bankart repair in modern practice **3 Latarjet procedure** • Coracoid transfer to the anterior glenoid • Used particularly when there is significant glenoid bone loss or recurrent instability --- **2 Recurrent Dislocation of Shoulder** **Definition** Repeated episodes of shoulder dislocation or subluxation following an initial traumatic dislocation **Causes** • Inadequate healing of capsule/labrum external rotation • Pain and instability • Reduced confidence in shoulder movements • Positive apprehension test **Management** **Conservative** • Activity modification • Shoulder immobilization when procedure • Remplissage or other bone/soft tissue procedures depending on associated lesions Recurrent instability is particularly common in young active patients after traumatic anterior dislocation --- **3 Dislocation of Elbow** **Mechanism of injury** • Commonly due to fall on an outstretched hand • Hyperextension and valgus/varus forces • Sports injuries • Road traffic accidents **Clinical deformity/intrinsic plus position • Wrist approximately 20 30 extension • MCP joints 70 90 flexion • IP joints extension • Thumb abducted 6 Early supervised ROM when safe 7 Scar management and and adducted with a force directed along the femur classically when the knee strikes the dashboard • Anterior dislocation forced abduction and external rotation of the hip • Central dislocation severe axial force directed through the femoral head causing it to be driven medially through the acetabulum usually with an acetabular fracture --- **1 Anterior Dislocation of Hip** **Definition** RTA or falls **Types** 1 Superior/anterior pubic 2 Inferior/anterior obturator **Clinical Features** • Severe hip pain • Inability to bear weight • Limb usually lies in abduction and external rotation • Superior type hip is relatively extended • Inferior type hip is flexed and abducted • Femoral head may be palpable anteriorly • Limb may appear shortened • Restricted and painful hip movements • Neurovascular examination is essential **Complications** • Femoral nerve/artery/vein injury • Femoral head fracture • Acetabular fracture • Avascular necrosis of femoral head • Post traumatic acetabulum It is the most common type of traumatic hip dislocation **Mechanism** • Hip is flexed adducted and internally rotated • Sudden force is transmitted along the femur • Classical example dashboard injury during an RTA **Clinical Features** • Severe hip pain • Inability to bear weight • Limb is • Flexed • Adducted • Internally rotated • Shortened • Prominent greater trochanter • Femoral head may be palpable posteriorly • Severe restriction of hip movements • Assess sciatic nerve function **Complications** • Sciatic nerve injury • Avascular necrosis of femoral head • Femoral head fracture • Acetabular fracture • Post traumatic osteoarthritis • Recurrent dislocation • Chondral injury • Associated knee injuries **Management** **Conservative/closed** • Urgent closed Dislocation is irreducible • Reduction is non concentric • Associated femoral head/neck or acetabular fracture requires fixation • Hip remains unstable after reduction --- **3 Central Dislocation of Hip** **Definition** Central dislocation is a medial displacement of the femoral head through a fractured acetabulum It is therefore essentially a fracture dislocation of the acetabulum rather than a simple dislocation **Mechanism** • Severe axial loading transmitted through the femoral shaft • Fall from height • RTA • Direct blow to the greater trochanter • Force drives the femoral head medially into/through the acetabular floor **Clinical Features** • Severe hip pain • Inability to bear weight • Marked restriction of hip movements • Swelling around hip • Limb may appear shortened • Abnormal **Management** **Initial** • ATLS assessment • Analgesia • Neurovascular examination • X ray pelvis/hip • CT scan to define acetabular fracture pattern **Conservative** • Skeletal traction may be used in selected stable minimally displaced injuries • Analgesics • Non weight bearing • Physiotherapy and gradual mobilization **Surgical** • Indicated for displaced acetabular fractures incongruent hip joint or instability • Open reduction and internal fixation ORIF of the acetabulum • Associated femoral head/neck fractures are treated appropriately • Total hip arthroplasty may be required in selected severe injuries or secondary arthritis /////////////////////////// **Fracture of Cervical Spine** **Definition** A cervical spine fracture is a break in the continuity of one or more cervical vertebrae with or without associated ligament injury dislocation or spinal cord injury Cervical spine trauma may cause spinal cord compression and neurological deficit including quadriplegia --- **Causes** • Road traffic accidents • Fall from height • Diving into shallow water • Sports injuries • Direct blow to the head or neck • Hyperflexion or hyperextension injuries • Axial loading of the cervical spine • Crush injuries --- **Mechanism of Injury** 1 Hyperflexion • Sudden forward bending of the neck • May cause vertebral body compression flexion distraction injury or fracture dislocation • Can produce spinal cord injury 2 Hyperextension • Sudden backward bending of the neck • Common in road traffic accidents and falls • May cause extension injuries and spinal cord compression 3 Axial compression • Force transmitted vertically through the head • Common in diving accidents and falls onto the head • May produce burst type fractures 4 Rotation • Rotational force may produce facet injuries and fracture dislocations 5 Combined mechanism • Flexion extension rotation and axial loading may occur together in high energy trauma --- **Clinical Features** **Local features** • Severe neck pain • Cervical muscle spasm • Tenderness over cervical spine • Swelling • Restricted neck movement • Deformity or abnormal neck position **Neurological features** Depending on the level and severity of spinal cord injury • Weakness or paralysis of limbs • Loss of sensation • Tingling/numbness • Loss of reflexes initially • Respiratory difficulty • Bladder and bowel dysfunction **Quadriplegia** Quadriplegia/tetraplegia is paralysis or significant impairment of motor and/or sensory function in the four limbs and trunk due to cervical spinal cord injury High cervical injuries may cause • Paralysis of all four limbs • Loss of sensation • Respiratory muscle paralysis • Loss of bladder and bowel control • Autonomic dysfunction The neurological level and completeness of spinal cord injury should be assessed using the ASIA/ISNCSCI neurological examination --- **Management of Cervical Spine Fracture** **1 Initial Management** **A Immobilization** Until cervical spine injury is excluded maintain spinal precautions • Keep patient supine • Maintain manual in line stabilization during handling and airway procedures • Apply a properly fitted rigid cervical collar when indicated • Avoid unnecessary neck movements • Log roll the patient while maintaining spinal alignment • Assess airway breathing and circulation • Perform repeated neurological examinations Rigid cervical immobilization is particularly important when there is neurological deficit or suspected significant cervical injury **B Investigation** • Cervical spine CT scan is commonly used to identify fractures and alignment abnormalities • MRI is useful for spinal cord disc ligament and soft tissue abnormalities particularly when neurological deficit is present --- **2 Management for Stabilization** **Conservative management** Used for stable fractures without significant displacement or neurological compromise • Rigid cervical collar • Cervical orthosis/brace • Analgesics • Activity restriction • Regular radiographs/CT as required • Physiotherapy after adequate healing Stable cervical compression fractures may be treated with a cervical collar for several weeks **Halo immobilization** • Halo vest may provide rigid external immobilization • Used in selected stable or reducible cervical injuries • Requires careful monitoring for complications **Surgical stabilization** Indications • Unstable fracture • Significant displacement or deformity • Fracture dislocation • Progressive neurological deficit • Spinal cord compression • Failure of conservative treatment • Significant ligamentous disruption Procedures • Anterior cervical decompression and fusion • Posterior cervical fixation and fusion • Combined anterior and posterior stabilization when required • Removal of compressive bone/disc fragments when indicated The choice of surgical approach depends on the fracture pattern instability neurological status and site of spinal cord compression --- **3 Management of Quadriplegia** **Immediate management** 1 Maintain cervical immobilization and spinal alignment 2 Maintain a patent airway 3 Provide oxygen and ventilatory support when required 4 Monitor respiratory function continuously 5 Maintain adequate circulation and blood pressure 6 Perform complete neurological assessment 7 CT/MRI to identify spinal cord compression 8 Urgent spine/neurosurgical consultation 9 Surgical decompression and stabilization when indicated 10 Prevent secondary complications **Prevention of complications** • Regular repositioning • Pressure sore REPAIR** **Introduction to Soft Tissue Healing** **Definition of Inflammation** Inflammation is a protective response of living vascularized tissue to injury infection or irritation which removes the injurious stimulus and initiates the process of healing and repair --- **1 Causes of Inflammation** • Trauma and mechanical injury • Burns • Infection • Chemical irritants • Foreign bodies • Tissue necrosis • Ischaemia • Immune reactions --- **2 Types of Inflammation** **A Acute inflammation** • Rapid onset • Usually lasts for a short duration • Predominantly involves neutrophils • Characterized by vascular changes exudation of fluid and inflammatory cells **B Chronic inflammation** • Develops gradually or persists for a longer duration • Predominantly involves lymphocytes macrophages and plasma cells • Associated with tissue destruction and fibrosis --- **3 Cardinal Signs of Inflammation** 1 Rubor redness 2 Calor heat 3 Tumor swelling 4 Dolor pain 5 Functio laesa loss of function --- of blood flow **Cellular response** • Margination of leukocytes • Rolling • Adhesion • Transmigration/diapedesis • Chemotaxis • Phagocytosis • Destruction/removal of microorganisms and damaged tissue 2 Scar formation **Regeneration** Replacement of damaged cells by cells of the same type restoring normal tissue structure and function **Scar formation** Replacement of damaged tissue by connective tissue resulting in fibrosis and scar formation --- **6 Soft Tissue Healing** Soft tissue healing is the process by which injured skin muscle tendon ligament and other soft tissues restore their structural integrity and function following injury Healing occurs through overlapping phases **Phase 1 Haemostasis** Immediately after injury • Vasoconstriction • Platelet aggregation • Formation of blood clot • Fibrin clot formation • Provides temporary wound stability • Releases growth factors that initiate healing --- **Phase 2 Inflammatory Phase** Approximately first few days • Vasodilation and increased vascular permeability • Neutrophils migrate to the wound • Macrophages subsequently predominate • Removal of bacteria dead cells and debris • Release of cytokines and growth factors • Prepares the wound for tissue formation --- **Phase 3 Proliferative Phase** Usually begins within a few days and continues for several weeks Main events • Fibroblast proliferation • Collagen synthesis • Formation of granulation tissue • Angiogenesis • Re epithelialization • Wound contraction Initially the wound contains predominantly type III collagen --- **Phase 4 Remodeling/Maturation** Begins after the proliferative phase and may continue for months to years • Collagen is reorganized • Type III collagen is gradually replaced by stronger type I collagen • Collagen cross linking increases • Vascularity decreases • Scar becomes paler and flatter • Tensile strength progressively increases but does not normally return completely to that of uninjured tissue The inflammatory proliferative and remodeling phases overlap rather than occurring as completely separate stages --- **7 Factors Affecting Soft Tissue Healing** **Local factors** • Poor blood supply • Infection • Tissue damage • Foreign body • Excessive tension • Repeated trauma • Haematoma • Excessive movement **Systemic factors** • Age • Poor nutrition • Diabetes mellitus • Smoking • Anaemia • Immunosuppression • Certain Example clean surgical incision **Secondary intention** • Wound edges cannot be approximated • Greater tissue loss • Extensive granulation tissue • More wound contraction • Larger scar **Tertiary intention** • Wound is initially left open because of contamination/infection and is closed later after the wound is adequately clean ///////////// **1 Sprain** **Definition** Injury to a ligament contact sports **LCL** • Varus stress applied to the knee • May occur with high energy trauma **Clinical Features** • Pain and tenderness over the injured ligament • Local swelling • Pain on stress testing • Medial instability with valgus stress in MCL injury • Lateral instability with varus stress in LCL injury • Difficulty in weight bearing --- **5 Lateral Ligament Injury of Ankle** contusion** • Direct fall or blow to buttock • Pain and tenderness • Swelling and bruising • Pain while sitting or walking **C Calf contusion** • Direct blow to calf • Pain and swelling • Bruising • Amputation is the partial or complete removal of a limb or part of a limb through a surgical procedure or as a result of trauma The main aims of amputation are to remove non viable or diseased tissue amputation 2 Middle phalanx amputation 3 Proximal phalanx amputation 4 Metacarpal amputation 5 Ray amputation removal of a digit with its corresponding metacarpal 6 Transmetacarpal amputation through the metacarpals **B Wrist and Forearm** 7 Wrist disarticulation separation through the wrist joint 8 Transradial amputation through the forearm below the elbow **C Elbow and Arm** 9 Elbow disarticulation through the elbow joint 10 Transhumeral amputation through the arm above the elbow **D Shoulder** 11 Shoulder disarticulation removal of the upper limb through the shoulder joint 12
