Transmetatarsal amputation 4 Lisfranc amputation through the tarsometatarsal joints 5 Chopart amputation through the transverse tarsal joint 6 Symes amputation ankle disarticulation with preservation of the heel pad **B Leg** 7 Transtibial amputation through the tibia and fibula below the knee **C Knee** 8 Knee disarticulation amputation through the knee joint **D Thigh and Hip** 9 Transfemoral amputation through the femur above the knee 10 Hip disarticulation removal of the limb through the hip joint 11 Hemipelvectomy removal of the lower limb with part of the pelvis --- **3 Indications for Amputation** • Severe traumatic injury • Peripheral vascular disease with irreversible tissue loss • Uncontrolled infection/gangrene • Malignant tumour • Severe congenital deformity • Non functional painful limb • Severe burns or crush injury • Irreversible ischemia --- **4 Principles of Selecting the Level** The level should be selected to • Remove all non viable or diseased tissue • Preserve maximum useful limb length • Preserve viable skin and soft tissue coverage • Maintain adequate blood supply • Preserve important joints whenever possible • Produce a stable painless and functional residual limb • Allow effective prosthetic fitting ///////////////////// **Traumatic Spinal Cord Injuries** **Definition** Traumatic spinal cord injury SCI is an acute injury to the spinal cord caused by an external mechanical force resulting in temporary or permanent impairment of motor sensory and autonomic functions below the level of injury --- **Causes** • Road traffic accidents • Falls from height • Sports injuries especially diving • Direct blow to the spine • Gunshot or penetrating injuries • Crush injuries • Hyperflexion or hyperextension injuries • Fracture dislocation of the vertebral column --- **Clinical Features** Clinical presentation depends mainly on the level severity and completeness of spinal cord injury **1 Motor disturbances** • Muscle weakness or paralysis below the level of injury • Paraplegia paralysis of both lower limbs • Quadriplegia/tetraplegia paralysis of all four limbs following cervical cord injury • Loss of voluntary movements • Muscle weakness may be flaccid initially because of spinal shock • Later spasticity and hyperreflexia may develop in upper motor neuron lesions --- **2 Sensory disturbances** • Loss or reduction of sensation below the level of injury • Loss of • Pain • Temperature • Touch • Pressure • Vibration • Proprioception • Paraesthesia or numbness • A clearly defined sensory level may be present --- **3 Reflex changes** **Spinal shock** Immediately after a significant acute SCI • Flaccid paralysis • Loss of deep tendon reflexes • Loss of superficial reflexes • Absent bulbocavernosus reflex may occur • Areflexia below the level of injury As spinal shock resolves reflexes may return and become exaggerated in upper motor neuron injuries --- **4 Autonomic disturbances** **Bladder dysfunction** • Urinary retention • Urinary incontinence • Neurogenic bladder **Bowel dysfunction** • Constipation • Faecal incontinence • Neurogenic bowel **Sexual dysfunction** • Erectile/ejaculatory dysfunction • Altered sexual sensation Other autonomic abnormalities may include impaired sweating and temperature regulation --- **5 Respiratory Features** Respiratory impairment depends on the level of injury • Difficulty in deep inspiration • Weak cough • Retained respiratory secretions • Reduced vital capacity • Respiratory muscle paralysis • Respiratory failure in high cervical injuries Injury involving C3 C5 can compromise diaphragmatic function because the phrenic nerve arises from these cervical segments --- **6 Cardiovascular Features** Particularly with cervical and high thoracic injuries • Hypotension • Bradycardia • Peripheral vasodilation • Neurogenic shock • Cardiac rhythm disturbances Neurogenic shock results from loss of sympathetic outflow and is particularly associated with injuries above approximately T6 --- **7 Clinical Patterns of Incomplete SCI** **A Central Cord Syndrome** • Usually follows cervical hyperextension injury • Upper limbs are affected more than lower limbs • Hand weakness may be prominent • Sensory disturbance may occur **B Brown Séquard Syndrome** Due to hemisection of the spinal cord • Ipsilateral motor weakness • Ipsilateral loss of proprioception/vibration • Contralateral loss of pain and temperature **C Anterior Cord Syndrome** • Motor paralysis below the lesion • Loss of pain and temperature • Relative preservation of dorsal column functions such as vibration and proprioception --- **8 Complete and Incomplete Injury** **Complete SCI** • No sensory or motor function is preserved in the sacral segments S4 S5 • No sacral sparing • Classified as AIS/ASIA Grade A **Incomplete SCI** • Some sensory and/or motor function is preserved below the neurological level including sacral function • Classified as AIS B D depending on the amount of preserved function • AIS E normal motor and sensory examination --- **9 Clinical Examination** Assessment should include • Level of neurological injury • Motor power • Sensory examination • Deep tendon reflexes • Anal sensation and voluntary anal contraction • Muscle tone • Respiratory function • Bladder and bowel function • Autonomic function The International Standards for Neurological Classification of Spinal Cord Injury ISNCSCI/ASIA examination is used to determine the neurological level and severity of injury --- **10 Important Complications** • Respiratory failure • Neurogenic shock • Spinal shock • Pressure sores • Deep vein thrombosis and pulmonary embolism • Urinary tract infection • Neurogenic bladder and bowel • Contractures • Spasticity • Autonomic dysreflexia • Chronic pain • Permanent paralysis

07 Pneumothorax
Definition:The abnormal presence or accumulation of free air or gas within the pleural cavity between the parietal and visceral
pleura, disrupting negative intrapleural pressure and causing partial or complete ipsilateral lung collapse.
Major Types:
Spontaneous: Primary (rupture of subpleural apical blebs in healthy young adults) or Secondary (complication of COPD,
TB, abscess, or cystic fibrosis).
Traumatic: Penetrating or blunt thoracic trauma, including iatrogenic causes (central venous catheterization, pleural tap).
Tension: Medical emergency where a one-way valve effect builds positive intrapleural pressure, shifts the mediastinum,
and compromises venous return.
08 Respiratory Failure
Definition:An acute or chronic failure of the respiratory system to maintain adequate gas exchange, defined objectively as
arterial hypoxemia (PaO2 < 60 mmHg) with or without hypercapnia (PaCO2 > 50 mmHg) at rest on room air at sea level.
Major Types:
Type 1 (Hypoxemic):PaO2 < 60 mmHg with normal or reduced PaCO2 ; caused by V/Q mismatch or shunt (e.g., ARDS,
severe pneumonia, acute pulmonary edema).
Type 2 (Hypercapnic):PaCO2 > 50 mmHg with concurrent hypoxemia; caused by alveolar hypoventilation or ventilatory
pump failure (e.g., severe COPD, Guillain-Barré, opioid overdose).
09 Interstitial Lung Disease (ILD)
Definition:A heterogeneous group of non-neoplastic pulmonary disorders characterized by diffuse chronic inflammation,
cellular infiltration, and progressive collagen deposition/fibrosis within the alveolar walls and perilobular interstitium.
Common Types:Idiopathic Pulmonary Fibrosis (IPF), connective tissue disease-associated ILD (systemic sclerosis,
rheumatoid arthritis), sarcoidosis, hypersensitivity pneumonitis, and occupational pneumoconioses (silicosis, asbestosis).
10 Cystic Fibrosis (CF)
Definition:An autosomal recessive multisystem disorder caused by mutations in the CFTR gene on chromosome 7, leading to
abnormal epithelial chloride and bicarbonate transport and secretion of viscous mucus.
Major Respiratory Manifestations:Thick endobronchial mucus obstruction; recurrent chronic bacterial infections
(Pseudomonas aeruginosa, S. aureus); diffuse bronchiectasis; recurrent hemoptysis; and chronic rhinosinusitis with nasal
polyposis.
PART II: CARDIOVASCULAR PATHOLOGY & HEMODYNAMICS
11 Atherosclerosis
Definition:A chronic, progressive inflammatory disease of large and medium-sized elastic and muscular arteries characterized
by the formation of fibrofatty intimal plaques (atheromas) that compromise lumen caliber and vessel elasticity.
Major Risk Factors:
Modifiable: Dyslipidemia (elevated LDL, low HDL), systemic hypertension, cigarette smoking, diabetes mellitus, visceral
obesity, and physical inactivity.
Non-modifiable: Advancing age, male sex, and familial or genetic predisposition to premature coronary artery disease.

12 Thrombosis and Embolism
Thrombosis:The pathological formation of a solid or semisolid mass (thrombus) composed of fibrin, aggregated platelets, and
cellular elements within the unruptured vascular tree or cardiac chambers during life.
Embolism:The physical occlusion of a vascular lumen by a detached intravascular physical mass (thromboembolus, fat
droplet, air bubble, amniotic fluid) carried by the blood current away from its point of origin.
13 Ischemic Heart Disease (IHD)
Definition:A spectrum of cardiac disorders resulting from an absolute or relative imbalance between myocardial oxygen
demand and coronary arterial blood supply, predominantly caused by fixed atherosclerotic narrowing.
Major Risk Factors:Hypercholesterolemia/dyslipidemia, systemic arterial hypertension, tobacco cigarette smoking, diabetes
mellitus, metabolic syndrome, advancing age, and family history of early ischemic heart disease.
14 Congenital Heart Disease (CHD)
Definition:Macroscopic structural or functional defects of the heart or great intrathoracic vessels that are present at birth,
resulting from faulty embryonic cardiovascular morphogenesis.
Classification:
Acyanotic (Left-to-Right Shunt / Obstructive): Ventricular Septal Defect (VSD), Atrial Septal Defect (ASD), Patent Ductus
Arteriosus (PDA), Coarctation of the Aorta, Pulmonary Stenosis.
Cyanotic (Right-to-Left Shunt): Tetralogy of Fallot (TOF), Transposition of the Great Arteries (TGA), Tricuspid Atresia,
Truncus Arteriosus, Total Anomalous Pulmonary Venous Return (TAPVR).
15 Rheumatic Heart Disease (RHD)
Definition:Chronic, permanent cardiac valvular damage resulting from single or recurrent episodes of acute rheumatic fever,
an autoimmune inflammatory reaction triggered by Group A β-hemolytic streptococcal pharyngitis.
Common Complications:Chronic valvular stenoses or regurgitations (predominantly mitral and aortic valves), congestive
cardiac failure, atrial fibrillation with atrial thrombus formation, infective endocarditis, and cardioembolic stroke.
16 Cardiac Failure (Heart Failure)
Definition:A complex clinical syndrome caused by structural or functional impairment of ventricular filling or blood ejection,
rendering the heart incapable of meeting the metabolic demands of tissues at normal venous pressures.
Major Types:
By Ejection Fraction: Heart Failure with Reduced EF (HFrEF, LVEF ≤ 40%) vs. Heart Failure with Preserved EF (HFpEF, 
LVEF ≥ 50%).
By Ventricular Dominance: Left-sided heart failure (pulmonary congestion) vs. Right-sided heart failure (systemic venous
congestion).
By Time-Course: Acute decompensated heart failure vs. Chronic stable heart failure.
17 Cardiac Arrest
Definition:The abrupt cessation of effective mechanical cardiac pump activity resulting in the immediate collapse of systemic
blood flow, characterized by unresponsiveness, absent carotid pulse, and apnea or agonal breathing.
Immediate Emergency Response:
Confirm arrest, shout for help, and activate the emergency response system (Code Blue / AED retrieval).
Initiate immediate high-quality CPR: chest compressions at 100–120/min, 5–6 cm depth, 30:2 ratio with ventilations.
Attach AED/defibrillator; analyze rhythm and deliver immediate DC shock if shockable (VF or pulseless VT).

18 Cardiomyopathy
Definition:A diverse group of intrinsic myocardial disorders associated with mechanical and/or electrical cardiac dysfunction,
not secondary to coronary disease, systemic hypertension, valvular lesions, or congenital heart disease.
Major Types:Dilated Cardiomyopathy (DCM), Hypertrophic Cardiomyopathy (HCM), Restrictive Cardiomyopathy (RCM), and
Arrhythmogenic Right Ventricular Cardiomyopathy (ARVC).
19 Infective Endocarditis (IE)
Definition:A serious, invasive microbial infection of the endocardial surface of the heart, characterized by the formation of
bulky, friable vegetations composed of fibrin, platelets, and microorganisms on the cardiac valves.
Common Complications:Acute valvular regurgitation, congestive heart failure, perivalvular ring abscesses, systemic septic
embolization (cerebral stroke, splenic/renal infarction), mycotic aneurysms, and glomerulonephritis.
20 Shock
Definition:A life-threatening state of acute systemic circulatory failure characterized by inadequate tissue and cellular
microvascular perfusion, resulting in cellular dysoxia, anaerobic metabolism, and progressive multi-organ failure.
Major Types:
Hypovolemic: Depletion of intravascular volume (acute hemorrhage, severe dehydration, plasma loss in burns).
Cardiogenic: Primary pump failure (acute myocardial infarction, severe acute myocarditis, malignant arrhythmias).
Distributive: Profound systemic vasodilation (septic shock, anaphylactic shock, neurogenic spinal shock).
Obstructive: Physical mechanical impedance to cardiac filling or output (cardiac tamponade, tension pneumothorax,
pulmonary embolism).
PART III: EMERGENCY CARE, CRITICAL CARE & CLINICAL DIAGNOSTICS
21 Hemorrhage
Definition:The escape or extravasation of whole blood from the intravascular lumen into extravascular tissues, body cavities,
or the external environment following disruption, trauma, or ulceration of vessel walls.
Major Types:
By Vessel: Arterial (pulsatile, bright red), Venous (steady, dark red), Capillary (generalized oozing).
By Location: External (visible bleeding) vs. Internal (hidden in serous cavities/tissues: hemothorax, hemoperitoneum).
By Timing: Primary (at time of trauma), Reactionary (within 24 hours), Secondary (7–14 days later due to sepsis).
22 Septicemia
Definition:A severe, life-threatening systemic infection caused by the active multiplication and persistence of virulent bacteria
and their toxins in the circulating blood, precipitating a dysregulated systemic host inflammatory response.
Common Clinical Features:High swinging fever with shaking chills (rigors) or hypothermia (< 36°C), resting tachycardia (> 90
bpm), tachypnea (> 20 bpm), systemic arterial hypotension, altered mental status, diaphoresis, and progressive oliguria.
23 Basic Life Support (BLS)
Definition:The standardized level of non-invasive emergency medical care provided to victims of cardiopulmonary arrest,
acute airway obstruction, or drowning prior to the availability of advanced cardiac life support (ACLS).
Main Components:Early recognition of cardiac arrest and activation of emergency response; high-quality cardiopulmonary
resuscitation (CPR) with emphasis on chest compressions; early automated external defibrillation (AED); and foreign-body
airway clearance maneuvers.

24 Cardiopulmonary Resuscitation (CPR)
Definition:An emergency life-saving procedure consisting of external rhythmic manual chest compressions combined with
positive-pressure rescue ventilations delivered to a victim in cardiac or respiratory arrest.
Primary Purpose:To maintain artificial forward perfusion to the coronary arteries and brain, sustaining minimal vital organ
cellular oxygenation and viability until spontaneous circulation (ROSC) is restored or definitive therapy is delivered.
25 Mechanical Ventilation
Definition:An advanced supportive medical intervention in which an automated machine (ventilator) is used to assist or
completely replace spontaneous pulmonary gas exchange and work of breathing.
Two Major Indications:
Acute respiratory failure refractory to conservative therapy (severe hypoxemic ARDS or acute hypercapnic COPD
decompensation).
Airway protection and loss of neurological respiratory drive (severe coma with GCS ≤ 8, acute drug toxicity, or general
anesthesia).
26 Arterial Blood Gas (ABG) Analysis
Definition:A quantitative point-of-care laboratory evaluation performed on whole arterial blood (commonly sampled from the
radial artery) to measure partial pressures of gases (PaO2 , PaCO2), pH, and bicarbonate concentrations (HCO3
−).
Clinical Significance:Provides rapid objective assessment of alveolar ventilation, pulmonary oxygenation efficiency, and acid
base homeostasis (metabolic/respiratory acidosis and alkalosis), guiding ventilator management and critical care therapy.
27 Electrocardiogram (ECG)
Definition:A non-invasive diagnostic recording of the bioelectrical potentials and cardiac vector voltages generated by
myocardial depolarization and repolarization, recorded through skin surface electrodes.
Major Waves:
P wave: Atrial depolarization.
QRS complex: Rapid ventricular depolarization (and masked atrial repolarization).
T wave: Ventricular repolarization. (U wave: Inconstant, repolarization of Purkinje fibers / papillary muscles).
28 Oxygen Therapy
Definition:The controlled medical administration of supplemental oxygen at concentrations higher than ambient air (FiO2 >
21%) to prevent, treat, or reverse tissue hypoxia and alleviate cardiopulmonary work.
Common Indications:Documented acute hypoxemia (SpO2 < 90% or PaO2 < 60 mmHg); acute myocardial infarction; systemic
shock states; severe trauma; and acute carbon monoxide poisoning.
PART IV: DERMATOLOGY & INFECTIOUS DISEASES
29 Psoriasis
Definition:A chronic, immune-mediated, non-contagious systemic inflammatory dermatosis driven by T-helper lymphocytes,
resulting in marked hyperproliferation and abnormal differentiation of epidermal keratinocytes.
Characteristic Clinical Feature:Sharply demarcated, erythematous plaques topped with silvery-white, micaceous scales on
extensor surfaces, exhibiting pinpoint capillary bleeding upon scale removal (Auspitz sign) and lesion development at sites of
injury (Koebner phenomenon).

30 Eczema (Dermatitis)
Definition:A non-contagious, inflammatory skin disorder characterized histologically by epidermal spongiosis and clinically by
intense pruritus, erythema, edema, and vesiculation acutely, progressing to lichenification chronically.
Common Types:Atopic dermatitis, Allergic contact dermatitis, Irritant contact dermatitis, Seborrheic dermatitis, and Dyshidrotic
eczema (pompholyx).
31 Urticaria (Hives)
Definition:A transient vascular cutaneous reaction characterized by the abrupt appearance of intensely pruritic, erythematous,
edematous plaques with central pallor (wheals) caused by mast-cell histamine release.
Common Triggers:Food allergens (shellfish, nuts, eggs), drugs (penicillin, NSAIDs, ACE inhibitors), viral or parasitic
infections, insect envenomation, and physical triggers (dermographism, heat, cold, localized pressure).
32 Acne (Acne Vulgaris)
Definition:A chronic inflammatory disease of the pilosebaceous units driven by follicular hyperkeratinization, sebum
overproduction under androgenic influence, Cutibacterium acnes proliferation, and perifollicular inflammation.
Common Types:
Non-inflammatory: Open comedones (blackheads) and closed comedones (whiteheads).
Inflammatory: Papular acne, pustular acne, and nodulocystic acne (including severe forms like acne conglobata).
33 Vitiligo
Definition:An acquired, progressive chronic autoimmune skin disease characterized by the targeted immune-mediated
destruction of epidermal melanocytes, leading to complete absence of melanin pigment.
Characteristic Clinical Presentation:Asymptomatic, well-circumscribed, chalk-white or amelanotic macules and patches of
normal cutaneous texture, frequently exhibiting bilateral symmetrical distribution over extensor surfaces, hands, and periorificial
areas.
34 Leprosy (Hansen's Disease)
Definition:A chronic granulomatous infection caused by Mycobacterium leprae, an obligate intracellular acid-fast bacillus
displaying unique tropism for the skin, upper respiratory mucosa, and peripheral nerve Schwann cells.
Major Neurological Complications:Peripheral sensorimotor neuropathy with painless glove-and-stocking sensory loss, nerve
thickening, neuropathic plantar ulcerations, and peripheral paralyses: claw hand (ulnar nerve), wrist drop (radial nerve), foot
drop (common peroneal nerve), and lagophthalmos (facial nerve).
PART V: CLINICAL NUTRITION, MATERNAL HEALTH & OB-GYN
35 Protein-Energy Malnutrition (PEM)
Definition:A broad spectrum of nutritional deficiency disorders resulting from insufficient dietary intake, poor absorption, or
hypercatabolic wasting of proteins and energy needed to sustain growth and physiological homeostasis.
Major Types:
Kwashiorkor: Predominant protein deficiency with adequate carbohydrates; presents with generalized pitting edema,
"flaky-paint" dermatosis, sparse depigmented hair, moon facies, and hepatomegaly.
Marasmus: Severe deficiency of both total calories and protein; presents with extreme somatic muscle wasting, loss of
subcutaneous fat, and wizened "old-man" facies without edema.
Marasmic Kwashiorkor: Severe muscle and fat wasting combined with peripheral edema.

36 Vitamin Deficiency Disease
Definition:A specific pathologic nutritional disorder caused by chronic inadequate dietary intake, impaired gastrointestinal
absorption, or metabolic derangement of one or more vital micronutrients (vitamins).
Two Examples:
Scurvy: Vitamin C (ascorbic acid) deficiency; impaired collagen synthesis resulting in swollen bleeding gums, perifollicular
petechiae, subperiosteal hematomas, and delayed wound healing.
Rickets (in children) / Osteomalacia (in adults): Vitamin D deficiency; impaired mineralization of bone matrix and growth
plates, leading to bowing of long legs and rachitic rosary.
37 Antenatal Care (ANC)
Definition:Comprehensive, continuous clinical, nutritional, and preventive healthcare provided by skilled medical professionals
to a pregnant woman throughout the gestational period from conception until labor.
Core Objectives:Monitor maternal-fetal physical well-being; detect and manage high-risk obstetrical complications early (pre
eclampsia, gestational diabetes, severe anemia); provide micronutrient prophylaxis (iron-folate); and prepare the mother for
safe delivery and breastfeeding.
38 Postnatal Care (PNC)
Definition:The specialized medical, diagnostic, and supportive health surveillance provided to the mother and newborn infant
immediately after parturition through the puerperium (traditionally 6 weeks or 42 days postpartum).
Clinical Importance:Immediate detection and prevention of major postpartum morbidities (postpartum hemorrhage, puerperal
sepsis, thromboembolism, postpartum depression), neonatal evaluation, reinforcement of exclusive breastfeeding, and
postpartum contraception counseling.
39 Menopause
Definition:The permanent, physiological cessation of menses resulting from the irreversible exhaustion of ovarian follicular
reserves and loss of ovarian estradiol production, established clinically after 12 consecutive months of amenorrhea.
Common Symptoms:Vasomotor symptoms (hot flashes, night sweats), sleep disturbances, urogenital atrophy (vaginal
dryness, dyspareunia, urinary frequency), mood swings and irritability, and decreased libido.
40 Infertility
Definition:A disease of the male or female reproductive tract defined by the failure to achieve a successful clinical pregnancy
after 12 continuous months or more of regular, unprotected heterosexual intercourse without contraception.
Major Causes:
Female Factors (40–50%): Ovulatory dysfunction (PCOS), tubal occlusion/pelvic adhesions (PID), endometriosis, uterine
fibroids.
Male Factors (30–40%): Semen abnormalities (oligo/astheno/teratozoospermia), varicocele, endocrine disorders,
obstructive azoospermia.
Combined / Unexplained Factors (10–20%).

41 Urinary Incontinence
Definition:The involuntary, uncontrollable loss or leakage of urine that is objectively demonstrable and causes physical
hygiene, emotional, or social impairment.
Major Types:
Stress Incontinence: Involuntary leakage during coughing, laughing, or lifting due to pelvic floor laxity or urethral
hypermobility.
Urge Incontinence: Involuntary leakage preceded by an urgent, sudden urge to void, caused by detrusor overactivity.
Overflow Incontinence: Involuntary dribbling from a chronically overdistended bladder (obstruction or underactive
bladder).
Functional Incontinence: Incontinence secondary to physical, cognitive, or environmental impediments preventing normal
toilet access.
42 Hysterectomy
Definition:The surgical excision and removal of the uterus, categorized as total (body and cervix removed) or subtotal/
supracervical (body removed, cervix preserved), via abdominal, vaginal, or laparoscopic routes.
Common Indications:Symptomatic uterine leiomyomas (fibroids) unresponsive to medical therapy, refractory abnormal
uterine bleeding, gynecological malignancies (endometrial, cervical, or ovarian cancer), severe uterine prolapse, and
debilitating endometriosis/adenomyosis.
43 Dilatation and Curettage (D&C)
Definition:A minor gynecological operative procedure involving the gradual mechanical enlargement/dilatation of the cervical
canal followed by the scraping or vacuum evacuation (curettage) of the endometrial lining.
Key Indications:
Diagnostic: Evaluation of postmenopausal bleeding, abnormal uterine bleeding, or suspected endometrial hyperplasia and
neoplasia.
Therapeutic: Evacuation of retained products of conception following incomplete or missed abortion, management of acute
heavy uterine bleeding, or polyp excision.
44 Pre-eclampsia
Definition:A multisystem disorder of pregnancy characterized by the new development of arterial hypertension (≥ 140/90
mmHg) presenting after 20 weeks of gestation in a previously normotensive female, accompanied by proteinuria and/or
maternal organ dysfunction.
Major Clinical Features:Persistent gestational hypertension, significant proteinuria (≥ 300 mg/24 h), rapid pathological facial
and non-dependent hand edema, throbbing frontal headache, scotomata and visual blurriness, epigastric or right upper
quadrant abdominal tenderness, and thrombocytopenia.
45 Sexually Transmitted Diseases (STDs)
Definition:A heterogeneous group of communicable infectious syndromes caused by bacteria, viruses, parasites, or fungi that
are predominantly spread from person to person through unprotected sexual intercourse (vaginal, anal, or oral).
Two Classical Examples:
Syphilis: A chronic systemic venereal infection caused by the spirochete Treponema pallidum, presenting primarily with an
indurated, painless chancre.
Gonorrhea: An acute purulent mucosal infection of the genitourinary tract caused by the Gram-negative diplococcus 
Neisseria gonorrhoeae.

PART I: RESPIRATORY PATHOLOGY & PULMONARY DISORDERS
01 Bronchial Asthma
Definition:A chronic inflammatory disorder of the airways characterized by bronchial hyperresponsiveness, chronic
inflammation, and recurrent episodes of reversible airflow obstruction and bronchospasm.
Common Triggers:Inhaled allergens (pollen, dust mites, animal dander), viral respiratory tract infections, cold ambient air,
physical exertion, atmospheric smoke/pollutants, and medications (aspirin, non-selective beta-blockers).
02 Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease (COPD)
Definition:A common, preventable, and treatable pulmonary disease characterized by persistent, usually progressive airflow
limitation caused by a combination of small airway disease (obstructive bronchiolitis) and parenchymal destruction
(emphysema).
Major Risk Factors:Tobacco cigarette smoking (primary risk factor), exposure to biomass fuel smoke and poorly ventilated
indoor cooking, occupational dusts and chemical fumes, ambient air pollution, and genetic α1-antitrypsin deficiency.
03 Tuberculosis (TB)
Definition:A chronic, communicable granulomatous bacterial infection caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis, primarily
affecting the pulmonary parenchyma but capable of hematogenous or lymphatic dissemination to extrapulmonary organs.
Common Modes of Transmission:Inhalation of microscopic airborne droplet nuclei (1 to 5 μm in diameter) expelled when a
patient with active pulmonary or laryngeal tuberculosis coughs, sneezes, speaks, or sings.
04 Bronchiectasis
Definition:A chronic pulmonary disorder characterized by permanent, abnormal dilation and destruction of the elastic and
muscular components of the bronchial walls, driven by a vicious cycle of recurrent infection and transmural inflammation.
Common Clinical Features:Chronic persistent cough productive of copious, foul-smelling, purulent sputum; recurrent
hemoptysis; progressive dyspnea; coarse inspiratory crackles and rhonchi on auscultation; and digital clubbing.
05 Emphysema
Definition:An anatomically defined pulmonary disorder characterized by abnormal, permanent enlargement of the airspaces
distal to the terminal bronchioles, accompanied by destruction of alveolar walls without gross fibrosis.
Major Pathological Changes:Proteolytic breakdown of alveolar elastin fibers, loss of alveolar gas-exchanging surface area,
loss of radial elastic traction causing expiratory airway collapse, pulmonary capillary bed depletion, and bullae formation.
06 Pleural Effusion
Definition:An abnormal accumulation of fluid within the pleural space exceeding the physiological volume (> 15 mL), reflecting
an imbalance between pleural fluid production and lymphatic absorption.
Common Causes:
Transudative: Congestive heart failure, liver cirrhosis with ascites, nephrotic syndrome, severe hypoalbuminemia.
Exudative: Parapneumonic bacterial effusion, pulmonary tuberculosis, malignancy (bronchogenic carcinoma, metastases),
pulmonary embolism.

Initiate immediate high-quality CPR: chest compressions at 100–120/min, 5–6 cm depth, 30:2 ratio with ventilations.
Attach AED/defibrillator; analyze rhythm and deliver immediate DC shock if shockable (VF or pulseless VT).

18 Cardiomyopathy
Definition:A diverse group of intrinsic myocardial disorders associated with mechanical and/or electrical cardiac dysfunction,
not secondary to coronary disease, systemic hypertension, valvular lesions, or congenital heart disease.
Major Types:Dilated Cardiomyopathy (DCM), Hypertrophic Cardiomyopathy (HCM), Restrictive Cardiomyopathy (RCM), and
Arrhythmogenic Right Ventricular Cardiomyopathy (ARVC).
19 Infective Endocarditis (IE)
Definition:A serious, invasive microbial infection of the endocardial surface of the heart, characterized by the formation of
bulky, friable vegetations composed of fibrin, platelets, and microorganisms on the cardiac valves.
Common Complications:Acute valvular regurgitation, congestive heart failure, perivalvular ring abscesses, systemic septic
embolization (cerebral stroke, splenic/renal infarction), mycotic aneurysms, and glomerulonephritis.
20 Shock
Definition:A life-threatening state of acute systemic circulatory failure characterized by inadequate tissue and cellular
microvascular perfusion, resulting in cellular dysoxia, anaerobic metabolism, and progressive multi-organ failure.
Major Types:
Hypovolemic: Depletion of intravascular volume (acute hemorrhage, severe dehydration, plasma loss in burns).
Cardiogenic: Primary pump failure (acute myocardial infarction, severe acute myocarditis, malignant arrhythmias).
Distributive: Profound systemic vasodilation (septic shock, anaphylactic shock, neurogenic spinal shock).
Obstructive: Physical mechanical impedance to cardiac filling or output (cardiac tamponade, tension pneumothorax,
pulmonary embolism).
PART III: EMERGENCY CARE, CRITICAL CARE & CLINICAL DIAGNOSTICS
21 Hemorrhage
Definition:The escape or extravasation of whole blood from the intravascular lumen into extravascular tissues, body cavities,
or the external environment following disruption, trauma, or ulceration of vessel walls.
Major Types:
By Vessel: Arterial (pulsatile, bright red), Venous (steady, dark red), Capillary (generalized oozing).
By Location: External (visible bleeding) vs. Internal (hidden in serous cavities/tissues: hemothorax, hemoperitoneum).
By Timing: Primary (at time of trauma), Reactionary (within 24 hours), Secondary (7–14 days later due to sepsis).
22 Septicemia
Definition:A severe, life-threatening systemic infection caused by the active multiplication and persistence of virulent bacteria
and their toxins in the circulating blood, precipitating a dysregulated systemic host inflammatory response.
Common Clinical Features:High swinging fever with shaking chills (rigors) or hypothermia (< 36°C), resting tachycardia (> 90
bpm), tachypnea (> 20 bpm), systemic arterial hypotension, altered mental status, diaphoresis, and progressive oliguria.
23 Basic Life Support (BLS)
Definition:The standardized level of non-invasive emergency medical care provided to victims of cardiopulmonary arrest,
acute airway obstruction, or drowning prior to the availability of advanced cardiac life support (ACLS).
Main Components:Early recognition of cardiac arrest and activation of emergency response; high-quality cardiopulmonary
resuscitation (CPR) with emphasis on chest compressions; early automated external defibrillation (AED); and foreign-body
airway clearance maneuvers.

24 Cardiopulmonary Resuscitation (CPR)
Definition:An emergency life-saving procedure consisting of external rhythmic manual chest compressions combined with
positive-pressure rescue ventilations delivered to a victim in cardiac or respiratory arrest.
Primary Purpose:To maintain artificial forward perfusion to the coronary arteries and brain, sustaining minimal vital organ
cellular oxygenation and viability until spontaneous circulation (ROSC) is restored or definitive therapy is delivered.
25 Mechanical Ventilation
Definition:An advanced supportive medical intervention in which an automated machine (ventilator) is used to assist or
completely replace spontaneous pulmonary gas exchange and work of breathing.
Two Major Indications:
Acute respiratory failure refractory to conservative therapy (severe hypoxemic ARDS or acute hypercapnic COPD
decompensation).
Airway protection and loss of neurological respiratory drive (severe coma with GCS ≤ 8, acute drug toxicity, or general
anesthesia).
26 Arterial Blood Gas (ABG) Analysis
Definition:A quantitative point-of-care laboratory evaluation performed on whole arterial blood (commonly sampled from the
radial artery) to measure partial pressures of gases (PaO2 , PaCO2), pH, and bicarbonate concentrations (HCO3
−).
Clinical Significance:Provides rapid objective assessment of alveolar ventilation, pulmonary oxygenation efficiency, and acid
base homeostasis (metabolic/respiratory acidosis and alkalosis), guiding ventilator management and critical care therapy.
27 Electrocardiogram (ECG)
Definition:A non-invasive diagnostic recording of the bioelectrical potentials and cardiac vector voltages generated by
myocardial depolarization and repolarization, recorded through skin surface electrodes.
Major Waves:
P wave: Atrial depolarization.
QRS complex: Rapid ventricular depolarization (and masked atrial repolarization).
T wave: Ventricular repolarization. (U wave: Inconstant, repolarization of Purkinje fibers / papillary muscles).
28 Oxygen Therapy
Definition:The controlled medical administration of supplemental oxygen at concentrations higher than ambient air (FiO2 >
21%) to prevent, treat, or reverse tissue hypoxia and alleviate cardiopulmonary work.
Common Indications:Documented acute hypoxemia (SpO2 < 90% or PaO2 < 60 mmHg); acute myocardial infarction; systemic
shock states; severe trauma; and acute carbon monoxide poisoning.
PART IV: DERMATOLOGY & INFECTIOUS DISEASES
29 Psoriasis
Definition:A chronic, immune-mediated, non-contagious systemic inflammatory dermatosis driven by T-helper lymphocytes,
resulting in marked hyperproliferation and abnormal differentiation of epidermal keratinocytes.
Characteristic Clinical Feature:Sharply demarcated, erythematous plaques topped with silvery-white, micaceous scales on
extensor surfaces, exhibiting pinpoint capillary bleeding upon scale removal (Auspitz sign) and lesion development at sites of
injury (Koebner phenomenon).

30 Eczema (Dermatitis)
Definition:A non-contagious, inflammatory skin disorder characterized histologically by epidermal spongiosis and clinically by
intense pruritus, erythema, edema, and vesiculation acutely, progressing to lichenification chronically.
Common Types:Atopic dermatitis, Allergic contact dermatitis, Irritant contact dermatitis, Seborrheic dermatitis, and Dyshidrotic
eczema (pompholyx).
31 Urticaria (Hives)
Definition:A transient vascular cutaneous reaction characterized by the abrupt appearance of intensely pruritic, erythematous,
edematous plaques with central pallor (wheals) caused by mast-cell histamine release.
Common Triggers:Food allergens (shellfish, nuts, eggs), drugs (penicillin, NSAIDs, ACE inhibitors), viral or parasitic
infections, insect envenomation, and physical triggers (dermographism, heat, cold, localized pressure).
32 Acne (Acne Vulgaris)
Definition:A chronic inflammatory disease of the pilosebaceous units driven by follicular hyperkeratinization, sebum
overproduction under androgenic influence, Cutibacterium acnes proliferation, and perifollicular inflammation.
Common Types:
Non-inflammatory: Open comedones (blackheads) and closed comedones (whiteheads).
Inflammatory: Papular acne, pustular acne, and nodulocystic acne (including severe forms like acne conglobata).
33 Vitiligo
Definition:An acquired, progressive chronic autoimmune skin disease characterized by the targeted immune-mediated
destruction of epidermal melanocytes, leading to complete absence of melanin pigment.
Characteristic Clinical Presentation:Asymptomatic, well-circumscribed, chalk-white or amelanotic macules and patches of
normal cutaneous texture, frequently exhibiting bilateral symmetrical distribution over extensor surfaces, hands, and periorificial
areas.
34 Leprosy (Hansen's Disease)
Definition:A chronic granulomatous infection caused by Mycobacterium leprae, an obligate intracellular acid-fast bacillus
displaying unique tropism for the skin, upper respiratory mucosa, and peripheral nerve Schwann cells.
Major Neurological Complications:Peripheral sensorimotor neuropathy with painless glove-and-stocking sensory loss, nerve
thickening, neuropathic plantar ulcerations, and peripheral paralyses: claw hand (ulnar nerve), wrist drop (radial nerve), foot
drop (common peroneal nerve), and lagophthalmos (facial nerve).
PART V: CLINICAL NUTRITION, MATERNAL HEALTH & OB-GYN
35 Protein-Energy Malnutrition (PEM)
Definition:A broad spectrum of nutritional deficiency disorders resulting from insufficient dietary intake, poor absorption, or
hypercatabolic wasting of proteins and energy needed to sustain growth and physiological homeostasis.
Major Types:
Kwashiorkor: Predominant protein deficiency with adequate carbohydrates; presents with generalized pitting edema,
"flaky-paint" dermatosis, sparse depigmented hair, moon facies, and hepatomegaly.
Marasmus: Severe deficiency of both total calories and protein; presents with extreme somatic muscle wasting, loss of
subcutaneous fat, and wizened "old-man" facies without edema.
Marasmic Kwashiorkor: Severe muscle and fat wasting combined with peripheral edema.

36 Vitamin Deficiency Disease
Definition:A specific pathologic nutritional disorder caused by chronic inadequate dietary intake, impaired gastrointestinal
absorption, or metabolic derangement of one or more vital micronutrients (vitamins).
Two Examples:
Scurvy: Vitamin C (ascorbic acid) deficiency; impaired collagen synthesis resulting in swollen bleeding gums, perifollicular
petechiae, subperiosteal hematomas, and delayed wound healing.
Rickets (in children) / Osteomalacia (in adults): Vitamin D deficiency; impaired mineralization of bone matrix and growth
plates, leading to bowing of long legs and rachitic rosary.
37 Antenatal Care (ANC)
Definition:Comprehensive, continuous clinical, nutritional, and preventive healthcare provided by skilled medical professionals
to a pregnant woman throughout the gestational period from conception until labor.
Core Objectives:Monitor maternal-fetal physical well-being; detect and manage high-risk obstetrical complications early (pre
eclampsia, gestational diabetes, severe anemia); provide micronutrient prophylaxis (iron-folate); and prepare the mother for
safe delivery and breastfeeding.
38 Postnatal Care (PNC)
Definition:The specialized medical, diagnostic, and supportive health surveillance provided to the mother and newborn infant
immediately after parturition through the puerperium (traditionally 6 weeks or 42 days postpartum).
Clinical Importance:Immediate detection and prevention of major postpartum morbidities (postpartum hemorrhage, puerperal
sepsis, thromboembolism, postpartum depression), neonatal evaluation, reinforcement of exclusive breastfeeding, and
postpartum contraception counseling.
39 Menopause
Definition:The permanent, physiological cessation of menses resulting from the irreversible exhaustion of ovarian follicular
reserves and loss of ovarian estradiol production, established clinically after 12 consecutive months of amenorrhea.
Common Symptoms:Vasomotor symptoms (hot flashes, night sweats), sleep disturbances, urogenital atrophy (vaginal
dryness, dyspareunia, urinary frequency), mood swings and irritability, and decreased libido.
40 Infertility
Definition:A disease of the male or female reproductive tract defined by the failure to achieve a successful clinical pregnancy
after 12 continuous months or more of regular, unprotected heterosexual intercourse without contraception.
Major Causes:
Female Factors (40–50%): Ovulatory dysfunction (PCOS), tubal occlusion/pelvic adhesions (PID), endometriosis, uterine
fibroids.
Male Factors (30–40%): Semen abnormalities (oligo/astheno/teratozoospermia), varicocele, endocrine disorders,
obstructive azoospermia.
Combined / Unexplained Factors (10–20%).

41 Urinary Incontinence
Definition:The involuntary, uncontrollable loss or leakage of urine that is objectively demonstrable and causes physical
hygiene, emotional, or social impairment.
Major Types:
Stress Incontinence: Involuntary leakage during coughing, laughing, or lifting due to pelvic floor laxity or urethral
hypermobility.
Urge Incontinence: Involuntary leakage preceded by an urgent, sudden urge to void, caused by detrusor overactivity.
Overflow Incontinence: Involuntary dribbling from a chronically overdistended bladder (obstruction or underactive
bladder).
Functional Incontinence: Incontinence secondary to physical, cognitive, or environmental impediments preventing normal
toilet access.
42 Hysterectomy
Definition:The surgical excision and removal of the uterus, categorized as total (body and cervix removed) or subtotal/
supracervical (body removed, cervix preserved), via abdominal, vaginal, or laparoscopic routes.
Common Indications:Symptomatic uterine leiomyomas (fibroids) unresponsive to medical therapy, refractory abnormal
uterine bleeding, gynecological malignancies (endometrial, cervical, or ovarian cancer), severe uterine prolapse, and
debilitating endometriosis/adenomyosis.
43 Dilatation and Curettage (D&C)
Definition:A minor gynecological operative procedure involving the gradual mechanical enlargement/dilatation of the cervical
canal followed by the scraping or vacuum evacuation (curettage) of the endometrial lining.
Key Indications:
Diagnostic: Evaluation of postmenopausal bleeding, abnormal uterine bleeding, or suspected endometrial hyperplasia and
neoplasia.
Therapeutic: Evacuation of retained products of conception following incomplete or missed abortion, management of acute
heavy uterine bleeding, or polyp excision.
44 Pre-eclampsia
Definition:A multisystem disorder of pregnancy characterized by the new development of arterial hypertension (≥ 140/90
mmHg) presenting after 20 weeks of gestation in a previously normotensive female, accompanied by proteinuria and/or
maternal organ dysfunction.
Major Clinical Features:Persistent gestational hypertension, significant proteinuria (≥ 300 mg/24 h), rapid pathological facial
and non-dependent hand edema, throbbing frontal headache, scotomata and visual blurriness, epigastric or right upper
quadrant abdominal tenderness, and thrombocytopenia.
45 Sexually Transmitted Diseases (STDs)
Definition:A heterogeneous group of communicable infectious syndromes caused by bacteria, viruses, parasites, or fungi that
are predominantly spread from person to person through unprotected sexual intercourse (vaginal, anal, or oral).
Two Classical Examples:
Syphilis: A chronic systemic venereal infection caused by the spirochete Treponema pallidum, presenting primarily with an
indurated, painless chancre.
Gonorrhea: An acute purulent mucosal infection of the genitourinary tract caused by the Gram-negative diplococcus 
Neisseria gonorrhoeae.

COPD Guillain Barre opioid overdose --- **09 Interstitial Lung Disease ILD** **Definition** A heterogeneous group of non neoplastic pulmonary disorders characterized by diffuse chronic inflammation cellular infiltration and progressive collagen deposition / fibrosis within the alveolar walls and perilobular interstitium **Common Types** Idiopathic Pulmonary Fibrosis IPF connective tissue disease associated ILD systemic sclerosis rheumatoid arthritis sarcoidosis hypersensitivity pneumonitis and occupational pneumoconioses silicosis asbestosis --- **10 Cystic Fibrosis CF** **Definition** An autosomal recessive multisystem disorder caused by mutations in the CFTR gene on chromosome 7 leading to abnormal epithelial chloride and bicarbonate transport and secretion of viscous mucus **Major Respiratory Manifestations** Thick endobronchial mucus obstruction recurrent chronic bacterial infections Pseudomonas aeruginosa S aureus diffuse bronchiectasis recurrent hemoptysis and chronic rhinosinusitis with nasal polyposis --- **PART II CARDIOVASCULAR PATHOLOGY HEMODYNAMICS** --- **11 Atherosclerosis** **Definition** A chronic progressive inflammatory disease of large and medium sized elastic and muscular arteries characterized by the formation of fibrofatty intimal plaques atheromas that compromise lumen caliber and vessel elasticity **Major Risk Factors** **Modifiable** Dyslipidemia elevated LDL low HDL systemic hypertension cigarette smoking diabetes mellitus visceral obesity and physical inactivity **Non modifiable** Advancing age male sex and familial or genetic predisposition to premature coronary artery disease --- **12 Thrombosis and Embolism** **Thrombosis** The pathological formation of a solid or semisolid mass thrombus composed of fibrin aggregated platelets and cellular elements within the unruptured vascular tree or cardiac chambers during life **Embolism** The physical occlusion of a vascular lumen by a detached intravascular physical mass thromboembolus fat droplet air bubble amniotic fluid carried by the blood current away from its point of origin --- **13 Ischemic Heart Disease IHD** **Definition** A spectrum of cardiac disorders resulting from an absolute or relative imbalance between myocardial oxygen demand and coronary arterial blood supply predominantly caused by fixed atherosclerotic narrowing **Major Risk Factors** Hypercholesterolemia dyslipidemia systemic arterial hypertension tobacco cigarette smoking diabetes mellitus metabolic syndrome advancing age and family history of early ischemic heart disease --- **14 Congenital Heart Disease CHD** **Definition** Macroscopic structural or functional defects of the heart or great intrathoracic vessels that are present at birth resulting from faulty embryonic cardiovascular morphogenesis **Classification** **Acyanotic Left to Right Shunt / Obstructive** Ventricular Septal Defect VSD Atrial Septal Defect ASD Patent Ductus Arteriosus PDA Coarctation of the Aorta Pulmonary Stenosis **Cyanotic Right to Left Shunt** Tetralogy of Fallot TOF Transposition of the Great Arteries TGA Tricuspid Atresia Truncus Arteriosus Total Anomalous Pulmonary Venous Return TAPVR --- **15 Rheumatic Heart Disease RHD** **Definition** Chronic permanent cardiac valvular damage resulting from single or recurrent episodes of acute rheumatic fever an autoimmune inflammatory reaction triggered by Group A beta hemolytic streptococcal pharyngitis **Common Complications** Chronic valvular stenoses or regurgitations predominantly mitral and aortic valves congestive cardiac failure atrial fibrillation with atrial thrombus formation infective endocarditis and cardioembolic stroke --- **16 Cardiac Failure Heart Failure** **Definition** A complex clinical syndrome caused by structural or functional impairment of ventricular filling or blood ejection rendering the heart incapable of meeting the metabolic demands of tissues at normal venous pressures **Major Types** **By Ejection Fraction** Heart Failure with Reduced EF HFrEF LVEF 40 vs Heart Failure with Preserved EF HFpEF LVEF 50 **By Ventricular Dominance** Left sided heart failure pulmonary congestion vs Right sided heart failure systemic venous congestion **By Time Course** Acute decompensated heart failure vs Chronic stable heart failure --- **17 Cardiac Arrest** **Definition** The abrupt cessation of effective mechanical cardiac pump activity resulting in the immediate collapse of systemic blood flow characterized by unresponsiveness absent carotid pulse and apnea or agonal breathing **Immediate Emergency Response** Confirm arrest shout for help and activate the emergency response system Code Blue / AED retrieval Initiate immediate high quality CPR chest compressions at 100 120 / min 5 6 cm depth 30 2 ratio with ventilations Attach AED / defibrillator analyze rhythm and deliver immediate DC shock if shockable VF or pulseless VT --- **18 Cardiomyopathy** **Definition** A diverse group of intrinsic myocardial disorders associated with mechanical and / or electrical cardiac dysfunction not secondary to coronary disease systemic hypertension valvular lesions or congenital heart disease **Major Types** Dilated Cardiomyopathy DCM Hypertrophic Cardiomyopathy HCM Restrictive Cardiomyopathy RCM and Arrhythmogenic Right Ventricular Cardiomyopathy ARVC --- **19 Infective Endocarditis IE** **Definition** A serious invasive microbial infection of the endocardial surface of the heart characterized by the formation of bulky friable vegetations composed of fibrin platelets and microorganisms on the cardiac valves **Common Complications** Acute valvular regurgitation congestive heart failure perivalvular ring abscesses systemic septic embolization cerebral stroke splenic / renal infarction mycotic aneurysms and glomerulonephritis --- **20 Shock** **Definition** A life threatening state of acute systemic circulatory failure characterized by inadequate tissue and cellular microvascular perfusion resulting in cellular dysoxia anaerobic metabolism and progressive multi organ failure **Major Types** **Hypovolemic** Depletion of intravascular volume acute hemorrhage severe dehydration plasma loss in burns **Cardiogenic** Primary pump failure acute myocardial infarction severe acute myocarditis malignant arrhythmias **Distributive** Profound systemic vasodilation septic shock anaphylactic shock neurogenic spinal shock **Obstructive** Physical mechanical impedance to cardiac filling or output cardiac tamponade tension pneumothorax pulmonary embolism --- **PART III EMERGENCY CARE CRITICAL CARE CLINICAL DIAGNOSTICS** --- **21 Hemorrhage** **Definition** The escape or extravasation of whole blood from the intravascular lumen into extravascular tissues body cavities or the external environment following disruption trauma or ulceration of vessel walls **Major Types** **By Vessel** Arterial pulsatile bright red Venous steady dark red Capillary generalized oozing **By Location** External visible bleeding vs Internal hidden in serous cavities / tissues hemothorax hemoperitoneum **By Timing** Primary at time of trauma Reactionary within 24 hours Secondary 7 14 days later due to sepsis --- **22 Septicemia** **Definition** A severe life threatening systemic infection caused by the active multiplication and persistence of virulent bacteria and their toxins in the circulating blood precipitating a dysregulated systemic host inflammatory response **Common Clinical Features** High swinging fever with shaking chills rigors or hypothermia 36 C resting tachycardia 90 bpm tachypnea 20 bpm systemic arterial hypotension altered mental status diaphoresis and progressive oliguria --- **23 Basic Life Support BLS** **Definition** The standardized level of non invasive emergency medical care provided to victims of cardiopulmonary arrest acute airway obstruction or drowning prior to the availability of advanced cardiac life support ACLS **Main Components** Early recognition of cardiac arrest and activation of emergency response high quality cardiopulmonary resuscitation CPR with emphasis on chest compressions early automated external defibrillation AED and foreign body airway clearance maneuvers --- **24 Cardiopulmonary Resuscitation CPR** **Definition** An emergency life saving procedure consisting of external rhythmic manual chest compressions combined with positive pressure rescue ventilations delivered to a victim in cardiac or respiratory arrest **Primary Purpose** To maintain artificial forward perfusion to the coronary arteries and brain sustaining minimal vital organ cellular oxygenation and viability until spontaneous circulation ROSC is restored or definitive therapy is delivered --- **25 Mechanical Ventilation** **Definition** An advanced supportive medical intervention in which an automated machine ventilator is used to assist or completely replace spontaneous pulmonary gas exchange and work of breathing **Two Major Indications** Acute respiratory failure refractory to conservative therapy severe hypoxemic ARDS or acute hypercapnic COPD decompensation Airway protection and loss of neurological respiratory drive severe coma with GCS 8 acute drug toxicity or general anesthesia --- **26 Arterial Blood Gas ABG Analysis** **Definition** A quantitative point of care laboratory evaluation performed on whole arterial blood commonly sampled from the radial artery to measure partial pressures of gases PaO2 PaCO2 pH and bicarbonate concentrations HCO3 **Clinical Significance** Provides rapid objective assessment of alveolar ventilation pulmonary oxygenation efficiency and acid base homeostasis metabolic / respiratory acidosis and alkalosis guiding ventilator management and critical care therapy --- **27 Electrocardiogram ECG** **Definition** A non invasive diagnostic recording of the bioelectrical potentials and cardiac vector voltages generated by myocardial depolarization and repolarization recorded through skin surface electrodes **Major Waves** **P wave** Atrial depolarization **QRS complex** Rapid ventricular depolarization and masked atrial repolarization **T wave** Ventricular repolarization U wave Inconstant repolarization of Purkinje fibers / papillary muscles --- **28 Oxygen Therapy** **Definition** The controlled medical administration of supplemental oxygen at concentrations higher than ambient air FiO2 21 to prevent treat or reverse tissue hypoxia and alleviate cardiopulmonary work **Common Indications** Documented acute hypoxemia SpO2 90 or PaO2 60 mmHg acute myocardial infarction systemic shock states severe trauma and acute carbon monoxide poisoning --- **PART IV DERMATOLOGY INFECTIOUS DISEASES** --- **29 Psoriasis** **Definition** A chronic immune mediated non contagious systemic inflammatory dermatosis driven by T helper lymphocytes resulting in marked hyperproliferation and abnormal differentiation of epidermal keratinocytes **Characteristic Clinical Feature** Sharply demarcated erythematous plaques topped with silvery white micaceous scales on extensor surfaces exhibiting pinpoint capillary bleeding upon scale removal Auspitz sign and lesion development at sites of injury Koebner phenomenon --- **30 Eczema Dermatitis** **Definition** A non contagious inflammatory skin disorder characterized histologically by epidermal spongiosis and clinically by intense pruritus erythema edema and vesiculation acutely progressing to lichenification chronically **Common Types** Atopic dermatitis Allergic contact dermatitis Irritant contact dermatitis Seborrheic dermatitis and Dyshidrotic eczema pompholyx --- **31 Urticaria Hives** **Definition** A transient vascular cutaneous reaction characterized by the abrupt appearance of intensely pruritic erythematous edematous plaques with central pallor wheals caused by mast cell histamine release **Common Triggers** Food allergens shellfish nuts eggs drugs penicillin NSAIDs ACE inhibitors viral or parasitic infections insect envenomation and physical triggers dermographism heat cold localized pressure --- **32 Acne Acne Vulgaris** **Definition** A chronic inflammatory disease of the pilosebaceous units driven by follicular hyperkeratinization sebum overproduction under androgenic influence Cutibacterium acnes proliferation and perifollicular inflammation **Common Types** **Non inflammatory** Open comedones blackheads and closed comedones whiteheads **Inflammatory** Papular acne pustular acne and nodulocystic acne including severe forms like acne conglobata --- **33 Vitiligo** **Definition** An acquired progressive chronic autoimmune skin disease characterized by the targeted immune mediated destruction of epidermal melanocytes leading to complete absence of melanin pigment **Characteristic Clinical Presentation** Asymptomatic well circumscribed chalk white or amelanotic macules and patches of normal cutaneous texture frequently exhibiting bilateral symmetrical distribution over extensor surfaces hands and periorificial areas --- **34 Leprosy Hansens Disease** **Definition** A chronic granulomatous infection caused by Mycobacterium leprae an obligate intracellular acid fast bacillus displaying unique tropism for the skin upper respiratory mucosa and peripheral nerve Schwann cells **Major Neurological Complications** Peripheral sensorimotor neuropathy with painless glove and stocking sensory loss nerve thickening neuropathic plantar ulcerations and peripheral paralyses claw hand ulnar nerve wrist drop radial nerve foot drop common peroneal nerve and lagophthalmos facial nerve --- **PART V CLINICAL NUTRITION MATERNAL HEALTH OB GYN** --- **35 Protein Energy Malnutrition PEM** **Definition** A broad spectrum of nutritional deficiency disorders resulting from insufficient dietary intake poor absorption or hypercatabolic wasting of proteins and energy needed to sustain growth and physiological homeostasis **Major Types** **Kwashiorkor** Predominant protein deficiency with adequate carbohydrates presents with generalized pitting edema flaky paint dermatosis sparse depigmented hair moon facies and hepatomegaly **Marasmus** Severe deficiency of both total calories and protein presents with extreme somatic muscle wasting loss of subcutaneous fat and wizened old man facies without edema **Marasmic Kwashiorkor** Severe muscle and fat wasting combined with peripheral edema --- **36 Vitamin Deficiency Disease** **Definition** A specific pathologic nutritional disorder caused by chronic inadequate dietary intake impaired gastrointestinal absorption or metabolic derangement of one or more vital micronutrients vitamins **Two Examples** **Scurvy** Vitamin C ascorbic acid deficiency impaired collagen synthesis resulting in swollen bleeding gums perifollicular petechiae subperiosteal hematomas and delayed wound healing **Rickets in children / Osteomalacia in adults** Vitamin D deficiency impaired mineralization of bone matrix and growth plates leading to bowing of long legs and rachitic rosary --- **37 Antenatal Care ANC** **Definition** Comprehensive continuous clinical nutritional and preventive healthcare provided by skilled medical professionals to a pregnant woman throughout the gestational period from conception until labor **Core Objectives** Monitor maternal fetal physical well being detect and manage high risk obstetrical complications early pre eclampsia gestational diabetes severe anemia provide micronutrient prophylaxis iron folate and prepare the mother for safe delivery and breastfeeding --- **38 Postnatal Care PNC** **Definition** The specialized medical diagnostic and supportive health surveillance provided to the mother and newborn infant immediately after parturition through the puerperium traditionally 6 weeks or 42 days postpartum **Clinical Importance** Immediate detection and prevention of major postpartum morbidities postpartum hemorrhage puerperal sepsis thromboembolism postpartum depression neonatal evaluation reinforcement of exclusive breastfeeding and postpartum contraception counseling --- **39 Menopause** **Definition** The permanent physiological cessation of menses resulting from the irreversible exhaustion of ovarian follicular reserves and loss of ovarian estradiol production established clinically after 12 consecutive months of amenorrhea **Common Symptoms** Vasomotor symptoms hot flashes night sweats sleep disturbances urogenital atrophy vaginal dryness dyspareunia urinary frequency mood swings and irritability and decreased libido --- **40 Infertility** **Definition** A disease of the male or female reproductive tract defined by the failure to achieve a successful clinical pregnancy after 12 continuous months or more of regular unprotected heterosexual intercourse without contraception **Major Causes** **Female Factors 40 50** Ovulatory dysfunction PCOS tubal occlusion / pelvic adhesions PID endometriosis uterine fibroids **Male Factors 30 40** Semen abnormalities oligo / astheno / teratozoospermia varicocele endocrine disorders obstructive azoospermia **Combined / Unexplained Factors 10 20** --- **41 Urinary Incontinence** **Definition** The involuntary uncontrollable loss or leakage of urine that is objectively demonstrable and causes physical hygiene emotional or social impairment **Major Types** **Stress Incontinence** Involuntary leakage during coughing laughing or lifting due to pelvic floor laxity or urethral hypermobility **Urge Incontinence** Involuntary leakage preceded by an urgent sudden urge to void caused by detrusor overactivity **Overflow Incontinence** Involuntary dribbling from a chronically overdistended bladder obstruction or underactive bladder **Functional Incontinence** Incontinence secondary to physical cognitive or environmental impediments preventing normal toilet access --- **42 Hysterectomy** **Definition** The surgical excision and removal of the uterus categorized as total body and cervix removed or subtotal / supracervical body removed cervix preserved via abdominal vaginal or laparoscopic routes **Common Indications** Symptomatic uterine leiomyomas fibroids unresponsive to medical therapy refractory abnormal uterine bleeding gynecological malignancies endometrial cervical or ovarian cancer severe uterine prolapse and debilitating endometriosis / adenomyosis --- **43 Dilatation and Curettage D C** **Definition** A minor gynecological operative procedure involving the gradual mechanical enlargement / dilatation of the cervical canal followed by the scraping or vacuum evacuation curettage of the endometrial lining **Key Indications** **Diagnostic** Evaluation of postmenopausal bleeding abnormal uterine bleeding or suspected endometrial hyperplasia and neoplasia **Therapeutic** Evacuation of retained products of conception following incomplete or missed abortion management of acute heavy uterine bleeding or polyp excision --- **44 Pre eclampsia** **Definition** A multisystem disorder of pregnancy characterized by the new development of arterial hypertension 140 / 90 mmHg presenting after 20 weeks of gestation in a previously normotensive female accompanied by proteinuria and / or maternal organ dysfunction **Major Clinical Features** Persistent gestational hypertension significant proteinuria 300 mg / 24 h rapid pathological facial and non dependent hand edema throbbing frontal headache scotomata and visual blurriness epigastric or right upper quadrant abdominal tenderness and thrombocytopenia --- **45 Sexually Transmitted Diseases STDs** **Definition** A heterogeneous group of communicable infectious syndromes caused by bacteria viruses parasites or fungi that are predominantly spread from person to person through unprotected sexual intercourse vaginal anal or oral **Two Classical Examples** **Syphilis** A chronic systemic venereal infection caused by the spirochete Treponema pallidum presenting primarily with an indurated painless chancre **Gonorrhea** An acute purulent mucosal infection of the genitourinary tract caused by the Gram negative diplococcus Neisseria gonorrhoeae

Medical & Allied Health Sciences: Master Examination Guide
Comprehensive 32-Question Master Bank (05-Mark Long-Form Model Answers)
QUESTIONS 01 – 32 5-MARK EXAMINATION FORMAT SYSTEMIC PATHOLOGY • CRITICAL CARE • DERMATOLOGY • OB-GYN
PART I: RESPIRATORY PATHOLOGY & PULMONARY MEDICINE (Q01 – Q07)
Q 01 Acute Bronchitis
Definition: An acute, self-limiting inflammation of the tracheobronchial mucosa presenting characteristically with persistent cough with or
without sputum production.
Etiology:
Viral (>90%): Influenza A/B, Parainfluenza, RSV, Rhinovirus, Adenovirus, Coronavirus.
Bacterial (<10%):Mycoplasma pneumoniae, Chlamydophila pneumoniae, Bordetella pertussis.
Non-Infectious: Chemical fumes, dusts, tobacco smoke, air pollutants.
Clinical Features: Persistent cough (initially dry/hacking, later mucoid or purulent, lasting 1–3 weeks); retrosternal burning soreness on
coughing; low-grade fever, malaise, myalgias; scattered expiratory wheezes/rhonchi and coarse crackles that clear upon coughing.
Investigations: Primarily clinical diagnosis. Chest X-ray (PA view) is usually normal; indicated to exclude pneumonia if tachypnea,
tachycardia, high fever, or consolidation signs are present. Sputum PCR only for suspected B. pertussis.
Complications: Secondary bronchopneumonia, acute asthma/COPD exacerbation, chronic post-infectious bronchial
hyperresponsiveness (>4 weeks).
Management: Supportive hydration and steam inhalation; Paracetamol/Ibuprofen for chest soreness and fever; Dextromethorphan for
disruptive dry cough; inhaled Salbutamol for bronchospasm/wheeze. Routine antibiotics are not recommended unless elderly with
comorbidities or confirmed pertussis (Azithromycin).
Q 02 Bronchial Pneumonia (Bronchopneumonia)
Definition: Acute suppurative inflammation of the pulmonary parenchyma centered around terminal and respiratory bronchioles,
presenting with patchy, multifocal consolidation involving multiple pulmonary lobes.
Causes: Bacterial: Streptococcus pneumoniae, Staphylococcus aureus, Klebsiella pneumoniae, Pseudomonas aeruginosa, H.
influenzae. Predisposing factors include extremes of age, aspiration, malnutrition, post-viral airway injury, and immobilization.
Clinical Presentation: High-grade fever with chills/rigors, productive cough with purulent/rust-colored sputum, progressive dyspnea,
pleuritic chest pain; tachypnea, localized dullness on percussion, bronchial breath sounds, increased vocal resonance, and coarse
inspiratory crackles.
Investigations: Chest X-ray (shows bilateral patchy, mottled opacities centered around bronchi); Sputum Gram stain and culture/
sensitivity; blood cultures; CBC (leukocytosis with left shift, elevated CRP/ESR); ABG for hypoxemia.
Complications: Parapneumonic effusion, empyema thoracis, lung abscess formation, sepsis/septic shock, Type 1 respiratory failure,
and ARDS.
Treatment: Supplemental O2 (target SpO2 ≥92%); IV fluids and chest physiotherapy; Empiric antibiotics: IV Ceftriaxone or Amoxicillin
clavulanate plus Azithromycin (community-acquired); Piperacillin-tazobactam or Meropenem plus Vancomycin for hospital-acquired/
MRSA; tailored to culture sensitivities for 7–10 days.

Medical & Allied Health Sciences Examination Series • 5-Mark Long-Form Outlines Page 1 of 12
Q 03 Pleural Effusion
Definition: Pathological accumulation of excess fluid within the pleural cavity (>15 mL) resulting from an imbalance between fluid
formation and absorption.
Types & Causes:
Transudative (Altered Starling forces): Congestive heart failure, liver cirrhosis with ascites, nephrotic syndrome, severe
hypoalbuminemia.
Exudative (Inflammatory/vascular permeability): Parapneumonic infection, tuberculosis, bronchogenic/metastatic carcinoma,
pulmonary infarction/PE, autoimmune diseases (SLE, RA).
Clinical Features: Progressive exertional dyspnea, pleuritic chest pain, dry cough; decreased chest expansion on affected side,
contralateral mediastinal shift (massive effusion), stony dull percussion note, absent/diminished breath sounds and vocal resonance.
Investigations: Chest X-ray (costophrenic angle blunting >175 mL, homogenous opacity with lateral upward-curving meniscus sign);
Thoracic Ultrasound; Diagnostic thoracocentesis using Light's Criteria for exudates (Fluid/Serum Protein >0.5, Fluid/Serum LDH >0.6,
or Fluid LDH >2/3 upper limit of serum LDH); ADA (>40 U/L indicates TB), cytology, and microbiology.
Management: Treat etiology (diuretics for CHF; ATT for TB; chemotherapy for malignancy); Therapeutic thoracocentesis (drain ≤1,000
1,500 mL/session); Intercostal chest drain (ICD) for empyema (pH <7.20) or hemothorax; Chemical pleurodesis (talc, bleomycin) for
recurrent malignant effusions.
Q 04 Pneumothorax
Definition: Accumulation of free air within the pleural space between the parietal and visceral pleura, causing partial or complete lung
collapse.
Types & Causes:
Spontaneous: Primary (rupture of subpleural apical blebs in tall, young men); Secondary (COPD bullae, cavitary TB, cystic fibrosis).
Traumatic / Iatrogenic: Penetrating/blunt chest trauma, rib fractures, subclavian line placement, pleural biopsy, mechanical
barotrauma.
Tension Pneumothorax: One-way valve mechanism allowing air entry during inspiration but trapping air on expiration, generating
massive intrapleural pressure.
Clinical Features: Sudden unilateral sharp pleuritic chest pain and dyspnea; decreased expansion, hyperresonant percussion note,
absent/diminished breath sounds. Tension hallmark: cyanosis, hypotension, tachycardia, tracheal deviation to the contralateral side, and
distended neck veins.
Complications: Obstructive shock, severe hypoxemic respiratory failure, hemopneumothorax, re-expansion pulmonary edema.
Emergency Management:
Tension Pneumothorax: Immediate emergency needle decompression (14–16G cannula in 2nd ICS midclavicular line or 4th/5th ICS
anterior axillary line) without awaiting X-ray.
Definitive Tube Thoracostomy: Intercostal chest tube (ICD) with underwater seal inserted in the safe triangle.
High-flow supplemental oxygen (accelerates pleural air resorption); VATS pleurodesis for persistent leaks (>48h) or recurrence.
Q 05 Lung Abscess
Definition: Localized parenchymal microbial necrosis and cavity formation containing purulent necrotic debris and fluid.
Etiology: Aspiration of oral/gastric secretions containing anaerobes (Peptostreptococcus, Bacteroides, Fusobacterium) in patients with
impaired consciousness (alcoholism, stroke, epilepsy) or poor dentition; Necrotizing pneumonia (S. aureus, Klebsiella); Bronchial
obstruction by carcinoma; Septic emboli (tricuspid endocarditis).
Clinical Manifestations: High swinging fever with rigors and night sweats, malaise, progressive weight loss; cough productive of
copious, foul-smelling, putrid purulent sputum; hemoptysis; pallor, rapid finger clubbing, dullness to percussion, and cavernous/amphoric
breath sounds over cavity.
Investigations: Chest X-ray (thick-walled solitary cavity with a prominent air-fluid level surrounded by consolidation); CECT Chest
(delineates cavity and excludes empyema); Sputum microbiology (Gram, AFB, culture); Bronchoscopy to exclude obstructing
endobronchial neoplasm.
Complications: Empyema/pyopneumothorax, bronchopleural fistula, massive fatal hemoptysis, metastatic brain abscess, secondary
amyloidosis.
Treatment: Prolonged antimicrobial therapy (4–8 weeks): IV Ampicillin-sulbactam, Amoxicillin-clavulanate, or Clindamycin, transitioned
to oral; Postural drainage and chest physiotherapy; Percutaneous catheter drainage for refractory cavities >6 cm; Surgical lobectomy for
massive hemoptysis or suspected underlying malignancy.

Q 06 Respiratory Failure
Definition: Inability of the respiratory system to maintain adequate gas exchange, defined as arterial PaO2 <60 mmHg with or without
PaCO2 >50 mmHg on ambient air at sea level.
Types & Causes:
Type 1 (Hypoxemic): PaO2 <60 mmHg with normal/low PaCO2. Caused by V/Q mismatch and right-to-left shunting: ARDS, severe
pneumonia, acute pulmonary edema, massive PE, diffuse interstitial fibrosis.
Type 2 (Hypercapnic): PaCO2 >50 mmHg with companion hypoxemia. Caused by alveolar hypoventilation/pump failure: severe
COPD, acute severe asthma, opioid overdose, myasthenia gravis, Guillain-Barré, severe kyphoscoliosis.
Clinical Features: Hypoxemia: dyspnea, tachypnea, tachycardia, central cyanosis, restlessness, confusion. Hypercapnia: bounding
pulses, warm flushed hands, morning headache, asterixis (flapping tremor), somnolence, and CO2 narcosis/coma.
Investigations: Arterial Blood Gas (ABG) analysis (confirms diagnosis, defines acidosis/alkalosis and compensation); Continuous pulse
oximetry; Chest X-ray and CT thorax; Spirometry.
Management: Controlled oxygen therapy (target SpO2 94–98% in Type 1; strictly 88–92% using a Venturi mask in Type 2 COPD to
preserve hypoxic drive); Non-Invasive Ventilation (BiPAP) for hypercapnic COPD exacerbations; Invasive mechanical ventilation if severe
acidosis (pH <7.25), exhaustion, or coma; Bronchodilators, systemic steroids, diuretics, and antidotes (Naloxone).
Q 07 Occupational Lung Diseases
Definition: Preventable non-neoplastic and neoplastic disorders caused by repeated inhalation of mineral dusts, organic particles,
fumes, or toxic gases in the work environment.
Causes & Common Types:
Silicosis: Inhalation of crystalline SiO2 in stone cutting, sandblasting, quarrying, foundry work; produces fibrotic silicotic nodules and
high risk of tuberculosis (silicotuberculosis).
Asbestosis: Inhalation of asbestos fibers in shipbuilding, demolition, roofing; causes bibasilar interstitial fibrosis, calcified pleural
plaques, and malignant mesothelioma.
Coal Workers' Pneumoconiosis (CWP): Coal dust inhalation leading to anthracosis and progressive massive fibrosis.
Organic: Byssinosis (cotton dust, "Monday chest tightness"), Farmer's lung (thermophilic actinomycetes in moldy hay).
Clinical Features: Insidious exertional dyspnea, chronic dry or productive cough (melanoptysis in CWP), wheezing, bibasilar end
inspiratory crackles, reduced chest expansion, digital clubbing, and late cor pulmonale.
Prevention: Engineering controls (wet drilling, local exhaust ventilation, toxic material substitution); Administrative controls (worker
rotation); PPE (certified N95/HEPA particulate respirators); Periodic medical screening with spirometry and chest X-rays (ILO
classification).
Management: Immediate permanent removal from dust exposure; Bronchodilators and supplemental O2; Pneumococcal and influenza
vaccination; Tuberculosis screening; Pulmonary rehabilitation; Medico-legal compensation.
PART II: CARDIOVASCULAR PATHOLOGY & HEMODYNAMICS (Q08 – Q15)
Q 08 Atherosclerosis
Definition: Chronic inflammatory disease of large/medium muscular and elastic arteries characterized by intimal fibrofatty plaques
(atheromas) narrowing the lumen and weakening the arterial wall.
Major Risk Factors: Modifiable: Dyslipidemia (high LDL, low HDL), systemic hypertension, cigarette smoking, diabetes mellitus, visceral
obesity, sedentary life. Non-modifiable: Advancing age, male sex, family history of premature CAD.
Clinical Manifestations: Coronary: stable angina, acute myocardial infarction; Cerebral: TIAs, ischemic stroke; Peripheral: intermittent
claudication, critical limb ischemia; Renal: renovascular hypertension.
Complications: Acute plaque rupture with occlusive luminal thrombosis, aneurysmal dilatation/rupture (abdominal aorta),
atheroembolism, and progressive ischemic cardiomyopathy.
Investigations: Fasting lipid profile, HbA1c, hs-CRP; ECG and treadmill exercise test (TMT); Carotid Doppler (intima-media thickness)
and Ankle-Brachial Index (ABI <0.9); Coronary CT angiography and conventional catheter angiography.
Management: Lifestyle: Mediterranean diet, aerobic exercise, smoking cessation; Pharmacotherapy: High-intensity statins (Atorvastatin
40–80 mg to achieve LDL <55 mg/dL), low-dose Aspirin (75–100 mg), ACE inhibitors, tight glycemic/BP control; Revascularization: PCI
with drug-eluting stents, CABG, or endarterectomy.
