Q 09 Thrombosis and Embolism
Definitions: Thrombosis is the intravascular formation of a solid/semisolid mass of fibrin, platelets, and cells in intact unruptured vessels
during life. Embolism is the mechanical occlusion of a vessel by a detached intravascular mass transported away from its origin.
Causes (Virchow's Triad): 1. Endothelial injury (atherosclerosis, trauma, vasculitis); 2. Altered blood flow (venous stasis from
immobility, turbulence from aneurysms); 3. Hypercoagulability (Factor V Leiden, malignancy, antiphospholipid syndrome, oral
contraceptives). Emboli arise from dislodged DVTs, cardiac mural thrombi (atrial fibrillation), fat (fractures), air, or septic vegetations.
Clinical Features: DVT: Unilateral calf swelling, calf pain, erythema, tenderness, positive Homans sign; Pulmonary Embolism: acute
dyspnea, pleuritic chest pain, tachypnea, tachycardia, hemoptysis, syncope; Acute Arterial Embolism (6 Ps): Pain, Pallor, Pulselessness,
Paresthesia, Paralysis, Poikilothermia.
Complications: Fatal massive PE with obstructive shock, ischemic stroke, acute mesenteric ischemia, post-thrombotic syndrome.
Diagnosis: Compression Duplex ultrasound (DVT); quantitative D-dimer assay; CT Pulmonary Angiography (CTPA, gold standard for
PE); Arterial Doppler and CT angiography.
Management: Anticoagulation: LMWH (Enoxaparin 1 mg/kg SC q12h) or unfractionated heparin, transitioned to DOACs (Apixaban,
Rivaroxaban) or Warfarin (target INR 2.0–3.0) for 3–6 months; Thrombolysis (r-tPA / Alteplase) for massive PE with shock or acute
ischemic stroke <4.5h; Catheter thrombectomy, surgical embolectomy, and IVC filter placement.
Q 10 Ischemic Heart Disease (IHD)
Definition: Cardiac syndromes resulting from an imbalance between myocardial oxygen supply and demand, predominantly caused by
fixed atherosclerotic narrowing of epicardial coronary arteries.
Risk Factors: Dyslipidemia, hypertension, cigarette smoking, diabetes mellitus, visceral obesity, metabolic syndrome, male sex, older
age, family history.
Clinical Features: Stable angina: retrosternal tightness/pressure radiating to left arm/neck/jaw, provoked by exertion, relieved by rest or
sublingual nitroglycerin within 2–5 min; Acute Coronary Syndromes (NSTEMI/STEMI): severe crushing retrosternal pain lasting >20 min,
occurring at rest, accompanied by diaphoresis, nausea, dyspnea, and syncope.
Investigations: 12-lead ECG (ST elevation in STEMI, ST depression/T inversion in ischemia/NSTEMI); Cardiac biomarkers (hs-cTnI, hs
cTnT, CK-MB); Echocardiography (regional wall motion abnormalities, LVEF); Coronary angiography (gold standard).
Complications: Malignant ventricular arrhythmias (VT/VF), sudden cardiac death, cardiogenic shock, congestive heart failure, papillary
muscle rupture with acute mitral regurgitation, ventricular free-wall/septal rupture.
Treatment: Acute ACS: Oxygen (if SpO2 <90%), sublingual Nitroglycerin, chewable Aspirin (300 mg) plus P2Y12 inhibitor (Ticagrelor
180 mg or Clopidogrel 600 mg), Enoxaparin; Primary PCI (<90 min door-to-balloon) or thrombolysis (<120 min); Long-term: dual
antiplatelet therapy, high-intensity statin, cardioselective beta-blocker, and ACE inhibitor.
Q 11 Cardiac Failure (Heart Failure)
Definition: Complex clinical syndrome resulting from structural or functional impairment of ventricular filling or blood ejection, leaving the
heart unable to meet the metabolic demands of tissues at normal venous pressures.
Types & Causes:
Types: HFrEF (systolic, LVEF ≤40%); HFpEF (diastolic, LVEF ≥50%); Left-sided vs. Right-sided; Acute vs. Chronic.
Causes: Coronary artery disease and myocardial infarction (most common), chronic hypertension, valvular heart disease, dilated
cardiomyopathies, cor pulmonale.
Clinical Manifestations: Left-sided (Pulmonary congestion): exertional dyspnea, orthopnea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea (PND),
bibasilar crackles, S3 gallop; Right-sided (Systemic venous congestion): elevated JVP, bilateral pitting pedal edema, congestive
hepatomegaly, ascites.
Complications: Acute pulmonary edema, ventricular arrhythmias, cardiorenal syndrome, cardiac cirrhosis, mural thrombi with systemic
embolism.
Management: Lifestyle: dietary sodium (<2 g/day) and fluid restriction, weight monitoring; Guideline-Directed Medical Therapy (GDMT 
4 Pillars for HFrEF): 1. ARNI (Sacubitril-valsartan) or ACEi/ARB; 2. Beta-blocker (Carvedilol, Bisoprolol, Metoprolol succinate); 3. MRA
(Spironolactone); 4. SGLT2 inhibitor (Dapagliflozin/Empagliflozin); Diuretics (Furosemide) for volume overload; Device therapy: ICD and
CRT-D; LVAD or heart transplantation.

Q 12 Rheumatic Heart Disease (RHD)
Definition: Chronic permanent cardiac valvular damage resulting from single or recurrent episodes of acute rheumatic fever (ARF)
initiated by untreated Group A β-hemolytic streptococcal (GAS) pharyngitis.
Etiology & Pathogenesis:Streptococcus pyogenes. Driven by molecular mimicry: streptococcal M-protein cross-reacts with human
cardiac myosin and sarcolemma, producing pancarditis with pathognomonic granulomatous Aschoff bodies.
Clinical Features: History of ARF (Jones criteria). Valvular involvement (Mitral >90%, then Aortic): 
Mitral Stenosis: Exertional dyspnea, hemoptysis, malar flush, tapping apex beat, loud S1, opening snap, low-pitched rumbling mid
diastolic murmur at the apex.
Mitral Regurgitation: Holosystolic murmur radiating to axilla; Aortic lesions cause early diastolic decrescendo murmur.
Complications: Congestive heart failure, atrial fibrillation, left atrial mural thrombi with stroke, and infective endocarditis.
Investigations: Doppler Echocardiography (shows thickened valve leaflets, chordal shortening, "hockey-stick" anterior mitral leaflet,
pressure gradients); 12-lead ECG (left atrial enlargement / P-mitrale, AF); Chest X-ray (straightening of left heart border, double right
contour); Elevated ASO titer.
Management: Secondary penicillin prophylaxis: Benzathine penicillin G (1.2 million units IM q3–4 weeks) for at least 10 years or until
age 40; Medical: diuretics, beta-blockers/digoxin for AF, Warfarin anticoagulation (target INR 2.0–3.0); Surgery/Intervention:
Percutaneous Transvenous Mitral Commissurotomy (PTMC) or surgical prosthetic valve replacement.
Q 13 Cardiomyopathies
Definition: Heterogeneous group of intrinsic myocardial disorders associated with mechanical/electrical cardiac dysfunction, not
secondary to coronary disease, hypertension, or valvular disease.
Types & Causes:
Dilated (DCM): Ventricular dilatation with systolic dysfunction (LVEF <40%). Causes: idiopathic, titin mutations, viral myocarditis,
chronic alcoholism, doxorubicin toxicity, peripartum.
Hypertrophic (HCM): Asymmetric septal hypertrophy with preserved/hyperdynamic systolic function. Autosomal dominant mutation
in sarcomeric genes (β-MHC, MYBPC3).
Restrictive (RCM): Rigid, non-compliant ventricular walls causing impaired diastolic filling. Infiltrative causes: amyloidosis,
sarcoidosis, hemochromatosis.
ARVC: Fibrofatty replacement of RV myocardium predisposing to ventricular arrhythmias.
Clinical Manifestations: DCM: biventricular heart failure (dyspnea, edema, cardiomegaly, S3); HCM: dyspnea, chest pain, exertional
syncope, harsh systolic ejection murmur that intensifies with Valsalva; sudden cardiac death in athletes; RCM: severe right-sided failure,
high JVP with Kussmaul's sign.
Investigations: Echocardiography (ventricular dilation in DCM; asymmetric septal thickness ≥15 mm with systolic anterior motion of
mitral valve in HCM; bi-atrial dilatation in RCM); Cardiac MRI (Late Gadolinium Enhancement for fibrosis/amyloid); Holter ECG.
Treatment: DCM: standard GDMT (ARNI, beta-blockers, MRA, SGLT2i), ICD/CRT; HCM: non-vasodilating beta-blockers (Metoprolol),
Verapamil, Mavacamten, surgical septal myectomy, prophylactic ICD; RCM: cautious diuretics, Tafamidis for amyloidosis.

Q 14 Cardiac Arrest
Definition: Abrupt, unexpected cessation of mechanical cardiac pump activity resulting in circulatory collapse, sudden
unresponsiveness, absent central arterial pulse, and apnea or agonal gasping.
Immediate Assessment:
1. Confirm scene safety; 2. Check responsiveness (tap shoulders and shout); 3. Simultaneously assess breathing and carotid pulse
(minimum 5 sec, maximum 10 sec); 4. If pulseless and breathless, activate emergency response (Call Code Blue / EMS) and call for
an AED.
Emergency Management:
High-Quality CPR (C-A-B): Rate 100–120/min, depth 5–6 cm, allow full recoil, minimize interruptions, 30:2 compression-ventilation
ratio.
Defibrillation for Shockable Rhythms (VF / Pulseless VT): Deliver 1 unsynchronized shock (120–200 J biphasic or 360 J
monophasic); resume CPR immediately for 2 minutes without pulse check; Epinephrine 1 mg IV q3–5min after 2nd shock;
Amiodarone 300 mg IV (second dose 150 mg) for shock-refractory VF/pVT.
Non-Shockable Rhythms (Asystole / PEA): CPR in 2-min cycles; Epinephrine 1 mg IV immediately and q3–5min; Defibrillation is 
contraindicated.
Treat Reversible Causes (Hs & Ts): Hypovolemia, Hypoxia, Hydrogen ion (acidosis), Hypo/hyperkalemia, Hypothermia; Tension
pneumothorax, Tamponade, Toxins, Thrombosis (coronary/pulmonary).
Post-ROSC Care: Hemodynamic support (MAP ≥65 mmHg), targeted temperature management (32–36°C for 24h), emergency
coronary angiography.
Q 15 Cardiopulmonary Resuscitation (CPR) & Basic Life Support (BLS)
Principles: Maintains artificial coronary and cerebral perfusion via rhythmic external chest compressions and ventilations to preserve
tissue viability until ROSC is achieved. Follows the C-A-B sequence (Chest compressions prioritized over Airway and Breathing). Chain
of Survival: Early Recognition & Activation → High-Quality CPR → Rapid Defibrillation → Advanced Resuscitation → Post-Arrest Care →
Recovery.
Core Metrics of High-Quality CPR: Rate: 100–120/min; Depth: 5–6 cm (adult); Full chest recoil between compressions (avoid leaning);
Chest compression fraction >60% (target >80%); Avoid hyperventilation (500–600 mL tidal volume visible chest rise over 1 second).
Step-by-Step BLS Procedure:
1. Confirm scene safety; 2. Check responsiveness; 3. Call for help, activate EMS / Code Blue, retrieve AED; 4. Check carotid pulse
and breathing (5–10 sec); 5. If no pulse: begin chest compressions on lower half of sternum, interlocked fingers, elbows locked,
shoulders vertical; 6. Open airway (Head-Tilt–Chin-Lift; Jaw-Thrust if spinal trauma); 7. Deliver 2 rescue breaths after every 30
compressions (30:2 ratio); 8. Attach AED as soon as available, clear patient during rhythm analysis, deliver shock if indicated, and
immediately resume compressions; 9. Switch rescuers every 2 minutes (5 cycles) to prevent fatigue.
PART III: CRITICAL CARE, DIAGNOSTICS & EMERGENCY SURGERY (Q16 – Q21)
Q 16 Mechanical Ventilation
Definition: Supportive intervention using an automated positive-pressure device to assist or replace spontaneous alveolar ventilation
and pulmonary gas exchange.
Indications: Severe hypoxemic respiratory failure (ARDS, pulmonary edema); Hypercapnic respiratory failure (severe COPD,
myasthenic crisis); Airway protection / coma (GCS ≤8); General anesthesia and shock states to reduce work of breathing.
Basic Principles: Positive pressure ventilation pushes gas into lungs. Parameters: Tidal Volume (Vt, 6–8 mL/kg; 4–6 mL/kg in ARDS
lung-protective strategy), Respiratory Rate (12–16/min), FiO2 (21–100%), PEEP (5–15 cmH2O to prevent alveolar collapse), I:E ratio
(1:2).
Types & Modes: Non-Invasive (NIV: CPAP, BiPAP via mask); Invasive (via ETT/tracheostomy): Volume-Controlled (VCV), Pressure
Controlled (PCV), SIMV, and Pressure Support Ventilation (PSV).
Complications: Ventilator-Associated Pneumonia (VAP >48h post-intubation), Barotrauma/Volutrauma (pneumothorax,
pneumomediastinum), Hemodynamic hypotension (reduced venous return from positive intrathoracic pressure), and Tracheal stenosis.
Monitoring: Continuous pulse oximetry, capnography (EtCO2), serial ABGs; Peak airway pressure (<35 cmH2O), Plateau pressure
(Pplat ≤30 cmH2O); Sedation scoring (RASS), ETT depth.

Q 17 Arterial Blood Gas (ABG) Analysis
Definition & Significance: Quantitative point-of-care laboratory assessment performed on heparinized arterial blood (radial artery)
measuring gas partial pressures and pH to assess oxygenation, alveolar ventilation, and acid-base status.
Normal Ranges: pH: 7.35–7.45; PaCO2: 35–45 mmHg; HCO3-: 22–26 mEq/L; PaO2: 80–100 mmHg; Base Excess: -2 to +2 mEq/L;
SaO2: 95–100%.
Interpretation of Primary Disorders:
Respiratory Acidosis: pH <7.35, PaCO2 >45 mmHg. Due to hypoventilation (COPD, asthma, opioid overdose, neuromuscular
weakness).
Respiratory Alkalosis: pH >7.45, PaCO2 <35 mmHg. Due to hyperventilation (anxiety/panic, pulmonary embolism, early salicylate
toxicity, sepsis).
Metabolic Acidosis: pH <7.35, HCO3- <22 mEq/L. High Anion Gap (DKA, lactic acidosis, uremia, toxic alcohols); Normal Anion Gap
(severe diarrhea, RTA).
Metabolic Alkalosis: pH >7.45, HCO3- >26 mEq/L. Due to H+ loss (severe vomiting, NG suction, loop diuretics,
hyperaldosteronism).
Q 18 Electrocardiogram (ECG)
Basic Principles: Non-invasive graphic recording of cardiac bioelectrical potentials and vector voltages produced by myocardial
depolarization and repolarization, measured via 10 skin electrodes arranged in 12 standard leads (6 limb, 6 precordial).
Major Waves, Complexes & Intervals:
P wave: Atrial depolarization (<0.12s, <2.5 mm).
PR interval: AV nodal conduction delay (0.12–0.20s). Prolonged in 1st-degree AV block; short in WPW.
QRS complex: Ventricular depolarization (<0.12s). Widened in bundle branch blocks and VT.
ST segment: Isoelectric plateau phase. Elevation indicates STEMI/pericarditis; depression indicates ischemia/NSTEMI.
T wave: Ventricular repolarization. Peaked in hyperkalemia; inverted/flat in ischemia or hypokalemia.
QT interval: Total ventricular electrical cycle (depolarization + repolarization; QTc ≤0.44s men, ≤0.46s women).
Clinical Significance: Diagnostic standard for Acute Coronary Syndromes (STEMI vs. NSTEMI); dysrhythmias (AF, VT, VF, heart
blocks); chamber enlargement (LVH); electrolyte disorders (hyper/hypokalemia); and drug toxicities (digoxin).
Q 19 Shock
Definition: Life-threatening acute circulatory failure characterized by inadequate tissue and cellular microvascular perfusion, resulting in
cellular hypoxia, anaerobic metabolism (lactic acidosis), and multi-organ failure.
Types & Causes:
Hypovolemic: Hemorrhagic (trauma, GI bleed); Non-hemorrhagic (burn plasma loss, severe dehydration).
Cardiogenic: Myocardial infarction (>40% LV loss), end-stage cardiomyopathy, severe acute mitral regurgitation.
Distributive: Septic shock (bacterial endotoxemia), anaphylactic shock (Type 1 hypersensitivity), neurogenic shock (high spinal cord
injury).
Obstructive: Tension pneumothorax, massive pulmonary embolism, cardiac tamponade.
Clinical Features: Systemic hypotension (SBP <90 mmHg or MAP <65 mmHg), tachycardia (>100 bpm; bradycardia in neurogenic),
tachypnea, cold clammy pale skin with delayed capillary refill (>3s; warm flushed in early septic shock), progressive oliguria (<0.5 mL/kg/
h), confusion/coma.
Complications: Acute kidney injury, ARDS, DIC, mesenteric ischemia, MODS, and death.
Management: Airway & high-flow O2; IV access (two 14–16G cannulas) & fluid resuscitation (30 mL/kg balanced crystalloids for
hypovolemia/sepsis; restrict in cardiogenic shock); Norepinephrine (first-line vasopressor targeting MAP ≥65 mmHg); Dobutamine for
cardiogenic inotropic support; Epinephrine IM (0.3–0.5 mg 1:1,000) for anaphylaxis; Emergency cause-specific relief: blood transfusion
for trauma, needle decompression for tension pneumothorax, pericardiocentesis for tamponade, PCI for cardiogenic MI.

Q 20 Burns
Classification:
Depth: Superficial (1st degree: red, dry, painful, heals <6d); Superficial partial-thickness (2nd degree: pink, weeping, thin blisters,
very painful); Deep partial-thickness (mottled white/red, reduced sensation, scarring); Full-thickness (3rd degree: leathery, charred,
dry, anesthetic); 4th degree (involves muscle/bone).
Wallace's Rule of Nines (% TBSA in adults): Head & neck: 9%; Each arm: 9%; Anterior trunk: 18%; Posterior trunk: 18%; Each leg:
18%; Perineum: 1%. (Patient's palm = 1%).
Clinical Assessment: Primary survey (ABCDE); Rule out inhalation injury (facial burns, singed nasal hairs, soot in sputum, stridor);
Calculate % TBSA (excluding 1st degree).
Complications: Hypovolemic burn shock, carbon monoxide toxicity, compartment syndrome from circumferential eschar, burn wound
sepsis (Pseudomonas, S. aureus), Curling's stress ulcer, contractures, Marjolin's carcinoma.
Principles of Management:
Stop burning, cool with tap water (15–20 min, no ice); Early intubation if inhalation injury suspected.
Parkland Formula Resuscitation (>15–20% TBSA): Total Ringer's Lactate in 24 hours = 4 mL × Weight (kg) × % TBSA. Give 50%
in first 8 hours (from burn time), remaining 50% over next 16 hours. Titrate to urine output (0.5–1.0 mL/kg/h).
Wound debridement, topical Silver Sulfadiazine cream; IV Morphine; Tetanus prophylaxis; Emergency escharotomy for circumferential
chest/limb burns; Early tangential excision and skin grafting (3–7 days).
Q 21 Septicemia
Definition: Life-threatening systemic infection characterized by the active multiplication and persistence of pathogenic microbes and
toxins in the bloodstream, triggering a dysregulated host response and acute end-organ dysfunction.
Causes: Gram-negative bacilli (E. coli, Klebsiella, Pseudomonas, Acinetobacter); Gram-positive cocci (S. aureus/MRSA, S.
pneumoniae, Enterococcus); Fungi (Candida). Primary foci: pneumonia, urosepsis, intra-abdominal peritonitis, central line infections.
Clinical Manifestations: High swinging fever with rigors or hypothermia (<36°C), resting tachycardia (>90 bpm), tachypnea (>20 bpm),
hypotension (SBP <90 mmHg), warm flushed skin transitioning to cold mottled cyanosis, petechiae/purpura, delirium, and oliguria.
Complications: Septic shock (hypotension requiring vasopressors with serum lactate >2 mmol/L), DIC, ARDS, acute tubular necrosis,
and MODS.
Investigations: Blood cultures (2 sets drawn prior to antibiotics), paired sputum/urine cultures; CBC (leukocytosis >12,000/μL or
leukopenia <4,000/μL, thrombocytopenia); Serum lactate (>2 mmol/L); Elevated Procalcitonin and CRP; PT/INR, aPTT, D-dimer.
Management (Surviving Sepsis Hour-1 Bundle):
1. Measure blood lactate; 2. Blood cultures before antibiotics; 3. Administer empiric broad-spectrum IV antimicrobials within 1 hour
(e.g., Piperacillin-tazobactam plus Vancomycin); 4. Rapid 30 mL/kg balanced crystalloids for hypotension or lactate ≥4 mmol/L; 5.
Norepinephrine to maintain MAP ≥65 mmHg; 6. Prompt infectious source control (drain abscesses, remove infected lines).
PART IV: DERMATOLOGY & CLINICAL NUTRITION (Q22 – Q26)
Q 22 Psoriasis
Etiology & Pathogenesis: Chronic immune-mediated dermatosis characterized by accelerated epidermal cell turnover (3–5 days vs.
normal 28 days) driven by T-helper lymphocytes (Th1/Th17) releasing TNF-α, IL-17, and IL-23. Strongly linked to HLA-Cw6. Triggers:
physical trauma (Koebner phenomenon), streptococcal pharyngitis, stress, drugs (beta-blockers, lithium, NSAIDs, steroid withdrawal).
Clinical Features: Sharply demarcated salmon-pink erythematous plaques covered by silvery-white micaceous scales on extensor
surfaces (knees, elbows, scalp, sacrum). Signs: Auspitz sign (pinpoint bleeding on removing scales) and Koebner phenomenon. Nail
changes (pitting, onycholysis, subungual hyperkeratosis, oil-drop sign). Variants: plaque, guttate, inverse, pustular, and erythrodermic.
Complications: Psoriatic arthritis (PsA in 30%), life-threatening erythroderma (>90% TBSA involvement), severe metabolic syndrome,
cardiovascular disease, and depression.
Treatment: Topical: potent corticosteroids (Clobetasol), Calcipotriol (vitamin D3 analogue), keratolytics (salicylic acid), calcineurin
inhibitors (tacrolimus for flexures); Phototherapy: Narrowband UVB (311 nm) or PUVA; Systemic: Methotrexate (7.5–25 mg/week),
Cyclosporine, Acitretin; Biologics: anti-TNF (Adalimumab), anti-IL-17 (Secukinumab), anti-IL-23 (Guselkumab).

Q 23 Eczema and Dermatitis
Definition & Causes: Non-contagious inflammatory skin condition histologically marked by epidermal spongiosis (intercellular edema)
and intense pruritus. Driven by genetic skin barrier defects (filaggrin [FLG] mutations), Th2-skewed inflammation, elevated IgE, contact
allergens (nickel, fragrances, rubber), chemical irritants, and S. aureus colonization.
Common Types: Atopic dermatitis (associated with asthma and allergic rhinitis); Contact dermatitis (Allergic [Type IV hypersensitivity]
vs. Irritant [direct chemical/detergent disruption]); Seborrheic dermatitis (greasy scaly plaques on scalp/face linked to Malassezia);
Dyshidrotic eczema / pompholyx (pruritic vesicles on finger sides/palms/soles); Nummular / discoid eczema (coin-shaped plaques).

Q 26 Protein-Energy Malnutrition (PEM)
Definition & Causes: Spectrum of nutritional deficiency disorders resulting from inadequate intake/absorption of protein and caloric
energy to meet bodily growth and metabolic needs. Caused by poverty, food insecurity, faulty early weaning onto dilute starches,
recurrent gastroenteritis, and measles/TB infections.
Types & Clinical Features:
Kwashiorkor (Protein deficiency with adequate calories): Generalized bilateral pitting edema; "moon face"; "crazy-pavement" /
"flaky-paint" dermatosis; sparse, dry, hypopigmented hair with alternating light/dark bands (flag sign); marked hepatomegaly (fatty
liver infiltration); profound misery, apathy, and anorexia.
Marasmus (Severe deficiency of both calories and protein): Severe somatic muscle wasting and total loss of subcutaneous fat;
wizened, shrunken "old-man" facies; prominent ribs ("accordion cage"); loose folds of redundant skin over buttocks ("baggy pants"); 
absence of edema; voracious appetite.
Marasmic Kwashiorkor: Severe tissue wasting coexisting with peripheral pitting edema.
Complications: Hypoglycemia (<54 mg/dL), hypothermia (<35.5°C), severe electrolyte derangements (hypokalemia, hypomagnesemia,
sodium retention), occult severe sepsis, heart failure, and acute keratomalacia.
Management (WHO 10-Step Guidelines):
Stabilization (Days 1–7): Treat hypoglycemia (10% dextrose), warm child, gentle oral rehydration with ReSoMal (no rapid IV fluids);
supplement potassium/magnesium; broad-spectrum antibiotics; Vitamin A; initial starter feeding with low-protein F-75 diet (75 kcal/
100 mL); strictly withhold iron during stabilization.
Rehabilitation (Weeks 2–6): Transition to energy-dense F-100 diet (100 kcal/100 mL) or RUTF for catch-up growth; add iron
supplementation; emotional stimulation.

Q 27 Physiological Changes in Pregnancy, Antenatal & Postnatal Care
Physiological Changes During Pregnancy:
Cardiovascular: Cardiac output rises 30–50%; heart rate increases 10–15 bpm; SVR drops (progesterone-mediated vasodilation),
lowering diastolic BP in 2nd trimester; supine hypotension syndrome from IVC compression.
Hematological: Plasma volume increases 50%, RBC mass rises 20–30% → physiological hemodilution anemia; hypercoagulable
state (elevated fibrinogen, factors VII, VIII, X → 5x increased VTE risk).
Respiratory & Renal: Progesterone stimulates hyperventilation (mild respiratory alkalosis); GFR increases 50%, lowering serum
creatinine (<0.6 mg/dL).
Antenatal Care (ANC): Comprehensive healthcare surveillance from conception until labor. Objectives: monitor maternal-fetal health;
detect and manage high-risk obstetrical conditions early (pre-eclampsia, gestational diabetes, severe anemia, Rh isoimmunization);
provide prophylaxis (iron-folate, calcium, Td/Tdap immunization); birth preparedness and complication readiness.
Postnatal Care (PNC): Specialized medical care provided during the 6-week puerperium (42 days post-delivery). Importance: early
detection and management of postpartum hemorrhage (PPH), puerperal sepsis, venous thromboembolism, and postpartum depression;
establish and support exclusive breastfeeding; neonatal surveillance (jaundice, cord care, immunization); postpartum contraception
counseling.
Q 28 Stages and Physiological Changes of Labor
The Four Stages of Labor:
1st Stage (Cervical Dilatation): Onset of regular uterine contractions to full cervical dilatation (10 cm). Divided into Latent phase
(slow dilatation up to 4–5 cm) and Active phase (rapid dilatation ≥1 cm/h).
2nd Stage (Fetal Expulsion): Full dilatation (10 cm) to complete delivery of the fetus. Propelled by Cardinal Movements:
Engagement, Descent, Flexion, Internal rotation, Extension, Restitution, External rotation, and Expulsion.
3rd Stage (Placental): Complete delivery of baby to complete delivery of placenta and membranes (normal ≤30 min). Managed
with AMTSL: Oxytocin (10 IU IM), controlled cord traction, and fundal massage.
4th Stage (Observation): Immediate 1–2 hours postpartum for monitoring maternal hemodynamics, uterine contraction tone, and
vaginal bleeding.
Major Physiological Changes During Labor: Uterine muscular action shows fundal dominance with rhythmic contraction (transient
shortening) and retraction (permanent shortening without relaxation), creating a thick upper active segment and thin lower passive
segment separated by the physiological retraction ring; Cervical effacement (shortening/thinning) and dilatation driven by hydrostatic bag
of waters and fetal head pressure; Hemodynamic "autotransfusion" of 300–500 mL blood into maternal circulation during each
contraction increasing cardiac output and blood pressure; Hyperventilation causing respiratory alkalosis followed by metabolic lactic
acidosis.

Q 29 Menopause
Definition & Physiology: Permanent cessation of menses resulting from loss of ovarian follicular activity, clinically diagnosed
retrospectively after 12 consecutive months of amenorrhea (mean age 51y). Ovarian depletion of follicles causes circulating estradiol
(E2) to fall, removing hypothalamic-pituitary negative feedback and producing hypergonadotropism with marked elevation of FSH (>30
40 IU/L) and LH.
Clinical Manifestations:
Vasomotor: Hot flashes (intense sudden heat, flushing, sweating, chills from hypothalamic thermoregulatory instability), night sweats,
sleep disturbances.
Genitourinary Syndrome of Menopause (GSM): Vaginal epithelial atrophy, dryness, dyspareunia, pruritus, loss of rugae, elevated
pH >5.0, urinary frequency/urgency, and recurrent UTIs.
Psychological & Physical: Irritability, mood swings, depression, forgetfulness, loss of libido, breast atrophy, skin collagen loss, and
arthralgias.
Complications: Accelerated osteoporosis and fragility fractures (trabecular bone loss from osteoclast disinhibition); Cardiovascular
disease (atherogenic lipid shifts: elevated LDL, decreased HDL; loss of estrogen vascular protection).
Management: Lifestyle: weight-bearing exercise, calcium (1,200 mg/day), vitamin D (800–1,000 IU/day), trigger avoidance; Hormone
Replacement Therapy (HRT): Estrogen-only for hysterectomized women; Combined Estrogen-Progestin for women with an intact uterus
(progestin prevents endometrial cancer); Non-hormonal alternatives: SSRIs/SNRIs (Venlafaxine), Gabapentin, Fezolinetant (NK3
receptor antagonist); Topical vaginal estrogen creams for GSM.
Q 30 Common Gynecological Infections & Uterine/Vaginal Disorders
Common Gynecological Infections:
Bacterial Vaginosis: Dysbiosis with loss of Lactobacillus and overgrowth of anaerobes (G. vaginalis). Thin grayish-white discharge
with "fishy" odor. Diagnosis by Amsel's criteria: pH >4.5, positive Whiff test (KOH), Clue cells on wet mount. Rx: oral/topical
Metronidazole.
Vulvovaginal Candidiasis:C. albicans. Intense vulvovaginal pruritus, erythema, thick white curd-like "cottage cheese" discharge,
normal pH (<4.5), pseudohyphae on 10% KOH. Rx: single-dose oral Fluconazole (150 mg) or Clotrimazole pessary.
Trichomoniasis:T. vaginalis (flagellated protozoan, STD). Frothy greenish-yellow malodorous discharge, severe pruritus, 
"strawberry cervix". Rx: oral Metronidazole; treat partner.
Pelvic Inflammatory Disease (PID): Ascending infection (Chlamydia, Gonorrhea). Bilateral pelvic pain, high fever, purulent
discharge, marked cervical motion tenderness ("chandelier sign"). Rx: IM Ceftriaxone plus oral Doxycycline plus oral
Metronidazole for 14 days.
Uterine & Vaginal Disorders:
Uterine Fibroids (Leiomyomas): Benign smooth muscle tumors. Menorrhagia, dysmenorrhea, pelvic pressure, bulk symptoms. Rx:
Tranexamic acid, Levonorgestrel IUD, GnRH agonists, myomectomy, hysterectomy.
Endometriosis & Adenomyosis: Ectopic endometrial tissue outside uterus or in myometrium. Severe dysmenorrhea, chronic pelvic
pain, deep dyspareunia, subfertility. Rx: Progestins, OCPs, laparoscopic ablation.
Pelvic Organ Prolapse: Vaginal bulge, pelvic heaviness, cystocele/rectocele. Rx: Kegel exercises, supportive pessaries, pelvic floor
repair.

Q 31 Hysterectomy and Dilatation & Curettage (D&C)
Hysterectomy:
Definition: Surgical removal of the uterus (Total: body + cervix; Subtotal: body only; Radical: uterus, cervix, parametrium, upper
vagina, lymph nodes). Performed via abdominal, vaginal, or laparoscopic routes.
Indications: Symptomatic uterine fibroids failing medical therapy, refractory abnormal uterine bleeding (AUB), gynecological
malignancies (endometrial/cervical cancer), severe adenomyosis/endometriosis, advanced uterovaginal prolapse, emergency
intractable postpartum hemorrhage.
Complications: Hemorrhage, ureteric injury (proximity to uterine arteries), bladder/bowel injury, pelvic hematoma/abscess, surgical
site infection, DVT/PE, vaginal vault prolapse, and psychosexual distress.
Dilatation and Curettage (D&C):
Definition: Minor operative procedure involving progressive mechanical dilatation of the cervical canal followed by scraping and
evacuation of endometrial tissue with a curette.
Indications: Diagnostic: evaluation of postmenopausal bleeding, abnormal uterine bleeding in women >40y, suspected endometrial
hyperplasia/carcinoma; Therapeutic: evacuation of retained products of conception (incomplete/missed miscarriage), molar
pregnancy evacuation, temporary control of acute refractory uterine bleeding, polyp removal.
Complications:Uterine perforation (risk of bowel/vessel injury), cervical laceration/incompetence, acute endometritis/salpingitis, 
Asherman's syndrome (intrauterine synechiae from over-vigorous curettage causing amenorrhea/infertility), and hemorrhage.
Q 32 Urinary Incontinence in Women
Definition: Involuntary, objectively demonstrable loss or leakage of urine causing physical hygiene, social, or psychological distress.
Types & Causes:
Stress Incontinence (SUI, ~50%): Leakage on effort, exertion, coughing, sneezing, or laughing without detrusor contraction. Caused
by pelvic floor muscle laxity, urethral hypermobility, and intrinsic sphincteric deficiency (risk factors: multiparity, vaginal deliveries,
postmenopausal estrogen deficiency, obesity, chronic cough).
Urge Incontinence (UUI / Overactive Bladder, ~20%): Involuntary leakage preceded by an intense, sudden, uncontrollable urge to
void. Caused by detrusor overactivity (idiopathic, stroke, Parkinson's, MS, UTI, bladder stones).
Mixed Incontinence (~30%): Features of both stress and urge incontinence.
Overflow: Involuntary dribbling from a chronically overfilled, distended bladder due to bladder outlet obstruction (pelvic prolapse) or
hypotonic detrusor (diabetic neuropathy).
Functional: Inability to reach toilet due to severe physical or cognitive disability (dementia, severe arthritis).
Clinical Features: Leakage on strain/cough (SUI); urinary urgency, daytime frequency (>8 times), and nocturia (UUI); continuous
dribbling (overflow); perineal skin dermatitis, secondary UTIs, anxiety, and social withdrawal.
Management:
Conservative & Behavioral (First-line): Lifestyle: weight loss, fluid moderation, avoid caffeine/alcohol; Pelvic Floor Muscle
Training (Kegel exercises): at least 3 sets of 8–12 maximal contractions daily for ≥3 months (first-line for SUI); Bladder training
(timed voiding) for UUI.
Pharmacological: For UUI: Antimuscarinics (Oxybutynin, Tolterodine, Solifenacin) or β3-agonist (Mirabegron); Local topical vaginal
estrogen for postmenopausal women; SUI: Duloxetine (SNRI).
Interventional & Surgical: Intravesical OnabotulinumtoxinA injections or sacral neuromodulation for refractory UUI; Mid-Urethral
Sling (MUS: TVT / TOT) synthetic mesh placement (gold standard for refractory SUI); Burch colposuspension; Periurethral bulking
agents.

hyperresponsiveness (>4 weeks).
Management: Supportive hydration and steam inhalation; Paracetamol/Ibuprofen for chest soreness and fever; Dextromethorphan for
disruptive dry cough; inhaled Salbutamol for bronchospasm/wheeze. Routine antibiotics are not recommended unless elderly with
comorbidities or confirmed pertussis (Azithromycin).
Q 02 Bronchial Pneumonia (Bronchopneumonia)
Definition: Acute suppurative inflammation of the pulmonary parenchyma centered around terminal and respiratory bronchioles,
presenting with patchy, multifocal consolidation involving multiple pulmonary lobes.
Causes: Bacterial: Streptococcus pneumoniae, Staphylococcus aureus, Klebsiella pneumoniae, Pseudomonas aeruginosa, H.
influenzae. Predisposing factors include extremes of age, aspiration, malnutrition, post-viral airway injury, and immobilization.
Clinical Presentation: High-grade fever with chills/rigors, productive cough with purulent/rust-colored sputum, progressive dyspnea,
pleuritic chest pain; tachypnea, localized dullness on percussion, bronchial breath sounds, increased vocal resonance, and coarse
inspiratory crackles.
Investigations: Chest X-ray (shows bilateral patchy, mottled opacities centered around bronchi); Sputum Gram stain and culture/
sensitivity; blood cultures; CBC (leukocytosis with left shift, elevated CRP/ESR); ABG for hypoxemia.
Complications: Parapneumonic effusion, empyema thoracis, lung abscess formation, sepsis/septic shock, Type 1 respiratory failure,
and ARDS.
Treatment: Supplemental O2 (target SpO2 ≥92%); IV fluids and chest physiotherapy; Empiric antibiotics: IV Ceftriaxone or Amoxicillin
clavulanate plus Azithromycin (community-acquired); Piperacillin-tazobactam or Meropenem plus Vancomycin for hospital-acquired/
MRSA; tailored to culture sensitivities for 7–10 days.

Q 03 Pleural Effusion
Definition: Pathological accumulation of excess fluid within the pleural cavity (>15 mL) resulting from an imbalance between fluid
formation and absorption.
Types & Causes:
Transudative (Altered Starling forces): Congestive heart failure, liver cirrhosis with ascites, nephrotic syndrome, severe
hypoalbuminemia.
Exudative (Inflammatory/vascular permeability): Parapneumonic infection, tuberculosis, bronchogenic/metastatic carcinoma,
pulmonary infarction/PE, autoimmune diseases (SLE, RA).
Clinical Features: Progressive exertional dyspnea, pleuritic chest pain, dry cough; decreased chest expansion on affected side,
contralateral mediastinal shift (massive effusion), stony dull percussion note, absent/diminished breath sounds and vocal resonance.
Investigations: Chest X-ray (costophrenic angle blunting >175 mL, homogenous opacity with lateral upward-curving meniscus sign);
Thoracic Ultrasound; Diagnostic thoracocentesis using Light's Criteria for exudates (Fluid/Serum Protein >0.5, Fluid/Serum LDH >0.6,
or Fluid LDH >2/3 upper limit of serum LDH); ADA (>40 U/L indicates TB), cytology, and microbiology.
Management: Treat etiology (diuretics for CHF; ATT for TB; chemotherapy for malignancy); Therapeutic thoracocentesis (drain ≤1,000
1,500 mL/session); Intercostal chest drain (ICD) for empyema (pH <7.20) or hemothorax; Chemical pleurodesis (talc, bleomycin) for
recurrent malignant effusions.
Q 04 Pneumothorax
Definition: Accumulation of free air within the pleural space between the parietal and visceral pleura, causing partial or complete lung
collapse.
Types & Causes:
Spontaneous: Primary (rupture of subpleural apical blebs in tall, young men); Secondary (COPD bullae, cavitary TB, cystic fibrosis).
Traumatic / Iatrogenic: Penetrating/blunt chest trauma, rib fractures, subclavian line placement, pleural biopsy, mechanical
barotrauma.
Tension Pneumothorax: One-way valve mechanism allowing air entry during inspiration but trapping air on expiration, generating
massive intrapleural pressure.
Clinical Features: Sudden unilateral sharp pleuritic chest pain and dyspnea; decreased expansion, hyperresonant percussion note,
absent/diminished breath sounds. Tension hallmark: cyanosis, hypotension, tachycardia, tracheal deviation to the contralateral side, and
distended neck veins.
Complications: Obstructive shock, severe hypoxemic respiratory failure, hemopneumothorax, re-expansion pulmonary edema.
Emergency Management:
Tension Pneumothorax: Immediate emergency needle decompression (14–16G cannula in 2nd ICS midclavicular line or 4th/5th ICS
anterior axillary line) without awaiting X-ray.
Definitive Tube Thoracostomy: Intercostal chest tube (ICD) with underwater seal inserted in the safe triangle.
High-flow supplemental oxygen (accelerates pleural air resorption); VATS pleurodesis for persistent leaks (>48h) or recurrence.
Q 05 Lung Abscess
Definition: Localized parenchymal microbial necrosis and cavity formation containing purulent necrotic debris and fluid.
Etiology: Aspiration of oral/gastric secretions containing anaerobes (Peptostreptococcus, Bacteroides, Fusobacterium) in patients with
impaired consciousness (alcoholism, stroke, epilepsy) or poor dentition; Necrotizing pneumonia (S. aureus, Klebsiella); Bronchial
obstruction by carcinoma; Septic emboli (tricuspid endocarditis).
Clinical Manifestations: High swinging fever with rigors and night sweats, malaise, progressive weight loss; cough productive of
copious, foul-smelling, putrid purulent sputum; hemoptysis; pallor, rapid finger clubbing, dullness to percussion, and cavernous/amphoric
breath sounds over cavity.
Investigations: Chest X-ray (thick-walled solitary cavity with a prominent air-fluid level surrounded by consolidation); CECT Chest
(delineates cavity and excludes empyema); Sputum microbiology (Gram, AFB, culture); Bronchoscopy to exclude obstructing
endobronchial neoplasm.
Complications: Empyema/pyopneumothorax, bronchopleural fistula, massive fatal hemoptysis, metastatic brain abscess, secondary
amyloidosis.
Treatment: Prolonged antimicrobial therapy (4–8 weeks): IV Ampicillin-sulbactam, Amoxicillin-clavulanate, or Clindamycin, transitioned
to oral; Postural drainage and chest physiotherapy; Percutaneous catheter drainage for refractory cavities >6 cm; Surgical lobectomy for
massive hemoptysis or suspected underlying malignancy.

Q 06 Respiratory Failure
Definition: Inability of the respiratory system to maintain adequate gas exchange, defined as arterial PaO2 <60 mmHg with or without
PaCO2 >50 mmHg on ambient air at sea level.
Types & Causes:
Type 1 (Hypoxemic): PaO2 <60 mmHg with normal/low PaCO2. Caused by V/Q mismatch and right-to-left shunting: ARDS, severe
pneumonia, acute pulmonary edema, massive PE, diffuse interstitial fibrosis.
Type 2 (Hypercapnic): PaCO2 >50 mmHg with companion hypoxemia. Caused by alveolar hypoventilation/pump failure: severe
COPD, acute severe asthma, opioid overdose, myasthenia gravis, Guillain-Barré, severe kyphoscoliosis.
Clinical Features: Hypoxemia: dyspnea, tachypnea, tachycardia, central cyanosis, restlessness, confusion. Hypercapnia: bounding
pulses, warm flushed hands, morning headache, asterixis (flapping tremor), somnolence, and CO2 narcosis/coma.
Investigations: Arterial Blood Gas (ABG) analysis (confirms diagnosis, defines acidosis/alkalosis and compensation); Continuous pulse
oximetry; Chest X-ray and CT thorax; Spirometry.
Management: Controlled oxygen therapy (target SpO2 94–98% in Type 1; strictly 88–92% using a Venturi mask in Type 2 COPD to
preserve hypoxic drive); Non-Invasive Ventilation (BiPAP) for hypercapnic COPD exacerbations; Invasive mechanical ventilation if severe
acidosis (pH <7.25), exhaustion, or coma; Bronchodilators, systemic steroids, diuretics, and antidotes (Naloxone).
Q 07 Occupational Lung Diseases
Definition: Preventable non-neoplastic and neoplastic disorders caused by repeated inhalation of mineral dusts, organic particles,
fumes, or toxic gases in the work environment.
Causes & Common Types:
Silicosis: Inhalation of crystalline SiO2 in stone cutting, sandblasting, quarrying, foundry work; produces fibrotic silicotic nodules and
high risk of tuberculosis (silicotuberculosis).
Asbestosis: Inhalation of asbestos fibers in shipbuilding, demolition, roofing; causes bibasilar interstitial fibrosis, calcified pleural
plaques, and malignant mesothelioma.
Coal Workers' Pneumoconiosis (CWP): Coal dust inhalation leading to anthracosis and progressive massive fibrosis.
Organic: Byssinosis (cotton dust, "Monday chest tightness"), Farmer's lung (thermophilic actinomycetes in moldy hay).
Clinical Features: Insidious exertional dyspnea, chronic dry or productive cough (melanoptysis in CWP), wheezing, bibasilar end
inspiratory crackles, reduced chest expansion, digital clubbing, and late cor pulmonale.
Prevention: Engineering controls (wet drilling, local exhaust ventilation, toxic material substitution); Administrative controls (worker
rotation); PPE (certified N95/HEPA particulate respirators); Periodic medical screening with spirometry and chest X-rays (ILO
classification).
Management: Immediate permanent removal from dust exposure; Bronchodilators and supplemental O2; Pneumococcal and influenza
vaccination; Tuberculosis screening; Pulmonary rehabilitation; Medico-legal compensation.
PART II: CARDIOVASCULAR PATHOLOGY & HEMODYNAMICS (Q08 – Q15)
Q 08 Atherosclerosis
Definition: Chronic inflammatory disease of large/medium muscular and elastic arteries characterized by intimal fibrofatty plaques
(atheromas) narrowing the lumen and weakening the arterial wall.
Major Risk Factors: Modifiable: Dyslipidemia (high LDL, low HDL), systemic hypertension, cigarette smoking, diabetes mellitus, visceral
obesity, sedentary life. Non-modifiable: Advancing age, male sex, family history of premature CAD.
Clinical Manifestations: Coronary: stable angina, acute myocardial infarction; Cerebral: TIAs, ischemic stroke; Peripheral: intermittent
claudication, critical limb ischemia; Renal: renovascular hypertension.
Complications: Acute plaque rupture with occlusive luminal thrombosis, aneurysmal dilatation/rupture (abdominal aorta),
atheroembolism, and progressive ischemic cardiomyopathy.
Investigations: Fasting lipid profile, HbA1c, hs-CRP; ECG and treadmill exercise test (TMT); Carotid Doppler (intima-media thickness)
and Ankle-Brachial Index (ABI <0.9); Coronary CT angiography and conventional catheter angiography.
Management: Lifestyle: Mediterranean diet, aerobic exercise, smoking cessation; Pharmacotherapy: High-intensity statins (Atorvastatin
40–80 mg to achieve LDL <55 mg/dL), low-dose Aspirin (75–100 mg), ACE inhibitors, tight glycemic/BP control; Revascularization: PCI
with drug-eluting stents, CABG, or endarterectomy.

Q 09 Thrombosis and Embolism
Definitions: Thrombosis is the intravascular formation of a solid/semisolid mass of fibrin, platelets, and cells in intact unruptured vessels
during life. Embolism is the mechanical occlusion of a vessel by a detached intravascular mass transported away from its origin.
Causes (Virchow's Triad): 1. Endothelial injury (atherosclerosis, trauma, vasculitis); 2. Altered blood flow (venous stasis from
immobility, turbulence from aneurysms); 3. Hypercoagulability (Factor V Leiden, malignancy, antiphospholipid syndrome, oral
contraceptives). Emboli arise from dislodged DVTs, cardiac mural thrombi (atrial fibrillation), fat (fractures), air, or septic vegetations.
Clinical Features: DVT: Unilateral calf swelling, calf pain, erythema, tenderness, positive Homans sign; Pulmonary Embolism: acute
dyspnea, pleuritic chest pain, tachypnea, tachycardia, hemoptysis, syncope; Acute Arterial Embolism (6 Ps): Pain, Pallor, Pulselessness,
Paresthesia, Paralysis, Poikilothermia.
Complications: Fatal massive PE with obstructive shock, ischemic stroke, acute mesenteric ischemia, post-thrombotic syndrome.
Diagnosis: Compression Duplex ultrasound (DVT); quantitative D-dimer assay; CT Pulmonary Angiography (CTPA, gold standard for
PE); Arterial Doppler and CT angiography.
Management: Anticoagulation: LMWH (Enoxaparin 1 mg/kg SC q12h) or unfractionated heparin, transitioned to DOACs (Apixaban,
Rivaroxaban) or Warfarin (target INR 2.0–3.0) for 3–6 months; Thrombolysis (r-tPA / Alteplase) for massive PE with shock or acute
ischemic stroke <4.5h; Catheter thrombectomy, surgical embolectomy, and IVC filter placement.
Q 10 Ischemic Heart Disease (IHD)
Definition: Cardiac syndromes resulting from an imbalance between myocardial oxygen supply and demand, predominantly caused by
fixed atherosclerotic narrowing of epicardial coronary arteries.
Risk Factors: Dyslipidemia, hypertension, cigarette smoking, diabetes mellitus, visceral obesity, metabolic syndrome, male sex, older
age, family history.
Clinical Features: Stable angina: retrosternal tightness/pressure radiating to left arm/neck/jaw, provoked by exertion, relieved by rest or
sublingual nitroglycerin within 2–5 min; Acute Coronary Syndromes (NSTEMI/STEMI): severe crushing retrosternal pain lasting >20 min,
occurring at rest, accompanied by diaphoresis, nausea, dyspnea, and syncope.
Investigations: 12-lead ECG (ST elevation in STEMI, ST depression/T inversion in ischemia/NSTEMI); Cardiac biomarkers (hs-cTnI, hs
cTnT, CK-MB); Echocardiography (regional wall motion abnormalities, LVEF); Coronary angiography (gold standard).
Complications: Malignant ventricular arrhythmias (VT/VF), sudden cardiac death, cardiogenic shock, congestive heart failure, papillary
muscle rupture with acute mitral regurgitation, ventricular free-wall/septal rupture.
Treatment: Acute ACS: Oxygen (if SpO2 <90%), sublingual Nitroglycerin, chewable Aspirin (300 mg) plus P2Y12 inhibitor (Ticagrelor
180 mg or Clopidogrel 600 mg), Enoxaparin; Primary PCI (<90 min door-to-balloon) or thrombolysis (<120 min); Long-term: dual
antiplatelet therapy, high-intensity statin, cardioselective beta-blocker, and ACE inhibitor.
Q 11 Cardiac Failure (Heart Failure)
Definition: Complex clinical syndrome resulting from structural or functional impairment of ventricular filling or blood ejection, leaving the
heart unable to meet the metabolic demands of tissues at normal venous pressures.
Types & Causes:
Types: HFrEF (systolic, LVEF ≤40%); HFpEF (diastolic, LVEF ≥50%); Left-sided vs. Right-sided; Acute vs. Chronic.
Causes: Coronary artery disease and myocardial infarction (most common), chronic hypertension, valvular heart disease, dilated
cardiomyopathies, cor pulmonale.
Clinical Manifestations: Left-sided (Pulmonary congestion): exertional dyspnea, orthopnea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea (PND),
bibasilar crackles, S3 gallop; Right-sided (Systemic venous congestion): elevated JVP, bilateral pitting pedal edema, congestive
hepatomegaly, ascites.
Complications: Acute pulmonary edema, ventricular arrhythmias, cardiorenal syndrome, cardiac cirrhosis, mural thrombi with systemic
embolism.
Management: Lifestyle: dietary sodium (<2 g/day) and fluid restriction, weight monitoring; Guideline-Directed Medical Therapy (GDMT 
4 Pillars for HFrEF): 1. ARNI (Sacubitril-valsartan) or ACEi/ARB; 2. Beta-blocker (Carvedilol, Bisoprolol, Metoprolol succinate); 3. MRA
(Spironolactone); 4. SGLT2 inhibitor (Dapagliflozin/Empagliflozin); Diuretics (Furosemide) for volume overload; Device therapy: ICD and
CRT-D; LVAD or heart transplantation.

Q 12 Rheumatic Heart Disease (RHD)
Definition: Chronic permanent cardiac valvular damage resulting from single or recurrent episodes of acute rheumatic fever (ARF)
initiated by untreated Group A β-hemolytic streptococcal (GAS) pharyngitis.
Etiology & Pathogenesis:Streptococcus pyogenes. Driven by molecular mimicry: streptococcal M-protein cross-reacts with human
cardiac myosin and sarcolemma, producing pancarditis with pathognomonic granulomatous Aschoff bodies.
Clinical Features: History of ARF (Jones criteria). Valvular involvement (Mitral >90%, then Aortic): 
Mitral Stenosis: Exertional dyspnea, hemoptysis, malar flush, tapping apex beat, loud S1, opening snap, low-pitched rumbling mid
diastolic murmur at the apex.
Mitral Regurgitation: Holosystolic murmur radiating to axilla; Aortic lesions cause early diastolic decrescendo murmur.
Complications: Congestive heart failure, atrial fibrillation, left atrial mural thrombi with stroke, and infective endocarditis.
Investigations: Doppler Echocardiography (shows thickened valve leaflets, chordal shortening, "hockey-stick" anterior mitral leaflet,
pressure gradients); 12-lead ECG (left atrial enlargement / P-mitrale, AF); Chest X-ray (straightening of left heart border, double right
contour); Elevated ASO titer.
Management: Secondary penicillin prophylaxis: Benzathine penicillin G (1.2 million units IM q3–4 weeks) for at least 10 years or until
age 40; Medical: diuretics, beta-blockers/digoxin for AF, Warfarin anticoagulation (target INR 2.0–3.0); Surgery/Intervention:
Percutaneous Transvenous Mitral Commissurotomy (PTMC) or surgical prosthetic valve replacement.
Q 13 Cardiomyopathies
Definition: Heterogeneous group of intrinsic myocardial disorders associated with mechanical/electrical cardiac dysfunction, not
secondary to coronary disease, hypertension, or valvular disease.
Types & Causes:
Dilated (DCM): Ventricular dilatation with systolic dysfunction (LVEF <40%). Causes: idiopathic, titin mutations, viral myocarditis,
chronic alcoholism, doxorubicin toxicity, peripartum.
Hypertrophic (HCM): Asymmetric septal hypertrophy with preserved/hyperdynamic systolic function. Autosomal dominant mutation
in sarcomeric genes (β-MHC, MYBPC3).
Restrictive (RCM): Rigid, non-compliant ventricular walls causing impaired diastolic filling. Infiltrative causes: amyloidosis,
sarcoidosis, hemochromatosis.
ARVC: Fibrofatty replacement of RV myocardium predisposing to ventricular arrhythmias.
Clinical Manifestations: DCM: biventricular heart failure (dyspnea, edema, cardiomegaly, S3); HCM: dyspnea, chest pain, exertional
syncope, harsh systolic ejection murmur that intensifies with Valsalva; sudden cardiac death in athletes; RCM: severe right-sided failure,
high JVP with Kussmaul's sign.
Investigations: Echocardiography (ventricular dilation in DCM; asymmetric septal thickness ≥15 mm with systolic anterior motion of
mitral valve in HCM; bi-atrial dilatation in RCM); Cardiac MRI (Late Gadolinium Enhancement for fibrosis/amyloid); Holter ECG.
Treatment: DCM: standard GDMT (ARNI, beta-blockers, MRA, SGLT2i), ICD/CRT; HCM: non-vasodilating beta-blockers (Metoprolol),
Verapamil, Mavacamten, surgical septal myectomy, prophylactic ICD; RCM: cautious diuretics, Tafamidis for amyloidosis.

Q 14 Cardiac Arrest
Definition: Abrupt, unexpected cessation of mechanical cardiac pump activity resulting in circulatory collapse, sudden
unresponsiveness, absent central arterial pulse, and apnea or agonal gasping.
Immediate Assessment:
1. Confirm scene safety; 2. Check responsiveness (tap shoulders and shout); 3. Simultaneously assess breathing and carotid pulse
(minimum 5 sec, maximum 10 sec); 4. If pulseless and breathless, activate emergency response (Call Code Blue / EMS) and call for
an AED.
Emergency Management:
High-Quality CPR (C-A-B): Rate 100–120/min, depth 5–6 cm, allow full recoil, minimize interruptions, 30:2 compression-ventilation
ratio.
Defibrillation for Shockable Rhythms (VF / Pulseless VT): Deliver 1 unsynchronized shock (120–200 J biphasic or 360 J
monophasic); resume CPR immediately for 2 minutes without pulse check; Epinephrine 1 mg IV q3–5min after 2nd shock;
Amiodarone 300 mg IV (second dose 150 mg) for shock-refractory VF/pVT.
Non-Shockable Rhythms (Asystole / PEA): CPR in 2-min cycles; Epinephrine 1 mg IV immediately and q3–5min; Defibrillation is 
contraindicated.
Treat Reversible Causes (Hs & Ts): Hypovolemia, Hypoxia, Hydrogen ion (acidosis), Hypo/hyperkalemia, Hypothermia; Tension
pneumothorax, Tamponade, Toxins, Thrombosis (coronary/pulmonary).
Post-ROSC Care: Hemodynamic support (MAP ≥65 mmHg), targeted temperature management (32–36°C for 24h), emergency
coronary angiography.
Q 15 Cardiopulmonary Resuscitation (CPR) & Basic Life Support (BLS)
Principles: Maintains artificial coronary and cerebral perfusion via rhythmic external chest compressions and ventilations to preserve
tissue viability until ROSC is achieved. Follows the C-A-B sequence (Chest compressions prioritized over Airway and Breathing). Chain
of Survival: Early Recognition & Activation → High-Quality CPR → Rapid Defibrillation → Advanced Resuscitation → Post-Arrest Care →
Recovery.
Core Metrics of High-Quality CPR: Rate: 100–120/min; Depth: 5–6 cm (adult); Full chest recoil between compressions (avoid leaning);
Chest compression fraction >60% (target >80%); Avoid hyperventilation (500–600 mL tidal volume visible chest rise over 1 second).
Step-by-Step BLS Procedure:
1. Confirm scene safety; 2. Check responsiveness; 3. Call for help, activate EMS / Code Blue, retrieve AED; 4. Check carotid pulse
and breathing (5–10 sec); 5. If no pulse: begin chest compressions on lower half of sternum, interlocked fingers, elbows locked,
shoulders vertical; 6. Open airway (Head-Tilt–Chin-Lift; Jaw-Thrust if spinal trauma); 7. Deliver 2 rescue breaths after every 30
compressions (30:2 ratio); 8. Attach AED as soon as available, clear patient during rhythm analysis, deliver shock if indicated, and
immediately resume compressions; 9. Switch rescuers every 2 minutes (5 cycles) to prevent fatigue.
PART III: CRITICAL CARE, DIAGNOSTICS & EMERGENCY SURGERY (Q16 – Q21)
Q 16 Mechanical Ventilation
Definition: Supportive intervention using an automated positive-pressure device to assist or replace spontaneous alveolar ventilation
and pulmonary gas exchange.
Indications: Severe hypoxemic respiratory failure (ARDS, pulmonary edema); Hypercapnic respiratory failure (severe COPD,
myasthenic crisis); Airway protection / coma (GCS ≤8); General anesthesia and shock states to reduce work of breathing.
Basic Principles: Positive pressure ventilation pushes gas into lungs. Parameters: Tidal Volume (Vt, 6–8 mL/kg; 4–6 mL/kg in ARDS
lung-protective strategy), Respiratory Rate (12–16/min), FiO2 (21–100%), PEEP (5–15 cmH2O to prevent alveolar collapse), I:E ratio
(1:2).
Types & Modes: Non-Invasive (NIV: CPAP, BiPAP via mask); Invasive (via ETT/tracheostomy): Volume-Controlled (VCV), Pressure
Controlled (PCV), SIMV, and Pressure Support Ventilation (PSV).
Complications: Ventilator-Associated Pneumonia (VAP >48h post-intubation), Barotrauma/Volutrauma (pneumothorax,
pneumomediastinum), Hemodynamic hypotension (reduced venous return from positive intrathoracic pressure), and Tracheal stenosis.
Monitoring: Continuous pulse oximetry, capnography (EtCO2), serial ABGs; Peak airway pressure (<35 cmH2O), Plateau pressure
(Pplat ≤30 cmH2O); Sedation scoring (RASS), ETT depth.

Q 17 Arterial Blood Gas (ABG) Analysis
Definition & Significance: Quantitative point-of-care laboratory assessment performed on heparinized arterial blood (radial artery)
measuring gas partial pressures and pH to assess oxygenation, alveolar ventilation, and acid-base status.
Normal Ranges: pH: 7.35–7.45; PaCO2: 35–45 mmHg; HCO3-: 22–26 mEq/L; PaO2: 80–100 mmHg; Base Excess: -2 to +2 mEq/L;
SaO2: 95–100%.
Interpretation of Primary Disorders:
Respiratory Acidosis: pH <7.35, PaCO2 >45 mmHg. Due to hypoventilation (COPD, asthma, opioid overdose, neuromuscular
weakness).
Respiratory Alkalosis: pH >7.45, PaCO2 <35 mmHg. Due to hyperventilation (anxiety/panic, pulmonary embolism, early salicylate
toxicity, sepsis).
Metabolic Acidosis: pH <7.35, HCO3- <22 mEq/L. High Anion Gap (DKA, lactic acidosis, uremia, toxic alcohols); Normal Anion Gap
(severe diarrhea, RTA).
Metabolic Alkalosis: pH >7.45, HCO3- >26 mEq/L. Due to H+ loss (severe vomiting, NG suction, loop diuretics,
hyperaldosteronism).
Q 18 Electrocardiogram (ECG)
Basic Principles: Non-invasive graphic recording of cardiac bioelectrical potentials and vector voltages produced by myocardial
depolarization and repolarization, measured via 10 skin electrodes arranged in 12 standard leads (6 limb, 6 precordial).
Major Waves, Complexes & Intervals:
P wave: Atrial depolarization (<0.12s, <2.5 mm).
PR interval: AV nodal conduction delay (0.12–0.20s). Prolonged in 1st-degree AV block; short in WPW.
QRS complex: Ventricular depolarization (<0.12s). Widened in bundle branch blocks and VT.
ST segment: Isoelectric plateau phase. Elevation indicates STEMI/pericarditis; depression indicates ischemia/NSTEMI.
T wave: Ventricular repolarization. Peaked in hyperkalemia; inverted/flat in ischemia or hypokalemia.
QT interval: Total ventricular electrical cycle (depolarization + repolarization; QTc ≤0.44s men, ≤0.46s women).
Clinical Significance: Diagnostic standard for Acute Coronary Syndromes (STEMI vs. NSTEMI); dysrhythmias (AF, VT, VF, heart
blocks); chamber enlargement (LVH); electrolyte disorders (hyper/hypokalemia); and drug toxicities (digoxin).
Q 19 Shock
Definition: Life-threatening acute circulatory failure characterized by inadequate tissue and cellular microvascular perfusion, resulting in
cellular hypoxia, anaerobic metabolism (lactic acidosis), and multi-organ failure.
Types & Causes:
Hypovolemic: Hemorrhagic (trauma, GI bleed); Non-hemorrhagic (burn plasma loss, severe dehydration).
Cardiogenic: Myocardial infarction (>40% LV loss), end-stage cardiomyopathy, severe acute mitral regurgitation.
Distributive: Septic shock (bacterial endotoxemia), anaphylactic shock (Type 1 hypersensitivity), neurogenic shock (high spinal cord
injury).
Obstructive: Tension pneumothorax, massive pulmonary embolism, cardiac tamponade.
Clinical Features: Systemic hypotension (SBP <90 mmHg or MAP <65 mmHg), tachycardia (>100 bpm; bradycardia in neurogenic),
tachypnea, cold clammy pale skin with delayed capillary refill (>3s; warm flushed in early septic shock), progressive oliguria (<0.5 mL/kg/
h), confusion/coma.
Complications: Acute kidney injury, ARDS, DIC, mesenteric ischemia, MODS, and death.
Management: Airway & high-flow O2; IV access (two 14–16G cannulas) & fluid resuscitation (30 mL/kg balanced crystalloids for
hypovolemia/sepsis; restrict in cardiogenic shock); Norepinephrine (first-line vasopressor targeting MAP ≥65 mmHg); Dobutamine for
cardiogenic inotropic support; Epinephrine IM (0.3–0.5 mg 1:1,000) for anaphylaxis; Emergency cause-specific relief: blood transfusion
for trauma, needle decompression for tension pneumothorax, pericardiocentesis for tamponade, PCI for cardiogenic MI.

Q 20 Burns
Classification:
Depth: Superficial (1st degree: red, dry, painful, heals <6d); Superficial partial-thickness (2nd degree: pink, weeping, thin blisters,
very painful); Deep partial-thickness (mottled white/red, reduced sensation, scarring); Full-thickness (3rd degree: leathery, charred,
dry, anesthetic); 4th degree (involves muscle/bone).
Wallace's Rule of Nines (% TBSA in adults): Head & neck: 9%; Each arm: 9%; Anterior trunk: 18%; Posterior trunk: 18%; Each leg:
18%; Perineum: 1%. (Patient's palm = 1%).
Clinical Assessment: Primary survey (ABCDE); Rule out inhalation injury (facial burns, singed nasal hairs, soot in sputum, stridor);
Calculate % TBSA (excluding 1st degree).
Complications: Hypovolemic burn shock, carbon monoxide toxicity, compartment syndrome from circumferential eschar, burn wound
sepsis (Pseudomonas, S. aureus), Curling's stress ulcer, contractures, Marjolin's carcinoma.
Principles of Management:
Stop burning, cool with tap water (15–20 min, no ice); Early intubation if inhalation injury suspected.
Parkland Formula Resuscitation (>15–20% TBSA): Total Ringer's Lactate in 24 hours = 4 mL × Weight (kg) × % TBSA. Give 50%
in first 8 hours (from burn time), remaining 50% over next 16 hours. Titrate to urine output (0.5–1.0 mL/kg/h).
Wound debridement, topical Silver Sulfadiazine cream; IV Morphine; Tetanus prophylaxis; Emergency escharotomy for circumferential
chest/limb burns; Early tangential excision and skin grafting (3–7 days).
Q 21 Septicemia
Definition: Life-threatening systemic infection characterized by the active multiplication and persistence of pathogenic microbes and
toxins in the bloodstream, triggering a dysregulated host response and acute end-organ dysfunction.
Causes: Gram-negative bacilli (E. coli, Klebsiella, Pseudomonas, Acinetobacter); Gram-positive cocci (S. aureus/MRSA, S.
pneumoniae, Enterococcus); Fungi (Candida). Primary foci: pneumonia, urosepsis, intra-abdominal peritonitis, central line infections.
Clinical Manifestations: High swinging fever with rigors or hypothermia (<36°C), resting tachycardia (>90 bpm), tachypnea (>20 bpm),
hypotension (SBP <90 mmHg), warm flushed skin transitioning to cold mottled cyanosis, petechiae/purpura, delirium, and oliguria.
Complications: Septic shock (hypotension requiring vasopressors with serum lactate >2 mmol/L), DIC, ARDS, acute tubular necrosis,
and MODS.
Investigations: Blood cultures (2 sets drawn prior to antibiotics), paired sputum/urine cultures; CBC (leukocytosis >12,000/μL or
leukopenia <4,000/μL, thrombocytopenia); Serum lactate (>2 mmol/L); Elevated Procalcitonin and CRP; PT/INR, aPTT, D-dimer.
Management (Surviving Sepsis Hour-1 Bundle):
1. Measure blood lactate; 2. Blood cultures before antibiotics; 3. Administer empiric broad-spectrum IV antimicrobials within 1 hour
(e.g., Piperacillin-tazobactam plus Vancomycin); 4. Rapid 30 mL/kg balanced crystalloids for hypotension or lactate ≥4 mmol/L; 5.
Norepinephrine to maintain MAP ≥65 mmHg; 6. Prompt infectious source control (drain abscesses, remove infected lines).
PART IV: DERMATOLOGY & CLINICAL NUTRITION (Q22 – Q26)
Q 22 Psoriasis
Etiology & Pathogenesis: Chronic immune-mediated dermatosis characterized by accelerated epidermal cell turnover (3–5 days vs.
normal 28 days) driven by T-helper lymphocytes (Th1/Th17) releasing TNF-α, IL-17, and IL-23. Strongly linked to HLA-Cw6. Triggers:
physical trauma (Koebner phenomenon), streptococcal pharyngitis, stress, drugs (beta-blockers, lithium, NSAIDs, steroid withdrawal).
Clinical Features: Sharply demarcated salmon-pink erythematous plaques covered by silvery-white micaceous scales on extensor
surfaces (knees, elbows, scalp, sacrum). Signs: Auspitz sign (pinpoint bleeding on removing scales) and Koebner phenomenon. Nail
changes (pitting, onycholysis, subungual hyperkeratosis, oil-drop sign). Variants: plaque, guttate, inverse, pustular, and erythrodermic.
Complications: Psoriatic arthritis (PsA in 30%), life-threatening erythroderma (>90% TBSA involvement), severe metabolic syndrome,
cardiovascular disease, and depression.
Treatment: Topical: potent corticosteroids (Clobetasol), Calcipotriol (vitamin D3 analogue), keratolytics (salicylic acid), calcineurin
inhibitors (tacrolimus for flexures); Phototherapy: Narrowband UVB (311 nm) or PUVA; Systemic: Methotrexate (7.5–25 mg/week),
Cyclosporine, Acitretin; Biologics: anti-TNF (Adalimumab), anti-IL-17 (Secukinumab), anti-IL-23 (Guselkumab).

Q 23 Eczema and Dermatitis
Definition & Causes: Non-contagious inflammatory skin condition histologically marked by epidermal spongiosis (intercellular edema)
and intense pruritus. Driven by genetic skin barrier defects (filaggrin [FLG] mutations), Th2-skewed inflammation, elevated IgE, contact
allergens (nickel, fragrances, rubber), chemical irritants, and S. aureus colonization.
Common Types: Atopic dermatitis (associated with asthma and allergic rhinitis); Contact dermatitis (Allergic [Type IV hypersensitivity]
vs. Irritant [direct chemical/detergent disruption]); Seborrheic dermatitis (greasy scaly plaques on scalp/face linked to Malassezia);
Dyshidrotic eczema / pompholyx (pruritic vesicles on finger sides/palms/soles); Nummular / discoid eczema (coin-shaped plaques).
Clinical Features: Acute: intense itching, erythema, edema, clustered papules, weeping serous vesicles, and crusting. Chronic: dry
xerotic skin, lichenification (thickened leathery skin with exaggerated markings from scratching), excoriations, and painful fissures.
Management: Trigger avoidance; liberal use of ceramide emollients immediately after bathing; Topical corticosteroids (hydrocortisone
for face; mometasone/betamethasone for body flares); Topical calcineurin inhibitors (Tacrolimus); Oral antihistamines for pruritus;
Phototherapy (NB-UVB); Systemic immunosuppressants (Methotrexate, Cyclosporine) or Biologics (Dupilumab anti-IL-4Rα); Oral
antibiotics for secondary impetiginization.
Q 24 Bacterial, Fungal, and Viral Skin Infections
Bacterial Skin Infections:
Impetigo (S. aureus, S. pyogenes): Thin-walled vesicles rupturing into pathognomonic honey-colored golden crusts on face/
perioral zone. Rx: topical Mupirocin (2%) or oral Cephalexin.
Cellulitis & Erysipelas: Spreading erythema, warmth, pain, and edema with fever. Erysipelas is superficial with raised sharp borders;
cellulitis is deep. Rx: Flucloxacillin, Cefazolin, or Vancomycin (MRSA).
Folliculitis, Furuncles & Carbuncles (S. aureus): Suppurative hair follicle inflammation and necrotic boils. Rx: warm compresses,
incision & drainage, anti-staphylococcal antibiotics.
Fungal Skin Infections:
Dermatophytosis (Tinea / Ringworm): Annular erythematous plaques with raised, scaly, advancing borders and central clearing
(Tinea corporis, cruris, pedis, capitis). Rx: topical Terbinafine or Clotrimazole; oral Terbinafine/Itraconazole for extensive disease or
tinea capitis (Griseofulvin).
Candidiasis (C. albicans): Beefy-red intertriginous plaques with peripheral satellite pustules in moist body folds. Rx: keep dry,
topical Nystatin/Clotrimazole; oral Fluconazole.
Viral Skin Infections:
Herpes Simplex (HSV-1/2): Grouped vesicles on an erythematous base ("dewdrops on a rose petal") that ulcerate painfully. Rx: oral
Acyclovir (400 mg 5x/day) or Valacyclovir.
Herpes Zoster (VZV reactivation): Unilateral, dermatomal eruption of lancinating pain and grouped vesicles. Rx: oral Valacyclovir
(1,000 mg TID for 7d); Pregabalin for neuralgia.
Viral Warts (HPV 1, 2, 4): Hyperkeratotic exophytic papules with black dots (thrombosed capillaries). Rx: Salicylic acid, cryotherapy.
Q 25 Vitamin and Mineral Deficiency Disorders
Major Vitamin Deficiencies & Manifestations:
Vitamin A: Nyctalopia (night blindness), Bitot's spots, xerophthalmia, keratomalacia (corneal ulceration and permanent blindness).
Vitamin B1 (Thiamine): Wet Beriberi (high-output heart failure, edema); Dry Beriberi (peripheral neuropathy); Wernicke-Korsakoff

Vitamin B3 (Niacin):Pellagra (4 Ds): Photosensitive Dermatitis (Casal's necklace), Diarrhea, Dementia, Death.

Q 26 Protein-Energy Malnutrition (PEM)
Definition & Causes: Spectrum of nutritional deficiency disorders resulting from inadequate intake/absorption of protein and caloric
energy to meet bodily growth and metabolic needs. Caused by poverty, food insecurity, faulty early weaning onto dilute starches,
recurrent gastroenteritis, and measles/TB infections.
Types & Clinical Features:
Kwashiorkor (Protein deficiency with adequate calories): Generalized bilateral pitting edema; "moon face"; "crazy-pavement" /
"flaky-paint" dermatosis; sparse, dry, hypopigmented hair with alternating light/dark bands (flag sign); marked hepatomegaly (fatty
liver infiltration); profound misery, apathy, and anorexia.
Marasmus (Severe deficiency of both calories and protein): Severe somatic muscle wasting and total loss of subcutaneous fat;
wizened, shrunken "old-man" facies; prominent ribs ("accordion cage"); loose folds of redundant skin over buttocks ("baggy pants"); 
absence of edema; voracious appetite.
Marasmic Kwashiorkor: Severe tissue wasting coexisting with peripheral pitting edema.
Complications: Hypoglycemia (<54 mg/dL), hypothermia (<35.5°C), severe electrolyte derangements (hypokalemia, hypomagnesemia,
sodium retention), occult severe sepsis, heart failure, and acute keratomalacia.
Management (WHO 10-Step Guidelines):
Stabilization (Days 1–7): Treat hypoglycemia (10% dextrose), warm child, gentle oral rehydration with ReSoMal (no rapid IV fluids);
supplement potassium/magnesium; broad-spectrum antibiotics; Vitamin A; initial starter feeding with low-protein F-75 diet (75 kcal/
100 mL); strictly withhold iron during stabilization.
Rehabilitation (Weeks 2–6): Transition to energy-dense F-100 diet (100 kcal/100 mL) or RUTF for catch-up growth; add iron
supplementation; emotional stimulation.
PART V: MATERNAL HEALTH, LABOR & GYNECOLOGY (Q27 – Q32)
Q 27 Physiological Changes in Pregnancy, Antenatal & Postnatal Care
Physiological Changes During Pregnancy:
Cardiovascular: Cardiac output rises 30–50%; heart rate increases 10–15 bpm; SVR drops (progesterone-mediated vasodilation),
lowering diastolic BP in 2nd trimester; supine hypotension syndrome from IVC compression.
Hematological: Plasma volume increases 50%, RBC mass rises 20–30% → physiological hemodilution anemia; hypercoagulable
state (elevated fibrinogen, factors VII, VIII, X → 5x increased VTE risk).
Respiratory & Renal: Progesterone stimulates hyperventilation (mild respiratory alkalosis); GFR increases 50%, lowering serum
creatinine (<0.6 mg/dL).
Antenatal Care (ANC): Comprehensive healthcare surveillance from conception until labor. Objectives: monitor maternal-fetal health;
detect and manage high-risk obstetrical conditions early (pre-eclampsia, gestational diabetes, severe anemia, Rh isoimmunization);
provide prophylaxis (iron-folate, calcium, Td/Tdap immunization); birth preparedness and complication readiness.
Postnatal Care (PNC): Specialized medical care provided during the 6-week puerperium (42 days post-delivery). Importance: early
detection and management of postpartum hemorrhage (PPH), puerperal sepsis, venous thromboembolism, and postpartum depression;
establish and support exclusive breastfeeding; neonatal surveillance (jaundice, cord care, immunization); postpartum contraception
counseling.
Q 28 Stages and Physiological Changes of Labor
The Four Stages of Labor:
1st Stage (Cervical Dilatation): Onset of regular uterine contractions to full cervical dilatation (10 cm). Divided into Latent phase
(slow dilatation up to 4–5 cm) and Active phase (rapid dilatation ≥1 cm/h).
2nd Stage (Fetal Expulsion): Full dilatation (10 cm) to complete delivery of the fetus. Propelled by Cardinal Movements:
Engagement, Descent, Flexion, Internal rotation, Extension, Restitution, External rotation, and Expulsion.
3rd Stage (Placental): Complete delivery of baby to complete delivery of placenta and membranes (normal ≤30 min). Managed
with AMTSL: Oxytocin (10 IU IM), controlled cord traction, and fundal massage.
4th Stage (Observation): Immediate 1–2 hours postpartum for monitoring maternal hemodynamics, uterine contraction tone, and
vaginal bleeding.
Major Physiological Changes During Labor: Uterine muscular action shows fundal dominance with rhythmic contraction (transient
shortening) and retraction (permanent shortening without relaxation), creating a thick upper active segment and thin lower passive
segment separated by the physiological retraction ring; Cervical effacement (shortening/thinning) and dilatation driven by hydrostatic bag
of waters and fetal head pressure; Hemodynamic "autotransfusion" of 300–500 mL blood into maternal circulation during each
contraction increasing cardiac output and blood pressure; Hyperventilation causing respiratory alkalosis followed by metabolic lactic
acidosis.

Q 29 Menopause
Definition & Physiology: Permanent cessation of menses resulting from loss of ovarian follicular activity, clinically diagnosed
retrospectively after 12 consecutive months of amenorrhea (mean age 51y). Ovarian depletion of follicles causes circulating estradiol
(E2) to fall, removing hypothalamic-pituitary negative feedback and producing hypergonadotropism with marked elevation of FSH (>30
40 IU/L) and LH.
Clinical Manifestations:
Vasomotor: Hot flashes (intense sudden heat, flushing, sweating, chills from hypothalamic thermoregulatory instability), night sweats,
sleep disturbances.
Genitourinary Syndrome of Menopause (GSM): Vaginal epithelial atrophy, dryness, dyspareunia, pruritus, loss of rugae, elevated
pH >5.0, urinary frequency/urgency, and recurrent UTIs.
Psychological & Physical: Irritability, mood swings, depression, forgetfulness, loss of libido, breast atrophy, skin collagen loss, and
arthralgias.
Complications: Accelerated osteoporosis and fragility fractures (trabecular bone loss from osteoclast disinhibition); Cardiovascular
disease (atherogenic lipid shifts: elevated LDL, decreased HDL; loss of estrogen vascular protection).
Management: Lifestyle: weight-bearing exercise, calcium (1,200 mg/day), vitamin D (800–1,000 IU/day), trigger avoidance; Hormone
Replacement Therapy (HRT): Estrogen-only for hysterectomized women; Combined Estrogen-Progestin for women with an intact uterus
(progestin prevents endometrial cancer); Non-hormonal alternatives: SSRIs/SNRIs (Venlafaxine), Gabapentin, Fezolinetant (NK3
receptor antagonist); Topical vaginal estrogen creams for GSM.
Q 30 Common Gynecological Infections & Uterine/Vaginal Disorders
Common Gynecological Infections:
Bacterial Vaginosis: Dysbiosis with loss of Lactobacillus and overgrowth of anaerobes (G. vaginalis). Thin grayish-white discharge
with "fishy" odor. Diagnosis by Amsel's criteria: pH >4.5, positive Whiff test (KOH), Clue cells on wet mount. Rx: oral/topical
Metronidazole.
Vulvovaginal Candidiasis:C. albicans. Intense vulvovaginal pruritus, erythema, thick white curd-like "cottage cheese" discharge,
normal pH (<4.5), pseudohyphae on 10% KOH. Rx: single-dose oral Fluconazole (150 mg) or Clotrimazole pessary.
Trichomoniasis:T. vaginalis (flagellated protozoan, STD). Frothy greenish-yellow malodorous discharge, severe pruritus, 
"strawberry cervix". Rx: oral Metronidazole; treat partner.
Pelvic Inflammatory Disease (PID): Ascending infection (Chlamydia, Gonorrhea). Bilateral pelvic pain, high fever, purulent
discharge, marked cervical motion tenderness ("chandelier sign"). Rx: IM Ceftriaxone plus oral Doxycycline plus oral
Metronidazole for 14 days.
Uterine & Vaginal Disorders:
Uterine Fibroids (Leiomyomas): Benign smooth muscle tumors. Menorrhagia, dysmenorrhea, pelvic pressure, bulk symptoms. Rx:
Tranexamic acid, Levonorgestrel IUD, GnRH agonists, myomectomy, hysterectomy.
Endometriosis & Adenomyosis: Ectopic endometrial tissue outside uterus or in myometrium. Severe dysmenorrhea, chronic pelvic
pain, deep dyspareunia, subfertility. Rx: Progestins, OCPs, laparoscopic ablation.
Pelvic Organ Prolapse: Vaginal bulge, pelvic heaviness, cystocele/rectocele. Rx: Kegel exercises, supportive pessaries, pelvic floor
repair.

Q 31 Hysterectomy and Dilatation & Curettage (D&C)
Hysterectomy:
Definition: Surgical removal of the uterus (Total: body + cervix; Subtotal: body only; Radical: uterus, cervix, parametrium, upper
vagina, lymph nodes). Performed via abdominal, vaginal, or laparoscopic routes.
Indications: Symptomatic uterine fibroids failing medical therapy, refractory abnormal uterine bleeding (AUB), gynecological
malignancies (endometrial/cervical cancer), severe adenomyosis/endometriosis, advanced uterovaginal prolapse, emergency
intractable postpartum hemorrhage.
Complications: Hemorrhage, ureteric injury (proximity to uterine arteries), bladder/bowel injury, pelvic hematoma/abscess, surgical
site infection, DVT/PE, vaginal vault prolapse, and psychosexual distress.
Dilatation and Curettage (D&C):
Definition: Minor operative procedure involving progressive mechanical dilatation of the cervical canal followed by scraping and
evacuation of endometrial tissue with a curette.
Indications: Diagnostic: evaluation of postmenopausal bleeding, abnormal uterine bleeding in women >40y, suspected endometrial
hyperplasia/carcinoma; Therapeutic: evacuation of retained products of conception (incomplete/missed miscarriage), molar
pregnancy evacuation, temporary control of acute refractory uterine bleeding, polyp removal.
Complications:Uterine perforation (risk of bowel/vessel injury), cervical laceration/incompetence, acute endometritis/salpingitis, 
Asherman's syndrome (intrauterine synechiae from over-vigorous curettage causing amenorrhea/infertility), and hemorrhage.
Q 32 Urinary Incontinence in Women
Definition: Involuntary, objectively demonstrable loss or leakage of urine causing physical hygiene, social, or psychological distress.
Types & Causes:
Stress Incontinence (SUI, ~50%): Leakage on effort, exertion, coughing, sneezing, or laughing without detrusor contraction. Caused
by pelvic floor muscle laxity, urethral hypermobility, and intrinsic sphincteric deficiency (risk factors: multiparity, vaginal deliveries,
postmenopausal estrogen deficiency, obesity, chronic cough).
Urge Incontinence (UUI / Overactive Bladder, ~20%): Involuntary leakage preceded by an intense, sudden, uncontrollable urge to
void. Caused by detrusor overactivity (idiopathic, stroke, Parkinson's, MS, UTI, bladder stones).
Mixed Incontinence (~30%): Features of both stress and urge incontinence.
Overflow: Involuntary dribbling from a chronically overfilled, distended bladder due to bladder outlet obstruction (pelvic prolapse) or
hypotonic detrusor (diabetic neuropathy).
Functional: Inability to reach toilet due to severe physical or cognitive disability (dementia, severe arthritis).
Clinical Features: Leakage on strain/cough (SUI); urinary urgency, daytime frequency (>8 times), and nocturia (UUI); continuous
dribbling (overflow); perineal skin dermatitis, secondary UTIs, anxiety, and social withdrawal.
Management:
Conservative & Behavioral (First-line): Lifestyle: weight loss, fluid moderation, avoid caffeine/alcohol; Pelvic Floor Muscle
Training (Kegel exercises): at least 3 sets of 8–12 maximal contractions daily for ≥3 months (first-line for SUI); Bladder training
(timed voiding) for UUI.
Pharmacological: For UUI: Antimuscarinics (Oxybutynin, Tolterodine, Solifenacin) or β3-agonist (Mirabegron); Local topical vaginal
estrogen for postmenopausal women; SUI: Duloxetine (SNRI).
Interventional & Surgical: Intravesical OnabotulinumtoxinA injections or sacral neuromodulation for refractory UUI; Mid-Urethral
Sling (MUS: TVT / TOT) synthetic mesh placement (gold standard for refractory SUI); Burch colposuspension; Periurethral bulking
agents.
