Diagnostic Shows the forward slip Used to calculate Meyerdings grade and the slip angle Oblique X rays Shows the pars defect in isthmic types Scotty dog with a broken collar Dynamic X rays Flexion/Extension To assess for spinal instability abnormal movement between vertebrae MRI To evaluate disc status nerve root compression and central canal dimensions **Management** **A Conservative / Medical Management** Indicated for Grade I and II slips with mild symptoms Rest activity restriction avoid heavy lifting/contact sports NSAIDs and analgesics Lumbosacral corset for support Physiotherapy Abdominal and core strengthening exercises hamstring stretching **B Surgical Management** Indications Progressive slip especially in children Grade III or higher severe intractable back/leg pain neurological deficit Decompression and Fusion Standard of Care The compressed nerve roots are decompressed The unstable segment e g L5 S1 is fused using bone graft posterolateral fusion and stabilized with titanium pedicle screws and rods Reduction In severe grades the slipped vertebra may be partially pulled back into alignment before fusion though this carries a risk of nerve stretching --- **6 Lumbago / Lumbosacral Strain** **Introduction and Definition** Definition Lumbago is a descriptive term for pain in the lower back Lumbosacral strain specifically refers to mechanical back pain resulting from injury stretching or partial tearing of the muscles fascia or ligaments of the lower back It is the most common cause of acute low back pain **Aetiology / Causes** Acute Strain Sudden forceful lifting especially with the spine in a twisted or awkward position Sudden uncoordinated movement or a fall Chronic Strain Poor posture prolonged sitting or standing in unergonomic positions obesity increased lumbar lordosis weak core muscles or wearing high heels Psychological factors Stress and depression can manifest as chronic muscular back pain **Pathophysiology** The spinal column relies on a complex network of muscles erector spinae and ligaments supraspinous interspinous for stability When demand exceeds capacity micro tears occur in these soft tissues This leads to localized bleeding inflammation and local swelling The body responds with a reflex muscle spasm to splint and protect the injured area which in itself is highly painful and restricts movement **Clinical Features** **Symptoms** Pain Acute sharp or dull aching pain localized to the lower back Onset Often sudden after a specific event e g I lifted a heavy box and felt a pop but can be gradual in chronic strain Radiation The pain may radiate to the buttocks or posterior thigh but does not go below the knee non radicular Stiffness Severe difficulty in bending forward or getting out of bed **Signs** Posture The patient may stand with a tilt or flattened lumbar lordosis to avoid stretching the injured muscle Tenderness Diffuse localized tenderness over the paraspinal muscles Muscle Spasm Visible or palpable tight bands of muscle beside the spine Neurological Exam Completely normal normal power reflexes and sensation SLR is negative though it may cause back tightness **Investigations** The diagnosis is primarily clinical X rays AP and Lateral Usually completely normal May show a straightening of the normal lumbar lordosis due to muscle spasm Ordered primarily to rule out red flag conditions like fractures tumors or infections MRI Not indicated for acute lumbago unless symptoms persist beyond 4 6 weeks or neurological signs develop **Management** **A Conservative / Medical Management** Curative in almost all cases Short term Rest Bed rest for 1 2 days on a firm mattress Prolonged bed rest is discouraged as it leads to muscle deconditioning Early Mobilization The patient is encouraged to walk and resume light activities as soon as tolerated Medications Analgesics Paracetamol NSAIDs Ibuprofen Diclofenac to reduce inflammation Muscle relaxants Thiocolchicoside to break the pain spasm cycle Local Therapy Ice packs in the first 48 hours to reduce inflammation followed by heat therapy to relax muscles Physiotherapy Back extension exercises core strengthening and posture correction once the acute phase passes Patient education on proper lifting techniques lift with knees not back **B Surgical Management** There is no role for surgery in a pure lumbosacral muscle strain --- **7 Sacralisation Lumbosacral Transitional Vertebra LSTV** **Introduction and Definition** Definition Sacralisation is a congenital anomaly where the lowest fifth lumbar vertebra L5 is partially or completely fused with the first sacral segment S1 or the iliac crest It is a type of Lumbosacral Transitional Vertebra LSTV Because L5 takes on the characteristics of the sacrum the lumbar spine appears to have only four mobile vertebrae **Aetiology / Causes** Congenital It occurs during embryonic development due to a failure of segmentation of the somites Genetic predisposition Often runs in families representing a variant of normal spinal development **Pathophysiology** Sacralisation can be unilateral or bilateral and the fusion can be bony complete or fibrous pseudoarthrosis Biomechanical Alteration Normally L5 S1 is a highly mobile segment that absorbs a lot of stress When L5 is fused to the sacrum this segment becomes rigid Consequently the mechanical stress of spinal movement is transferred to the level above L4 L5 Over time this increased stress at L4 L5 leads to accelerated disc degeneration hypermobility and facet arthropathy at that specific level a condition known as Bertolottis Syndrome Additionally a pseudoarthrosis between a large L5 transverse process and the sacrum can become a direct source of localized pain **Clinical Features** Often Asymptomatic Found incidentally on X rays taken for other reasons Low Back Pain If symptomatic patients present with mechanical low back pain Bertolottis Syndrome Back pain with or without radiculopathy originating from the hypermobile L4 L5 level above the sacralisation Localized Pain Unilateral pain if there is inflammation at the site of a pseudoarthrosis between the transverse process and sacrum Signs May have restricted spinal mobility Local tenderness over the lumbosacral junction Neurological exam is typically normal **Investigations** X ray AP view of Lumbosacral spine Diagnostic Evaluated using the Castellvi classification Broadening of the L5 transverse process greater than 19mm Pseudoarthrosis with the sacrum/ilium Complete bony fusion with the sacrum MRI Ordered if disc herniation is suspected at the level above L4 L5 **Management** **A Conservative / Medical Management** Reassurance The patient should be reassured that it is a common congenital variant and not a disease Symptomatic relief Analgesics and NSAIDs for acute pain Physiotherapy Core strengthening and pelvic tilt exercises to improve spinal biomechanics and protect the L4 L5 level Local Injections A steroid injection into the pseudoarthrosis if present can provide diagnostic confirmation and therapeutic relief **B Surgical Management** Indications Very rare Considered only if conservative treatment fails and the pain is severely debilitating Excision Resection of the enlarged transverse process or pseudoarthrosis Spinal Fusion Fusion of the L4 L5 segment if it is severely degenerated and unstable --- **8 Lumbarisation Lumbosacral Transitional Vertebra LSTV** **Introduction and Definition** Definition Lumbarisation is a congenital anomaly where the first sacral segment S1 fails to fuse completely with the rest of the sacrum As a result S1 acts like a separate mobile vertebra taking on the characteristics of a lumbar vertebra The patient effectively appears to have a sixth lumbar vertebra and a shortened sacrum **Aetiology / Causes** Congenital Arises from a defect in embryonic segmentation It is the anatomical opposite of sacralisation though they are both classed as transitional vertebrae **Pathophysiology** Like sacralisation lumbarisation alters the normal biomechanics of the lower spine The extra mobile segment can lead to instability The new L6 S2 joint or what was supposed to be S1 S2 is not designed to handle the mechanical loads and shear forces of a lumbar disc This can lead to premature degenerative changes facet arthritis and disc prolapse at this transitional level or the levels above it **Clinical Features** Asymptomatic Mostly an incidental finding Mechanical Back Pain Due to altered mechanics instability or early degenerative changes in the extra mobile segment Signs No specific clinical signs differentiate it from standard lumbago without X rays Neurological exam is typically normal **Investigations** Plain X rays AP and Lateral Counting the vertebrae from the lower ribs downwards reveals six lumbar type vertebrae that are not fused to the sacrum MRI To assess disc health at the transitional segments if the patient has radicular symptoms **Management** The management principles are identical to sacralisation **A Conservative / Medical Management** Reassurance Analgesics NSAIDs during painful episodes Physiotherapy focusing on core stability and back muscle strengthening to support the extra mobile segment **B Surgical Management** Extremely rare Only indicated if there is a prolapsed disc or severe instability causing neurological compression at the transitional level requiring decompression and fusion --- **9 Coccydynia** **Introduction and Definition** Definition Coccydynia is a painful condition localized to the coccyx tailbone and the surrounding sacrococcygeal region **Aetiology / Causes** Direct Trauma Most Common A fall directly onto the buttocks e g falling on ice falling down stairs which can result in a contusion sprain or fracture dislocation of the sacrococcygeal joint Childbirth Vaginal delivery can stretch or injure the coccyx as the babys head passes through the pelvis Repetitive Strain Prolonged sitting on hard narrow or uncomfortable surfaces e g cycling Idiopathic In some cases no specific cause is found could be due to degenerative changes or bony spurs **Pathophysiology** The sacrococcygeal joint normally has a small amount of movement flexion and extension Trauma causes a sprain or partial tear of the sacrococcygeal ligaments leading to hypermobility or subluxation of the joint This creates chronic inflammation The pain is exacerbated when the patient sits as the weight forces the coccyx into extension pulling on the inflamed ligaments **Clinical Features** **Symptoms** Localized Pain Severe pain directly over the tailbone Sitting Pain Exacerbated by sitting especially leaning backward on a hard surface Transitional Pain Sharp pain when moving from a sitting to a standing position as the pelvic muscles attached to the coccyx contract Pain with Defecation May occur due to pressure from the rectum **Signs** Point Tenderness Exquisite tenderness precisely over the coccyx or the sacrococcygeal joint when palpated from the outside Per Rectal PR Examination If required the coccyx can be grasped between the thumb outside and index finger inside the rectum moving it elicits severe pain confirms the diagnosis **Investigations** X rays Lateral View Shows the shape and angulation of the coccyx May reveal a fracture anterior subluxation or a bony spur However often X rays are normal Dynamic X rays Sitting vs Standing Can demonstrate abnormal hypermobility of the sacrococcygeal joint when weight is applied **Management** **A Conservative / Medical Management** Usually successful Cushions The most important treatment Use of a donut cushion or a U shaped coccyx cushion to offload weight from the tailbone while sitting Postural modification Leaning slightly forward while sitting Medications NSAIDs for pain and inflammation Heat Therapy Hot sitz baths or local heating pads Local Injections Injection of a local anesthetic mixed with a corticosteroid directly into the sacrococcygeal joint or around the painful ligaments Provides excellent relief in refractory cases Manipulation Gentle manual manipulation of the coccyx via the rectum under anesthesia rarely done now **B Surgical Management** Indications Chronic intractable coccydynia that has failed months of aggressive conservative treatment Coccygectomy Surgical excision of the mobile portion of the coccyx Care must be taken to preserve the sphincter muscles --- **10 Hemivertebra** **Introduction and Definition** Definition A hemivertebra is a severe congenital anomaly of the spine where only one half one side of a vertebral body develops It acts like a wedge inserted into one side of the spinal column leading to a congenital spinal deformity most commonly congenital scoliosis lateral curvature or kyphoscoliosis **Aetiology / Causes** Embryological Failure Occurs during the first 6 weeks of gestation It is caused by the failure of formation of one of the two lateral chondrification centers of the vertebral body Often associated with other congenital anomalies VACTERL association Vertebral Anal Cardiac Tracheal Esophageal Renal and Limb defects **Pathophysiology** A normal vertebra is shaped like a block keeping the spine straight A hemivertebra is wedge shaped Because one side of the spine has extra bony material the hemivertebra and the other side is deficient the spine curves away from the side of the hemivertebra Furthermore the hemivertebra has its own growth plates As the child grows the hemivertebra grows asymmetrically acting as a progressive wedge that continuously worsens the scoliotic curve **Classification of Hemivertebrae** Fully Segmented Has normal discs above and below it High risk of progression because both growth plates are active Semi segmented Fused to the vertebra above or below Moderate risk of progression Non segmented Fused to both the vertebra above and below Lowest risk of progression Incarcerated The hemivertebra is tucked into the spine without disrupting the overall alignment much **Clinical Features** Spinal Deformity The parents usually notice a lump on the back uneven shoulders or a visible curve in the spine scoliosis in infancy or early childhood Progression The deformity worsens rapidly during periods of growth spurts Neurological symptoms Usually absent initially Severe neglected curves can eventually cause spinal cord tethering or compression Signs Asymmetrical trunk rib hump on forward bending test Adams test **Investigations** X rays AP and Lateral of whole spine Diagnostic Shows the wedge shaped anomalous bone and the degree of scoliosis measured by Cobbs angle MRI of the Spine Mandatory to rule out associated neural axis abnormalities like tethered cord syringomyelia or diastematomyelia which are common with congenital spine defects Ultrasound Renal and Cardiac To rule out associated VACTERL anomalies **Management** Because congenital curves are rigid and do not respond to bracing management is largely observational or surgical **A Conservative Management** Observation Indicated for non segmented or incarcerated hemivertebrae that are not progressing Serial X rays every 6 months to monitor for curve progression Braces are ineffective for congenital scoliosis **B Surgical Management** Indications Documented progression of the curve fully segmented hemivertebrae in young children or severe curves at presentation Hemivertebra Excision The anomalous wedge of bone is surgically completely removed via an anterior posterior or combined approach Short Segment Spinal Fusion After excision the spine above and below the defect is brought together straightened and fused using pedicle screws and rods This corrects the deformity and prevents further asymmetric growth In Situ Fusion Fusing the spine as it is without excising the hemivertebra in very young children to arrest the growth and stop the progression of the curve

PART I — SHOULDER Regional Conditions of the Shoulder — 20-Mark University Exam Answer Introduction The shoulder is a highly mobile joint complex consisting mainly of the glenohumeral, acromioclavicular, sternoclavicular and scapulothoracic articulations. Because of its wide range of movement and dependence on soft tissues for stability, it is commonly affected by painful disorders involving the joint capsule, rotator cuff tendons, biceps tendon and subacromial bursa. The important regional shoulder conditions include: 1. Periarthritis shoulder / Adhesive capsulitis 2. Rotator cuff tendinitis 3. Supraspinatus tendinitis 4. Infraspinatus tendinitis 5. Bicipital tendinitis 6. Subacromial bursitis 1. Periarthritis Shoulder / Adhesive Capsulitis Definition Adhesive capsulitis is a painful condition of the shoulder characterized by progressive pain, stiffness and marked restriction of both active and passive glenohumeral movements, particularly external rotation. It is commonly called frozen shoulder. Clinical Features • Gradual onset of shoulder pain. • Pain is often worse at night and may disturb sleep. • Progressive stiffness of the shoulder. • Difficulty with combing hair, dressing, reaching overhead and reaching behind the back. • Both active and passive ROM are restricted. • External rotation is usually the most restricted movement, followed by abduction and internal rotation. • Capsular pattern: External rotation > abduction > internal rotation. • Muscle weakness may develop secondary to pain and disuse. Page 1 BPT University Exam Notes• Scapular movements may become excessive as compensation. Stages 1. Freezing stage: increasing pain and progressive loss of movement. 2. Frozen stage: pain may decrease but marked stiffness persists. 3. Thawing stage: gradual recovery of ROM and function. Management Medical management • Patient education and activity modification. • Analgesics and NSAIDs as prescribed. • Corticosteroid injection, particularly in the painful early stage. • Hydrodilatation in selected patients. • Manipulation under anesthesia or arthroscopic capsular release in resistant cases. Physiotherapy management • Pain-relieving modalities as appropriate. • Gentle pendular exercises. • Gentle active-assisted ROM. • Avoid aggressive stretching that increases pain. • Joint mobilization and capsular stretching. • Active and active-assisted ROM. • Wand/pulley exercises. • Scapular mobility exercises. • Progressive stretching and strengthening. • Rotator cuff and scapular muscle strengthening. • Functional and home exercise programme. 2. Rotator Cuff Tendinitis Definition Rotator cuff tendinitis is an inflammatory or degenerative condition involving one or more tendons of the supraspinatus, infraspinatus, teres minor and subscapularis, commonly producing shoulder pain during elevation and rotation. The supraspinatus tendon is most frequently involved. Clinical Features • Pain over the shoulder, commonly around the anterolateral aspect. • Pain increases with overhead activities. • Painful arc during shoulder abduction, commonly between 60° and 120°. Page 2 BPT University Exam Notes• Pain may increase at night. • Weakness due to pain and inhibition. • Restricted active movement may occur. • Passive ROM is usually relatively preserved. • Tenderness over the affected tendon. • Positive rotator cuff provocation tests may be present. • Difficulty with lifting, reaching and overhead activities. Management • Relative rest and activity modification. • Avoid repetitive overhead activities. • Ice during the painful phase. • Analgesics/NSAIDs as prescribed. • Gentle ROM and pendulum exercises. • Stretching. • Rotator cuff strengthening. • Scapular stabilizer strengthening. • Progressive resisted exercises. • Postural correction. • Gradual return to overhead activities. • Specialist assessment for persistent symptoms or structural pathology. 3. Supraspinatus Tendinitis Definition Supraspinatus tendinitis is an inflammatory or degenerative disorder of the supraspinatus tendon, usually occurring near its passage beneath the acromion, causing pain particularly during shoulder elevation. Clinical Features • Pain over the anterolateral aspect of the shoulder. • Pain increases during abduction and overhead activities. • Painful arc, commonly from approximately 60°–120°. • Pain may be worse at night. • Tenderness over the supraspinatus tendon. • Pain or weakness during resisted abduction. • Difficulty lifting the arm. • Positive empty-can/Jobe test may reproduce pain or weakness. • Passive ROM is generally less affected than active ROM. • Severe cases may produce weakness of abduction. Page 3 BPT University Exam NotesManagement • Relative rest from painful overhead activities. • Ice during acute painful periods. • Analgesics/NSAIDs as prescribed. • Gentle ROM exercises. • Stretching. • Progressive supraspinatus and rotator cuff strengthening. • Isometric → isotonic → functional strengthening. • Scapular stabilization exercises. • Postural correction. • Gradual return to overhead activities. • Corticosteroid injection may be considered in selected cases. • Persistent or associated structural lesions may require specialist assessment. 4. Infraspinatus Tendinitis Definition Infraspinatus tendinitis is inflammation or degeneration of the infraspinatus tendon, resulting in pain and dysfunction mainly during external rotation of the shoulder. Clinical Features • Posterior shoulder pain. • Pain may radiate toward the lateral arm. • Pain increases during external rotation. • Pain during overhead activities. • Tenderness over the posterior shoulder/infraspinatus tendon. • Pain or weakness on resisted external rotation. • Difficulty with activities requiring external rotation. • Weakness may occur because of pain. • Passive ROM is usually relatively preserved. Management • Relative rest and avoidance of aggravating activities. • Ice for pain where appropriate. • Analgesics/NSAIDs as prescribed. • Gentle shoulder ROM. • Stretching exercises. • Isometric external rotation exercises initially. • Progressive resisted external rotation. Page 4 BPT University Exam Notes• Rotator cuff and scapular stabilizer strengthening. • Postural correction. • Gradual functional and sports-specific rehabilitation. 5. Bicipital Tendinitis Definition Bicipital tendinitis is inflammation or degenerative irritation of the tendon of the long head of the biceps brachii, particularly within the intertubercular/bicipital groove. Clinical Features • Pain in the anterior shoulder. • Pain may radiate down the anterior aspect of the arm. • Pain increases with shoulder flexion, elbow flexion, forearm supination and overhead activities. • Tenderness over the bicipital groove. • Pain on resisted elbow flexion. • Pain on resisted forearm supination. • Positive Speed's test may reproduce symptoms. • Yergason's test may also reproduce pain. • Weakness may occur due to pain. • Night pain can occur. • Difficulty lifting objects or performing repetitive overhead activities. Management • Relative rest and activity modification. • Avoid repetitive lifting and overhead activities. • Ice during painful periods. • Analgesics/NSAIDs as prescribed. • Gentle shoulder ROM and stretching. • Progressive biceps strengthening after pain decreases. • Rotator cuff and scapular stabilization. • Postural correction. • Gradual return to functional activities. • Injection or surgical management may be considered depending on underlying pathology. 6. Subacromial Bursitis Definition Page 5 BPT University Exam NotesSubacromial bursitis is inflammation of the subacromial bursa, a fluid-filled structure that reduces friction between the rotator cuff tendons and the acromion during shoulder movement. Clinical Features • Shoulder pain, commonly over the lateral/anterior shoulder. • Pain increases with overhead activities. • Painful arc, often around 60°–120° of abduction. • Night pain may be present. • Tenderness around the subacromial region. • Pain with active shoulder elevation. • Difficulty reaching overhead. • Difficulty dressing and grooming. • Muscle guarding may occur. • Weakness may be present due to pain inhibition. Management Medical management • Relative rest. • Activity modification. • Ice. • Analgesics/NSAIDs as prescribed. • Corticosteroid injection may be considered in selected cases. Physiotherapy management • Pain-relieving modalities when indicated. • Gentle ROM and pendular exercises. • Stretching. • Rotator cuff and scapular stabilizer strengthening. • Postural correction. • Correction of movement patterns. • Progressive functional exercises. • Gradual return to overhead activities. Comparison of Important Clinical Features • Adhesive capsulitis: joint capsule; restriction of both active and passive ROM. • Rotator cuff tendinitis: rotator cuff tendons; pain with elevation/overhead activity. • Supraspinatus tendinitis: supraspinatus tendon; painful arc and painful resisted abduction. • Infraspinatus tendinitis: infraspinatus tendon; pain with resisted external rotation. • Bicipital tendinitis: long head of biceps; anterior shoulder pain and bicipital groove tenderness. Page 6 BPT University Exam Notes• Subacromial bursitis: subacromial bursa; painful elevation/abduction. General Physiotherapy Principles 1. Pain management: cryotherapy where appropriate, heat in selected chronic/stiff conditions, adjunctive electrotherapy where indicated, and activity modification. 2. Restoration of ROM: pendular, active-assisted, wand and pulley exercises; capsular stretching in adhesive capsulitis. 3. Strengthening: isometric → isotonic → resisted → functional strengthening. 4. Scapular rehabilitation: retraction, depression, controlled upward rotation, serratus anterior and lower trapezius strengthening. 5. Postural correction. 6. Functional rehabilitation: ADLs, overhead activity, work-specific and sports-specific exercises. Conclusion Regional shoulder conditions commonly involve the capsule, rotator cuff tendons, biceps tendon and subacromial bursa. Careful assessment of pain location, painful arc, active and passive ROM, resisted movements and special tests helps differentiate them. Management is primarily conservative and includes pain control, activity modification, restoration of mobility, progressive strengthening, scapular stabilization, postural correction and functional rehabilitation. Tennis Elbow — Lateral Epicondylitis Definition Tennis elbow is a painful overuse disorder of the tendons originating from the common extensor origin at the lateral epicondyle of the humerus, most commonly involving the extensor carpi radialis brevis. It is usually a tendinopathy rather than a purely inflammatory condition. Etiology/Risk Factors • Repetitive wrist extension. • Repetitive gripping. • Racquet sports. • Manual work. • Repetitive computer or occupational activities. • Sudden increase in activity. • Poor technique during sports. Clinical Features • Pain over the lateral epicondyle, sometimes radiating down the lateral forearm. • Pain aggravated by gripping, wrist extension, lifting, turning a screwdriver and shaking hands. • Tenderness over the lateral epicondyle/common extensor origin. • Reduced grip strength due to pain. • Pain on resisted wrist extension. • Difficulty performing occupational activities. Investigations • Mainly clinical. • X-ray to exclude bony pathology. • Ultrasound/MRI in persistent or unclear cases. Management • Activity modification and relative rest. • Ice during painful periods. Page 8 BPT University Exam Notes• Analgesics/NSAIDs as prescribed. • Counterforce brace or wrist splint in selected cases. • Wrist/forearm stretching. • Isometric wrist extension. • Progressive eccentric/concentric extensor strengthening. • Grip strengthening. • Manual therapy. • Ergonomic correction. • Gradual return to sport/work. 2. Golfer's Elbow — Medial Epicondylitis Definition Golfer's elbow is a tendinopathy involving the common flexor-pronator tendon origin at the medial epicondyle of the humerus, producing medial elbow pain. Etiology • Repetitive wrist flexion. • Repetitive forearm pronation. • Golf. • Throwing sports. • Manual occupations. • Repetitive gripping. Clinical Features • Pain over medial epicondyle, possibly radiating down medial forearm. • Tenderness at common flexor origin. • Pain during wrist flexion, forearm pronation and gripping. • Reduced grip strength. • Pain on resisted wrist flexion/pronation. • Occasionally ulnar nerve symptoms may coexist. Management • Activity modification, ice and analgesics as prescribed. • Brace if indicated. • Stretching of wrist flexors. • Isometric → progressive resisted strengthening. • Grip strengthening. • Eccentric training. • Manual therapy. Page 9 BPT University Exam Notes• Ergonomic correction. • Gradual return to activity. 3. Olecranon Bursitis — Student's Elbow Definition Olecranon bursitis is inflammation of the olecranon bursa, located between the skin and olecranon process of the ulna. It is commonly called student's elbow because prolonged leaning on the elbows can irritate the bursa. Causes • Repeated pressure. • Trauma. • Prolonged elbow leaning. • Infection. • Gout or inflammatory arthritis. Clinical Features • Swelling over posterior elbow. • Soft/fluctuant swelling over olecranon. • Pain or tenderness. • Warmth and redness if inflamed/infected. • Usually preserved elbow ROM. • Septic cases may cause fever and systemic symptoms. Investigations • Clinical examination. • Aspiration and fluid analysis when infection/gout is suspected. • Blood investigations in suspected infection. • Imaging when necessary. Management Non-infective: avoid pressure, activity modification, ice, compression/padding, analgesics and selected aspiration; recurrent cases may require surgery. Septic bursitis: medical assessment, antibiotics and drainage/aspiration when indicated. Physiotherapy: protection, gentle ROM, avoidance of direct pressure, and gradual strengthening after acute symptoms settle. 4. Triceps Tendinitis Definition Page 10 BPT University Exam NotesTriceps tendinitis is an overuse tendinopathy affecting the distal triceps tendon near its insertion into the olecranon, causing posterior elbow pain. Causes • Repetitive elbow extension. • Weightlifting. • Throwing. • Repetitive pushing. • Sudden increase in exercise load. Clinical Features • Posterior elbow pain. • Tenderness near triceps insertion. • Pain during resisted elbow extension. • Pain during pushing activities. • Weakness due to pain. • Pain after repetitive activity. • Occasionally swelling. Management • Relative rest and ice. • Activity modification. • Analgesics/NSAIDs. • Gentle ROM. • Triceps stretching. • Isometric exercises initially. • Progressive resisted strengthening. • Eccentric loading. • Gradual return to sport/work. WRIST AND HAND 5. De Quervain's Tenosynovitis Definition De Quervain's tenosynovitis is a painful stenosing tenosynovitis affecting the first dorsal compartment of the wrist, involving the abductor pollicis longus and extensor pollicis brevis tendons. Causes/Risk Factors • Repetitive thumb movements. Page 11 BPT University Exam Notes• Repetitive wrist motion. • Lifting infants. • Occupational overuse. • Repetitive gripping. Clinical Features • Pain over radial side of wrist, possibly radiating toward thumb/forearm. • Swelling over first dorsal compartment. • Pain with thumb movement. • Pain during gripping and lifting. • Reduced grip strength. • Tenderness over radial styloid. • Positive Finkelstein test. Management • Activity modification. • Thumb-spica splint. • Ice. • Analgesics/NSAIDs. • Corticosteroid injection when indicated. • Gentle ROM, thumb exercises, tendon gliding, stretching and progressive strengthening. • Surgical release in persistent cases. 6. Ganglion Definition A ganglion is a benign cystic swelling containing gelatinous fluid, commonly arising from a joint capsule or tendon sheath, particularly around the wrist. Clinical Features • Smooth rounded swelling, commonly dorsal wrist. • May change in size. • May be painless. • Pain may occur with wrist movement or pressure. • Possible weakness or discomfort. • Usually firm/fluctuant. • May transilluminate. Investigations • Clinical examination. Page 12 BPT University Exam Notes• Ultrasound. • MRI when diagnosis is uncertain. Management • Observation if asymptomatic. • Activity modification. • Splinting for painful cases. • Aspiration in selected cases. • Surgical excision for recurrent/symptomatic ganglion. • Physiotherapy for pain, ROM, strengthening, functional modification and scar management after surgery. 7. Trigger Finger / Trigger Thumb Definition Trigger finger is a stenosing tenosynovitis in which thickening of the flexor tendon/pulley system causes difficulty in smooth tendon gliding, producing catching, locking or snapping during finger movement. Clinical Features • Pain/tenderness at volar MCP region. • Clicking or snapping. • Finger catches during flexion/extension. • Locking in flexion in advanced cases. • Morning stiffness. • Palpable flexor tendon nodule. • Difficulty opening/closing the hand. Management • Activity modification. • Rest. • Splinting. • Analgesics. • Tendon-gliding exercises. • Gentle ROM. • Corticosteroid injection when indicated. • Surgical A1 pulley release for persistent/severe cases. • Postoperative scar management and mobilization. 8. Mallet Finger Definition Page 13 BPT University Exam NotesMallet finger is an injury to the terminal extensor mechanism at the distal interphalangeal joint, usually resulting in inability to actively extend the DIP joint. Causes • Sudden forced flexion of an actively extended finger. • Sports injuries. • Avulsion fracture may occur. Clinical Features • Drooping fingertip. • Inability to actively extend DIP. • Pain and swelling may occur. • Passive extension is usually possible. • Chronic cases may develop swan-neck deformity. Investigations • X-ray to identify avulsion fracture and joint involvement. Management • DIP joint splinting in extension. • Continuous splinting for the prescribed period. • Maintain PIP mobility. • Surgical treatment in selected large/displaced fractures or joint instability. • Physiotherapy: splint compliance, PIP/MCP mobility, gradual DIP ROM after immobilization and progressive strengthening. 9. Carpal Tunnel Syndrome Definition Carpal tunnel syndrome is a compressive neuropathy of the median nerve at the wrist as it passes through the carpal tunnel. Causes/Risk Factors • Repetitive wrist use. • Diabetes. • Pregnancy. • Rheumatoid arthritis. • Hypothyroidism. • Wrist trauma. • Space-occupying lesions. Page 14 BPT University Exam Notes• Increased pressure within carpal tunnel. Clinical Features • Numbness/tingling in thumb, index, middle and radial half of ring finger. • Night symptoms. • Hand weakness. • Dropping objects. • Difficulty with fine motor activities. • Thenar muscle wasting in advanced cases. • Reduced thumb opposition. • Positive Phalen test. • Positive Tinel sign may occur. Investigations • Nerve conduction studies/EMG. • Ultrasound. • Imaging if structural pathology is suspected. Management • Activity modification. • Neutral wrist splint, especially at night. • Analgesics. • Corticosteroid injection in selected cases. • Median nerve-gliding and tendon-gliding exercises. • Ergonomic correction. • Wrist ROM. • Carpal tunnel release for severe or persistent cases. 10. Dupuytren's Contracture Definition Dupuytren's contracture is a progressive fibrotic disorder of the palmar fascia, producing nodules and cords that cause flexion contractures of the fingers, most commonly ring and little fingers. Clinical Features • Palmar nodules. • Palmar cords. • Progressive finger flexion contracture. • Difficulty placing hand flat on a table. • Difficulty washing face, wearing gloves or putting hand into pockets. Page 15 BPT University Exam Notes• Usually painless. • Reduced hand function. Management • Observation in mild disease. • Splinting in selected cases. • ROM, stretching and functional training. • Postoperative rehabilitation. • Needle fasciotomy/collagenase treatment in selected settings. • Surgical fasciectomy for significant contracture. Iliotibial Band Syndrome Definition IT band syndrome is an overuse condition causing pain around the lateral aspect of the knee, resulting from irritation of tissues between the iliotibial band and lateral femoral region during repetitive knee flexion and extension. Causes • Running. • Cycling. • Repetitive knee flexion-extension. • Sudden increase in training. • Poor biomechanics. • Weak hip abductors. Clinical Features • Lateral knee pain. • Pain during running, especially downhill. • Pain worsens with repetitive activity. • Tenderness over lateral femoral epicondyle. • Pain around 20–30° of knee flexion may occur. • Tight IT band. • Hip abductor weakness. Management • Relative rest. • Ice. Page 16 BPT University Exam Notes• Activity modification. • Correct training errors. • Stretching. • Hip abductor and gluteal strengthening. • Core strengthening. • Running biomechanics correction. • Gradual return to sport. 12. Piriformis Syndrome Definition Piriformis syndrome is a condition in which the piriformis muscle irritates or compresses the sciatic nerve, producing buttock pain with possible radiating symptoms. Clinical Features • Deep buttock pain. • Pain may radiate down posterior thigh. • Pain aggravated by prolonged sitting. • Pain during running/walking. • Tenderness over piriformis. • Pain with hip flexion, adduction and internal rotation. • Possible paresthesia. • Reduced tolerance for sitting. Management • Activity modification. • Ice/heat as appropriate. • Analgesics. • Piriformis stretching. • Hip mobility exercises. • Gluteal and core strengthening. • Neural mobilization when appropriate. • Postural correction. • Gradual return to activity. 13. Trochanteric Bursitis / Greater Trochanteric Pain Syndrome Definition Trochanteric bursitis is pain around the greater trochanter, traditionally attributed to inflammation of the trochanteric bursa. Clinically, lateral hip pain often represents greater trochanteric pain syndrome, which can also involve the gluteal tendons. Page 17 BPT University Exam NotesClinical Features • Lateral hip pain. • Tenderness over greater trochanter. • Pain when lying on affected side. • Pain during walking/running. • Difficulty climbing stairs. • Pain during prolonged standing. • Pain with resisted hip abduction. • Possible IT band tightness. Management • Avoid prolonged pressure on affected side. • Activity modification. • Ice. • Analgesics/NSAIDs. • Hip abductor, gluteal and pelvic stabilization exercises. • Flexibility work where appropriate. • Gait retraining. • Gradual functional progression. • Injection may be considered in selected cases. Osteochondritis Dissecans Definition Osteochondritis dissecans is a condition in which a segment of subchondral bone and its overlying articular cartilage becomes damaged and may become partially or completely separated from the surrounding bone. Common Site Lateral aspect of medial femoral condyle is common. Causes/Risk Factors • Repetitive microtrauma. • Sports activities. • Abnormal joint loading. • Vascular factors may contribute. Page 18 BPT University Exam NotesClinical Features • Activity-related knee pain. • Swelling/effusion. • Tenderness. • Catching or locking in unstable lesions. • Reduced ROM. • Limp. • Quadriceps weakness. • Mechanical symptoms in advanced disease. Investigations • X-ray. • MRI. • CT in selected cases. Management • Activity restriction. • Avoid impact loading. • Physiotherapy. • Maintain ROM. • Quadriceps and hip strengthening. • Surgical options in selected lesions: drilling, fixation, debridement and osteochondral grafting. 15. Prepatellar Bursitis Definition Prepatellar bursitis is inflammation of the bursa located between the patella and overlying skin, commonly caused by repetitive kneeling. It is also called housemaid's knee. Clinical Features • Swelling directly over patella. • Anterior knee pain/tenderness. • Fluctuant swelling. • Pain with kneeling. • Redness/warmth in acute inflammation or infection. • Knee joint ROM may be relatively preserved. Management • Avoid kneeling. Page 19 BPT University Exam Notes• Knee padding. • Ice. • Compression. • Analgesics. • Aspiration when indicated. • Antibiotics for septic bursitis. • Physiotherapy after acute symptoms settle. • Strengthening and functional rehabilitation. 16. Suprapatellar Bursitis Definition Suprapatellar bursitis is inflammation of the suprapatellar bursa, located above the patella and communicating with the knee joint in many individuals. Clinical Features • Swelling above patella. • Anterior knee pain. • Tenderness. • Pain during knee flexion. • Possible joint effusion. • Reduced knee movement due to pain/swelling. Management • Rest/activity modification. • Ice. • Compression. • Analgesics/NSAIDs. • Treatment of underlying inflammatory/infective cause. • ROM exercises. • Quadriceps strengthening. • Gradual functional training. 17. Popliteal Tendinitis Definition Popliteal tendinitis is an overuse injury of the popliteus tendon, producing posterolateral knee pain. Clinical Features • Posterolateral knee pain. Page 20 BPT University Exam Notes• Pain during running, especially downhill. • Pain during knee flexion/rotation. • Tenderness around posterolateral knee. • Pain may increase with weight-bearing. • Possible feeling of instability. Management • Relative rest. • Ice. • Activity modification. • Analgesics as prescribed. • Gentle ROM. • Hamstring and calf flexibility. • Progressive strengthening of knee and hip musculature. • Proprioceptive training. • Gradual return to running/sport. 18. Patellar Tendinitis Definition Patellar tendinitis/tendinopathy is an overuse disorder of the patellar tendon, commonly at its attachment to the inferior pole of the patella. Clinical Features • Anterior knee pain. • Localized tenderness at inferior pole of patella. • Pain during jumping, running and squatting. • Pain during stairs. • Pain during resisted knee extension. • Reduced functional performance. Chondromalacia Patella Definition Chondromalacia patella refers to softening and degenerative changes of the articular cartilage on the posterior surface of the patella, commonly associated with patellofemoral pain and abnormal patellar loading. Clinical Features • Anterior knee pain. • Pain during stairs, squatting, running, jumping or prolonged sitting. • Crepitus. • Patellar tenderness. • Pain with appropriate patellar compression testing. • Possible quadriceps and hip muscle weakness. Plantar Fasciitis / Calcaneal Spur Definition Plantar fasciitis is a degenerative/overuse condition of the plantar fascia, commonly producing pain at its medial calcaneal attachment. Achilles Tendinitis / Achilles Tendinopathy Definition Achilles tendinopathy is a painful overuse disorder of the Achilles tendon, usually involving degenerative changes associated with repetitive mechanical loading. Causes/Risk Factors • Running and jumping. • Sudden increase in training. • Poor training progression. • Tight calf muscles. • Inappropriate footwear. • Reduced ankle dorsiflexion. • Previous tendon problems. Clinical Features • Pain at Achilles tendon. • Mid-portion or insertional pain. • Morning stiffness. Page 27 BPT University Exam Notes• Pain during running/jumping. • Tenderness. • Tendon thickening may occur. • Pain during resisted plantarflexion. • Reduced calf strength. • Difficulty with repeated heel raises. Management • Relative rest/load modification. • Ice for symptom relief. • Appropriate footwear. • Heel lift temporarily in selected cases. • Calf stretching where appropriate. • Progressive tendon loading. • Isometric exercises initially when painful. • Heavy-slow resistance/eccentric loading. • Calf strengthening. • Balance and functional training. • Gradual return to running/jumping. 26. Metatarsalgia Definition Metatarsalgia is pain arising from the forefoot/metatarsal head region, usually caused by excessive loading of the metatarsal heads. Causes • Excessive running/jumping. • Improper footwear. • High heels. • Pes cavus. • Hallux valgus. • Altered foot biomechanics. • Increased body weight. • Fat-pad changes. Clinical Features • Pain under metatarsal heads. • Burning or aching forefoot pain. • Pain worsens with walking/running. Page 28 BPT University Exam Notes• Feeling of walking on a pebble may occur. • Callus formation. • Tenderness. • Reduced tolerance for prolonged standing. Management • Activity modification. • Proper footwear. • Avoid high heels. • Metatarsal pads. • Orthotics when indicated. • Ice. • Calf and foot stretching. • Foot intrinsic strengthening. • Gait correction. • Gradual return to activity. • Treat underlying foot deformity. 27. Morton's Neuroma Definition Morton's neuroma is a painful perineural fibrotic enlargement/irritation of a common digital nerve, most commonly occurring between the third and fourth toes. 1. Congenital Talipes Equinovarus (CTEV / Clubfoot)
Introduction & Definition
CTEV is a complex congenital deformity of the foot characterized by four distinct components: Equinus (plantarflexion at the ankle), Varus (inversion of the subtalar joint), Adduction (of the forefoot), and Cavus (exaggerated medial longitudinal arch). It is commonly remembered by the mnemonic "CAVE".

Clinical Features
The foot is turned downwards and inwards, resembling a club.
Deep creases are visible on the medial border and posterior aspect of the heel.
The heel is small and empty (calcaneus is pulled up).
The calf muscles (especially on the affected side) are visibly atrophied and underdeveloped.
It is a rigid deformity that cannot be passively corrected to a neutral position.
Can be unilateral or bilateral.
Investigations
Clinical Diagnosis: Diagnosis is primarily clinical immediately at birth.
X-rays (AP and Lateral views of the foot in stress dorsiflexion): Used to assess the severity and document the baseline bony alignment (Kite's angle, talocalcaneal angle). X-rays are also used to monitor the progress of correction.
Complications
If untreated, the child walks on the dorsolateral aspect of the foot.
Formation of painful, large callosities and bursa over the weight-bearing area.
Awkward, limping gait.
"Rocker-bottom foot" (iatrogenic complication if the midfoot is forced into dorsiflexion before the heel equinus is corrected).
Severe psychological and cosmetic impact.
Medical / Conservative Management
Ponseti Method (Gold Standard): Serial manipulation and casting starting within the first week of life. The deformities are corrected in a specific order: Cavus, Adductus, Varus, and finally Equinus. Casts are changed weekly.
Splinting: After full correction, the foot is maintained in a Denis Browne splint or Foot Abduction Brace (full-time for 3 months, then at night until 4 years of age) to prevent relapse.
Surgical Management
Percutaneous Tendoachilles Tenotomy: Often required as the final step of the Ponseti method to correct residual equinus.
Posteromedial Soft Tissue Release (PMSTR): Done for resistant or neglected cases in children (6 months to 2 years), involving surgical release of tight medial and posterior ligaments/tendons.
Bony Surgeries: For older, neglected children (e.g., wedge resection, triple arthrodesis, or Ilizarov ring fixator).
2. Congenital Dislocation of Hip (CDH / DDH)
Introduction & Definition
Now correctly termed Developmental Dysplasia of the Hip (DDH), this represents a spectrum of hip abnormalities ranging from a shallow, dysplastic acetabulum to subluxation, and completely dislocated femoral head.

Clinical Features
Neonates/Infants:
Asymmetrical thigh and gluteal skin folds.
Limited abduction of the affected hip.
Ortolani Test Positive: A palpable "clunk" as the dislocated hip is reduced back into the socket during abduction.
Barlow Test Positive: The hip can be dislocated out of the socket with posterior pressure and adduction.
Older Children (Walking age):
Painless limp.
Shortening of the affected limb (Galeazzi sign positive).
Waddling gait (if bilateral) or Trendelenburg lurch.
Trendelenburg test is positive (pelvis drops on the opposite side when standing on the affected leg).
Investigations
Ultrasound (Infants < 6 months): The investigation of choice because the femoral head is not yet ossified. Used to assess acetabular depth and hip stability (Graf's classification).
X-rays (Children > 6 months): An AP pelvis radiograph is used. Pathological findings include a broken Shenton's line, an increased acetabular index, and the femoral head lying outside the inner lower quadrant formed by Hilgenreiner's and Perkin's lines.
Complications
Avascular Necrosis (AVN) of the femoral head (often iatrogenic from forced abduction).
Premature osteoarthritis of the hip in young adulthood.
Permanent limb length discrepancy and limping.
Severe limp and compensatory scoliosis.

Severe impairment of independent mobility and self-care.

formation → periosteal elevation → sequestrum formation → involucrum formation → sinus formation Important terms Sequestrum Dead separated piece of infected bone Involucrum New bone formed around a sequestrum by the periosteum Cloaca Opening in the involucrum through which pus or sequestrum may discharge **Clinical Features** **Acute osteomyelitis** Local • Severe localized bone pain • Tenderness • Swelling • Warmth • Redness • Restricted movement of nearby joint • Muscle spasm Systemic • Fever • Chills • Malaise • Irritability • Tachycardia • Loss of appetite **Chronic osteomyelitis** • Persistent bone pain • Recurrent swelling • Discharging sinus • Purulent discharge • Recurrent fever • Non healing wound • Limb deformity • Reduced function • Local tenderness • Skin pigmentation/scarring • Sequestrum may occasionally be palpable **Investigations** **Blood investigations** • CBC leukocytosis in acute infection • ESR raised • CRP raised • Blood culture identifies causative organism • Blood glucose **Imaging** • X ray • Ultrasound for soft tissue collection • MRI highly sensitive for early osteomyelitis • CT useful for cortical destruction and sequestrum • Bone scan where indicated **Microbiological investigation** • Pus/wound culture • Bone biopsy and culture important in chronic or uncertain cases **Complications** **Acute** • Septicemia • Septic shock • Subperiosteal abscess • Soft tissue abscess • Pathological fracture • Growth disturbance in children • Joint infection **Chronic** • Recurrent sinus • Sequestrum • Involucrum • Pathological fracture • Bone deformity • Limb shortening • Secondary amyloidosis • Malignant transformation of chronic sinus classically squamous cell carcinoma Marjolin ulcer • Chronic pain • Functional disability **Medical Management** **Acute osteomyelitis** • Hospitalization when clinically indicated • Blood and tissue cultures • Appropriate intravenous antibiotics initially • Antibiotics modified according to culture and sensitivity • Analgesics • Antipyretics • Adequate hydration and nutrition • Immobilization of affected limb if necessary • Treatment of underlying disease **Chronic osteomyelitis** • Long term culture directed antibiotics • Wound care • Nutritional support • Diabetes control • Treatment of vascular insufficiency • Analgesia • Physiotherapy after acute infection is controlled **Surgical Management** Indications • Abscess • Sequestrum • Failure of antibiotics • Chronic sinus • Necrotic tissue • Infected implant • Pathological fracture Procedures • Incision and drainage • Surgical debridement • Sequestrectomy • Curettage • Saucerization • Removal of infected implants when appropriate • Dead space management • Bone grafting • Local antibiotic delivery • Soft tissue flap coverage • Stabilization of pathological fracture when required **Flow Chart** Infection of bone ↓ Inflammatory response ↓ Edema + increased intraosseous pressure ↓ Vascular compromise ↓ Bone necrosis ↓ Abscess / sequestrum ↓ Chronic infection ↓ Involucrum + sinus formation ↓ Debridement + antibiotics ± reconstruction **Conclusion** Osteomyelitis is a potentially destructive bone infection Early diagnosis appropriate culture directed antibiotics and timely drainage/debridement are essential to prevent chronic infection deformity and functional disability --- **2 BRODIES ABSCESS** **Definition** Brodies abscess is a localized form of subacute osteomyelitis characterized by a localized intraosseous abscess usually occurring in the metaphysis of a long bone especially the tibia The common causative organism is Staphylococcus aureus **Etiology** Usually caused by • Staphylococcus aureus Predisposing factors • Previous minor trauma • Hematogenous infection • Reduced immunity • Diabetes • Previous inadequately treated infection **Common Sites** • Upper end of tibia common • Lower end of femur • Other long bones • Occasionally small bones **Pathophysiology** Bacterial infection ↓ Localized inflammatory response ↓ Intraosseous abscess formation ↓ Granulation tissue around abscess ↓ Reactive sclerosis of surrounding bone Because the infection is localized and relatively slow systemic manifestations may be minimal **Clinical Features** • Localized deep bone pain • Pain may be worse at night • Local tenderness • Mild swelling • Symptoms may persist for weeks or months • Fever usually absent or mild • Restriction of nearby joint movement may occur • Symptoms may be relieved temporarily by salicylates/analgesics **Investigations** **Blood** • CBC may be normal • ESR may be mildly elevated • CRP may be elevated **X ray** Typical appearance • Well defined radiolucent cavity • Surrounding sclerosis • Usually metaphyseal location **MRI** Shows • Abscess cavity • Bone marrow edema • Soft tissue involvement **CT** Useful for • Defining cortical involvement • Surgical planning **Biopsy** May be required to • Confirm diagnosis • Exclude tumor • Obtain culture **Differential Diagnosis** • Osteosarcoma • Ewing sarcoma • Osteoid osteoma • Chronic osteomyelitis • Bone cyst • Tuberculosis of bone **Complications** • Chronic osteomyelitis • Recurrence • Extension into soft tissues • Pathological fracture uncommon • Growth disturbance in children • Deformity **Medical Management** • Culture directed antibiotics • Analgesics • Rest/temporary immobilization if required • Treatment of predisposing conditions • Follow up imaging **Surgical Management** Surgery may be required when • Abscess is large • Symptoms persist despite antibiotics • Diagnosis is uncertain • There is extensive bone destruction • Recurrence occurs Procedures • Curettage of abscess cavity • Drainage • Removal of infected tissue • Cavity filling with bone graft or suitable substitute when indicated • Antibiotic therapy **Flow Chart** Subacute bacterial infection ↓ Localized bone infection ↓ Intraosseous abscess ↓ Surrounding sclerosis ↓ Persistent localized pain ↓ X ray/MRI diagnosis ↓ Antibiotics ± curettage/drainage **Conclusion** Brodies abscess should be suspected in patients with persistent localized bone pain and a well defined lytic lesion surrounded by sclerosis Early diagnosis prevents progression to chronic osteomyelitis --- **3 TUBERCULOUS ARTHRITIS / TB OF SPINE AND MAJOR JOINTS** **Definition** Tuberculosis of bone and joints is a chronic granulomatous infection caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis usually resulting from hematogenous spread from a primary focus commonly the lungs Tuberculosis may affect • Spine Potts disease • Hip • Knee • Ankle • Shoulder • Elbow • Wrist and other joints **A TUBERCULOSIS OF SPINE POTTS SPINE** **Definition** Potts spine is tuberculosis of the vertebral column characterized by destruction of vertebral bodies and intervertebral discs often leading to vertebral collapse kyphotic deformity and neurological complications **Etiology** Causative organism • Mycobacterium tuberculosis Usually spreads to the spine through • Hematogenous spread • Lymphatic spread • Extension from adjacent structures **Common Sites** • Lower thoracic spine • Thoracolumbar junction • Lumbar spine **Pathophysiology** TB infection ↓ Granuloma formation in vertebral body ↓ Caseous necrosis ↓ Vertebral destruction ↓ Disc involvement ↓ Vertebral collapse ↓ Kyphosis / gibbus deformity ↓ Cold abscess ± spinal cord compression ↓ Neurological deficit **Clinical Features** **General** • Low grade fever • Night sweats • Loss of appetite • Weight loss • Malaise **Spinal** • Persistent back pain • Local tenderness • Stiffness • Muscle spasm • Restricted spinal movement • Deformity • Kyphosis • Gibbus deformity **Neurological** • Weakness • Sensory disturbance • Radicular pain • Paraplegia • Bowel/bladder dysfunction in severe disease **Cold abscess** May appear as • Paravertebral swelling • Psoas abscess • Groin swelling **Investigations** **Blood** • CBC • ESR • CRP • Tuberculosis related microbiological testing as appropriate **Imaging** • X ray spine • MRI spine best for neural compression abscess and soft tissue involvement • CT bony destruction and surgical planning **Microbiological/histological** • Biopsy • Tissue culture • Molecular testing where appropriate **Complications** • Vertebral collapse • Kyphosis • Gibbus deformity • Spinal cord compression • Paraplegia • Nerve root compression • Cold abscess • Sinus formation • Instability • Chronic pain • Severe neurological disability **Medical Management** **Anti tubercular therapy** Multidrug anti tubercular therapy ATT is the cornerstone of treatment using an appropriate regimen according to current national/institutional guidelines **Other measures** • Analgesics • Nutritional support • Rest during active painful stage • Bracing when appropriate • Management of neurological deficits • Monitoring treatment response **Surgical Management** Indications • Progressive neurological deficit • Significant spinal cord compression • Severe instability • Severe or progressive deformity • Large abscess requiring drainage • Failure of appropriate medical treatment • Mechanical instability Procedures • Abscess drainage • Debridement • Decompression • Stabilization • Instrumented fusion • Corrective surgery for severe deformity **B TUBERCULOUS ARTHRITIS OF MAJOR JOINTS** **Definition** Tuberculous arthritis is a chronic granulomatous infection of a synovial joint caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis producing synovial inflammation cartilage destruction and progressive joint damage **Common Joints** • Hip • Knee • Ankle • Shoulder • Elbow • Wrist **Clinical Features** The onset is generally insidious **General** • Low grade fever • Weight loss • Malaise • Reduced appetite **Local** • Pain • Swelling • Stiffness • Reduced range of movement • Muscle wasting • Joint tenderness **Characteristic** • A cold swelling may occur with comparatively little redness or warmth **Advanced disease** • Sinus formation • Joint destruction • Deformity • Subluxation/dislocation • Ankylosis • Limb shortening especially with hip disease **Investigations** • CBC • ESR/CRP • X ray • MRI • Ultrasound for effusion • Joint aspiration • Synovial fluid analysis • AFB testing/culture where appropriate • Molecular tests • Synovial biopsy **Classical radiological findings** The classical description of tuberculous arthritis includes • Periarticular osteoporosis • Peripheral osseous erosions • Gradual joint space narrowing **Complications** • Cartilage destruction • Joint deformity • Subluxation • Dislocation • Ankylosis • Sinus formation • Abscess • Pathological fracture • Limb shortening • Severe functional disability **Medical Management** • Appropriate multidrug ATT • Analgesics • Rest during acute painful stage • Nutritional support • Treatment of associated TB • Physiotherapy after acute inflammation is controlled **Physiotherapy principles** • Maintain safe joint mobility • Prevent contractures • Maintain muscle strength • Gradual functional training • Avoid excessive loading of a severely destroyed joint **Surgical Management** Depending on disease stage • Aspiration/drainage of abscess • Synovectomy in selected cases • Debridement • Arthrodesis for severely destroyed joints • Joint replacement in selected patients after adequate infection control • Spinal decompression and stabilization for Potts spine when indicated **Conclusion** TB of the spine and major joints is a slowly progressive destructive disease Early diagnosis and adequate ATT can prevent deformity and neurological or functional disability --- **4 PYOGENIC ARTHRITIS** **Definition** Pyogenic arthritis is an acute or chronic inflammatory infection of a synovial joint caused by pyogenic microorganisms resulting in accumulation of infected synovial fluid/pus and potential destruction of articular cartilage The terms pyogenic arthritis and septic arthritis are often used interchangeably **Etiology** Common organisms • Staphylococcus aureus most common • Streptococci • Gram negative bacilli • Neisseria gonorrhoeae in appropriate populations • Other organisms depending on age and risk factors **Routes of Infection** 1 Hematogenous Most common route 2 Direct inoculation ◦ Penetrating injury ◦ Joint injection ◦ Surgery 3 Contiguous spread ◦ Osteomyelitis ◦ Soft tissue infection ◦ Bursitis **Risk Factors** • Diabetes • Immunosuppression • Older age • Recent surgery • Joint prosthesis • IV drug use • Skin infection • Pre existing joint disease • Trauma **Pathophysiology** Bacterial entry into joint ↓ Synovial inflammation ↓ Neutrophil accumulation ↓ Purulent effusion ↓ Raised intra articular pressure ↓ Reduced cartilage nutrition ↓ Cartilage destruction ↓ Subchondral bone destruction ↓ Joint deformity / ankylosis **Clinical Features** **Acute presentation** • Severe joint pain • Rapidly developing swelling • Warmth • Redness • Tenderness • Marked restriction of movement • Severe pain on passive movement **Systemic** • Fever • Chills • Malaise • Tachycardia **Common joints** • Knee • Hip • Shoulder • Elbow • Ankle **Investigations** **Blood** • CBC • ESR • CRP • Blood cultures **Joint aspiration essential investigation** Synovial fluid may show • Turbid/purulent appearance • High leukocyte count • Predominantly neutrophils • Gram stain • Culture and sensitivity **Imaging** • X ray • Ultrasound • MRI where required **Complications** • Cartilage destruction • Joint space loss • Osteomyelitis • Joint deformity • Ankylosis • Sepsis • Septic shock • Pathological fracture • Growth disturbance in children • Permanent disability **Medical Management** This is an orthopedic emergency • Urgent joint aspiration • Blood cultures • Prompt empirical antibiotics after appropriate cultures then modify according to results • Analgesics • Antipyretics • Fluid management if systemically ill • Treatment of underlying conditions • Temporary immobilization in the acute painful stage **Surgical Management** Main objectives • Drain pus • Reduce bacterial load • Relieve intra articular pressure • Prevent cartilage destruction Procedures • Needle aspiration • Arthroscopic lavage and drainage • Open arthrotomy and drainage when indicated • Debridement • Repeat drainage if necessary **After infection is controlled** • Gradual mobilization • ROM exercises • Muscle strengthening • Functional rehabilitation **Flow Chart** Bacterial invasion of joint ↓ Synovitis ↓ Purulent effusion ↓ Raised intra articular pressure ↓ Cartilage destruction ↓ Joint destruction ↓ Early antibiotics + drainage ↓ Rehabilitation **Conclusion** Pyogenic arthritis is a joint threatening emergency Early aspiration appropriate antibiotics and adequate drainage are essential to preserve joint function --- **5 SEPTIC ARTHRITIS** **Definition** Septic arthritis is an infection of a joint caused by microorganisms producing inflammation and destruction of the synovium cartilage and sometimes subchondral bone Important examination point Pyogenic arthritis and septic arthritis are commonly used as synonyms Septic arthritis is the broader clinical term while pyogenic arthritis generally emphasizes bacterial suppurative infection **Etiology** Infective organisms • Staphylococcus aureus • Streptococci • Gram negative organisms • Gonococci • Other organisms in immunocompromised patients Routes • Hematogenous spread • Direct inoculation • Spread from adjacent osteomyelitis • Surgical contamination • Prosthetic joint infection **Risk Factors** • Diabetes mellitus • Immunosuppression • Rheumatoid arthritis • Prosthetic joint • Recent joint surgery • Skin infection • Intravenous drug use • Extremes of age • Previous septic arthritis **Clinical Features** **Local** • Severe joint pain • Swelling • Warmth • Redness • Tenderness • Restricted active and passive ROM • Severe pain on passive movement **Systemic** • Fever • Chills • Malaise • Tachycardia • Leukocytosis **Hip septic arthritis** May present with • Severe hip/groin pain • Refusal to bear weight • Painful hip movement • Flexion and external rotation posture in some cases **Investigations** **Blood** • CBC • ESR • CRP • Blood cultures **Joint aspiration Most important investigation** • Appearance • Cell count • Differential count • Gram stain • Culture and sensitivity • Crystal analysis where clinically appropriate **Imaging** • X ray • Ultrasound • MRI **Complications** • Articular cartilage destruction • Osteomyelitis • Joint deformity • Fibrous/bony ankylosis • Subluxation/dislocation • Growth plate damage • Sepsis • Septic shock • Permanent loss of joint function **Medical Management** • Urgent orthopedic evaluation • Joint aspiration • Blood cultures • Prompt IV antibiotics then culture directed therapy • Analgesia • Fluid/electrolyte management • Treatment of underlying diseases • Nutritional support **Surgical Management** Drainage methods • Repeated needle aspiration in selected joints • Arthroscopic drainage and lavage • Open arthrotomy Indications for operative drainage • Large purulent collection • Failure of aspiration • Deep joint infection • Hip infection • Inadequate clinical response • Loculated infection • Associated abscess **Rehabilitation** After infection is adequately controlled **Early** • Pain control • Gentle ROM • Positioning • Prevention of contractures **Later** • Active ROM • Isometric exercises • Progressive strengthening • Weight bearing progression • Gait training • Functional activities --- **6 SYPHILITIC INFECTION OF JOINTS** **Definition** Syphilitic arthritis is a rare musculoskeletal manifestation of infection with Treponema pallidum in which syphilis produces inflammatory or destructive changes involving joints bones or surrounding tissues It may occur in different stages of syphilis particularly as a manifestation of late/congenital syphilis **Etiology** Causative organism • Treponema pallidum Transmission • Sexual transmission • Congenital transmission from infected mother to fetus **Types of Joint Involvement** 1 Acute syphilitic arthritis May occur during secondary syphilis 2 Chronic syphilitic arthropathy May occur in late disease 3 Charcot arthropathy A neuropathic arthropathy associated with tabes dorsalis a late neurological manifestation of syphilis 4 Congenital syphilitic skeletal disease May affect ◦ Long bones ◦ Joints ◦ Epiphyses/metaphyses **Pathophysiology** Treponema pallidum infection ↓ Systemic infection ↓ Inflammatory response ↓ Synovial and periarticular involvement ↓ Chronic tissue damage In late neurosyphilis Dorsal column sensory loss ↓ Loss of proprioception and protective sensation ↓ Repetitive joint trauma ↓ Progressive neuropathic arthropathy ↓ Joint destruction and deformity **Clinical Features** **Acute syphilitic arthritis** • Joint pain • Joint swelling • Stiffness • Effusion • Restricted movement • May involve multiple joints • Constitutional symptoms may occur **Chronic syphilitic arthropathy** • Chronic joint pain or discomfort • Swelling • Progressive deformity • Restricted movement **Charcot joint** Characteristic features • Recurrent painless or relatively painless trauma • Swelling • Warmth • Deformity • Crepitus • Subluxation/dislocation • Severe radiological destruction • The knee and hip can be affected among other joints **Investigations** **Serological tests** Non treponemal tests • VDRL • RPR Treponemal tests • TPHA/TPPA • FTA ABS or equivalent treponemal assays **Joint investigations** • Joint aspiration when indicated • Synovial fluid analysis • Culture to exclude pyogenic infection **Imaging** • X ray • MRI when required **Neurological evaluation** If Charcot arthropathy is suspected • Sensory examination • Proprioception • Reflexes • Neurological assessment **Differential Diagnosis** • Rheumatoid arthritis • Osteoarthritis • Septic arthritis • Tuberculous arthritis • Gout • Neuropathic arthropathy due to other causes **Complications** • Joint destruction • Deformity • Subluxation • Dislocation • Pathological fracture • Instability • Loss of function • Secondary osteoarthritis • Neurological disability in associated neurosyphilis **Medical Management** **Specific treatment** Penicillin based therapy is the standard treatment for syphilis with the exact preparation dose and duration determined by the stage and clinical form of disease Management may include • Appropriate penicillin therapy • Treatment of sexual partners according to public health guidance • Screening for other sexually transmitted infections • Neurological evaluation when indicated • Analgesics • Management of secondary complications **For Charcot arthropathy** • Protection from excessive loading • Off loading • Appropriate orthosis • Footwear modification where applicable • Management of associated neurological disease **Surgical Management** Surgery is generally directed toward the resulting structural damage rather than eradication of the infection itself May include • Synovectomy in selected cases • Debridement when indicated • Arthrodesis for severe instability • Joint reconstruction • Joint replacement in selected patients after appropriate infection treatment • Correction of severe deformity **Rehabilitation** • Protection of affected joint • Pain management • Maintaining safe ROM • Muscle strengthening • Orthotic support • Gait training • Assistive devices when required • Patient education regarding joint protection

Possible factors: Developmental abnormality Genetic factors Previous trauma Chronic irritation Associated syndromes, particularly Gardner syndrome CLINICAL FEATURES Small osteomas may be asymptomatic. When symptomatic: Slow-growing hard swelling Painless mass Facial asymmetry Headache in some cranial lesions Sinus obstruction Visual symptoms if orbital structures are involved Cosmetic deformity • • • • • • • • • • • • • • • • Orthopaedics & Metabolic Bone Diseases — University Exam Notes Page 1 of 17INVESTIGATIONS • • • • X-ray: Dense, well-defined bony lesion CT scan: Best for defining the size, location and relationship to surrounding structures. COMPLICATIONS • • • • • • Cosmetic deformity Pressure on adjacent structures Sinus obstruction Visual impairment Rare neurological complications Recurrence after incomplete excision MEDICAL MANAGEMENT • • Asymptomatic: Observation, Periodic clinical/imaging follow-up Symptomatic: Analgesics for pain, Treatment of associated sinus symptoms SURGICAL MANAGEMENT Indications: Pain, Functional impairment, Significant cosmetic deformity, Rapid or uncertain growth, Compression of adjacent structures. It is the most common primary malignant bone tumour in many clinical series, particularly among adolescents. CLASSIFICATION 1. Conventional high-grade osteosarcoma • • • Osteoblastic Chondroblastic Fibroblastic 2. CERVICOBRACHIAL SYNDROME Definition Cervicobrachial syndrome is a clinical condition characterized by pain, paraesthesia, numbness, weakness or other neurological symptoms originating from the cervical spine or surrounding structures and radiating into the shoulder, arm, forearm or hand. Causes / Etiology • Cervical intervertebral disc prolapse • Cervical spondylosis and osteophytes • Foraminal or spinal canal stenosis • Whiplash and other cervical trauma • Muscle spasm and postural dysfunction • Brachial plexus lesions • Tumour, infection or inflammatory disorders • Thoracic outlet disorders Pathophysiology Cervical pathology → nerve-root irritation/compression → inflammation and impaired nerve conduction → pain and paraesthesia → weakness and functional limitation. Clinical Features • Neck pain with radiation to shoulder/upper limb • Burning, shooting or electric-shock-like pain • Paraesthesia and numbness in a dermatomal pattern • Muscle weakness and reduced grip strength • Reduced deep tendon reflexes corresponding to the affected root • Restricted cervical ROM and muscle spasm • Symptoms may worsen with cervical movement or compression Investigations • Cervical X-ray for degenerative or bony changes • MRI for disc pathology, nerve-root or cord compression • CT for bony/foraminal abnormalities • EMG/NCV when nerve involvement needs clarification • Neurological examination of dermatomes, myotomes and reflexes Complications • Chronic pain Page 1• Persistent sensory deficit • Motor weakness and muscle wasting • Loss of hand function • Reduced work capacity • Cervical myelopathy in severe cord compression Conservative / Medical Management • Relative rest and activity modification • Analgesics/NSAIDs as indicated • Muscle relaxants in selected cases • Neuropathic pain medication when appropriate • Selected use of cervical collar in acute cases Physiotherapy Management • Pain relief with TENS or thermal modalities when appropriate • Gentle cervical ROM • Deep neck flexor and cervical stabilization exercises • Scapular stabilization and upper-limb strengthening • Postural and ergonomic correction • Cervical traction in selected patients without contraindications • Neural mobilization when appropriate • Home exercise programme Surgical Management • Indications: progressive neurological deficit, severe persistent radicular pain despite appropriate conservative treatment, significant structural compression, myelopathy or instability • Anterior cervical discectomy and fusion (ACDF) • Cervical disc replacement in selected patients • Posterior cervical foraminotomy • Cervical decompression/laminectomy or laminoplasty when indicated Conclusion Early identification of neurological deficits, appropriate investigation, posture and exercise-based rehabilitation, and timely surgical referral in progressive or severe cases are essential. Page 22. THORACIC OUTLET SYNDROME Definition Thoracic outlet syndrome (TOS) is a group of disorders caused by compression of the brachial plexus and/or subclavian vessels as they pass through the thoracic outlet, producing neurological or vascular symptoms in the upper limb. Types • Neurogenic TOS – brachial plexus involvement • Venous TOS – subclavian vein involvement • Arterial TOS – subclavian artery involvement Causes / Risk Factors • Cervical rib or first-rib abnormality • Fibrous bands or abnormal scalene muscles • Forward head and rounded-shoulder posture • Clavicular/first-rib trauma • Repetitive overhead activity • Heavy lifting and occupational overuse Pathophysiology Anatomical abnormality or postural dysfunction → narrowing of thoracic outlet → neurovascular compression → neurological and/or vascular symptoms. SPECIAL TESTS — LUMBO-SACRAL REGION I. TEST FOR LUMBAR INSTABILITY 1. PASSIVE LUMBAR EXTENSION TEST PURPOSE To assess lumbar spine instability. PROCEDURE • • • • Patient lies prone. Examiner lifts both the patient’s legs together by holding around the ankles. The legs are elevated while the knees remain extended. Observe the patient’s symptoms and lumbar response. POSITIVE SIGN • • Development/reproduction of low-back pain Feeling of heaviness or instability in the lumbar region. INDICATES Lumbar segmental instability. II. TESTS FOR MUSCLE DYSFUNCTION 2. 90–90 STRAIGHT LEG RAISING TEST PURPOSE To assess hamstring muscle tightness/flexibility. PROCEDURE • • • • Patient lies supine. Flex the hip and knee to approximately 90°. Stabilize the thigh. Slowly extend the knee while maintaining hip flexion. POSITIVE SIGN • • Inability to achieve full knee extension. Increased resistance/tightness in the posterior thigh. INDICATES Hamstring tightness/shortness. 3. TRENDELENBURG TEST PURPOSE To assess hip abductor muscle function, especially gluteus medius. PROCEDURE • • • Patient stands on one leg. Ask the patient to lift the opposite foot from the floor. Observe the position of the pelvis. POSITIVE SIGN • Pelvis drops on the side of the lifted/non-weight-bearing leg. INDICATES Weakness of the hip abductors of the weight-bearing leg, particularly gluteus medius.III. TESTS FOR NEUROLOGICAL DYSFUNCTION 4. STRAIGHT LEG RAISING TEST (SLR/LASÈGUE’S TEST) PURPOSE To assess lumbosacral nerve-root irritation, particularly due to PIVD. PROCEDURE • • • • Patient lies supine. Keep the knee fully extended. Slowly raise the patient’s straight leg by flexing the hip. Note the angle and symptoms produced. POSITIVE SIGN • Reproduction of radicular/sciatic pain, typically between about 30–70° of hip flexion. INDICATES Lumbosacral nerve-root irritation/compression, commonly associated with PIVD. 5. SLUMP TEST PURPOSE To assess neural tissue mechanosensitivity, particularly lumbosacral nerve-root involvement. PROCEDURE Patient sits with: 1. 2. 3. 4. 5. Hands behind back. Thoracic/lumbar spine flexed. Cervical spine flexed. One knee is extended. Ankle is dorsiflexed. The examiner progressively adds these components while observing symptoms. POSITIVE SIGN • • Reproduction of the patient’s familiar neural/radicular symptoms. Symptoms change with release of one component, particularly cervical extension or ankle movement. INDICATES Neural tissue/nerve-root involvement, such as lumbar radiculopathy. IV. TESTS FOR JOINT DYSFUNCTION6. SCHOBER’S TEST PURPOSE To assess lumbar spine flexion/mobility. PROCEDURE • • • • Patient stands erect. Mark the lumbosacral region and a point 10 cm above it. Ask the patient to bend forward maximally. Measure the distance between the marks again. POSITIVE SIGN Insufficient increase in distance during forward flexion. INDICATES Reduced lumbar flexion/mobility, commonly seen in conditions such as ankylosing spondylitis. 7. FABER / PATRICK’S TEST FABER = Flexion – ABduction – External Rotation PURPOSE To assess hip and sacroiliac joint pathology. PROCEDURE • • • • • ◦ ◦ Patient lies supine. Place the tested leg in: Hip flexion Abduction External rotation ◦ Place the lateral ankle over the opposite thigh. Stabilize the opposite pelvis. Gently press the flexed knee downward. POSITIVE SIGN • • • Pain reproduced in the hip/groin → suggests hip pathology. Pain in the sacroiliac region → may indicate SI joint pathology. Restricted ROM may also be significant. INDICATES Hip or sacroiliac joint dysfunction.8. GAENSLEN’S TEST PURPOSE To assess sacroiliac joint dysfunction/pathology. PROCEDURE • • • • Patient lies near the edge of the table.
