--- **I TESTS FOR HIP PATHOLOGY** --- **1 HIP SCOUR TEST** PURPOSE To assess for intraarticular hip pathology PROCEDURE • Patient lies supine • Flex the hip and knee • Apply a gentle axial load through the femur • Move the hip through flexion/extension and abduction/adduction while maintaining compression POSITIVE SIGN • Pain • Catching • Clicking • Crepitus • Restricted/abnormal movement INDICATES Possible intraarticular hip pathology such as degenerative or labral pathology --- **2 LEG ROLL TEST** PURPOSE To assess for intraarticular hip pathology and restriction of passive hip rotation PROCEDURE • Patient lies supine with the leg relaxed • Examiner gently rolls the leg from side to side producing internal and external rotation of the hip • Compare with the opposite side POSITIVE SIGN • Pain • Markedly increased or decreased hip rotation • Excessive external rotation compared with the opposite side INDICATES Possible hip joint pathology --- **II TEST FOR LABRAL LESION** --- **4 ANTERIOR LABRAL TEAR TEST** PURPOSE To assess for an acetabular labral lesion particularly an anterior labral lesion PROCEDURE • Patient lies supine • Flex the hip and bring it through the provocative combination of hip movement used to stress the anterior labrum • Reproduce the patients familiar symptoms • Compare with the opposite side POSITIVE SIGN • Reproduction of anterior hip/groin pain • Clicking catching or givingway sensation may occur INDICATES Possible acetabular labral lesion --- **III PEDIATRIC HIP PATHOLOGY** --- **5 BARLOWS TEST** PURPOSE To determine whether an infants hip is unstable and can be dislocated PROCEDURE • Infant lies supine • Flex the hip and knee • Stabilize the pelvis • Gently adduct the hip • Apply gentle posteriorly directed pressure through the femur POSITIVE SIGN • A palpable clunk as the femoral head dislocates INDICATES Dislocatable/unstable hip suggestive of developmental dysplasia of the hip DDH --- **6 GALEAZZI SIGN** PURPOSE To detect apparent femoral shortening particularly due to hip dislocation PROCEDURE • Infant lies supine • Flex both hips and knees to approximately 90 • Place the feet together • Compare the height of both knees POSITIVE SIGN • One knee is lower than the other INDICATES • Developmental hip dislocation/dysplasia • Femoral shortening • Other limblength discrepancy --- **7 ORTOLANI SIGN** PURPOSE To detect a dislocated hip that can be reduced PROCEDURE • Infant lies supine with hips and knees flexed • Stabilize the pelvis • Gently abduct the hip while applying pressure over the greater trochanter in an appropriate direction to reduce the femoral head POSITIVE SIGN • A palpable clunk as the femoral head reduces into the acetabulum INDICATES Reducible hip dislocation DDH Barlow vs Ortolani Barlow OUT dislocates Ortolani IN reduces --- **IV TESTS FOR MUSCLE DYSFUNCTION** --- **8 HIP LAG SIGN** PURPOSE To assess hip extensor muscle function particularly the ability to actively maintain hip extension PROCEDURE • Patient lies prone • Examiner passively extends the hip • Ask the patient to maintain the hip in the extended position after the examiner releases support POSITIVE SIGN • The patient cannot maintain the extended position • The hip falls back toward flexion INDICATES Hip extensor weakness/dysfunction --- **10 THOMAS TEST** PURPOSE To assess hip flexor tightness/hip flexion contracture PROCEDURE • Patient lies supine near the edge of the table • Patient flexes one hip and knee toward the chest to flatten the lumbar spine • Observe the position of the opposite leg POSITIVE SIGN • Opposite thigh rises from the table hip flexor tightness • Knee extends possible rectus femoris tightness • Hip abducts possible TFL/ITB tightness INDICATES Hip flexor muscle tightness/contracture --- **V TESTS FOR HIP DISPLACEMENT** --- **11 NELATONS LINE** PURPOSE To assess the position of the greater trochanter in relation to the pelvis PROCEDURE • Patient lies in the appropriate position with the hip examined • Draw an imaginary line from the ASIS to the ischial tuberosity • Assess the position of the greater trochanter relative to this line POSITIVE FINDING • Greater trochanter lies above Nelatons line INDICATES Possible superior displacement of the femur/hip dislocation --- **12 BRYANTS TRIANGLE** PURPOSE To detect proximal displacement of the greater trochanter and apparent shortening of the femur PROCEDURE • Patient lies supine • From the ASIS draw a perpendicular line to the bed • Draw a line from the greater trochanter to meet this perpendicular • Compare the triangles on both sides POSITIVE FINDING • Shortening of the base of Bryants triangle on the affected side INDICATES Possible hip dislocation or proximal displacement of the femur --- **VI SACROILIAC JOINT TESTS** --- **14 GAENSLENS TEST** PURPOSE To assess SI joint pathology PROCEDURE • Patient lies near the edge of the table • One hip is flexed toward the chest • The opposite leg hangs over the edge • Apply gentle pressure to produce opposite pelvic movements POSITIVE SIGN • Reproduction of pain around the SI joint INDICATES ---**SPECIAL TESTS KNEE JOINT** ---**I TESTS FOR LIGAMENT INTEGRITY** ---**A COLLATERAL LIGAMENTS** ---**1 VALGUS STRESS TEST** PURPOSE To assess the integrity of the medial collateral ligament MCL PROCEDURE • Patient lies supine • Knee is slightly flexed approximately 20 30 to unlock the joint • Stabilize the lateral aspect of the knee • Apply a valgus force to the lower leg while stabilizing the thigh POSITIVE SIGN • Excessive medial joint opening compared with the opposite side • Pain along the medial knee INDICATES MCL injury/insufficiency ---**2 VARUS STRESS TEST** PURPOSE To assess the integrity of the lateral collateral ligament LCL PROCEDURE • Patient lies supine • Knee is slightly flexed approximately 20 30 • Stabilize the medial aspect of the knee • Apply a varus force to the lower leg POSITIVE SIGN • Excessive lateral joint opening • Pain along the lateral knee INDICATES LCL injury/insufficiency ---**B CRUCIATE LIGAMENTS** ---**3 LACHMAN TEST** PURPOSE To assess the integrity of the anterior cruciate ligament ACL PROCEDURE • Patient lies supine • Knee flexed approximately 20 30 • Stabilize the femur with one hand • Hold the proximal tibia with the other hand • Pull the tibia anteriorly POSITIVE SIGN • Excessive anterior translation of tibia • Soft/absent firm end feel compared with the normal side INDICATES ACL injury/tear Very important Lachman is generally more sensitive for ACL injury than the anterior drawer test particularly in the acute knee ---**4 ANTERIOR DRAWER TEST** PURPOSE To assess the ACL PROCEDURE • Patient lies supine • Hip flexed and knee flexed to 90 • Stabilize the foot • Grasp the proximal tibia with both hands • Pull the tibia anteriorly POSITIVE SIGN • Excessive anterior movement of the tibia compared with the opposite side INDICATES ACL injury/insufficiency ---**5 POSTERIOR DRAWER TEST** PURPOSE To assess the integrity of the posterior cruciate ligament PCL PROCEDURE • Patient lies supine • Knee flexed to approximately 90 • Stabilize the foot • Place both hands around the proximal tibia • Push the tibia posteriorly POSITIVE SIGN • Excessive posterior translation of the tibia INDICATES PCL injury/insufficiency ---**II TESTS FOR MENISCAL INJURY** ---**6 MCMURRAYS TEST** PURPOSE To assess for medial and lateral meniscal lesions PROCEDURE • Patient lies supine • Fully flex the knee • For medial meniscus externally rotate the tibia and apply valgus stress while extending the knee • For lateral meniscus internally rotate the tibia and apply varus stress while extending the knee • Palpate the joint line POSITIVE SIGN • Pain • Palpable/audible click or clunk at the joint line INDICATES Possible meniscal tear ---**7 APLEYS COMPRESSION DISTRACTION TEST** PURPOSE To differentiate meniscal pathology from ligament pathology PROCEDURE Compression • Patient lies prone • Knee flexed to 90 • Stabilize the thigh • Apply downward compression through the heel • Rotate the tibia internally and externally Distraction • Maintain the same position • Apply traction to the tibia while rotating it POSITIVE SIGN Compression positive • Pain reproduced with compression/rotation Suggests meniscal pathology Distraction positive • Pain reproduced with traction/rotation Suggests ligament/capsular pathology ---**III JOINT EFFUSION PATELLOFEMORAL DYSFUNCTION** ---**8 FLUCTUATION TEST** PURPOSE To detect knee joint effusion particularly larger effusions PROCEDURE • Patient lies supine with the knee relaxed/extended • Examiner compresses the fluid from one side of the knee toward the opposite side • Observe/palpate for a fluid wave POSITIVE SIGN • A palpable/visible fluid wave or fluctuation INDICATES Knee joint effusion ---**9 PATELLAR TAP TEST** PURPOSE To detect knee joint effusion PROCEDURE • Patient lies supine with knee extended • Gently press/compress the suprapatellar region to move fluid beneath the patella • Tap the patella downward against the femur POSITIVE SIGN • Patella rebounds/floats and taps the femur producing a palpable tap INDICATES Significant knee joint effusion ---**10 CLARKES TEST / PATELLAR GRIND TEST** PURPOSE To assess patellofemoral dysfunction particularly chondromalacia/patellofemoral pain PROCEDURE • Patient lies supine with the knee extended • Examiner places the hand proximal to the patella • Apply gentle downward pressure to the patella • Ask the patient to contract the quadriceps POSITIVE SIGN • Pain behind/around the patella • Inability to maintain quadriceps contraction because of pain INDICATES Possible patellofemoral dysfunction/chondral pathology ---**IV OTHER MEASUREMENT** ---**11 Q ANGLE** PURPOSE To assess patellofemoral alignment and the lateral pull on the patella MEASUREMENT Q angle is formed by the intersection of • Line 1 ASIS centre of patella • Line 2 centre of patella tibial tubercle PROCEDURE • Patient positioned with the knee in the appropriate standardized position • Identify and mark • ASIS • Centre of patella • Tibial tubercle • Use a goniometer to measure the angle between the two lines POSITIVE/ABNORMAL FINDING An increased Q angle may indicate increased lateral patellar alignment/pull and may be associated with patellofemoral dysfunction INDICATES • Patellofemoral malalignment • Predisposition to lateral patellar tracking/instability

Here are the comprehensive, 20-mark university exam answers for both topics, formulated from the perspective of an expert physiotherapist. 

While David J. Magee’s renowned textbook, *"Orthopedic Physical Assessment,"* is primarily utilized for musculoskeletal conditions, its foundational framework for sequential assessment (Subjective History → Observation → Palpation → Measurements/Special Tests) is the gold standard across all physiotherapy disciplines. The following answers apply Magee's systematic, evidence-based assessment principles to the evaluation of cardiovascular and pulmonary dysfunction.

---

# **TOPIC A: Subjective Examination (20 Marks)**

**Definition:** 
Subjective Examination is the systematic process of gathering clinical data directly from the patient or their caregivers. As emphasized in David J. Magee's assessment framework, the subjective history is the most critical component of the evaluation, often providing up to 80% of the information necessary to formulate a clinical diagnosis. It guides the subsequent objective examination and helps the physiotherapist understand the patient's functional limitations.

### **1. Demographic Data (2 Marks)**
*   **Definition:** The statistical characteristics of a patient.
*   **Clinical Significance:**
    *   **Age:** Certain conditions are age-specific (e.g., COPD and coronary artery disease are more common in older adults, whereas asthma or cystic fibrosis may present in childhood).
    *   **Gender:** Males have a statistically higher risk for early-onset ischemic heart disease. 
    *   **Occupation:** Helps identify exposure to occupational hazards.

### **2. Chief Complaint (2 Marks)**
*   **Definition:** The primary symptom or problem that prompted the patient to seek physiotherapy, recorded in the patient’s own words.
*   **Clinical Significance:** Helps prioritize the treatment plan. Common cardiopulmonary chief complaints include dyspnea (shortness of breath), angina (chest pain), fatigue, claudication (leg pain on walking), and chronic cough.

### **3. History of Present Illness (HPI) & Functional Limitation (4 Marks)**
*   **Definition:** A detailed chronological account of the chief complaint from its onset to the present.
*   **Clinical Significance:** 
    *   **Onset and Duration:** Is the dyspnea sudden (e.g., pulmonary embolism, pneumothorax) or gradual (e.g., COPD, congestive heart failure)?
    *   **Aggravating and Relieving Factors:** Orthopnea (breathlessness on lying flat) relieved by sitting up suggests congestive heart failure. Angina relieved by rest suggests stable coronary disease.
    *   **Functional Limitation:** Evaluating how the illness impacts Activities of Daily Living (ADLs). The physiotherapist must quantify this using scales (e.g., NYHA Functional Classification for heart failure or the MRC Dyspnea Scale). *Example:* "Patient is unable to climb one flight of stairs without severe breathlessness."

### **4. Past Medical and Surgical History (3 Marks)**
*   **Definition:** A record of all previous illnesses, hospitalizations, and surgeries.
*   **Clinical Significance:** 
    *   **Medical:** History of hypertension, diabetes mellitus, asthma, or previous myocardial infarction (MI) significantly alters the risk profile and exercise prescription.
    *   **Surgical:** Previous thoracic or cardiac surgeries (e.g., CABG, lobectomy, thoracotomy) indicate structural alterations, potential scar tissue restrictions, and altered chest wall mechanics.

### **5. Family History (2 Marks)**
*   **Definition:** Information regarding the health status and causes of death of immediate blood relatives.
*   **Clinical Significance:** Highlights genetic predispositions to cardiopulmonary diseases such as familial hypercholesterolemia, congenital heart defects, asthma, or cystic fibrosis.

### **6. Occupational, Personal, and Habitual History (3 Marks)**
*   **Definition:** Details regarding the patient's lifestyle, habits, and work environment.
*   **Clinical Significance:**
    *   **Occupational:** Exposure to asbestos, coal dust, or silica can lead to pneumoconiosis (occupational lung diseases).
    *   **Personal/Habits:** Smoking history is critical. It must be quantified in **pack-years** (Number of packs per day × years smoked). Alcohol consumption, dietary habits, and physical activity levels (sedentary vs. active) directly impact cardiovascular risk.

### **7. Socio-Economic, Environmental, and Psychological History (2 Marks)**
*   **Definition:** The assessment of the patient's living conditions, financial status, and mental well-being.
*   **Clinical Significance:** 
    *   **Environmental:** Living in highly polluted areas or homes with poor ventilation/mold exacerbates pulmonary conditions. Presence of stairs in the home dictates the required functional discharge goals.
    *   **Psychological:** Chronic cardiopulmonary conditions often lead to anxiety (especially during dyspneic attacks) and depression, which can lower exercise tolerance and rehabilitation compliance.

### **8. Drug and Treatment History (2 Marks)**
*   **Definition:** A comprehensive list of current and past medications and therapies.
*   **Clinical Significance:** Physiotherapists must know if the patient is on bronchodilators, beta-blockers (which blunt the heart rate response to exercise), diuretics, or anticoagulants (risk of bleeding). Compliance with continuous positive airway pressure (CPAP) or oxygen therapy must also be noted.

# **TOPIC B: Objective Examination (20 Marks)**

**Definition:** 
The Objective Examination is the physical assessment performed by the physiotherapist to observe, palpate, percuss, and measure physical signs. According to Magee’s principles, this confirms or refutes the clinical hypotheses generated during the subjective history. 

### **1. Vital Parameters (4 Marks)**
Vital signs provide a baseline of the patient's physiological stability.
*   **Temperature:** Elevated temperatures indicate acute infections (e.g., pneumonia, acute bronchitis).
*   **Respiratory Rate (RR):** Normal is 12–20 breaths/min. *Tachypnea* (>20) indicates respiratory distress or hypoxia. *Bradypnea* (<12) may indicate central nervous system depression.
*   **Peripheral Pulses:** Assessed at the radial, carotid, and dorsalis pedis arteries. The physiotherapist checks for rate, rhythm (regular vs. irregular), volume, and character (e.g., bounding pulse in hypercapnia, thready pulse in shock).
*   **Blood Pressure (BP):** Assessed for hypertension (increased cardiac workload) or orthostatic hypotension (drop in BP upon standing), which is crucial before initiating mobilization.

### **2. Observation: Body Build, Trophic Changes, and Deformities (3 Marks)**
*   **Body Build:** Obesity restricts diaphragmatic excursion; cachexia (severe muscle wasting) is common in severe COPD or advanced heart failure.
*   **Trophic Changes:** 
    *   Cyanosis (bluish discoloration of lips/nail beds) indicates hypoxemia.
    *   Digital clubbing indicates chronic tissue hypoxia (e.g., bronchiectasis, cystic fibrosis).
    *   Shiny, hairless skin on the lower extremities with dependent rubor suggests peripheral arterial disease (PAD).
*   **Attitude of Limb & Bony Contours:** 
    *   *Head/Neck:* Jugular Venous Distension (JVD) indicates right-sided heart failure (cor pulmonale).
    *   *Chest Deformities:* Barrel chest (increased anterior-posterior diameter in emphysema), Pectus Excavatum (funnel chest), Pectus Carinatum (pigeon chest), and Kyphoscoliosis severely restrict lung mechanics.

### **3. Breathing Pattern and Cough/Sputum Examination (4 Marks)**
*   **Breathing Pattern:** 
    *   Rhythm checks for abnormalities like Cheyne-Stokes respiration (waxing/waning pattern with apnea) or Kussmaul’s breathing (deep, labored).
    *   Use of accessory muscles (sternocleidomastoid, scalenes) and pursed-lip breathing indicates severe respiratory effort and hyperinflation.
*   **Breath Hold Test:** Normal is >25 seconds. Reduced time indicates diminished cardiopulmonary reserve or restrictive lung disease.
*   **Cough and Sputum:** 
    *   *Cough:* Is it dry, productive, bovine, or barking? A weak, ineffective cough indicates respiratory muscle fatigue.
    *   *Sputum:* Evaluated for color, consistency, and volume. Purulent (yellow/green) indicates infection; rust-colored indicates lobar pneumonia; frothy-pink indicates pulmonary edema.

### **4. Palpation and Percussion (3 Marks)**
*   **Tactile and Vocal Fremitus:** The vibration felt on the chest wall when the patient speaks (e.g., saying "99"). 
    *   *Increased fremitus* indicates consolidation (e.g., pneumonia). 
    *   *Decreased fremitus* indicates increased air or fluid in the pleural space (e.g., pneumothorax, pleural effusion).
*   **Thoracic Mobility:** Palpating the ribs and thoracic spine for segmental mobility, stiffness, and pain.
*   **Percussion:** Tapping the chest wall to determine underlying tissue density.
    *   *Resonant:* Normal air-filled lungs.
    *   *Hyper-resonant:* Hyperinflation (COPD) or pneumothorax.
    *   *Dull/Stony Dull:* Solid organ, consolidation, or pleural effusion.

### **5. Auscultation (3 Marks)**
Listening to the internal sounds of the body using a stethoscope.
*   **Breath Sounds:** 
    *   *Normal:* Vesicular (soft, low-pitched over peripheral lung fields), Bronchial (harsh, over trachea).
    *   *Adventitious (Abnormal):* Crackles/Crepitations (fluid in alveoli/airways), Wheezes (bronchospasm/narrowing), Pleural friction rub (pleurisy).
*   **Heart Sounds:** 
    *   *Normal:* S1 (AV valve closure) and S2 (Semilunar valve closure).
    *   *Abnormal:* S3 gallop (indicates heart failure/volume overload), murmurs (valvular stenosis or regurgitation).

### **6. Measurements (3 Marks)**
*   **Chest Expansion:** Measured using a standard inch-tape at three levels: Axillary, Nipple, and Xiphisternum. Normal excursion is 3-5 cm. Decreased or asymmetrical expansion indicates restrictive lung diseases, lobar collapse, or unilateral paralysis.
*   **BMI and Waist-Hip Ratio:** 
    *   *BMI:* Weight (kg) / Height (m²). 
    *   *Waist-Hip Ratio:* Evaluates central obesity. Both are critical anthropometric measurements used to assess the risk of metabolic syndrome and cardiovascular disease. High ratios correlate directly with ischemic heart disease.

**Functional Assessment for Cardiovascular and Pulmonary Dysfunction** **Definition of Functional Assessment** Functional assessment evaluates an individuals capacity to perform activities of daily living and exercise determining the impact of cardiovascular and pulmonary dysfunction on overall quality of life and physical capability It provides objective data for exercise prescription and monitors disease progression or recovery **Borg Scale for Rate of Perceived Exertion RPE** • **Definition** The Borg RPE scale is a subjective tool used to measure an individuals perceived effort and fatigue during physical activity • **Scale Range** It ranges from 6 to 20 where 6 represents no exertion at all and 20 represents maximal exertion • **Theoretical Basis** The scale is designed to correlate with the individuals heart rate multiplied by 10 eg a rating of 12 corresponds roughly to a heart rate of 120 beats per minute • **Clinical Significance** It is crucial for patients taking medications like beta blockers which alter heart rate response allowing them to self monitor exercise intensity safely **Modified Borg Scale** • **Definition** A revised version of the original Borg scale that uses a non linear scale from 0 to 10 • **Scale Ratings** 0 is rest or no breathlessness 3 is moderate breathlessness 5 is severe and 10 is maximal breathlessness • **Clinical Application** It is highly sensitive to changes in dyspnea and leg fatigue making it the preferred scale for patients with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease COPD and heart failure during rehabilitation **Grades of Dyspnea** Dyspnea or shortness of breath is a primary limiting factor in cardiopulmonary diseases **Modified Medical Research Council mMRC Dyspnea Scale** • **Definition** A simple grading system that assesses the degree of baseline breathlessness related to physical activity • **Grade 0** I only get breathless with strenuous exercise • **Grade 1** I get short of breath when hurrying on the level or walking up a slight hill • **Grade 2** I walk slower than people of the same age on the level because of breathlessness or have to stop for breath when walking at my own pace on the level • **Grade 3** I stop for breath after walking about 100 meters or after a few minutes on the level • **Grade 4** I am too breathless to leave the house or I am breathless when dressing or undressing **New York Heart Association NYHA Functional Classification** • **Definition** A classification system that places patients in one of four categories based on how much they are limited during physical activity • **Class I** No limitation of physical activity Ordinary physical activity does not cause undue fatigue palpitation or dyspnea • **Class II** Slight limitation of physical activity Comfortable at rest but ordinary physical activity results in fatigue palpitation or dyspnea • **Class III** Marked limitation of physical activity Comfortable at rest but less than ordinary activity causes fatigue palpitation or dyspnea • **Class IV** Unable to carry on any physical activity without discomfort Symptoms of heart failure at rest If any physical activity is undertaken discomfort increases --- **Exercise Tolerance Test** **Definition of Exercise Tolerance Test** Exercise tolerance testing ETT or clinical exercise testing is a cardiovascular stress test that evaluates the hearts and lungs ability to respond to external physical stress in a controlled environment It helps in diagnosing ischemia assessing functional capacity and prescribing exercise **Field Tests for Exercise Capacity** **6 Minute Walk Test 6MWT** • **Definition** A submaximal exercise test that measures the distance a patient can quickly walk on a flat hard surface in 6 minutes • **Procedure** Conducted in a 30 meter hallway Patients are allowed to self pace and rest if needed • **Clinical Significance** It evaluates the global and integrated responses of all systems involved during exercise heavily correlating with functional capacity and morbidity in heart failure and COPD **12 Minute Walk Test** • **Definition** Also known as the Cooper 12 minute run/walk test it measures the maximum distance covered in 12 minutes • **Application** Primarily used for estimating VO2 max in healthy individuals or athletes but can be adapted for clinical populations to assess aerobic endurance **Shuttle Run Test** • **Definition** An incremental progressive field test where the patient walks or runs back and forth between two markers usually 10 meters apart • **Procedure** The pacing is dictated by audio signals or beeps that get progressively faster The test ends when the patient can no longer keep up with the beep • **Clinical Significance** It provides a highly accurate estimation of peak oxygen uptake VO2 max and stresses the cardiovascular system more than self paced walking tests **Step Test** • **Definition** A simple submaximal test using a step of standardized height to evaluate cardiovascular fitness based on heart rate recovery • **Procedure** The patient steps up and down at a set cadence for a specific duration eg 3 minutes Heart rate is measured immediately after the test and during recovery • **Clinical Application** Ideal for settings with limited space and equipment though it requires good balance and lower extremity joint integrity **Treadmill Test TMT and Maximal Exercise Testing** • **Definition** A laboratory based test using a treadmill with continuous ECG blood pressure and symptom monitoring to evaluate cardiac ischemia and maximal functional capacity **Theoretical Bases of Different Protocols for Maximal Exercise Testing** Maximal exercise protocols vary in their starting intensity and rate of progression to accommodate different fitness levels and clinical conditions **Bruce Protocol** • **Theoretical Basis** A maximal multi stage treadmill protocol characterized by large abrupt increases in workload It is designed to quickly bring healthy subjects or athletes to their maximal effort • **Procedure** Speed and incline increase every 3 minutes starting at 1 7 miles per hour mph and a 10 percent grade • **Clinical Application** Best suited for younger or physically active individuals being evaluated for coronary artery disease **Modified Bruce Protocol** • **Theoretical Basis** Designed for older adults or patients with known cardiac disease who cannot tolerate the initial high workload of the standard Bruce protocol • **Procedure** It adds two preliminary stages stage 1 starts at 1 7 mph with 0 percent grade and stage 2 is 1 7 mph with 5 percent grade • **Clinical Application** Prevents premature test termination due to musculoskeletal limitations or sudden cardiac stress allowing a safer and more gradual cardiovascular adaptation **Balke Protocol** • **Theoretical Basis** A constant speed protocol with gradual incremental increases in workload primarily driven by elevation changes rather than speed • **Procedure** The treadmill speed is kept constant usually 3 3 mph while the grade increases by 1 percent every minute • **Clinical Application** Highly effective for elderly patients deconditioned individuals and those with peripheral arterial disease PAD because the constant walking speed reduces the risk of tripping and provides a steady linear increase in myocardial oxygen demand --- **Book Reference** David J Maggi Functional Assessment for Cardiovascular and Pulmonary dysfunction

Subjective Examination: Demographic Data. Chief complaint, History of Present illness including functional limitation, Past Medical Surgical history, Family history, Occupational & Personal history, Socio-Economic, Environmental and Psychological History, Drug and Treatment History///// musculoskeletal —-Vital Parameters
 Temperature: State route used (axillary/oral) and presence of fever.
 Normal Value: 98.6°F (37°C) (Range: 97.8°F – 99.1°F / 36.5°C – 37.3°C)
 Respiratory Rate (RR): Count rate, rhythm, depth, and pattern (thoraco-abdominal in females, abdomino-thoracic in males).
 Normal Value: 12–20 breaths/min, regular, quiet, and unlabored.
 Peripheral Pulses: Palpate radial, dorsalis pedis, or posterior tibial; document rate, rhythm, volume, and bilateral symmetry.
 Normal Value: 60–100 beats/min, regular, Grade 2+ (normal, palpable bilaterally).
 Blood Pressure (BP): Record systolic/diastolic pressure, patient position (sitting/supine), and arm used.
 Normal Value: <120/80 mmHg (Systolic: 100–120 mmHg, Diastolic: 60–80 mmHg).
General Musculoskeletal Observations
 Body Built: Document somatotype (ectomorphic, mesomorphic, endomorphic) and calculated BMI.
 Normal Finding: Mesomorphic build; BMI 18.5–24.9 kg/m².
 Attitude of Limb: Note resting spatial position of the limb relative to anatomical neutral (e.g., antalgic posturing, guarding).
 Normal Finding: Symmetrical, resting comfortably in anatomical neutral without protective spasm.
 Bony Contours: Inspect continuity, prominence, and bilateral symmetry of standard bony landmarks.
 Normal Finding: Intact, smooth, and symmetrical, without step-offs, spurs, or abnormal prominence.
 Deformities: Identify structural (fixed) vs. postural (flexible) deformities, plane of deviation, and joint involved.
 Normal Finding: Absent; normal physiological axial and appendicular alignment.
 Trophic Changes: Assess skin texture, shine, hair loss, nail changes, pigmentation, or signs of autonomic dysfunction.
 Normal Finding: Warm, supple skin with normal turgor, uniform hair distribution, and smooth nails; no trophic ulcers, glossiness, or cyanosis.
Examination of Posture
 Postural Alignment: Observe alignment relative to a standard plumb line across anterior, lateral, and posterior views:
 Anterior: Head level, shoulder symmetry, pelvic level (ASIS), Q-angle, patellar alignment, arches of feet.
 Lateral: Alignment through earlobe \rightarrow acromion \rightarrow lumbar bodies \rightarrow greater trochanter \rightarrow anterior knee \rightarrow anterior lateral malleolus.
 Posterior: Scapular level, vertical spinal line, PSIS symmetry, popliteal folds, calcaneal alignment.
 Normal Finding: Balanced, symmetrical posture; alignment matches plumb line reference points; normal physiological curves (cervical lordosis, thoracic kyphosis, lumbar lordosis) with neutral pelvic tilt (7^\circ\text{--}15^\circ).
Palpation & Soft Tissue Examination
 Muscle Spasm: Palpate muscle belly for involuntary sustained contraction, taut bands, and resistance to stretch.
 Normal Finding: Normal resting muscle tone; tissue is soft, pliable, and non-reactive to passive elongation.
 Tenderness: Localize exact anatomical structure and grade using the Ritchie scale:
 Grade 0: No tenderness.
 Grade I: Complaint of pain without facial grimace.
 Grade II: Complaint of pain with facial grimace/wince.
 Grade III: Severe pain causing withdrawal of the body part.
 Grade IV: Patient resists or prevents palpation.
 Normal Finding: Grade 0 (non-tender to firm palpation).
 Edema / Swelling: Document intra-articular effusion vs. extra-articular edema; test for pitting (1+ to 4+ scale) and localized warmth.
 Normal Finding: Absent / Grade 0; no localized heat, pitting, or fluid fluctuation.
 Limb Girth / Muscle Wasting: Measure circumference in centimeters using a non-elastic tape at set distances from fixed bony landmarks (e.g., 5 cm, 10 cm, 15 cm from superior pole of patella or medial epicondyle). Compare bilaterally.
 Normal Finding: Bilateral symmetry (a difference of \le 0.5\text{--}1\text{ cm} on the dominant side is acceptable as physiological).
 Scar Examination: Note exact anatomical site, size (L \times W in cm), type (surgical, traumatic, hypertrophic, keloid), healing stage, mobility over underlying planes, and adherence.
 Normal Finding: If present post-operatively: mature, pale, flat, pliable, fully mobile over fascia, and non-tender. /////Range of Motion (ROM)
 What to Write: Document Active ROM (AROM) and Passive ROM (PROM) using a universal goniometer; note plane, degrees of excursion, presence of a painful arc, and compensatory movement patterns.
 Normal Finding: Full, pain-free physiological range matching standard anatomical norms without substitution; AROM equals PROM (e.g., Shoulder Flexion 0\text{--}180^\circ, Knee Flexion 0\text{--}135^\circ/140^\circ).
Joint Play & End Feel
 What to Write:
 Joint Play (Accessory Motion): Evaluate passive glide, distraction, roll, and spin in the loose-packed position (graded as normal, hypomobile, or hypermobile).
 End Feel (Cyriax): Document sensation at extreme passive limit (Soft, Firm, Hard) or pathological end-feel (Empty, Springy block, Boggy/Spasm).
 Normal Finding: Normal accessory excursion with painless gliding; physiological end feel appropriate for the joint tested:
 Soft (Tissue approximation): Knee flexion, elbow flexion.
 Firm (Capsular/Ligamentous): Shoulder external rotation, ankle dorsiflexion.
 Hard (Bony contact): Elbow extension.
Muscle Strength (Manual Muscle Testing - MMT)
 What to Write: Rate isolated muscle groups using the Daniels & Worthingham / MRC scale (Grade 0 to Grade 5); specify anti-gravity vs. gravity-eliminated test positions and response to the "break test."
 Normal Finding: Grade 5 (Normal) — completes full active ROM against gravity and tolerates maximum manual resistance without breaking.
Muscle Power
 What to Write: Rate the ability to generate force rapidly (\text{Force} \times \text{Velocity}); document functional explosive tests (e.g., vertical jump height, standing broad jump, medicine ball toss) or isokinetic dynamometry.
 Normal Finding: Symmetrical, high-velocity force generation; Limb Symmetry Index (LSI) \ge 90\text{--}100\% compared to the contralateral side; within age/sex normative percentiles.
Muscle Endurance
 What to Write: Assess the capacity of a muscle group to sustain repetitive contractions or hold a static posture over time (e.g., timed static plank, Biering-Sørensen test for trunk extensors, dynamic repetitions to fatigue at 60–70% 1RM).
 Normal Finding: Symmetrical holding capacity without compensatory tremors (e.g., Biering-Sørensen test sustained for >60\text{--}120\text{ seconds}).
Muscle Flexibility (Muscle Length Testing)
 What to Write: Record specific length assessment tests for 2-joint and postural muscles (e.g., Thomas test for iliopsoas, Ober’s test for ITB/TFL, Ely’s test for rectus femoris, 90-90 Straight Leg Raise for hamstrings).
 Normal Finding: Normal physiological muscle length without restricted joint range or compensatory substitution:
 Thomas Test: Thigh remains flat on table with knee flexed to \ge 80^\circ.
 90-90 SLR: Knee extends to within 10^\circ\text{--}20^\circ of full extension.
 Ober's Test: Thigh drops below the horizontal plane.
Isometric Resisted Testing (Cyriax Method)
 What to Write: Test muscle groups in a loose-packed/neutral joint position to isolate contractile elements; record pain and strength response using the four Cyriax categories:
 Strong and Painless (SPL)
 Strong and Painful (SPF)
 Weak and Painful (WPF)
 Weak and Painless (WPL)
 Normal Finding: Strong and Painless (SPL) — signifies intact, uninjured contractile tissue and normal neural conduction.
Limb-Length Discrepancy (LLD)
 What to Write: Measure both lower extremities in supine using a non-elastic tape measure:
 True (Anatomic) Length: Anterior Superior Iliac Spine (ASIS) to Medial Malleolus (clearing medial knee joint line).
 Apparent (Functional) Length: Xiphisternum or Umbilicus to Medial Malleolus.
 Normal Finding: Equal bilaterally; True LLD <1\text{ cm} (<0.5\text{ inches}) is considered clinically insignificant/physiological.
Pelvic Inclination (Pelvic Tilt)
 What to Write: Palpate and measure the sagittal alignment between the ASIS and Posterior Superior Iliac Spine (PSIS) in comfortable bipedal stance using an inclinometer.
 Normal Finding: Normal anterior pelvic tilt of 7^\circ\text{--}15^\circ (ASIS lies approximately 0.5\text{--}1\text{ cm} inferior to PSIS in horizontal plane); transverse level symmetrical bilaterally.
Examination of Balance
 What to Write: Document static and dynamic postural control:
 Static Balance: Single-Leg Stance (SLS) with eyes open/closed, Romberg and Sharpened Romberg tests.
 Dynamic Balance: Functional Reach Test (FRT), Timed Up and Go (TUG), Y-Balance Test.
 Normal Finding:
 Single-Leg Stance: Sustained for >30\text{ seconds} (eyes open), >10\text{--}20\text{ seconds} (eyes closed).
 Romberg Test: Negative (steady posture maintained for 30 seconds with eyes closed; minimal sway).
 Functional Reach Test: Reach distance >25\text{ cm} (>10\text{ inches}).
 Timed Up and Go (TUG): Completed in <10\text{ seconds}.
Gait Examination
 What to Write: Analyze stance phase (heel strike, foot flat, midstance, push-off) and swing phase (acceleration, midswing, deceleration); record cadence, step length, stride width, and check for pathological deviations (antalgic, Trendelenburg, high-steppage, circumduction).
 Normal Finding: Normal, symmetrical, smooth gait pattern:
 Cadence: 100–120 steps/min.
 Base of Support (Step Width): 5–10 cm.
 Stance-to-Swing Ratio: 60% stance, 40% swing.
 Equal stride length bilaterally, normal pelvis/trunk counter-rotation, and reciprocal arm swing.
External Aids & Assistive Devices
 What to Write: Record the presence and type of mobility device (standard walker, axillary/elbow crutches, quad cane, AFO, knee brace), prescribed weight-bearing status (NWB, PWB, TTWB, FWB), gait sequence used (2-point, 3-point, 4-point), and degree of user independence.
 Normal Finding: Independent community ambulator; no external walking aids, orthoses, or bracing required.///// Superficial Sensation (Touch, Pain, Temp):
 Test: Cotton wisp (light touch), pinprick (pain), hot/cold tubes (temperature) bilaterally.
 Normal: Intact bilaterally; prompt and accurate localization.
 Deep Sensation (Proprioception, Kinesthesia, Vibration):
 Test: Passive digit displacement (joint position/kinesthesia), 128 Hz tuning fork on bony prominences (vibration).
 Normal: Intact bilaterally; detects minor joint excursion (<1^\circ\text{--}2^\circ); symmetrical vibration perception.
 Cortical Sensation (Stereognosis, 2PD, Graphesthesia):
 Test: Object identification by touch, 2-point discrimination on fingertips, tracing numbers on palm.
 Normal: Intact bilaterally; 2-point discrimination <4\text{--}5\text{ mm} on fingertips.
 Dermatomes (Sensory Key Points):
 Test: Light touch and pinprick across standard ASIA levels (C2–T1 upper quadrant; L1–S5 lower quadrant).
 Normal: Score 2/2 (Intact bilaterally) across all levels; no sensory loss or hyperalgesia.
 Myotomes (Motor Root Screen):
 Test: 5-second isometric hold (C1–C4 neck/scapula, C5 shoulder, C6 elbow flex/wrist ext, C7 elbow ext/wrist flex, C8 thumb/fingers, T1 intrinsics; L1–L2 hip flex, L3 knee ext, L4 dorsiflex, L5 EHL, S1 plantarflex).
 Normal: Grade 5/5 bilaterally; strong and non-fatiguing.
 Deep Tendon Reflexes (DTRs):
 Test: Biceps (C5–C6), Brachioradialis (C5–C6), Triceps (C7–C8), Knee (L3–L4), Ankle (S1–S2) on a 0–4+ scale.
 Normal: Grade 2+ bilaterally; symmetrical, brisk response.
 Superficial Reflexes:
 Test: Plantar stroke (S1–S2), abdominal quadrant strokes (T7–T12).
 Normal: Plantar is Flexor (toes curl down); abdominal reflex is present and symmetrical.
 Pathological Reflexes (UMN Signs):
 Test: Babinski response, Hoffmann’s sign (middle finger flick), Ankle clonus (rapid dorsiflexion).
 Normal: Negative / Absent bilaterally; clonus absent (<2 beats).
////// Power Grips:
 Assessment: Test ability to form and maintain standard functional grasp patterns:
 Cylindrical Grip: Holding a bottle or cylinder (flexor digitorum superficialis/profundus, thenar/hypothenar lock).
 Spherical Grip: Holding a ball with digits abducted and spread (intrinsics plus long flexors).
 Hook Grip: Carrying a handle or bag (IP flexion without thumb opposition; relies purely on long digital flexors).
 Fist / Grasp: Clenching tightly around an object (requires 20^\circ\text{--}30^\circ wrist extension).
 Grip Strength Measurement: Jamar Hand Dynamometer (tested seated, shoulder adducted, elbow at 90^\circ, wrist in neutral to 30^\circ extension; average of 3 trials).
 Normal Value: Symmetrical, complete grip closure; Jamar values: 30–50 kg (males), 15–30 kg (females); dominant hand is typically \sim 10\% stronger than non-dominant.
 Precision Grips (Hand Pinches):
 Assessment: Test prehension patterns and measure force using a hydraulic pinch gauge:
 Tip-to-Tip (Terminal / Pincer) Pinch: Index fingertip to thumb tip (picking up a needle/pin; tests Anterior Interosseous Nerve / FDP & FPL).
 Pad-to-Pad (Palmar / 3-Jaw Chuck) Pinch: Thumb pad opposed to index and middle finger pads (holding a pencil or coin).
 Lateral (Key) Pinch: Thumb pad pressed against the lateral/radial aspect of the index middle phalanx (turning a key; tests Adductor Pollicis / Ulnar Nerve).
 Normal Value: Clean opposition without collapse of interphalangeal joints; Pinch gauge averages:
 Key Pinch: 7–10 kg
 Palmar (3-Jaw) Pinch: 5–8 kg
 Tip Pinch: 4–6 kg
 Routine Hand Motor Evaluation:
 Thenar Muscles (Median Nerve): Test Abductor Pollicis Brevis (thumb abduction perpendicular to palm) and Opponens Pollicis (thumb pulp to little finger base).
 Hypothenar & Intrinsics (Ulnar Nerve): Test Dorsal Interossei (finger abduction against resistance), Palmar Interossei (finger adduction/card test), and Lumbricals (MCP flexion with IP extension).
 Special Motor Signs:
 Froment's Sign: Pull paper from between thumb and index finger; assesses Adductor Pollicis.
 Normal Finding: Negative (thumb IP remains extended; no compensatory FPL hyperflexion).
 Normal Motor Finding: Grade 5/5 bilaterally on all intrinsic/extrinsic tests; complete thumb opposition (Kapandji score: 10/10).
 Routine Hand Sensory Evaluation:
 Autonomous Sensory Zones:
 Median Nerve: Volar pulp of the index finger.
 Ulnar Nerve: Volar pulp of the little finger.
 Radial Nerve: Dorsal aspect of the first web space.
 Static Two-Point Discrimination (Weber Test): Apply blunt prongs parallel to finger axis on the distal digital pulp with eyes closed.
 Normal Value: \le 5\text{ mm} (classified as Normal static 2PD).
 Moving Two-Point Discrimination (Dellon Test): Move prongs longitudinally from proximal to distal along the finger pad.
 Normal Value: 2\text{--}3\text{ mm}.
 Semmes-Weinstein Monofilament (Pressure Threshold): Apply monofilament perpendicular to skin until it bows for 1.5 seconds.
 Normal Value: 2.83 monofilament (0.07 g) indicates intact normal light touch.
 Stereognosis & Functional Hand Dexterity:
 Tactile Stereognosis: Place 5–6 common objects (key, coin, safety pin, paperclip, cotton ball) into the patient's hand one by one with eyes closed; ask for identification.
 Normal Finding: Immediate, accurate recognition within 2–3 seconds per object without vision.
 Functional Dexterity Tests:
 Moberg Pick-Up Test: Patient picks up small items and places them into a container (timed with eyes open, then repeated with eyes closed).
 Nine-Hole Peg Test (NHPT): Place and remove nine small pegs from holes as quickly as possible.
 Normal Value: Completed smoothly in <18\text{--}20\text{ seconds} with no drops or fumbling; bilateral performance within 10% symmetry.
/////////////Cardiovascular///// Vital Parameters:
 Temp: 98.6°F (37°C); afebrile.
 RR: 12–20 breaths/min; regular, quiet, unlabored.
 Pulse: 60–100 bpm; regular, Grade 2+ volume, bilaterally symmetrical.
 BP: <120/80 mmHg; no orthostatic drop.
 SpO_2: 95%–100% on room air.
 Body Built & General Inspection:
 Body Built: Mesomorphic (BMI 18.5–24.9 kg/m²); no cachexia or wasting.
 Attitude & Posture: Relaxed sitting/supine; no tripoding or orthopnea.
 Bony Contours: Smooth, intact, and symmetrical; no sternal/rib step-offs.
 Symmetry & Deformities: Trachea midline; JVP <3\text{--}4\text{ cm}; AP:Transverse ratio is 1:2; no clubbing (Schamroth negative).
 Trophic Changes: Warm, pink, capillary refill <2\text{ s}; no cyanosis or pitting edema.
 Breathing Pattern & Breath Holding:
 Pattern: Eupneic, diaphragmatic-costal; I:E ratio 1:2; no paradoxical motion.
 Accessory Muscle Use: Quiescent / absent at rest; no SCM, scalene, or intercostal indrawing.
 Breath Holding Test (BHT): Normal holding time >30\text{--}45\text{ seconds}.
 Cough & Sputum:
 Cough: Strong, crisp, effective, and self-clearing.
 Sputum: Scant, clear/mucoid, and odorless.
 Palpation (Fremitus & Chest Expansion):
 Tactile/Vocal Fremitus: Symmetrical, moderate, uniform vibration across all zones.
 Chest Expansion: Bilaterally symmetrical excursion; 3\text{--}5\text{ cm} difference between full expiration and full inspiration.
 Percussion:
 Percussion Note: Resonant bilaterally over all lung fields (dullness restricted to normal cardiac and liver borders).
//////Breath Sounds (Lung Auscultation)
 Normal Breath Sounds:
 Vesicular: Soft, low-pitched, rustling; heard over peripheral lung fields; Inspiration : Expiration = 3:1 (no pause between phases).
 Bronchial: Loud, high-pitched, tubular/hollow; heard over trachea/manubrium; Inspiration : Expiration = 1:2 (distinct pause between phases).
 Bronchovesicular: Intermediate pitch and intensity; heard over 1st–2nd intercostal spaces anteriorly and interscapular region; Inspiration : Expiration = 1:1.
 Normal Finding: Normal vesicular breath sounds heard bilaterally across all lung zones with no added sounds.
 Abnormal Breath Sounds:
 Bronchial Breathing in Periphery: Pathological; indicates lung consolidation, lobar pneumonia, or large superficial cavity.
 Diminished / Absent Sounds: Pleural effusion, pneumothorax, severe atelectasis, or hyperinflated COPD.
 Adventitious (Added) Sounds:
 Crackles (Rales): Discontinuous, non-musical clicking/popping sounds; fine crackles (pulmonary edema, interstitial fibrosis) vs. coarse crackles (bronchiectasis, chronic bronchitis).
 Wheezes (Rhonchi): Continuous, musical, high-pitched whistling (bronchospasm in asthma/COPD) or low-pitched snoring sounds (secretions in large airways).
 Pleural Friction Rub: Grating, creaking sound present in both inspiration and expiration (pleurisy/pleuritis).
 Stridor: Loud, high-pitched, musical monophonic sound heard predominantly during inspiration; emergency upper airway obstruction.
 Vocal Resonance:
 Test: Auscultate lung zones while the patient repeats "ninety-nine".
 Normal: Muffled, indistinct, soft vocal resonance bilaterally.
 Abnormal: Bronchophony (words heard loudly and distinctly), Egophony ("E" transmits as nasal "A" over consolidation), Whispered Pectoriloquy (whispered syllables heard clearly).
Heart Sounds (Cardiac Auscultation)
 Normal Heart Sounds:
 S1 ("Lub"): Closure of Mitral and Tricuspid (AV) valves; marks the onset of ventricular systole; loudest at the apex (5th intercostal space, midclavicular line).
 S2 ("Dub"): Closure of Aortic and Pulmonary (semilunar) valves; marks the onset of ventricular diastole; loudest at the base (2nd intercostal space, right/left sternal borders).
 Normal Finding: S1 and S2 clearly audible, regular rate and rhythm; no extra sounds or murmurs.
 Abnormal Heart Sounds:
 S3 (Ventricular Gallop): Low-pitched, early diastole ("Kentucky" rhythm); pathological in adults >40 years indicating left ventricular failure or fluid overload.
 S4 (Atrial Gallop): Low-pitched, late diastole ("Tennessee" rhythm); caused by atria contracting against a stiff, non-compliant ventricle (hypertension, LVH).
 Murmurs: Turbulent blood flow through stenotic or regurgitant valves; graded Grade 1 (faint) to Grade 6 (audible without stethoscope touching chest).
 Pericardial Friction Rub: Superficial, scratchy, high-pitched sound heard best at the left lower sternal border with patient leaning forward (pericarditis).
Chest Measurements & Symmetry
 Chest Expansion Measurement:
 Method: Non-elastic measuring tape used across three levels, measuring the difference from maximal expiration to maximal inspiration:
 Axillary Level: 2nd–3rd intercostal space.
 Mammary / Nipple Level: 4th intercostal space.
 Xiphisternal Level: 8th–10th rib margin / xiphisternal junction.

 Formula: \text{Weight (kg)} / [\text{Height (m)}]^2
 Classifications (WHO):
 Underweight: <18.5\text{ kg/m}^2
 Normal: 18.5\text{--}24.9\text{ kg/m}^2
 Overweight: 25.0\text{--}29.9\text{ kg/m}^2
 Obese: \ge 30.0\text{ kg/m}^2 (Asian cut-off for obesity: \ge 25.0\text{ kg/m}^2)
 Waist-to-Hip Ratio (WHR):
 Method: Waist measured at the narrowest circumference between the lower rib margin and iliac crest (umbilicus level); Hip measured at the widest horizontal circumference over the buttocks/greater trochanters.
 Formula: \text{Waist Circumference} / \text{Hip Circumference}

Investigations for Musculoskeletal Disorders BPT 3rd Year Physiotherapy | Easy-language university exam notes | 10-mark answers Reference: David J. Magee, Orthopedic Physical Assessment (assessment principles). Simplified study notes; not verbatim textbook content. Contents • 1. Blood Investigations and Markers • 2. Ultrasonography (USG) • 3. X-ray (Radiography) • 4. Computed Tomography (CT Scan) • 5. Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) Page 1 BPT Physiotherapy Study Notes1. Blood Investigations and Markers Definition: Blood investigations are laboratory tests performed on a blood sample to detect inflammation, infection, autoimmune disease, muscle injury, and metabolic problems affecting bones and joints. In simple words: Blood tests help identify whether a musculoskeletal problem may be due to infection, inflammation, an immune disorder, or a metabolic problem. Aims • Detect infection and inflammation. • Identify autoimmune diseases such as rheumatoid arthritis. • Assess bone and mineral metabolism. • Detect muscle damage. • Support diagnosis and differential diagnosis. • Monitor disease activity and response to treatment. Important blood investigations • CBC (Complete Blood Count): Measures red cells, white cells, hemoglobin, and platelets. Increased WBCs may suggest infection; low hemoglobin may indicate anemia; platelets may rise during inflammation. • ESR (Erythrocyte Sedimentation Rate): Measures how far red blood cells settle in one hour. It may rise in inflammatory disorders and infections. It is a nonspecific marker and cannot identify the exact disease. • CRP (C-Reactive Protein): A protein produced mainly by the liver during inflammation. It rises in infection and inflammatory disorders and is useful for monitoring treatment response. It usually changes faster than ESR. • RF (Rheumatoid Factor): An autoantibody that may be present in rheumatoid arthritis. It supports diagnosis but can also be positive in other conditions or some healthy older adults. • Anti-CCP: An antibody against citrullinated proteins. It is relatively specific for rheumatoid arthritis and can help with early diagnosis. • Serum uric acid: Measures urate in blood. It may be elevated in gout, but a high result alone does not confirm gout; joint-fluid crystal analysis may be needed. • CK (Creatine Kinase): An enzyme found mainly in skeletal muscle. It may increase with muscle damage, muscular dystrophy, inflammatory myopathy, or severe muscle injury. • ALP (Alkaline Phosphatase): An enzyme found in bone and liver. It may rise with increased bone turnover, Paget disease, some metabolic bone disorders, or fracture healing. • Calcium, phosphate, and vitamin D: Help assess bone mineral metabolism. Vitamin D supports calcium absorption; these tests may be used when metabolic bone disease or deficiency is suspected. • HLA-B27: A genetic marker associated with ankylosing spondylitis and related disorders. It supports diagnosis when symptoms fit but does not confirm disease by itself. Other useful tests • ANA and anti-dsDNA when systemic autoimmune connective-tissue disease is suspected. • Renal function tests to assess kidney function and help guide medication choices. • PTH when calcium or phosphate abnormalities require investigation. • Blood cultures when bloodstream infection or bone/joint infection is suspected. Examples: RA—RF, anti-CCP, ESR, CRP; osteomyelitis—CBC, ESR, CRP, cultures; gout—urate plus joint-fluid analysis; suspected muscle disease—CK; metabolic bone disease—calcium, phosphate, ALP, vitamin D, and sometimes PTH. Page 2 BPT Physiotherapy Study NotesPhysiotherapy importance: Results help recognize systemic illness, guide referral and precautions, and support rehabilitation planning. Interpret them with history, examination, and imaging. Conclusion: Blood tests support the diagnosis of musculoskeletal disorders but usually cannot establish the diagnosis alone. Page 3 BPT Physiotherapy Study Notes2. Ultrasonography (USG) Definition: USG is an imaging technique that uses high-frequency sound waves to create images of muscles, tendons, ligaments, joints, and other soft tissues. In simple words: It uses sound waves to look inside the body without radiation. Principle • A transducer sends sound waves into tissues. • Different tissues reflect the waves differently. • The transducer receives returning echoes. • A computer converts the echoes into an image. Procedure • Position the patient to expose the area. • Apply gel to the skin. • Move the transducer over the area in different directions. • The examiner may ask the patient to move to observe structures dynamically. Indications • Rotator cuff and other tendon injuries. • Muscle strains, tears, and hematomas. • Bursitis and tenosynovitis. • Joint effusion. • Ganglion cysts and selected peripheral nerve problems. • Guidance for selected injections or aspirations. Possible findings • Tendon thickening or tear. • Disruption of muscle fibers. • Fluid around a joint. • Bursal swelling. • Abnormal tendon movement. Advantages • No ionizing radiation. • Usually painless and non-invasive. • Real-time and dynamic assessment. • Can compare both sides. • Relatively inexpensive and portable. • Can guide selected procedures. Limitations • Operator-dependent. • Deep structures may be difficult to assess. Page 4 BPT Physiotherapy Study Notes• Bone blocks sound waves. • Cannot adequately assess bone marrow. • Not suitable for every internal joint structure. Physiotherapy importance: Supports assessment of soft-tissue injuries, helps with rehabilitation planning, and may help monitor selected changes. It complements rather than replaces clinical examination. Conclusion: USG is especially useful for superficial soft tissues and movement-related assessment. Page 5 BPT Physiotherapy Study Notes3. X-ray (Radiography) Definition: X-ray is an imaging technique using ionizing radiation to produce images of bones and joints. In simple words: It is mainly used to see bones, fractures, and joint alignment. Principle • X-rays pass through the body and are absorbed differently by different tissues. • Dense bone absorbs more radiation and appears white; soft tissues appear gray and air appears black. Procedure • Position the body part. • Place it between the X-ray source and detector. • Take the required view, often two views at right angles. • Assess bone alignment, joint spaces, and abnormalities. Common views • AP (anteroposterior), lateral, and oblique views. • Weight-bearing views when clinically indicated. Indications and findings • Fracture: Site, pattern, displacement, and alignment. • Dislocation: Abnormal position of bones at a joint. • Osteoarthritis: Joint-space narrowing, osteophytes, subchondral sclerosis, and sometimes cysts. • Rheumatoid arthritis: Possible erosions, joint-space narrowing, and periarticular osteopenia. • Other: Spinal curvature, later changes of osteomyelitis, and some bone lesions. Advantages • Quick, widely available, and relatively inexpensive. • Good for bone, fractures, dislocations, and alignment. • Useful for monitoring fracture healing. Limitations • Uses ionizing radiation. • Produces two-dimensional images. • Limited soft-tissue detail. • Early disease or subtle fractures may not be visible. • Does not directly show cartilage, ligaments, or tendons well. Physiotherapy importance: Helps identify structural problems, understand alignment and healing, and follow medical precautions for loading and exercise. Conclusion: X-ray is commonly a first-line investigation for suspected bone and joint disorders. Page 6 BPT Physiotherapy Study Notes4. Computed Tomography (CT Scan) Definition: CT is an imaging technique that uses X-rays and computer processing to produce detailed cross-sectional images, with optional 3D reconstructions. In simple words: It combines X-ray information from many angles to show detailed slices of the body. Principle • An X-ray tube rotates around the patient. • Measurements are collected from different angles. • A computer reconstructs cross-sectional images and may create 3D views. Procedure • The patient lies on a motorized table. • The affected part is positioned in the scanner. • The scanner collects X-ray data while rotating. • A computer produces images in different planes. Indications • Complex, comminuted, and intra-articular fractures. • Pelvic, acetabular, calcaneal, and spinal fractures. • Detailed assessment of vertebral and other bony structures. • Bone destruction, abnormal bone formation, and selected tumors. • Preoperative planning and selected image-guided procedures. Advantages • Detailed cross-sectional bone images. • Useful for complex fractures and fracture displacement. • Allows 3D reconstruction. • Helpful for preoperative planning. Limitations • Uses ionizing radiation, generally more than plain X-ray. • Soft-tissue contrast is usually poorer than MRI. • More expensive than X-ray. • Metal implants can cause artifacts. • Some examinations require contrast material. Physiotherapy importance: Helps understand complex fracture patterns and bony involvement, supporting postoperative rehabilitation planning and precautions. Conclusion: CT is particularly useful for complex fractures and detailed bony anatomy. Page 7 BPT Physiotherapy Study Notes5. Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) Definition: MRI uses a strong magnetic field, radiofrequency waves, and computer processing to produce detailed images of body tissues. In simple words: MRI is especially useful for muscles, ligaments, tendons, cartilage, bone marrow, and spinal structures. Principle • Hydrogen nuclei respond to a strong magnetic field. • Radiofrequency pulses change their alignment temporarily. • As they return, they produce signals. • A computer converts these signals into detailed images. Procedure • Screen the patient for MRI safety, including implants and metallic objects. • Position the patient on the MRI table. • Acquire images in different planes and sequences. • Use contrast material only when indicated. Indications • Ligaments: ACL, PCL, collateral ligament, and selected shoulder injuries. • Tendons and muscles: Rotator cuff or Achilles tears, muscle tears, hematomas, and tendinopathy. • Joints: Meniscal tears, cartilage injury, effusion, synovitis, and osteonecrosis. • Spine: Disc herniation, spinal stenosis, nerve-root compression, spinal cord abnormalities, and infection. • Tumors: Extent of bone marrow and surrounding soft-tissue involvement. Possible findings • Ligament or tendon tears. • Muscle injury and cartilage damage. • Bone marrow edema. • Disc herniation or nerve compression. • Soft-tissue masses. Advantages • No ionizing radiation. • Excellent soft-tissue contrast. • Shows bone marrow abnormalities. • Useful for ligaments, tendons, cartilage, and spinal structures. • Images can be obtained in multiple planes. Limitations • Expensive and often takes longer than X-ray or CT. • Claustrophobia may be a problem. • Some implants or metallic foreign bodies need special safety assessment. Page 8 BPT Physiotherapy Study Notes• Movement can reduce image quality. • Some abnormalities also occur in people without symptoms. Physiotherapy importance: Supports assessment of soft-tissue and spinal conditions, helps plan rehabilitation precautions, and may guide referral. MRI findings must be matched with symptoms and examination. Conclusion: MRI is valuable for soft-tissue, bone marrow, and spinal disorders and does not use ionizing radiation.

Magee, Orthopedic Physical Assessment (assessment principles). Simplified study notes; not verbatim textbook content. Contents • 1. Blood Investigations and Markers • 2. Ultrasonography (USG) • 3. X-ray (Radiography) • 4. Computed Tomography (CT Scan) • 5. Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) Page 1 BPT Physiotherapy Study Notes1. Blood Investigations and Markers Definition: Blood investigations are laboratory tests performed on a blood sample to detect inflammation, infection, autoimmune disease, muscle injury, and metabolic problems affecting bones and joints. In simple words: Blood tests help identify whether a musculoskeletal problem may be due to infection, inflammation, an immune disorder, or a metabolic problem. Aims • Detect infection and inflammation. • Identify autoimmune diseases such as rheumatoid arthritis. • Assess bone and mineral metabolism. • Detect muscle damage. • Support diagnosis and differential diagnosis. • Monitor disease activity and response to treatment. Important blood investigations • CBC (Complete Blood Count): Measures red cells, white cells, hemoglobin, and platelets. Increased WBCs may suggest infection; low hemoglobin may indicate anemia; platelets may rise during inflammation. • ESR (Erythrocyte Sedimentation Rate): Measures how far red blood cells settle in one hour. It may rise in inflammatory disorders and infections. It is a nonspecific marker and cannot identify the exact disease. • CRP (C-Reactive Protein): A protein produced mainly by the liver during inflammation. It rises in infection and inflammatory disorders and is useful for monitoring treatment response. It usually changes faster than ESR. • RF (Rheumatoid Factor): An autoantibody that may be present in rheumatoid arthritis. It supports diagnosis but can also be positive in other conditions or some healthy older adults. • Anti-CCP: An antibody against citrullinated proteins. It is relatively specific for rheumatoid arthritis and can help with early diagnosis. • Serum uric acid: Measures urate in blood. It may be elevated in gout, but a high result alone does not confirm gout; joint-fluid crystal analysis may be needed. • CK (Creatine Kinase): An enzyme found mainly in skeletal muscle. It may increase with muscle damage, muscular dystrophy, inflammatory myopathy, or severe muscle injury. • ALP (Alkaline Phosphatase): An enzyme found in bone and liver. It may rise with increased bone turnover, Paget disease, some metabolic bone disorders, or fracture healing. • Calcium, phosphate, and vitamin D: Help assess bone mineral metabolism. Vitamin D supports calcium absorption; these tests may be used when metabolic bone disease or deficiency is suspected. • HLA-B27: A genetic marker associated with ankylosing spondylitis and related disorders. It supports diagnosis when symptoms fit but does not confirm disease by itself. Other useful tests • ANA and anti-dsDNA when systemic autoimmune connective-tissue disease is suspected. • Renal function tests to assess kidney function and help guide medication choices. • PTH when calcium or phosphate abnormalities require investigation. • Blood cultures when bloodstream infection or bone/joint infection is suspected. Examples: RA—RF, anti-CCP, ESR, CRP; osteomyelitis—CBC, ESR, CRP, cultures; gout—urate plus joint-fluid analysis; suspected muscle disease—CK; metabolic bone disease—calcium, phosphate, ALP, vitamin D, and sometimes PTH. Page 2 BPT Physiotherapy Study NotesPhysiotherapy importance: Results help recognize systemic illness, guide referral and precautions, and support rehabilitation planning. Interpret them with history, examination, and imaging. Conclusion: Blood tests support the diagnosis of musculoskeletal disorders but usually cannot establish the diagnosis alone. Page 3 BPT Physiotherapy Study Notes2. Ultrasonography (USG) Definition: USG is an imaging technique that uses high-frequency sound waves to create images of muscles, tendons, ligaments, joints, and other soft tissues. In simple words: It uses sound waves to look inside the body without radiation. Principle • A transducer sends sound waves into tissues. • Different tissues reflect the waves differently. • The transducer receives returning echoes. • A computer converts the echoes into an image. Procedure • Position the patient to expose the area. • Apply gel to the skin. • Move the transducer over the area in different directions. • The examiner may ask the patient to move to observe structures dynamically. Indications • Rotator cuff and other tendon injuries. • Muscle strains, tears, and hematomas. • Bursitis and tenosynovitis. • Joint effusion. • Ganglion cysts and selected peripheral nerve problems. • Guidance for selected injections or aspirations. Possible findings • Tendon thickening or tear. • Disruption of muscle fibers. • Fluid around a joint. • Bursal swelling. • Abnormal tendon movement. Advantages • No ionizing radiation. • Usually painless and non-invasive. • Real-time and dynamic assessment. • Can compare both sides. • Relatively inexpensive and portable. • Can guide selected procedures. Limitations • Operator-dependent. • Deep structures may be difficult to assess. Page 4 BPT Physiotherapy Study Notes• Bone blocks sound waves. • Cannot adequately assess bone marrow. • Not suitable for every internal joint structure. Physiotherapy importance: Supports assessment of soft-tissue injuries, helps with rehabilitation planning, and may help monitor selected changes. It complements rather than replaces clinical examination. Conclusion: USG is especially useful for superficial soft tissues and movement-related assessment. Page 5 BPT Physiotherapy Study Notes3. X-ray (Radiography) Definition: X-ray is an imaging technique using ionizing radiation to produce images of bones and joints. In simple words: It is mainly used to see bones, fractures, and joint alignment. Principle • X-rays pass through the body and are absorbed differently by different tissues. • Dense bone absorbs more radiation and appears white; soft tissues appear gray and air appears black. Procedure • Position the body part. • Place it between the X-ray source and detector. • Take the required view, often two views at right angles. • Assess bone alignment, joint spaces, and abnormalities. Common views • AP (anteroposterior), lateral, and oblique views. • Weight-bearing views when clinically indicated. Indications and findings • Fracture: Site, pattern, displacement, and alignment. • Dislocation: Abnormal position of bones at a joint. • Osteoarthritis: Joint-space narrowing, osteophytes, subchondral sclerosis, and sometimes cysts. • Rheumatoid arthritis: Possible erosions, joint-space narrowing, and periarticular osteopenia. • Other: Spinal curvature, later changes of osteomyelitis, and some bone lesions. Advantages • Quick, widely available, and relatively inexpensive. • Good for bone, fractures, dislocations, and alignment. • Useful for monitoring fracture healing. Limitations • Uses ionizing radiation. • Produces two-dimensional images. • Limited soft-tissue detail. • Early disease or subtle fractures may not be visible. • Does not directly show cartilage, ligaments, or tendons well. Physiotherapy importance: Helps identify structural problems, understand alignment and healing, and follow medical precautions for loading and exercise. Conclusion: X-ray is commonly a first-line investigation for suspected bone and joint disorders. Page 6 BPT Physiotherapy Study Notes4. Computed Tomography (CT Scan) Definition: CT is an imaging technique that uses X-rays and computer processing to produce detailed cross-sectional images, with optional 3D reconstructions. In simple words: It combines X-ray information from many angles to show detailed slices of the body. Principle • An X-ray tube rotates around the patient. • Measurements are collected from different angles. • A computer reconstructs cross-sectional images and may create 3D views. Procedure • The patient lies on a motorized table. • The affected part is positioned in the scanner. • The scanner collects X-ray data while rotating. • A computer produces images in different planes. Indications • Complex, comminuted, and intra-articular fractures. • Pelvic, acetabular, calcaneal, and spinal fractures. • Detailed assessment of vertebral and other bony structures. • Bone destruction, abnormal bone formation, and selected tumors. • Preoperative planning and selected image-guided procedures. Advantages • Detailed cross-sectional bone images. • Useful for complex fractures and fracture displacement. • Allows 3D reconstruction. • Helpful for preoperative planning. Limitations • Uses ionizing radiation, generally more than plain X-ray. • Soft-tissue contrast is usually poorer than MRI. • More expensive than X-ray. • Metal implants can cause artifacts. • Some examinations require contrast material. Physiotherapy importance: Helps understand complex fracture patterns and bony involvement, supporting postoperative rehabilitation planning and precautions. Conclusion: CT is particularly useful for complex fractures and detailed bony anatomy. Page 7 BPT Physiotherapy Study Notes5. Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) Definition: MRI uses a strong magnetic field, radiofrequency waves, and computer processing to produce detailed images of body tissues. In simple words: MRI is especially useful for muscles, ligaments, tendons, cartilage, bone marrow, and spinal structures. Principle • Hydrogen nuclei respond to a strong magnetic field. • Radiofrequency pulses change their alignment temporarily. • As they return, they produce signals. • A computer converts these signals into detailed images. Procedure • Screen the patient for MRI safety, including implants and metallic objects. • Position the patient on the MRI table. • Acquire images in different planes and sequences. • Use contrast material only when indicated. Indications • Ligaments: ACL, PCL, collateral ligament, and selected shoulder injuries. • Tendons and muscles: Rotator cuff or Achilles tears, muscle tears, hematomas, and tendinopathy. • Joints: Meniscal tears, cartilage injury, effusion, synovitis, and osteonecrosis. • Spine: Disc herniation, spinal stenosis, nerve-root compression, spinal cord abnormalities, and infection. • Tumors: Extent of bone marrow and surrounding soft-tissue involvement. Possible findings • Ligament or tendon tears. • Muscle injury and cartilage damage. • Bone marrow edema. • Disc herniation or nerve compression. • Soft-tissue masses. Advantages • No ionizing radiation. • Excellent soft-tissue contrast. • Shows bone marrow abnormalities. • Useful for ligaments, tendons, cartilage, and spinal structures. • Images can be obtained in multiple planes. Limitations • Expensive and often takes longer than X-ray or CT. • Claustrophobia may be a problem. • Some implants or metallic foreign bodies need special safety assessment. Page 8 BPT Physiotherapy Study Notes• Movement can reduce image quality. • Some abnormalities also occur in people without symptoms. Physiotherapy importance: Supports assessment of soft-tissue and spinal conditions, helps plan rehabilitation precautions, and may guide referral. MRI findings must be matched with symptoms and examination. Conclusion: MRI is valuable for soft-tissue, bone marrow, and spinal disorders and does not use ionizing radiation.

Compress both radial and ulnar arteries. Patient opens the hand. Release one artery at a time and observe colour return. Positive Sign Delayed or absent return of normal hand colour. Indicates Arterial insufficiency or vascular occlusion. 2. DIGITAL BLOOD FLOW TEST Purpose To assess circulation to the fingers. Procedure • • Compress the fingertip until it blanches. Release the pressure. Positive Sign Delayed capillary refill (>2 seconds). Indicates Reduced peripheral circulation. 3. FIGURE-OF-8 MEASUREMENT Purpose To assess hand and wrist swelling (edema). Procedure • Use a measuring tape in a standardized figure-of-8 pattern around the wrist and hand. Record the measurement. 1 • Positive Finding Increased measurement compared with the opposite side. Indicates Hand or wrist edema. 4. HAND VOLUME TEST Purpose To assess hand edema. Procedure • • Immerse the hand into a volumeter filled with water. Measure the volume of displaced water. Positive Finding Increased displaced volume. Indicates Hand swelling/edema. II. TESTS FOR THORACIC OUTLET SYNDROME 1. ADSON'S TEST Purpose To assess Thoracic Outlet Syndrome (TOS). Procedure • • Palpate the radial pulse. Patient extends the neck, rotates the head toward the tested side, and takes a deep breath. Positive Sign Reduced/absent radial pulse or reproduction of symptoms. Indicates Thoracic Outlet Syndrome. 2. ROOS STRESS TEST (EAST) Purpose To assess Thoracic Outlet Syndrome. Procedure Patient abducts shoulders to 90°, externally rotates them, and flexes elbows to 90°. 2 • Patient repeatedly opens and closes the hands for 3 minutes. Positive Sign Pain, numbness, tingling, heaviness, or inability to continue. Indicates Thoracic Outlet Syndrome.

Definition: Areas of skin supplied by sensory fibers from a single spinal nerve root.
Purpose: Helps identify sensory loss due to nerve root lesions.
Examples:
C6: Thumb.
C7: Middle finger.
C8: Little finger.
L4: Medial side of leg.
L5: Dorsum of foot and great toe.
S1: Lateral side of foot.
Normal: Sensation is intact in the tested dermatome.
5. Myotomes
Definition: Groups of muscles predominantly supplied by a single spinal nerve root.
Purpose: Assesses motor function of spinal nerve roots.
Examples:
C5: Shoulder abduction.
C6: Wrist extension.
C7: Elbow extension.
C8: Finger flexion.
L2: Hip flexion.
L3: Knee extension.
L4: Ankle dorsiflexion.
L5: Great toe extension.
S1: Ankle plantarflexion.
Normal: Full strength, usually 5/5 on MMT.)) ((Assessment of Hand Function
1. Hand Pinches
Definition: Holding an object between the thumb and fingers.
Types: Tip-to-tip, lateral pinch, three-jaw chuck pinch.
Assessment: Pinch gauge.
Example: Holding a key or picking up a coin.
2. Hand Grip
Definition: Ability to grasp and hold objects using the hand.
Types: Power grip and precision grip.
Assessment: Hand dynamometer.
Normal: Adequate grip strength for daily activities.
Example: Holding a bottle or squeezing a ball.
3. Routine Sensory-Motor Evaluation
Definition: Assessment of sensory and motor functions of the hand.
Motor assessment: Muscle strength, grip, pinch, thumb opposition and finger movements.
Sensory assessment: Light touch, pain, temperature, vibration and joint position sense.
Normal: Intact sensation, normal strength and coordinated movements.
Example: Weak thumb opposition may indicate median nerve involvement.
4. Stereognosis
Definition: Ability to identify an object by touch without seeing it.
Assessment: Patient identifies an object with eyes closed.
Normal: Correct identification of objects.
Example: Identifying a coin or key by touch.
Abnormal: Inability to recognize an object by touch is called astereognosis.))//////Cardiovascular and Pulmonary dysfunction —Symmetry/Deformities of Head, Neck, Extremities, Trophic changes. Examination of cough, sputum, tactile and vocal fremitus, mobility of thoracic spine and rib cage, percussion etc.((1. Auscultation
Definition: Listening to internal body sounds using a stethoscope.
Normal heart sounds:
S1: Closure of mitral and tricuspid valves, heard as “lub.”
S2: Closure of aortic and pulmonary valves, heard as “dub.”
Normal heart rate: 60–100 beats/minute in adults.
Abnormal heart sounds:
Murmur: Abnormal sound due to turbulent blood flow.
S3: May be normal in young adults but can indicate heart failure.
S4: May occur with reduced ventricular compliance.
Normal breath sounds:
Vesicular: Soft, low-pitched sounds over most lung fields.
Bronchial: Heard normally over the trachea.
Bronchovesicular: Heard near the major bronchi.
Abnormal breath sounds:
Crackles: Popping sounds, e.g., pulmonary edema or pneumonia.
Wheeze: Musical sound, e.g., asthma.
Rhonchi: Low-pitched sounds due to airway secretions.
Stridor: Harsh sound due to upper airway obstruction.
Reduced or absent breath sounds: May occur with pneumothorax or pleural effusion.
2. Chest Expansion
Definition: Measurement of the increase in chest circumference during inspiration.
Method: Measure chest circumference during maximal expiration and inspiration using a measuring tape.
Common sites: Axillary, nipple line and xiphisternal level.
Normal: Approximately 3–5 cm in healthy adults, depending on age and measurement site.
Example: Reduced chest expansion in COPD.
3. Symmetry of Chest Movement
Definition: Assessment of equal movement of both sides of the chest during breathing.
Method: Observe chest movement or place hands symmetrically over the chest.
Normal: Both sides expand equally during inspiration.
Abnormal: Unequal chest expansion.
Example: Reduced movement on one side in pleural effusion or pneumothorax.
4. Body Mass Index (BMI)
Definition: Measurement of body weight in relation to height.
Formula: BMI = Weight (kg) ÷ Height (m²).
Normal adult BMI (WHO): 18.5–24.9 kg/m².
Example: Weight 60 kg, height 1.65 m, BMI = 22.0 kg/m².
5. Waist–Hip Ratio (WHR)
Definition: Ratio of waist circumference to hip circumference.
Formula: WHR = Waist circumference ÷ Hip circumference.
Normal reference values (WHO):
Men: ≤0.90
Women: ≤0.85
Example: Waist 80 cm, hip 100 cm, WHR = 0.80.
Purpose: Assesses abdominal fat distribution and associated health risk.))
