1. Neck Disability Index (NDI)
• Definition and Overview
• Developed by Howard Vernon and Silvano Mior in 1991 as a modification of the Oswestry Low Back Pain Disability Questionnaire.
• It is a patient-reported, condition-specific outcome measure designed to quantify self-rated disability and functional limitation in patients experiencing acute, subacute, or chronic neck pain (including cervical spondylosis, radiculopathy, and whiplash-associated disorders).

• Structure and Clinical Domains
• Comprises 10 itemized sections evaluating physical daily activities and symptom impact:
• Pain Intensity (severity of baseline cervical aching/pain)
• Personal Care (washing, dressing, grooming without exacerbating symptoms)
• Lifting (handling light, medium, or heavy objects)
• Reading (sustained cervical flexion/postural tolerance)
• Headaches (frequency and duration of cervicogenic headaches)
• Concentration (ability to focus on cognitive tasks)
• Work (ability to perform occupational duties)
• Driving (head turning, blind-spot checks, postural endurance)
• Sleeping (sleep disruption due to neck symptoms)
• Recreation (participation in hobbies, sports, and leisure)

• Scoring Methodology and Formula
• Each of the 10 sections is rated on a 6-point ordinal scale ranging from 0 (no limitation/no pain) to 5 (complete limitation/worst pain).
• Maximum possible raw score = 50 (when all 10 sections are completed).
• If all 10 sections are answered:
• Percentage Disability = (Total Raw Score / 50) x 100
• Handling missing sections (e.g., patient does not drive):
• Minimum completed sections required for validity: 9 out of 10.
• Percentage Disability = (Total Raw Score / (5 x Number of completed sections)) x 100

• Score Interpretation
• 0 to 4 points (0% to 8%): No disability
• 5 to 14 points (10% to 28%): Mild functional disability
• 15 to 24 points (30% to 48%): Moderate functional disability
• 25 to 34 points (50% to 68%): Severe functional disability
• 35 to 50 points (70% to 100%): Complete functional disability / bedbound

• Relevance in Physiotherapy Practice
• Used as an objective baseline on day one of rehabilitation to establish functional limitations.
• Guides goal setting (e.g., progressing a patient from moderate to mild disability).
• Provides documentation required by clinical audits to substantiate continued manual therapy, cervical stabilization exercises, or postural re-education.

• Clinical Limitations
• Possesses a ceiling effect in elite athletes and high-demand physical workers who experience pain during high-velocity activities not captured by basic ADL questions.
• Section 8 (Driving) is frequently omitted by non-drivers, requiring re-calculation of the maximum denominator.

2. Shoulder Pain and Disability Index (SPADI)
• Definition and Overview
• Developed by Kathryn Roach and colleagues in 1991.
• A shoulder-specific, self-administered questionnaire designed to evaluate pain severity and functional disability caused by musculoskeletal pathologies of the shoulder complex (e.g., rotator cuff tendinopathy, subacromial impingement syndrome, adhesive capsulitis, and glenohumeral osteoarthritis).

• Structure and Components
• Consists of 13 total items grouped into 2 distinct subscales:
• Pain Subscale (5 items):
• How severe is your pain at its worst?
• How severe is your pain when lying on the involved side?
• How severe is your pain when reaching for something on a high shelf?
• How severe is your pain when touching the back of your neck?
• How severe is your pain when pushing with the involved arm?
• Disability Subscale (8 items):
• Washing your hair
• Washing your back
• Putting on an undershirt or jumper
• Putting on a shirt that buttons down the front
• Putting on your pants
• Placing an object on a high shelf
• Carrying a heavy object of 10 pounds (4.5 kg)
• Removing something from your back pocket

• Scoring Methodology and Calculation
• Scored using either a Visual Analogue Scale (VAS, 0 to 10 cm) or a Numeric Rating Scale (NRS, 0 to 10).
• 0 indicates "no pain / no difficulty"; 10 indicates "worst pain imaginable / so difficult that help was required."
• Subscale calculations:
• Pain Score (%) = (Sum of pain subscale items / 50) x 100
• Disability Score (%) = (Sum of disability subscale items / 80) x 100
• Total SPADI Score:
• Total SPADI (%) = (Sum of all 13 item scores / 130) x 100
• If items are skipped/omitted:
• Total SPADI (%) = (Total points scored / (10 x Number of items answered)) x 100

• Score Interpretation
• 0%: Best score, indicating completely normal function without shoulder pain.
• 100%: Worst score, indicating complete functional loss and severe, intractable pain.
• A reduction in percentage indicates clinical functional improvement.

• Relevance in Physiotherapy Practice
• Allows the therapist to distinguish whether a patient's primary impairment is pain-dominant (acute stage) or disability-dominant (chronic or adhesive stage), directly modifying treatment choices (e.g., modalities vs. aggressive mobilization).
• Takes less than 5 minutes for the patient to complete, making it ideal for busy outpatient clinics.

• Clinical Limitations
• Does not address high-level athletic performance, throwing mechanics, or overhead sports participation.
• Focuses solely on unilateral symptoms; less sensitive if bilateral shoulder dysfunction exists.

3. Disabilities of the Arm, Shoulder and Hand (DASH)
• Definition and Overview
• Developed in 1996 jointly by the Institute for Work & Health (IWH) and the American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons (AAOS).
• A comprehensive 30-item, upper-extremity-specific regional outcome tool designed to measure physical disability and symptoms across any single joint or combination of joints along the entire upper extremity kinetic chain (shoulder, elbow, wrist, and hand).

• Structure and Domains
• Comprises 30 mandatory core items covering three primary clinical domains:
• Degree of physical difficulty in performing gross and fine motor tasks (21 items, such as opening a tight jar, writing, turning a key, preparing a meal, pushing open a heavy door, carrying a briefcase, washing back, changing a lightbulb).
• Severity of clinical symptoms (5 items assessing pain intensity, activity-related pain, tingling/pins and needles, weakness, and joint stiffness).
• Psychosocial and occupational impact (4 items assessing social activities, work performance, sleep disturbance, and emotional impact/confidence).
• Optional Modules (4 items each):
• Work Module (for workers whose upper limb issues impact heavy or repetitive tasks).
• Sports / Performing Arts Module (for athletes, musicians, and performers).

• Scoring System and Formula
• Each of the 30 items is scored on a 5-point Likert scale:
• 1 = No difficulty / No symptom
• 2 = Mild difficulty / Mild symptom
• 3 = Moderate difficulty / Moderate symptom
• 4 = Severe difficulty / Severe symptom
• 5 = Unable to do / Extreme symptom
• Rule for missing data: At least 27 of the 30 items (90%) must be completed to compute a valid score.
• Formula for Core DASH:
• DASH Score = [((Sum of n responses) / n) - 1] x 25
• Where n is the number of completed items.
• Optional Modules Scoring:
• Scored independently using an identical mathematical formula to produce a separate score out of 100.

• Score Interpretation
• 0 = No disability (optimal upper limb performance).
• 100 = Maximum upper limb disability and severe symptoms.
• A lower score reflects improved clinical status.

• Relevance in Physiotherapy Practice
• Captures kinetic chain dysfunction (e.g., how a wrist fracture alters shoulder kinematics and daily upper-limb capacity).
• Enables standardized comparison between different upper quarter diagnoses under the same rehabilitation program.

• Clinical Limitations
• The 30-item core questionnaire can be time-consuming for elderly or fatigued patients (which led to the creation of the 11-item QuickDASH).
• Does not discriminate which specific anatomical joint of the arm is the primary pain generator.

4. Oswestry Disability Index (ODI)
• Definition and Overview
• Developed by John O’Brien and Jeremy Fairbank in 1980 (often referred to as the Oswestry Low Back Pain Questionnaire).
• Widely accepted as the international "gold standard" condition-specific patient-reported outcome measure for determining permanent or functional disability in acute and chronic low back pain (LBP), lumbar disc herniations, spinal canal stenosis, and post-lumbar fusion surgeries.

• Structure and Clinical Domains
• Composed of 10 clinical sections, each addressing a critical daily life domain impacted by lumbar pathology:
• Section 1: Pain Intensity
• Section 2: Personal Care (washing, dressing)
• Section 3: Lifting
• Section 4: Walking
• Section 5: Sitting
• Section 6: Standing
• Section 7: Sleeping
• Section 8: Sex Life (if applicable/acceptable to patient)
• Section 9: Social Life
• Section 10: Travelling

• Scoring Methodology and Calculation
• Each section contains 6 statements scored from 0 to 5:
• 0 indicates the least limitation or no pain.
• 5 indicates the greatest functional restriction or maximum pain.
• Maximum possible raw score = 50 (if all 10 sections are completed).
• Calculation when all sections are answered:
• ODI Percentage (%) = (Total Raw Score / 50) x 100
• Calculation when Section 8 (Sex Life) is omitted:
• ODI Percentage (%) = (Total Raw Score / 45) x 100

• Score Interpretation and Clinical Grading
• 0% to 20% (Minimal Disability): The patient can cope with most living activities. Treatment usually centers on ergonomics, core stabilization, and general fitness.
• 21% to 40% (Moderate Disability): The patient experiences pain with sitting, lifting, and standing. Conservative management (manual therapy, electrotherapy, active directional preference exercises) is indicated.
• 41% to 60% (Severe Disability): Pain remains the main problem; activities of daily living are significantly disrupted. Requires detailed diagnostic evaluation and structured intervention.
• 61% to 80% (Crippled): Back pain impinges on all aspects of the patient's life. Intervention requires advanced pain management, multidisciplinary care, or surgical consultation.
• 81% to 100% (Bedbound or Symptom Exaggeration): These patients are either completely bedridden or exaggerating their symptoms (requires screening for non-organic signs/Waddell signs).

• Relevance in Physiotherapy Practice
• Establishes functional baseline and tracks progress over weeks of lumbar core strengthening, McKenzie extension, or motor control stabilization.
• Serves as standard legal and disability documentation for return-to-work evaluations and medicolegal reporting.

• Clinical Limitations
• Patients from conservative cultures frequently leave the "Sex Life" section blank, necessitating manual formula adjustments.

1: 1. Blood Investigations and Cardiac Biomarkers
2: Definition
3: Blood investigations and biomarkers are laboratory tests performed on venous or arterial blood samples to evaluate organ function, systemic inflammation, hematological balance, and myocardial cellular damage or heart failure.
4: Key Cardiac and Hematological Markers
5: Cardiac Troponins (cTnI and cTnT):
6: Gold standard regulatory contractile proteins released exclusively upon cardiomyocyte necrosis.
7: Normal Value: cTnI is less than 0.04 ng/mL; high-sensitivity troponin (hs-cTn) is less than 14 ng/L.
8: Timeline: Rises within 3 to 4 hours post-myocardial injury, peaks at 18 to 24 hours, and remains elevated for 10 to 14 days.
9: Clinical Significance: Confirms Acute Myocardial Infarction (AMI); determines the extent of myocardial necrosis.
10: Creatine Kinase-MB (CK-MB):
11: Isoenzyme localized primarily in cardiac muscle tissue.
12: Normal Value: Less than 5% of total CK or 0 to 5 ng/mL.
13: Timeline: Rises within 4 to 6 hours, peaks at 18 to 24 hours, and normalizes within 48 to 72 hours.
14: Clinical Significance: Useful for detecting early re-infarction because it clears much faster than troponin.
15: B-Type Natriuretic Peptide (BNP and NT-proBNP):
16: Neurohormone secreted by ventricular myocytes in response to increased ventricular wall stretch and volume overload.
17: Normal Value: BNP is less than 100 pg/mL; NT-proBNP is less than 300 pg/mL.
18: Clinical Significance: Distinguishes dyspnea caused by congestive heart failure (elevated levels) from dyspnea of primary pulmonary origin.
19: Complete Blood Count (CBC) and Hemoglobin (Hb):
20: Normal Hemoglobin: 13 to 17 g/dL for males; 12 to 15 g/dL for females.
21: Clinical Significance: Anemia (Hb less than 8 g/dL) drastically impairs peripheral oxygen delivery, causing resting tachycardia, fatigue, and reduced exercise tolerance.
22: Inflammatory Markers (CRP and ESR):
23: High-Sensitivity C-Reactive Protein (hs-CRP): Values greater than 3.0 mg/L reflect systemic inflammation and elevated atherothrombotic risk.
24: Erythrocyte Sedimentation Rate (ESR): Elevated in pericarditis, infective endocarditis, and chronic pulmonary infections.
25: Coagulation Profile (D-Dimer, PT, INR):
26: D-Dimer: Normal is less than 500 ng/mL; elevated levels indicate active fibrinolysis and raise suspicion for deep vein thrombosis (DVT) or pulmonary embolism (PE).
27: International Normalized Ratio (INR): Normal is 0.8 to 1.2; therapeutic range for anticoagulated patients is 2.0 to 3.0.
28: Physiotherapy Implications and Exercise Precautions
29: Active myocardial infarction with progressively rising troponin levels is an absolute contraindication to physical therapy exercise.
30: Ambulation or phase I cardiac rehabilitation is deferred until cardiac enzymes peak and decline, and the patient remains hemodynamically stable for 24 hours.
31: If Hemoglobin is less than 8 g/dL, postpone active resistance training; limit interventions to gentle bedside bed-mobility or assisted transfers.
32: If INR is greater than 3.5, avoid vigorous chest physiotherapy, manual percussions, aggressive stretching, or high-impact mobilizations due to internal bleeding and hematoma risk.
33: Severely elevated BNP indicates decompensated heart failure; fluid overload requires avoiding head-down postural drainage and minimizing cardiovascular exertion.
34: 2. Arterial Blood Gas (ABG) Analysis
35: Definition
36: ABG analysis is an invasive diagnostic measurement of arterial blood assessing systemic oxygenation, alveolar ventilation, and metabolic or respiratory acid-base balance.
37: Standard Arterial Parameters and Reference Ranges
38: pH: 7.35 to 7.45 (indicates systemic hydrogen ion concentration).
39: PaCO2 (Partial pressure of arterial carbon dioxide): 35 to 45 mmHg (respiratory/ventilatory component).
40: PaO2 (Partial pressure of arterial oxygen): 80 to 100 mmHg on room air (arterial oxygenation status).
41: HCO3- (Bicarbonate concentration): 22 to 26 mEq/L (metabolic/renal component).
42: Base Excess (BE): -2 to +2 mEq/L (amount of buffer required to restore normal pH).
43: SaO2 (Arterial oxygen saturation): 95% to 100%.
44: Systematic Steps for ABG Interpretation
45: Step 1 (Check pH): A pH less than 7.35 indicates acidemia; a pH greater than 7.45 indicates alkalemia.
46: Step 2 (Check PaCO2): If altered in the direction opposite to pH (low pH with high PaCO2), the primary disorder is respiratory.
47: Step 3 (Check HCO3-): If altered in the same direction as pH (low pH with low HCO3-), the primary disorder is metabolic.
48: Step 4 (Determine Compensation):
49: Uncompensated: Abnormal pH, one component abnormal, other component normal.
50: Partially Compensated: Abnormal pH, both PaCO2 and HCO3- abnormal in the same compensatory direction.
51: Fully Compensated: Normal pH (within 7.35 to 7.45), but both PaCO2 and HCO3- remain abnormal.
52: Common Pathological Patterns
53: Respiratory Acidosis (pH less than 7.35, PaCO2 greater than 45 mmHg):
54: Causes: Alveolar hypoventilation, severe COPD, respiratory muscle fatigue, central nervous system depression, Guillain-Barré syndrome.
55: Respiratory Alkalosis (pH greater than 7.45, PaCO2 less than 35 mmHg):
56: Causes: Hyperventilation secondary to anxiety, hypoxemia, acute pulmonary embolism, severe pain.
57: Metabolic Acidosis (pH less than 7.35, HCO3- less than 22 mEq/L):
58: Causes: Diabetic ketoacidosis, lactic acidosis from septic or cardiogenic shock, chronic renal failure.
59: Metabolic Alkalosis (pH greater than 7.45, HCO3- greater than 26 mEq/L):
60: Causes: Prolonged vomiting, high-dose diuretic administration, severe hypokalemia.
61: Physiotherapy Significance
62: Identifies type I respiratory failure (hypoxemic: PaO2 less than 60 mmHg with normal/low PaCO2) vs. type II respiratory failure (hypercapnic: PaCO2 greater than 50 mmHg with acidosis).
63: Guides non-invasive ventilation (BiPAP) and aggressive airway clearance techniques for hypercapnic retained secretions in COPD.

69: Key Spirometric Parameters
70: Tidal Volume (TV): Normal volume inspired or expired during quiet breathing (~500 mL).
71: Vital Capacity (VC) / Forced Vital Capacity (FVC): Maximum volume of air exhaled forcefully following maximal inspiration (normal is greater than 80% predicted).
72: Forced Expiratory Volume in 1 Second (FEV1): Volume exhaled during the first second of an FVC maneuver (normal is greater than 80% predicted).
73: FEV1/FVC Ratio: Proportion of total vital capacity cleared in the first second; normal reference is 70% to 85% (0.70 to 0.85).
74: Peak Expiratory Flow Rate (PEFR): Maximum flow velocity reached during forced expiration; monitored in asthma management.
75: Diffusing Capacity of the Lungs for Carbon Monoxide (DLCO): Assesses alveolar-capillary membrane gas transfer (normal is greater than 75% predicted).

78: Characterized by expiratory flow limitation and increased airway resistance.
79: Criteria: FEV1/FVC ratio is less than 0.70 (70%); FEV1 is reduced; FVC may be normal or reduced; Total Lung Capacity (TLC) and Residual Volume (RV) are elevated due to air trapping and hyperinflation.

86: Extrinsic Causes: Kyphoscoliosis, ankylosing spondylitis, diaphragmatic paralysis, obesity hypoventilation syndrome.

93: In restrictive disease: Focus on inspiratory capacity enhancement, thoracic expansion exercises, incentive spirometry, and rib cage mobilization.

96: Definition
97: An electrocardiogram is a surface recording of the electrical potentials generated by cardiac muscle depolarization and repolarization over time, recorded via a standard 12-lead electrode configuration.
98: Normal ECG Deflections, Intervals, and Values
99: P Wave: Atrial depolarization; normal duration is less than 0.12 seconds (3 small boxes), amplitude is less than 2.5 mm.
100: PR Interval: Conduction travel time from the sinoatrial node through the AV node to ventricles; normal duration is 0.12 to 0.20 seconds (3 to 5 small boxes).
101: QRS Complex: Ventricular depolarization; normal duration is 0.06 to 0.10 seconds (less than 3 small boxes).
102: ST Segment: Interval between ventricular depolarization and repolarization; normally sits flat on the isoelectric baseline.
103: T Wave: Ventricular repolarization; smooth, asymmetrical deflection oriented in the same general direction as the main QRS deflection.

220: 0.41 to 0.90: Mild-to-moderate PAD (characteristic intermittent claudication during walking).

## BPT 3rd Year | 5-Mark University Exam Answers

- Definition: Sports-specific assessment is the systematic evaluation of an athlete’s physical fitness, functional abilities and performance-related components required for a particular sport.
- Purpose:
  - To assess fitness and sports performance.
  - To identify strengths and weaknesses.
  - To detect physical limitations and injury risk factors.
  - To monitor training progress and recovery.
  - To help plan individualized sports training and rehabilitation.

## 1. Cardiovascular Endurance

- Definition: Ability of the cardiovascular and respiratory systems to supply oxygen to working muscles during prolonged exercise.
- Purpose: To assess aerobic fitness and endurance capacity.
- Assessment tests:
  - Cooper 12-minute run test.
  - 20-metre multistage shuttle run test (Beep test).
  - 6-minute walk test.
- Parameters: Distance covered, heart rate, respiratory rate and recovery time.
- Example: Beep test for football players.

## 2. Muscular Strength

- Definition: Ability of a muscle or muscle group to produce maximum force against resistance.
- Purpose: To assess muscle force required for sports activities.
- Assessment tests:
  - One-repetition maximum (1RM) test.
  - Handgrip dynamometer test.
  - Isometric strength testing.
- Parameters: Maximum force produced and side-to-side differences.
- Example: 1RM squat test for weightlifters.

## 3. Flexibility

- Definition: Ability of a joint to move through its available range of motion.
- Purpose: To assess joint mobility and muscle flexibility required for sports movements.
- Assessment tests:
  - Sit-and-reach test.
  - Goniometric measurement.
  - Straight leg raise test.
- Parameters: Range of motion and muscle length.
- Example: Sit-and-reach test for gymnasts.

## 4. Speed

- Definition: Ability to perform a movement or cover a distance in the shortest possible time.
- Purpose: To assess rapid movement and sprinting ability.
- Assessment tests:
  - 30-metre sprint test.
  - 40-metre sprint test.
  - 10-metre sprint test.
- Parameters: Time taken to complete the distance.
- Example: 30-metre sprint test for sprinters and football players.

## 5. Agility

- Definition: Ability to change body direction rapidly and efficiently while maintaining balance and control.
- Purpose: To assess quick directional changes during sports activities.
- Assessment tests:
  - T-test.
  - Illinois agility test.
  - 505 agility test.
- Parameters: Time taken, movement control and directional changes.
- Example: T-test for basketball players.

## 6. Power

- Definition: Ability to produce maximum force in minimum time. Power is the product of force and velocity.
- Purpose: To assess explosive muscular performance.
- Assessment tests:
  - Vertical jump test.
  - Standing broad jump test.
  - Medicine ball throw test.
- Parameters: Jump height, distance or throwing distance.
- Example: Vertical jump test for volleyball players.

## 7. Balance

- Definition: Ability to maintain the body's centre of mass over its base of support.
- Types: Static balance and dynamic balance.
- Purpose: To assess postural control and stability during sports activities.
- Assessment tests:
  - Single-leg stance test.
  - Y-Balance test.
  - Star Excursion Balance Test (SEBT).
- Parameters: Time maintained, reach distance and postural stability.
- Example: Y-Balance test for football players.

## 8. Coordination

- Definition: Ability to perform smooth, accurate and controlled movements using different body parts.
- Purpose: To assess neuromuscular control and the integration of movements.
- Assessment tests:
  - Alternate hand wall-toss test.
  - Finger-to-nose test.
  - Alternate hand-foot tapping test.
- Parameters: Accuracy, timing, rhythm and movement smoothness.
- Example: Wall-toss test for tennis players.

## 9. Reaction Time

- Definition: Time taken to respond to a stimulus after it is presented.
- Types: Simple reaction time and choice reaction time.
- Purpose: To assess the speed of response to visual or auditory stimuli.
- Assessment tests:
  - Ruler drop test.
  - Computerized reaction-time test.
  - Sport-specific stimulus-response test.
- Parameters: Time taken to respond, usually measured in milliseconds.
- Example: Reaction-time test for a sprinter responding to the starting signal.

## References

- ACSM’s Guidelines for Exercise Testing and Prescription.
- Physiology of Sport and Exercise (Kenney, Wilmore and Costill).

**Types of Pain**

* **Somatic Pain:**
  * Arises from noxious stimulation of musculoskeletal, cutaneous, and deep somatic structures.
  * *Superficial Somatic:* Originates in skin or subcutaneous tissues; sharp, pricking, well-localized with clearly defined boundaries.
  * *Deep Somatic:* Originates in muscles, tendons, ligaments, periosteum, and joint capsules; dull, aching, poorly localized, and tends to refer to related sclerotomal structures.
* **Somatic Referred Pain:**
  * Pain perceived at a site distant from the actual primary site of somatic injury or dysfunction (e.g., cervical facet joint dysfunction referring into the shoulder girdle).
  * Follows an embryological segmental or sclerotomal pattern without mechanical irritation or compression of neural tissue.
  * Characterized by a diffuse, deep ache with no primary neurological signs (normal reflexes, sensation, and motor power).
* **Neurogenic (Neuropathic) Pain:**
  * Initiated or caused by a primary lesion, dysfunction, or mechanical irritation of the peripheral or central nervous system.
  * Described as sharp, shooting, lancinating, burning, stabbing, or electric shock-like sensations.
  * Follows discrete anatomical distributions (dermatomal tracts or peripheral nerve distributions) and frequently presents with positive or negative neurological symptoms (paresthesia, hyperalgesia, allodynia, hypesthesia, motor deficits).
* **Visceral Pain:**
  * Arises from the distension, ischemia, spasm, or inflammation of internal organs (thoracic, abdominal, or pelvic).
  * Poorly localized, deep, sickening, dull, and cramp-like.
  * Frequently accompanied by autonomic manifestations (nausea, diaphoresis, pallor, blood pressure changes) and visceral-somatic referral patterns (e.g., myocardial ischemia referring to the jaw/left arm; gallbladder referral to the right inferior scapular region).

**Subjective Assessment of Pain**

* **Location:**
  * Pinpointing the exact anatomical site and boundary using a standardized body chart; distinguishing localized pain from widespread or multi-site pain.
* **Duration:**
  * Timeframe since the onset of symptoms:
    * *Acute:* Less than 6 weeks (direct relation to tissue injury and healing).
    * *Subacute:* 6 to 12 weeks.
    * *Chronic / Persistent:* Greater than 3 to 6 months (outlasting normal physiological healing time).
* **Progression:**
  * The chronological course of the pain over time (improving, worsening, static, intermittent, episodic, or recurrent).
* **Distribution:**
  * Spatial pattern of symptoms (focal, segmental/sclerotomal, radiating along a dermatomal/peripheral nerve track, or non-anatomical/diffuse).
* **Quality:**
  * Subjective descriptive character of the sensation (e.g., sharp, dull ache, burning, throbbing, heavy, stabbing), indicating the underlying tissue source and neurophysiological mechanism.
* **Diurnal Variations:**
  * Behavior of symptoms across a 24-hour day-night cycle:
    * *Morning:* Stiffness and pain lasting more than 30 to 60 minutes points to inflammatory etiology (e.g., rheumatoid arthritis).
    * *Evening / End of day:* Pain aggravated by weight-bearing and activity points to mechanical or degenerative etiology (e.g., osteoarthritis).
    * *Night:* Constant, unremitting pain waking the patient from sound sleep is a clinical red flag requiring evaluation for non-mechanical pathology (e.g., malignancy, infection).
* **Modifying Factors:**
  * *Aggravating Factors:* Positions, functional movements, postures, or sustained loads that provoke or intensify the pain.
  * *Easing Factors:* Positions of relief, rest, thermal modalities, or medications that alleviate the pain.
* **Severity:**
  * Magnitude or intensity of the pain, assessed at present, at its best, and at its worst over a defined period (e.g., last 24 hours).
* **Nature of Pain:**
  * Underlying clinical mechanism generating the symptoms:
    * *Mechanical:* Pain varies predictably with physical loads, movements, and rest.
    * *Inflammatory:* Constant aching, marked morning stiffness, warmth, throbbing, eased slightly by gentle movement.
    * *Neuropathic:* Radicular, burning, electric sensations with neurosensory deficits.
    * *Nociplastic / Central Sensitization:* Disproportionate pain intensity with hypersensitivity and non-mechanical triggers.
* **Tissue Irritability:**
  * Clinical concept (Maitland) determining how easily symptoms are provoked and how readily they settle, dictating safe physical examination depth and treatment vigor:
    * *Vigor/Threshold:* The amount and intensity of activity required to bring on the pain.
    * *Severity:* The peak intensity of the provoked pain.
    * *Latency / Time to Ease:* The time required for pain to return to baseline once the provoking activity stops.
    * *Triage:* **High irritability** (provoked easily, severe, long time to ease; requires gentle handling); **Moderate irritability** (moderate load needed, moderate intensity, eases in minutes); **Low irritability** (high load required, mild pain, eases immediately).

**Objective Measurement & Documentation**

* **Visual Analogue Scale (V.A.S):**
  * *Format:* A continuous, horizontal, unnumbered line exactly 100 mm (10 cm) in length.
  * *Anchors:* Clearly demarcated endpoints labeled "No pain" (0 mm) at the left and "Worst pain imaginable" (100 mm) at the right.
  * *Administration:* The patient marks a single vertical tick across the line representing their current or peak pain level.
  * *Measurement & Documentation:* Measured with a millimeter ruler from the left anchor to the patient's mark; documented as a continuous value from 0 to 100 mm (or 0 to 10 cm). Highly sensitive to small clinical changes.
* **Numerical Rating Scale (N.R.S.):**

# Investigations for Musculoskeletal Disorders

**BPT 3rd Year | University Examination Notes**

## 1. Blood Investigations and Markers

### Definition
- Blood investigations are laboratory tests performed to identify inflammation, infection, autoimmune disorders, metabolic bone diseases and other abnormalities affecting the musculoskeletal system.

### A. Complete Blood Count (CBC)
- **Definition:** A blood test that measures red blood cells, white blood cells and platelets.
- **Purpose:**
  - To detect infection and inflammation.
  - To identify anemia associated with chronic diseases.
- **Important findings:**
  - Increased WBC count: May indicate infection.
  - Decreased hemoglobin: Indicates anemia.
  - Increased platelet count: May occur in inflammatory conditions.

### B. Erythrocyte Sedimentation Rate (ESR)
- **Definition:** A test that measures the rate at which red blood cells settle in a tube over one hour.
- **Purpose:**
  - To detect inflammation in the body.
  - To help assess inflammatory and infectious musculoskeletal disorders.
- **Increased ESR may be seen in:**
  - Rheumatoid arthritis.
  - Osteomyelitis.
  - Septic arthritis.
  - Polymyalgia rheumatica.

### C. C-Reactive Protein (CRP)
- **Definition:** A protein produced by the liver in response to inflammation.
- **Purpose:**
  - To detect acute inflammation.
  - To monitor disease activity and response to treatment.
- **Increased CRP may be seen in:**
  - Rheumatoid arthritis.
  - Septic arthritis.
  - Osteomyelitis.
  - Other infections and inflammatory conditions.

### D. Rheumatoid Factor (RF)
- **Definition:** An autoantibody commonly associated with rheumatoid arthritis.
- **Purpose:**
  - To support the diagnosis of rheumatoid arthritis.
- **Positive RF may be seen in:**
  - Rheumatoid arthritis.
  - Other autoimmune diseases.
  - Some chronic infections.
- **Note:** A positive RF alone does not confirm rheumatoid arthritis.

### E. Anti-Cyclic Citrullinated Peptide (Anti-CCP)
- **Definition:** An antibody test used to help diagnose rheumatoid arthritis.
- **Purpose:**
  - To support early diagnosis of rheumatoid arthritis.
  - To help identify patients at risk of more severe joint damage.
- **Important point:** Anti-CCP is relatively specific for rheumatoid arthritis.

### F. Serum Uric Acid
- **Definition:** A blood test that measures the level of uric acid in the blood.
- **Purpose:**
  - To support the evaluation of gout.
- **Increased uric acid may be seen in:**
  - Gout.
  - Hyperuricemia.
- **Note:** A normal uric acid level does not rule out an acute gout attack.

### G. Serum Calcium and Phosphorus
- **Definition:** Tests that measure calcium and phosphate levels in the blood.
- **Purpose:**
  - To assess bone mineral metabolism.
  - To investigate metabolic bone disorders.
- **Abnormal levels may be seen in:**
  - Osteomalacia.
  - Rickets.
  - Hyperparathyroidism.
  - Chronic kidney disease.

### H. Alkaline Phosphatase (ALP)
- **Definition:** An enzyme found mainly in the liver and bones.
- **Purpose:**
  - To assess bone formation and bone metabolism.
- **Increased ALP may be seen in:**
  - Paget's disease of bone.
  - Osteomalacia.
  - Healing fractures.
  - Increased bone turnover.

### I. Vitamin D Level
- **Definition:** A blood test that measures 25-hydroxyvitamin D.
- **Purpose:**
  - To assess vitamin D status.
  - To investigate metabolic bone diseases.
- **Low vitamin D may be associated with:**
  - Osteomalacia.
  - Rickets.
  - Reduced bone mineralization.

### J. Antinuclear Antibody (ANA)
- **Definition:** A test that detects antibodies directed against components of the cell nucleus.
- **Purpose:**
  - To help investigate systemic autoimmune diseases.
- **Positive ANA may be seen in:**
  - Systemic lupus erythematosus.
  - Other connective tissue diseases.

### K. HLA-B27
- **Definition:** A blood test that detects the HLA-B27 genetic marker.
- **Purpose:**
  - To support the diagnosis of spondyloarthritis.
- **Associated conditions:**
  - Ankylosing spondylitis.
  - Reactive arthritis.
  - Other forms of spondyloarthritis.
- **Note:** A positive result alone does not confirm the disease.

### L. Creatine Kinase (CK)

- **Definition:** An enzyme found mainly in skeletal muscles, heart and brain.
- **Purpose:**
  - To detect muscle damage.
  - To investigate muscle diseases.
- **Increased CK may be seen in:**
  - Muscular dystrophy.
  - Myositis.
  - Muscle injury.
  - Rhabdomyolysis.

### M. Other Important Blood Investigations

- **Serum creatinine:** Assesses kidney function, especially before certain medications and contrast investigations.
- **Blood glucose:** Helps assess diabetes, which may affect musculoskeletal healing.
- **Blood cultures:** Help identify the causative organism in suspected bone or joint infections.

---

## 2. Radiological and Imaging Investigations

### A. X-ray (Plain Radiography)

- **Definition:** An imaging technique that uses X-rays to produce images of bones and joints.
- **Principle:** X-rays pass through body tissues and are absorbed differently by different structures.
- **Indications:**
  - To detect fractures and dislocations.
  - To assess bone alignment and deformities.
  - To identify joint space narrowing.
  - To detect bone tumors and degenerative changes.
- **Advantages:**
  - Quick and widely available.
  - Relatively inexpensive.
  - Useful for initial assessment of bone injuries.
- **Limitations:**
  - Poor visualization of muscles, ligaments and tendons.
  - Uses ionizing radiation.
  - Early bone and soft-tissue abnormalities may not be visible.

### B. Computed Tomography (CT Scan)

- **Definition:** A diagnostic imaging technique that uses X-rays and computer processing to produce cross-sectional images of the body.
- **Principle:** Multiple X-ray images are obtained from different angles and reconstructed into detailed cross-sectional or 3D images.
- **Indications:**
  - To assess complex fractures.
  - To detect small bone fragments.
  - To evaluate spinal fractures.
  - To assess bone tumors.
  - To assist in preoperative planning.
- **Advantages:**
  - Provides detailed images of bones.
  - Helps assess complex fractures.
  - Can produce 3D images.
- **Limitations:**
  - Uses ionizing radiation.
  - Less effective than MRI for many soft-tissue injuries.
  - May require contrast in selected investigations.

### C. Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI)

- **Definition:** An imaging technique that uses a strong magnetic field and radio waves to produce detailed images of body structures.
- **Principle:** It detects signals from hydrogen nuclei in body tissues and converts them into detailed images.
- **Indications:**
  - To detect ligament and tendon injuries.
  - To assess intervertebral disc herniation.
  - To identify meniscal injuries.
  - To detect bone marrow abnormalities.
  - To investigate soft-tissue tumors and infections.
- **Advantages:**
  - Excellent visualization of soft tissues.
  - No ionizing radiation.
  - Provides detailed images of muscles, ligaments, tendons and cartilage.
- **Limitations:**
  - Expensive and less readily available.
  - Takes longer than X-ray or CT.
  - Some implanted devices and metallic foreign bodies may make MRI unsuitable or require special precautions.

### D. Ultrasonography (USG)

- **Definition:** An imaging technique that uses high-frequency sound waves to produce images of body structures.
- **Principle:** Sound waves are transmitted into the body, and the reflected echoes are used to create images.
- **Indications:**
  - To assess tendon injuries.
  - To detect joint effusion.
  - To identify muscle tears.
  - To detect bursitis and soft-tissue swelling.
  - To guide joint aspiration and injections.
- **Advantages:**
  - No ionizing radiation.
  - Real-time imaging.
  - Allows dynamic assessment during movement.
  - Relatively inexpensive and portable.
- **Limitations:**
  - Highly dependent on operator skill.
  - Limited visualization of deep structures.
  - Cannot adequately assess bone marrow or structures hidden behind bone.

---

## 3. Summary of Imaging Investigations

| Investigation | Main use |
|---|---|
| X-ray | Fractures, dislocations, bone alignment |
| CT scan | Complex fractures and detailed bone imaging |
| MRI | Ligaments, tendons, cartilage, discs and bone marrow |
| USG | Tendons, muscles, effusions and dynamic assessment |

**Clinical importance in physiotherapy:**

- Helps identify the underlying musculoskeletal pathology.
- Assists in selecting appropriate physiotherapy interventions.
- Helps identify contraindications and precautions.
- Supports monitoring of disease progression and recovery.
- Assists in determining the need for referral or further medical evaluation.

## 3. Modified Medical Research Council (mMRC) Dyspnea Scale

- **Definition:**
  - The mMRC Dyspnea Scale is a subjective assessment tool used to grade breathlessness according to its effect on daily physical activities.

- **Purpose:**
  - To assess the severity of dyspnea in respiratory disorders.
  - To evaluate functional limitation during daily activities.
  - To monitor disease progression and rehabilitation outcomes.
  - Commonly used in patients with COPD and other chronic respiratory diseases.

- **Grades of Dyspnea:**
  - **Grade 0:** Breathlessness occurs only during strenuous exercise.
  - **Grade 1:** Breathlessness occurs when hurrying on level ground or walking up a slight hill.
  - **Grade 2:** Walks slower than people of the same age on level ground due to breathlessness or has to stop for breath while walking at own pace.
  - **Grade 3:** Stops for breath after walking approximately 100 meters or after a few minutes on level ground.
  - **Grade 4:** Too breathless to leave the house or becomes breathless while dressing or undressing.

- **Clinical Significance:**
  - Higher grades indicate greater functional limitation due to breathlessness.
  - Useful in assessing COPD severity and functional disability.
  - Helps evaluate changes in symptoms during pulmonary rehabilitation.

- **Interpretation:**
  - Grade 0–1 – Minimal functional limitation.
  - Grade 2 – Moderate functional limitation.
  - Grade 3–4 – Severe functional limitation.

Source: National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine.
https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK593672/

---

## 4. New York Heart Association (NYHA) Functional Classification

- **Definition:**
  - The NYHA Functional Classification is a clinical assessment tool used to classify patients with cardiovascular disease according to the degree of limitation in physical activity caused by cardiac symptoms.

- **Purpose:**
  - To assess functional capacity in patients with heart disease.
  - To determine the severity of symptoms during physical activity.
  - To monitor the patient's clinical progress.
  - Commonly used in patients with heart failure.

- **Grades of NYHA Classification:**

- **Class I:**
  - No limitation of physical activity.
  - Ordinary physical activity does not cause undue fatigue, palpitation, dyspnea, or chest pain.

- **Class II:**
  - Slight limitation of physical activity.
  - Patient is comfortable at rest.
  - Ordinary physical activity causes fatigue, palpitation, dyspnea, or chest pain.

- **Class III:**
  - Marked limitation of physical activity.
  - Patient is comfortable at rest.
  - Less than ordinary physical activity causes fatigue, palpitation, dyspnea, or chest pain.

- **Class IV:**
  - Patient is unable to perform any physical activity without discomfort.
  - Symptoms may be present even at rest.
  - Any physical activity increases discomfort.

- **Clinical Significance:**
  - Helps assess the functional status of patients with cardiovascular disorders.
  - Useful in cardiac rehabilitation and exercise prescription.
  - Helps monitor improvement or deterioration in functional capacity.
  - Higher class indicates greater limitation in physical activity.

Source: American Heart Association.
https://www.heart.org/en/health-topics/heart-failure/what-is-heart-failure/classes-of-heart-failure

---

## 5. Difference Between mMRC and NYHA Classification

- **mMRC Scale:**
  - Primarily used to assess breathlessness-related functional limitation in respiratory disorders.
  - Consists of 5 grades: 0–4.
  - Focuses mainly on breathlessness during daily activities.

- **NYHA Classification:**
  - Primarily used to assess functional limitation in cardiovascular disorders, especially heart failure.
  - Consists of 4 classes: I–IV.
  - Focuses on symptoms such as dyspnea, fatigue, palpitation, and chest pain during physical activity.

- Both scales are subjective and should be interpreted alongside clinical examination and other functional assessments.

# Exercise Tolerance Tests and Maximal Exercise Testing Protocols

## 1. 12-Minute Walk Test (12MWT)

* **Definition:** The 12-Minute Walk Test is a submaximal exercise test used to assess functional exercise capacity by measuring the maximum distance a person can walk in 12 minutes.
* **Purpose:**

  * To assess cardiovascular and respiratory endurance.
  * To evaluate functional exercise capacity.
  * To monitor progress during pulmonary and cardiac rehabilitation.
* **Equipment:**

  * Measured walking track.
  * Stopwatch.
  * Measuring tape.
  * Pulse oximeter.
  * Heart rate monitor.
* **Procedure:**

  * Explain the test and demonstrate the walking technique.
  * Record baseline heart rate, blood pressure, respiratory rate, SpO₂ and perceived exertion.
  * Ask the patient to walk as far as possible for 12 minutes.
  * The patient may slow down, stop or rest if required.
  * Provide standardized encouragement.
  * Record the total distance covered in 12 minutes.
  * Monitor symptoms, heart rate and SpO₂ during and after the test.
* **Outcome measures:**

  * Total distance walked in meters.
  * Heart rate response.
  * Oxygen saturation.
  * Dyspnea and fatigue using the Borg scale.
* **Advantages:**

  * Simple, inexpensive and easy to perform.
  * Requires minimal equipment.
  * Useful for assessing functional capacity.
* **Limitations:**

  * Results are influenced by motivation, walking speed and encouragement.
  * Requires adequate space and patient ability to walk.
* **Clinical applications:**

  * COPD and other respiratory disorders.
  * Cardiac rehabilitation.
  * Assessment of functional limitations.

## 2. Shuttle Run Test

* **Definition:** The Shuttle Run Test is a field-based exercise test in which the individual runs or walks repeatedly between two marked points according to audio signals.
* **Purpose:**

  * To assess cardiovascular endurance and aerobic fitness.
  * To estimate maximal oxygen uptake (VO₂ max).
  * To evaluate exercise tolerance.
* **Types:**

  * 20-Meter Multistage Shuttle Run Test.
  * Incremental Shuttle Walk Test (ISWT).
* **Equipment:**

  * Flat, measured track.
  * Cones or markers.
  * Audio recording and speaker.
  * Stopwatch.
  * Heart rate monitor and pulse oximeter, when indicated.
* **Procedure:**

  * Mark two points at the required distance apart.
  * Explain and demonstrate the test.
  * The individual moves between the markers according to audio beeps.
  * The speed progressively increases in the multistage test.
  * Record the number of shuttles or level completed.
  * Monitor heart rate, symptoms and perceived exertion.
* **Outcome measures:**

  * Number of shuttles completed.
  * Total distance covered.
  * Final level or speed achieved.
  * Estimated VO₂ max, where validated for the specific protocol.
* **Advantages:**

  * Requires relatively little equipment.
  * Provides a standardized, progressive workload.
  * Useful for assessing aerobic fitness.
* **Limitations:**

  * Requires adequate balance, coordination and mobility.
  * Results may be affected by motivation and musculoskeletal problems.
  * Not suitable for all patients with severe cardiopulmonary disease.
* **Clinical applications:**

  * Sports fitness assessment.
  * Pulmonary rehabilitation.
  * Assessment of aerobic exercise capacity.

## 3. Step Test

* **Definition:** The Step Test is a submaximal exercise test used to assess cardiovascular endurance by measuring the physiological response to stepping up and down on a platform at a standardized rate.
* **Purpose:**

  * To assess cardiovascular endurance.
  * To evaluate aerobic fitness.
  * To assess heart rate recovery after exercise.
  * To monitor fitness and rehabilitation progress.
* **Types:**

  * Harvard Step Test.
  * YMCA 3-Minute Step Test.
  * Queens College Step Test.
* **Equipment:**

  * Step platform of standardized height.
  * Stopwatch or metronome.
  * Heart rate monitor.
  * Chair for recovery.
* **Procedure:**

  * Record resting heart rate and blood pressure.
  * Ask the subject to step up and down at a standardized rate.
  * Maintain the required stepping cadence for the specified duration.
  * Stop the test if the subject develops excessive fatigue, dizziness, chest pain or abnormal symptoms.
  * Record heart rate during recovery.
  * Calculate the fitness index or recovery score according to the selected protocol.
* **Outcome measures:**

  * Heart rate response.
  * Heart rate recovery.
  * Duration of exercise completed.
  * Fitness index, depending on the protocol.
* **Advantages:**

  * Simple and inexpensive.
  * Requires minimal equipment.
  * Useful for group fitness assessment.
* **Limitations:**

  * Results depend on step height, cadence and body weight.
  * Requires adequate balance and lower-limb strength.
  * May not be suitable for patients with severe cardiopulmonary or musculoskeletal conditions.
* **Clinical applications:**

  * Assessment of aerobic fitness.
  * Fitness screening.
  * Monitoring exercise training and rehabilitation.

## 4. Treadmill Test

* **Definition:** The Treadmill Test is an exercise test in which a person walks or runs on a treadmill while workload is progressively increased to assess cardiovascular and respiratory responses to exercise.
* **Purpose:**

  * To assess cardiovascular endurance and exercise capacity.
  * To evaluate heart rate and blood pressure responses.
  * To detect exercise-induced ECG abnormalities.
  * To assess symptoms such as chest pain, dyspnea and fatigue.
  * To estimate maximal oxygen uptake (VO₂ max) or metabolic equivalents (METs).
* **Equipment:**

  * Motorized treadmill.
  * Electrocardiogram (ECG) machine.
  * Blood pressure monitor.
  * Heart rate monitor.
  * Pulse oximeter, when indicated.
* **Procedure:**

  * Explain the test and obtain informed consent.
  * Record resting heart rate, blood pressure and ECG.
  * Ask the subject to walk on the treadmill at the initial workload.
  * Increase speed, incline or both according to the selected protocol.
  * Monitor ECG, heart rate, blood pressure, symptoms and perceived exertion.
  * Continue until maximal effort, the target endpoint or a termination criterion is reached.
  * Record recovery responses after stopping exercise.
* **Outcome measures:**

  * Exercise duration.
  * Maximum workload achieved.
  * Heart rate and blood pressure response.
  * ECG changes.
  * METs or estimated VO₂ max.
  * Symptoms and exercise tolerance.
* **Advantages:**

  * Provides controlled and progressive exercise.
  * Allows continuous ECG monitoring.
  * Useful for evaluating cardiovascular function and exercise capacity.
* **Limitations:**

  * Requires specialized equipment and trained personnel.
  * May be unsuitable for individuals with balance or gait problems.
  * Requires medical supervision when used for clinical cardiac stress testing.
* **Clinical applications:**

  * Cardiac stress testing.
  * Assessment of exercise tolerance.
  * Cardiopulmonary rehabilitation.
  * Evaluation of exercise-induced symptoms.

## 5. Theoretical Basis of Maximal Exercise Testing Protocols

* **Definition:** Maximal exercise testing protocols are standardized procedures in which exercise intensity is progressively increased until the individual reaches maximal effort or a clinically determined stopping point.
* **Purpose:**

  * To assess maximal exercise capacity.
  * To estimate or measure VO₂ max.
  * To evaluate cardiovascular and respiratory responses to increasing workload.
  * To identify exercise-induced abnormalities.
* **Physiological basis:**

  * During exercise, oxygen demand of working muscles increases.
  * Heart rate and stroke volume increase to raise cardiac output.
  * Cardiac output = Heart rate × Stroke volume.
  * Pulmonary ventilation increases to meet oxygen demand and remove carbon dioxide.
  * Oxygen uptake increases with workload until maximal oxygen uptake is reached or exercise is terminated.
  * Workload is commonly expressed in METs.
  * 1 MET = 3.5 mL O₂/kg/min, representing a conventional estimate of resting oxygen consumption.
* **Principles of protocol design:**

  * Workload should increase progressively.
  * Initial workload should match the individual's functional capacity.
  * Exercise duration should generally be sufficient to assess capacity without causing premature fatigue.
  * The protocol should be selected according to age, fitness, clinical condition and testing purpose.
  * ECG, heart rate, blood pressure and symptoms should be monitored during clinical stress testing.
* **Types of protocols:**

  * Step protocols: Workload increases at predetermined stages.
  * Ramp protocols: Workload increases continuously or in small increments.
  * Fixed-load protocols: Workload remains constant throughout the test.
* **Common maximal exercise testing protocols:**

  * Bruce Protocol.
  * Modified Bruce Protocol.
  * Balke Protocol.

## 6. Bruce Protocol

* **Definition:** The Bruce Protocol is a standardized maximal treadmill exercise test in which speed and treadmill incline increase every three minutes.
* **Purpose:**

  * To assess cardiovascular exercise capacity.
  * To evaluate exercise-induced ECG changes.
  * To estimate maximal aerobic capacity.
  * To assess functional capacity in individuals able to tolerate relatively high workloads.
* **Theoretical basis:**

  * Uses progressive increases in speed and incline to increase exercise intensity.
  * Each stage increases the metabolic demand placed on the cardiovascular and respiratory systems.
  * The three-minute stages allow physiological responses to develop before the next workload increase.
  * Workload is expressed in METs to estimate functional capacity.
* **Procedure:**

  * Record baseline ECG, heart rate and blood pressure.
  * Ask the subject to walk on the treadmill.
  * Increase speed and incline every three minutes.
  * Continue until maximal effort or a clinical termination criterion is reached.
  * Monitor ECG, heart rate, blood pressure and symptoms throughout the test.
* **Standard Bruce Protocol stages:**

  * Stage 1: 1.7 mph, 10% incline.
  * Stage 2: 2.5 mph, 12% incline.
  * Stage 3: 3.4 mph, 14% incline.
  * Stage 4: 4.2 mph, 16% incline.
  * Stage 5: 5.0 mph, 18% incline.
  * Stage 6: 5.5 mph, 20% incline.
  * Stage 7: 6.0 mph, 22% incline.
* **Advantages:**

  * Widely used and standardized.
  * Useful for assessing cardiovascular exercise capacity.
  * Provides workload estimates in METs.
* **Limitations:**

  * Initial workload and stage increments may be too high for sedentary or medically limited individuals.
  * Rapid workload increases may cause early fatigue.
  * Requires adequate walking ability and balance.
* **Clinical applications:**

  * Exercise stress testing.
  * Assessment of suspected coronary artery disease.
  * Evaluation of functional exercise capacity.

## 7. Modified Bruce Protocol

* **Definition:** The Modified Bruce Protocol is a modified treadmill exercise test that includes additional low-intensity stages before the standard Bruce stages.
* **Purpose:**

  * To assess exercise capacity in individuals with reduced exercise tolerance.
  * To evaluate patients who cannot tolerate the initial workload of the standard Bruce Protocol.
  * To assess cardiovascular responses at lower exercise intensities.
* **Theoretical basis:**

  * Provides a gradual increase in workload during the initial stages.
  * Reduces the sudden increase in metabolic demand seen in the standard Bruce Protocol.
  * Allows individuals with lower functional capacity to begin exercise at a more manageable intensity.
* **Procedure:**

  * Record baseline ECG, heart rate and blood pressure.
  * Begin with low-speed, low-incline treadmill walking.
  * Increase workload in stages, generally every three minutes.
  * Continue into the standard Bruce stages as tolerated.
  * Monitor ECG, heart rate, blood pressure and symptoms.
* **Modified Bruce Protocol stages:**

  * Stage 1: 1.7 mph, 0% incline.
  * Stage 2: 1.7 mph, 5% incline.
  * Stage 3: 1.7 mph, 10% incline.
  * Stage 4: 2.5 mph, 12% incline.
  * Stage 5: 3.4 mph, 14% incline.
  * Stage 6: 4.2 mph, 16% incline.
  * Stage 7: 5.0 mph, 18% incline.
* **Advantages:**

  * Suitable for individuals with lower exercise tolerance.
  * Provides a more gradual initial workload progression.
  * Allows assessment of patients who may not tolerate standard Bruce Stage 1.
* **Limitations:**

  * Requires treadmill equipment and monitoring.
  * Test duration may be longer.
  * Requires clinical supervision in patients undergoing cardiac stress testing.
* **Clinical applications:**

  * Cardiac rehabilitation assessment.
  * Patients with reduced functional capacity.
  * Individuals requiring a lower initial exercise workload.

## 8. Balke Protocol

* **Definition:** The Balke Protocol is a maximal treadmill exercise test in which treadmill speed is maintained at a relatively constant level while the incline is progressively increased.
* **Purpose:**

  * To assess maximal aerobic capacity.
  * To evaluate cardiovascular endurance.
  * To assess exercise capacity using a gradual increase in workload.
* **Theoretical basis:**

  * Maintains a relatively constant walking speed.
  * Progressively increases treadmill incline to increase exercise intensity.
  * Produces a gradual increase in metabolic demand.
  * Reduces the need for rapid changes in walking speed.
* **Procedure:**

  * Record baseline heart rate, blood pressure and ECG.
  * Begin treadmill walking at a selected speed.
  * Maintain the speed throughout the test.
  * Increase the treadmill incline at regular intervals.
  * Continue until maximal effort or a termination criterion is reached.
  * Record exercise duration, workload and physiological responses.
* **Common Balke-Ware treadmill protocol:**

  * Initial speed: approximately 3.3 mph.
  * Initial incline: 0%.
  * Incline is increased by approximately 1% each minute.
  * Speed remains constant during the test.
  * Variations exist according to the population and testing purpose.
* **Advantages:**

  * Provides gradual workload increments.
  * Useful for assessing aerobic capacity.
  * Maintains a relatively constant walking speed.
* **Limitations:**

  * Increasing incline may cause significant lower-limb fatigue.
  * Requires adequate walking ability.
  * Different Balke modifications may produce different results.
* **Clinical applications:**

  * Assessment of maximal aerobic capacity.
  * Cardiopulmonary exercise testing.
  * Evaluation of exercise tolerance.

## 9. Comparison of Bruce, Modified Bruce and Balke Protocols

* **Bruce Protocol:**

  * Speed and incline increase every three minutes.
  * Has relatively large workload increments.
  * Used for individuals who can tolerate higher exercise intensity.
* **Modified Bruce Protocol:**

  * Includes additional low-intensity stages before the standard Bruce stages.
  * Provides a more gradual initial increase in workload.
  * Used for individuals with reduced exercise tolerance.
* **Balke Protocol:**

  * Maintains a relatively constant treadmill speed.
  * Progressively increases incline.
  * Provides gradual workload progression.

## 10. Safety Precautions During Maximal Exercise Testing

* Obtain relevant medical history and assess contraindications before testing.
* Record baseline heart rate, blood pressure and ECG when clinically indicated.
* Ensure appropriate supervision and emergency equipment during clinical stress testing.
* Monitor heart rate, blood pressure, ECG, symptoms and perceived exertion.
* Stop the test if the individual develops chest pain, severe breathlessness, dizziness, abnormal ECG changes, a concerning blood pressure response or other significant symptoms.
* Provide an appropriate recovery period and monitor the patient after exercise.

## References

* American Thoracic Society/American College of Chest Physicians. ATS/ACCP Statement on Cardiopulmonary Exercise Testing.
* Treadmill Stress Testing, StatPearls, NCBI Bookshelf.
* Cardiopulmonary Exercise Testing in Congenital Heart Disease: Equipment and Test Protocols.

1: 1. Neck Disability Index (NDI)
2: Definition and Overview
3: Developed by Howard Vernon and Silvano Mior in 1991 as a modification of the Oswestry Low Back Pain Disability Questionnaire.
4: It is a patient-reported, condition-specific outcome measure designed to quantify self-rated disability and functional limitation in patients experiencing acute, subacute, or chronic neck pain (including cervical spondylosis, radiculopathy, and whiplash-associated disorders).
5: Structure and Clinical Domains
6: Comprises 10 itemized sections evaluating physical daily activities and symptom impact:
7: Pain Intensity (severity of baseline cervical aching/pain)
8: Personal Care (washing, dressing, grooming without exacerbating symptoms)
9: Lifting (handling light, medium, or heavy objects)
10: Reading (sustained cervical flexion/postural tolerance)
11: Headaches (frequency and duration of cervicogenic headaches)
12: Concentration (ability to focus on cognitive tasks)
13: Work (ability to perform occupational duties)
14: Driving (head turning, blind-spot checks, postural endurance)
15: Sleeping (sleep disruption due to neck symptoms)
16: Recreation (participation in hobbies, sports, and leisure)
17: Scoring Methodology and Formula
18: Each of the 10 sections is rated on a 6-point ordinal scale ranging from 0 (no limitation/no pain) to 5 (complete limitation/worst pain).
19: Maximum possible raw score = 50 (when all 10 sections are completed).
20: If all 10 sections are answered:
21: \text{Percentage Disability} = \left(\frac{\text{Total Raw Score}}{50}\right) \times 100
22: Handling missing sections (e.g., patient does not drive):
23: Minimum completed sections required for validity: 9 out of 10.
24: \text{Percentage Disability} = \left(\frac{\text{Total Raw Score}}{5 \times \text{Number of completed sections}}\right) \times 100
25: Score Interpretation
26: 0 to 4 points (0% to 8%): No disability
27: 5 to 14 points (10% to 28%): Mild functional disability
28: 15 to 24 points (30% to 48%): Moderate functional disability
29: 25 to 34 points (50% to 68%): Severe functional disability
30: 35 to 50 points (70% to 100%): Complete functional disability / bedbound
31: Psychometric Properties
32: Test-retest reliability: High, with an Intraclass Correlation Coefficient (ICC) between 0.73 and 0.98.
33: Construct validity: Strong positive correlation with the Visual Analogue Scale (VAS), McGill Pain Questionnaire, and Short-Form 36 (SF-36).
34: Minimal Clinically Important Difference (MCID): 5 points (or 10% change) in non-surgical cohorts; up to 7 to 8.5 points in post-surgical cervical spine patients.
35: Relevance in Physiotherapy Practice
36: Used as an objective baseline on day one of rehabilitation to establish functional limitations.
37: Guides goal setting (e.g., progressing a patient from moderate to mild disability).
38: Provides documentation required by clinical insurance audits to substantiate continued manual therapy, cervical stabilization exercises, or postural re-education.
39: Clinical Limitations
40: Possesses a ceiling effect in elite athletes and high-demand physical workers who experience pain during high-velocity activities not captured by basic ADL questions.
41: Section 8 (Driving) is frequently omitted by non-drivers, requiring re-calculation of the maximum denominator.
42: 2. Shoulder Pain and Disability Index (SPADI)
43: Definition and Overview
44: Developed by Kathryn Roach and colleagues in 1991.
45: A shoulder-specific, self-administered questionnaire designed to evaluate pain severity and functional disability caused by musculoskeletal pathologies of the shoulder complex (e.g., rotator cuff tendinopathy, subacromial impingement syndrome, adhesive capsulitis, and glenohumeral osteoarthritis).
46: Structure and Components
47: Consists of 13 total items grouped into 2 distinct subscales:
48: Pain Subscale (5 items):
49: How severe is your pain at its worst?
50: How severe is your pain when lying on the involved side?
51: How severe is your pain when reaching for something on a high shelf?
52: How severe is your pain when touching the back of your neck?
53: How severe is your pain when pushing with the involved arm?
54: Disability Subscale (8 items):
55: Washing your hair
56: Washing your back
57: Putting on an undershirt or jumper
58: Putting on a shirt that buttons down the front
59: Putting on your pants
60: Placing an object on a high shelf
61: Carrying a heavy object of 10 pounds (4.5 kg)
62: Removing something from your back pocket
63: Scoring Methodology and Calculation
64: Scored using either a Visual Analogue Scale (VAS, 0 to 10 cm) or a Numeric Rating Scale (NRS, 0 to 10).
65: 0 indicates "no pain / no difficulty"; 10 indicates "worst pain imaginable / so difficult that help was required."
66: Subscale calculations:
67: \text{Pain Score (\%)} = \left(\frac{\text{Sum of pain subscale items}}{50}\right) \times 100
68: \text{Disability Score (\%)} = \left(\frac{\text{Sum of disability subscale items}}{80}\right) \times 100
69: Total SPADI Score:
70: \text{Total SPADI (\%)} = \left(\frac{\text{Sum of all 13 item scores}}{130}\right) \times 100
71: If items are skipped/omitted:
72: \text{Total SPADI (\%)} = \left(\frac{\text{Total points scored}}{10 \times \text{Number of items answered}}\right) \times 100
73: Score Interpretation
74: 0%: Best score, indicating completely normal function without shoulder pain.
75: 100%: Worst score, indicating complete functional loss and severe, intractable pain.
76: A reduction in percentage indicates clinical functional improvement.
77: Psychometric Properties
78: Internal consistency: High (Cronbach's alpha typically > 0.90 for both subscales).
79: Test-retest reliability: Excellent (ICC between 0.84 and 0.89).
80: Minimal Clinically Important Difference (MCID): 8 to 13 points (a change of at least 10 points is generally considered clinically meaningful across most shoulder disorders).
81: Relevance in Physiotherapy Practice
82: Allows the therapist to distinguish whether a patient's primary impairment is pain-dominant (acute stage) or disability-dominant (chronic or adhesive stage), directly modifying treatment choices (e.g., modalities vs. aggressive mobilization).

87: 3. Disabilities of the Arm, Shoulder and Hand (DASH)
88: Definition and Overview
89: Developed in 1996 jointly by the Institute for Work & Health (IWH) and the American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons (AAOS).
90: A comprehensive 30-item, upper-extremity-specific regional outcome tool designed to measure physical disability and symptoms across any single joint or combination of joints along the entire upper extremity kinetic chain (shoulder, elbow, wrist, and hand).
91: Structure and Domains
92: Comprises 30 mandatory core items covering three primary clinical domains:
93: Degree of physical difficulty in performing gross and fine motor tasks (21 items, such as opening a tight jar, writing, turning a key, preparing a meal, pushing open a heavy door, carrying a briefcase, washing back, changing a lightbulb).

103: 3 = Moderate difficulty / Moderate symptom
104: 4 = Severe difficulty / Severe symptom

111: Scored independently using an identical mathematical formula to produce a separate score out of 100.
112: Score Interpretation
113: 0 = No disability (optimal upper limb performance).
114: 100 = Maximum upper limb disability and severe symptoms.
115: A lower score reflects improved clinical status.

117: Test-retest reliability: Excellent (ICC = 0.92 to 0.96 across various orthopedic upper extremity conditions).

119: Minimal Clinically Important Difference (MCID): 10 to 15 points.

122: Enables standardized comparison between different upper quarter diagnoses under the same rehabilitation program.

126: 4. Oswestry Disability Index (ODI)
127: Definition and Overview
128: Developed by John O’Brien and Jeremy Fairbank in 1980 (often referred to as the Oswestry Low Back Pain Questionnaire).
129: Widely accepted as the international "gold standard" condition-specific patient-reported outcome measure for determining permanent or functional disability in acute and chronic low back pain (LBP), lumbar disc herniations, spinal canal stenosis, and post-lumbar fusion surgeries.
130: Structure and Clinical Domains
131: Composed of 10 clinical sections, each addressing a critical daily life domain impacted by lumbar pathology:
132: Section 1: Pain Intensity
133: Section 2: Personal Care (washing, dressing)
134: Section 3: Lifting
135: Section 4: Walking
136: Section 5: Sitting
137: Section 6: Standing
138: Section 7: Sleeping
139: Section 8: Sex Life (if applicable/acceptable to patient)
140: Section 9: Social Life
141: Section 10: Travelling
142: Scoring Methodology and Calculation
143: Each section contains 6 statements scored from 0 to 5:
144: 0 indicates the least limitation or no pain.
145: 5 indicates the greatest functional restriction or maximum pain.
146: Maximum possible raw score = 50 (if all 10 sections are completed).
147: Calculation when all sections are answered:
148: \text{ODI Percentage (\%)} = \left(\frac{\text{Total Raw Score}}{50}\right) \times 100
149: Calculation when Section 8 (Sex Life) is omitted:
150: \text{ODI Percentage (\%)} = \left(\frac{\text{Total Raw Score}}{45}\right) \times 100
151: Score Interpretation and Clinical Grading
152: 0% to 20% (Minimal Disability): The patient can cope with most living activities. Treatment usually centers on ergonomics, core stabilization, and general fitness.
153: 21% to 40% (Moderate Disability): The patient experiences pain with sitting, lifting, and standing. Conservative management (manual therapy, electrotherapy, active directional preference exercises) is indicated.
154: 41% to 60% (Severe Disability): Pain remains the main problem; activities of daily living are significantly disrupted. Requires detailed diagnostic evaluation and structured intervention.
155: 61% to 80% (Crippled): Back pain impinges on all aspects of the patient's life. Intervention requires advanced pain management, multidisciplinary care, or surgical consultation.
156: 81% to 100% (Bedbound or Symptom Exaggeration): These patients are either completely bedridden or exaggerating their symptoms (requires screening for non-organic signs/Waddell signs).
157: Psychometric Properties
158: Test-retest reliability: Outstanding (r = 0.83 to 0.99).
159: Construct and content validity: Highly correlated with objective spinal mobility indices, VAS, and physical performance tests.
160: Minimal Clinically Important Difference (MCID): 10 to 12 points (or a 30% reduction from baseline).
161: Relevance in Physiotherapy Practice
162: Establishes functional baseline and tracks progress over weeks of lumbar core strengthening, McKenzie extension, or motor control stabilization.
163: Serves as standard legal and disability documentation for return-to-work evaluations and medicolegal reporting.
164: Clinical Limitations

170: A self-administered instrument specifically developed to evaluate both short-term post-traumatic knee injuries (such as ACL ruptures, meniscus tears, or chondral injuries in young, active people) and long-term joint damage (primary or post-traumatic knee osteoarthritis).

172: Contains 42 items organized into 5 separately analyzed subscales:
173: Symptoms and Stiffness (7 items: swelling, mechanical clicking/catching, morning joint stiffness).
174: Pain (9 items: frequency of pain, pain during twisting, bending, stairs, walking).
175: Function in Daily Living / ADL (17 items: domestic mobility, descending stairs, rising from sitting, getting in/out of bath, shopping).
176: Function in Sport and Recreation / Sport/Rec (5 items: squatting, running, jumping, twisting/pivoting on knee, kneeling).
177: Knee-Related Quality of Life / QoL (4 items: lifestyle modification, awareness of knee problem, emotional concern).
178: Scoring Methodology and Formula
179: Every item is scored on a 5-point Likert scale from 0 to 4:
180: 0 = None / Never
181: 1 = Mild / Rarely
182: 2 = Moderate / Sometimes
183: 3 = Severe / Often
184: 4 = Extreme / Always

191: 0 = Extreme knee problems / Complete functional impairment.
192: 100 = No knee problems / Optimal joint performance.
